### [1] [MemSlides: A Hierarchical Memory Driven Agent Framework for Personalized Slide Generation with Multi-turn Local Revision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17162)
*Ye Jin,Yangyang Xu,Jun Zhu,Yibo Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MemSlides is a hierarchical memory framework for personalized presentation agents that separates long-term memory (user profile memory + tool memory) from working memory, enabling stable persona alignment, multi-turn preference carryover, and reliable slide-local edits without full regeneration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing presentation generation systems condition mainly on immediate prompts/templates and lack mechanisms to: (1) preserve stable user preferences across tasks, (2) retain newly introduced constraints during multi-turn revision, and (3) execute reliable localized edits without regenerating entire slide decks.

Method: MemSlides introduces a hierarchical memory architecture with three components: (1) User profile memory stores intent-conditioned profiles for zero-round personalization; (2) Working memory carries active preferences and session constraints across revision rounds; (3) Tool memory stores reusable execution experience for localized editing. This is paired with scoped slide-local revision, where targeted updates operate on the minimal affected region rather than the full deck.

Result: In controlled experiments: user profile memory improved persona-alignment judgments on a multi-persona, multi-intent profile bank; tool-memory injection improved closed-loop modify behavior in diagnostic matched-pair settings; and qualitative cases demonstrated working memory's ability to carry over preferences across revision rounds.

Conclusion: Effective personalization in presentation authoring depends on separating persistent user profiles, session-level working memory, and reusable execution experience across generation and localized revision. The hierarchical memory design of MemSlides provides a viable architecture for achieving this separation.

Abstract: Personalized presentation generation requires more than conditioning on a current prompt or template: agents must preserve stable user preferences across tasks, retain newly introduced preferences and constraints during multi-turn revision, and carry out local edits reliably. We propose MemSlides, a hierarchical memory framework for personalized presentation agents that separates long-term memory from working memory and further divides long-term memory into user profile memory and tool memory. User profile memory stores intent-conditioned profiles for round-0 personalization, working memory carries active preferences and session constraints across revision rounds, and tool memory stores reusable execution experience for reliable localized editing. MemSlides pairs this memory design with scoped slide-local revision, so targeted updates act on the smallest affected region instead of repeatedly regenerating the full deck. In controlled experiments, user profile memory improves persona-alignment judgments on a multi-persona, multi-intent profile bank, tool-memory injection improves closed-loop modify behavior in diagnostic matched-pair settings, and qualitative cases illustrate working memory's ability to carryover preferences. Taken together, these results suggest that effective personalization in presentation authoring depends on separating persistent user profiles, session-level working memory, and reusable execution experience across generation and localized revision.

</details>


### [2] [PromptMN: Pseudo Prompting Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17164)
*Enkhzol Dovdon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PromptMN introduces a lightweight, %-prefixed directive DSL that annotates natural language prompts with structured roles, goals, constraints, and outputs. It occupies a middle ground between informal prompting and pseudocode, enabling inspectable, reusable prompts across the SDLC, and is validated on frontier models without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Natural language prompts are fragile — roles, goals, constraints, and expected outputs are often buried in prose or left implicit. In agentic and software development workflows, context ambiguities (rather than model limitations) are a major source of cascading failures. There is a need for a structured yet lightweight prompting approach that remains accessible to non-programmers (analysts, managers, stakeholders) while improving clarity, inspectability, and reusability.

Method: The authors design PromptMN, a pseudo-prompting DSL using %-prefixed typed directives (e.g., %role, %goal, %constraint, %input, %output, %plan, %priority, %requirement). Semantic resolution allows directives to be written in any order, with models interpreting them by function. PromptMN also supports reverse prompt engineering: asking a model to restate a desired outcome in PromptMN for inspection before execution. Feasibility is tested on Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.5 across tasks involving repetition, conditionals, methods, and prime-checking, without fine-tuning.

Result: All tested frontier models correctly resolved PromptMN instructions, including complex structures (repetition, conditionals, methods, prime-checking). The same vocabulary applied across diverse SDLC scenarios: new codebases, maintenance, and redesign. Reverse prompt engineering successfully surfaced inferred roles, goals, constraints, and missing assumptions.

Conclusion: PromptMN is a practical step toward clearer, more reviewable human-to-AI interaction. While large-scale validation remains future work, early results are promising and suggest that lightweight structured prompting can reduce ambiguity and repair cycles across the SDLC.

Abstract: Prompting has become the primary interface between humans and generative AI, yet many natural language prompts remain fragile: roles, goals, constraints, and expected outputs are often buried in prose or left implicit. In agentic and software development workflows, a misread at the first handoff can propagate through every step, since a significant portion of agent failures stem from context ambiguities rather than model limitations. This paper introduces PromptMN, a pseudo-prompting domain-specific language that annotates natural language with compact, %-prefixed typed directives covering roles, goals, requirements, priorities, constraints, plans, inputs, and outputs. Semantic resolution lets authors write in any order while the model interprets directives by function. PromptMN sits between informal prompting and programming-style pseudocode: structured enough to be inspectable and reusable, yet lightweight enough for analysts, managers, developers, and stakeholders across the software development lifecycle (SDLC). PromptMN also pairs with reverse prompt engineering. Asking a model to restate a desired outcome as PromptMN lets users inspect the inferred roles, goals, constraints, and missing assumptions before acting, reducing repair cycles and yielding a reusable artifact for aligning people and AI tools. PromptMN's feasibility is evaluated across several frontier models, including Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.5. The models correctly resolved PromptMN instructions, including complex structures such as repetition, conditionals, methods, and a prime-checking task, without fine-tuning. The same vocabulary applies across new codebases, maintenance, and redesign in the SDLC scenarios presented. While large-scale validation remains future work, these early results suggest PromptMN is a practical step toward clearer, more reviewable human-to-AI interaction.

</details>


### [3] [RepSelect: Robust LLM Unlearning via Representation Selectivity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17168)
*Filip Sondej,Yushi Yang,Adam Mahdi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Current LLM unlearning methods produce only shallow forgetting, easily reversed by fine-tuning or few-shot prompting. The paper identifies that existing approaches target shared representations between retain and forget sets. RepSelect solves this by isolating forget-set-specific representations via collapsing top principal components of weight gradients before each update, achieving 4-50x greater robustness against relearning and near-perfect resistance to few-shot attacks across multiple model families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM unlearning methods suffer from "shallow forgetting," where supposedly erased knowledge or values can be easily recovered through fine-tuning or few-shot prompting. The root cause is unknown, and no current method achieves genuinely deep, irreversible forgetting without harming general model capabilities.

Method: RepSelect (Representation Selectivity): During unlearning, the method isolates forget-set-specific representations by collapsing the top principal components of weight gradients before each parameter update. This prevents the unlearning process from disturbing representations shared with the retain set and limits what a fine-tuning attacker can later recover, focusing the gradient signal exclusively on forget-set-specific directions.

Result: Evaluated on two forget categories (biohazardous knowledge, abusive tendencies) across four model families (Llama 3, Qwen 3.5, Gemma 4 E4B, DeepSeek V2 Lite). Compared against five baselines (GradDiff, NPO, SimNPO, RMU, UNDIAL), RepSelect achieves a 4-50x larger reduction in post-relearning answer accuracy than the strongest baseline and demonstrates near-perfect robustness against few-shot prompting attacks.

Conclusion: Targeting selective representations via gradient principal component filtering is a critical step toward achieving deep and robust LLM forgetting that resists recovery attacks while preserving general capabilities.

Abstract: Making large language models (LLMs) deeply forget specific knowledge and values without sacrificing general capabilities remains a central challenge in unlearning. However, current methods are easily reversed by fine-tuning or few-shot prompting, suggesting their forgetting is only shallow. We identify the root cause. Existing methods target representations shared with both the retain set and the subspace recovered by a fine-tuning attacker, making unlearning both disruptive to general capabilities and easy to reverse. We propose RepSelect (Representation Selectivity), isolates forget-set-specific representations by collapsing top principal components of weight gradients before each update, leaving general capabilities intact while limiting what fine-tuning can recover. We evaluate across two forget categories, biohazardous knowledge and abusive tendencies, and four model families spanning dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures (Llama 3, Qwen 3.5, Gemma 4 E4B, DeepSeek V2 Lite). Compared to five popular baselines (GradDiff, NPO, SimNPO, RMU, UNDIAL), RepSelect achieves a 4-50x larger reduction in post-relearning answer accuracy than the strongest baseline, and is near-perfectly robust to few-shot prompting attacks. Targeting selective representations is thus an important step towards deep and robust LLM forgetting.

</details>


### [4] [From Parasocial Scripts to Dyadic Persistence in Autonomous AI-Agent Communities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17174)
*Mohammadsadegh Abolhasani,Hamid Reza Firoozfar,Reza Mousavi,Paul Jen-Hwa Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The study finds that parasocial interaction cues (attachment language, reciprocity bids, self-identification) are prevalent in AI-agent-dominated online communities and are robustly associated with original poster re-engagement and reciprocal reply structures, suggesting a behavioral discourse structure among LLM-enabled agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior research on parasocial interactions (PSIs) and parasocial relationships (PSRs) has focused on conventional media where one side (the audience) is human and the other (the media figure) is not. This study investigates whether PSI-style relational cues also emerge in online communities where both interacting sides are autonomous AI agents, extending PSI/PSR theory to fully synthetic agent-agent discourse.

Method: The authors analyzed 4,434 posts and 50,338 comments from the Moltbook platform using three theory-driven textual indicators: attachment/intimacy language, reciprocity bids, and self-identification to the original poster (OP). Three complementary methods were employed — keyword matching, few-shot large language model (LLM) annotation, and grouped-context LLM annotation. Robustness was tested via negative controls, nullification, clustered-standard-error re-estimation, multiple-testing correction, and a dyadic persistence test for sustained mutual recurrence.

Result: PSI colloquial cues were found to prevail in the AI-agent community. These cues were strongly associated with OP re-engagement and a reciprocal reply structure. All findings held across robustness checks. The dyadic persistence test confirmed that reciprocity bids aligned with sustained, OP-involving mutual recurrence, bridging interaction-level PSI scripts with PSR-consistent repeated dyadic patterns.

Conclusion: The evidence is interpreted as revealing a behavioral structure in discourse by LLM-enabled agents, demonstrating that parasocial interaction dynamics can manifest even in fully synthetic, agent-to-agent online settings. This extends PSI/PSR research beyond human-media-figure paradigms into AI-mediated social architectures.

Abstract: While parasocial interactions (PSIs) and parasocial relationships (PSRs) have been studied in conventional media settings, we investigate whether PSI- (colloquial) relational cues also exist in online communities where both sides are autonomous AI agents. We analyze 4,434 posts and 50,338 comments from Moltbook through three theory-based textual indicators: attachment/intimacy language, reciprocity bids, and self-identification to original poster (OP). The combined results across methods based on keyword matching, few-shot large language model (LLM) annotation, and grouped-context LLM annotation reveal that PSI colloquial cues prevail and are strongly associated with OP re-engagement and a reciprocal reply structure. These results are robust across negative controls, nullification, clustered-standard-error re-estimation, and multiple-testing correction. A dyadic persistence test further affirms reciprocity bids aligned with sustained OP-involving mutual recurrence, providing empirical evidence for bridging interaction-level PSI scripts with PSR-consistent repeated dyadic patterns. We interpret the evidence as a behavioral structure in discourse by LLM-enabled agents.

</details>


### [5] [Self-Generated Error Training for Token Editing in Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17175)
*Lin Yao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Self-generated T2T addresses the training-inference mismatch in token-to-token editing for block-diffusion language models by training the editor on the model's own draft errors rather than random corruptions, improving accuracy and reducing over-editing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLaDA2.1's T2T editor is trained on random vocabulary corruptions, but at inference it encounters the model's own fluent, high-confidence errors. This mismatch leads to failure modes like final-digit transcription errors after correct reasoning and excessive self-correction on short factual answers.

Method: Self-generated T2T: a no-gradient draft pass fills masked positions with predicted tokens; these self-generated corruptions then supervise a second recovery pass. Implemented as a short LoRA continued-pretraining pass on LLaDA2.1-mini, evaluated under official Q-Mode T2T with unchanged inference parameters.

Result: The method generally improves accuracy while reducing T2T edit intensity, mitigating both final-digit transcription errors after otherwise correct reasoning and excessive self-correction before short factual answers.

Conclusion: Training the T2T editor on self-generated draft errors rather than random corruptions effectively closes the train-test distribution gap, yielding more accurate and less intrusive token-level revisions during block-diffusion decoding.

Abstract: Token-to-token (T2T) editing lets LLaDA2.1 revise committed tokens during block-diffusion decoding. The released recipe trains this editor on random vocabulary corruptions, but at inference the editor sees the model's own fluent, high-confidence draft errors instead. We study this training-inference mismatch and propose self-generated T2T, which performs a no-gradient draft pass, fills masked positions with predicted tokens, and supervises recovery in a second pass under these self-generated corruptions. We implement the update as a short LoRA continued-pretraining pass on LLaDA2.1-mini and evaluate on several benchmarks under the official Q-Mode T2T procedure with unchanged inference parameters. The method generally improves accuracy while reducing T2T edit intensity, mitigating failure modes such as final-digit transcription errors after otherwise correct reasoning and excessive self-correction before short factual answers.

</details>


### [6] [Revisiting LLM Adaptation for 3D CT Report Generation: A Study of Scaling and Diagnostic Priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17213)
*Vanshali Sharma,Andrea M. Bejar,Halil Ertugrul Aktas,Quoc-Huy Trinh,Debesh Jha,Gorkem Durak,Ulas Bagci*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RAD3D-Prefix introduces a parameter-efficient framework for volumetric CT report generation that conditions a frozen LLM on diagnostic classification logits, outperforming baselines while using far fewer trainable parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extending LLMs/VLMs to 3D medical imaging is challenging due to high computational cost, volumetric dependencies, and semantic gaps between visual features and clinical terms. Fine-tuning on small medical datasets causes overfitting and "clinical hallucination" — fluent but factually incorrect outputs.

Method: RAD3D-Prefix is a lightweight diagnostic-prior conditioning module that fuses image embeddings with multi-label diagnostic classification logits. This prefix is fed into a frozen LLM, bridging the semantic gap while keeping the LLM untouched. The study systematically evaluates LLMs ranging from 96.1M to 1.6B parameters under different fine-tuning regimes.

Result: Fine-tuning benefits smaller LLMs most; for larger models (~1B+), freezing the LLM and training only lightweight projection layers yields the best performance–efficiency trade-off. RAD3D-Prefix outperforms parameter-efficient baselines on automatic metrics and in a clinical reader study, with strong out-of-domain generalization.

Conclusion: Parameter-efficient adaptation via diagnostic-prior conditioning effectively addresses the challenges of volumetric medical report generation, reducing overfitting and computational cost while maintaining clinical accuracy and generalization.

Abstract: Recent advances in multimodal learning, including large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), have demonstrated strong adaptability to natural images. However, extending their use to the medical domain, particularly for volumetric (3D) images, is challenging due to high computational complexity, volumetric dependencies and the semantic gap between visual features and clinical terminology. Naively fine-tuning LLMs on limited medical data often leads to overfitting and clinical hallucination, where linguistic fluency is prioritized over clinical factuality. In this study, we investigate parameter-efficient adaptation strategies for volumetric CT report generation and introduce RAD3D-Prefix, a lightweight diagnostic-prior conditioning framework that minimizes the need for extensive parameter training. This module integrates image embeddings with multi-label diagnostic classification logits, preserving critical clinical details while bridging the semantic gap. By keeping the LLM frozen, our method requires minimal trainable parameters and mitigates the risk of overfitting on small, domain-specific datasets. Through a systematic study spanning LLMs from 96.1M to 1.6B parameters, we find that fine-tuning is most beneficial for smaller LLMs, whereas freezing larger (~1B+ LLMs and training only lightweight projection layers provides a superior trade-off between performance, generalization, and computational efficiency. Across multiple automatic metrics and a clinical reader study, RAD3D-Prefix outperforms comparable parameter-efficient baselines and demonstrates strong out-of-domain generalization while using substantially fewer trainable parameters than fully fine-tuned alternatives.

</details>


### [7] [Speaking in Self-Assessing Tongues: On the Verbalized Confidence of LLMs in Machine Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17234)
*Ali Marashian,Alexis Palmer,Katharina von der Wense*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates the reliability of LLM confidence estimation in translation tasks by comparing internal signal-based methods with five novel verbalized confidence extraction methods. The authors evaluate both approaches on fine-grained error detection and calibration, finding similar performance but surprisingly little correlation between internal and verbalized confidence measures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for translation, but their self-assessed confidence is understudied. Existing unsupervised confidence methods relying on internal signals (e.g., predicted probabilities) suffer from two key limitations: (1) they reflect certainty among alternatives rather than actual correctness, and (2) they require access to internal model signals, which may not always be available. This motivates the need for verbalized, black-box-compatible confidence extraction methods.

Method: The authors devise five verbalized methods to extract per-token confidence from LLMs without requiring access to internal signals. These are compared against internal signal-based approaches (predicted probabilities). Reliability is evaluated along two dimensions: (1) fine-grained error detection — how well confidence scores identify actual translation errors at token/word/span granularity, and (2) calibration — how well confidence scores align with empirical correctness probabilities.

Result: Internal and verbalized methods perform similarly on both fine-grained error detection and calibration tasks, though results vary across different models. A key finding is that there is little to no correlation between internal and verbalized confidence measures, suggesting they capture fundamentally different aspects of model uncertainty.

Conclusion: Verbalized confidence methods are a viable alternative to internal signal-based approaches for translation tasks, offering the advantage of being black-box compatible. The lack of correlation between internal and verbalized measures indicates they may reflect distinct types of uncertainty, warranting further investigation into their complementary use.

Abstract: The rapid rise in popularity of large language models (LLMs) for translation calls for a thorough study of the reliability of their confidence in their own outputs. Unlike many generation tasks, translation errors and confidence levels can be useful at different levels of granularity (tokens, words, or spans). Unsupervised approaches based on internal signals like predicted probabilities can be misleading because they reflect certainty among alternatives rather than correctness. In addition, they require access to such internal signals. Here, we devise five verbalized methods of extracting an LLM's per-token confidence without those shortcomings and compare their reliability with that of the model's internal signals of certainty. We evaluate reliability using two forms of alignment: fine-grained error detection and calibration. For both, internal and verbalized methods perform similarly, although results vary by model. Interestingly, we find little to no correlation between internal and verbalized methods.

</details>


### [8] [MLLP-VRAIN UPV system for the IWSLT 2026 Simultaneous Speech Translation task](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17255)
*Jorge Iranzo-Sánchez,Gerard Mas-Mollà,Adrià Giménez,Jorge Civera,Albert Sanchis,Alfons Juan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The MLLP-VRAIN group's submission to IWSLT 2026 Simultaneous Speech Translation uses Parakeet and Qwen 3.5 models in a cascaded SimulST system with adaptive black-box policies, achieving a +5.82 XCOMET-XL improvement over last year, with further gains from context-track techniques (ASR word-boosting + RAG).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To build a robust cascaded solution for long-form simultaneous speech translation (SimulST) that achieves better quality-latency trade-offs, and to leverage domain-specific context (via the new context track) to further improve translation quality.

Method: A cascaded (ASR → MT) system using the Parakeet ASR model and Qwen 3.5 MT model, combined with adaptive "black-box" policy relaxations for quality-latency optimization. For the context track (En→De, It, Zh), the authors augment the system with ASR word-boosting and a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mechanism using offline pre-translated exemplars to inject domain-specific context into generation.

Result: On the MCIF En→De test set, the system achieves a +5.82 XCOMET-XL improvement over the previous year's submission. The context-track processing yields an additional +1.03 XCOMET-XL gain. The authors participated in all language directions and provided a detailed latency analysis.

Conclusion: The combination of modern Parakeet/Qwen 3.5 models with adaptive black-box policies yields substantial quality gains for cascaded SimulST. Furthermore, incorporating domain-specific context via word-boosting and RAG-based exemplar retrieval provides an effective, additive improvement on top of the base system.

Abstract: This work describes the participation of the MLLP-VRAIN research group in the shared task of the IWSLT 2026 Simultaneous Speech Translation track. Our submission utilizes the recently released Parakeet and Qwen 3.5 models to create a robust, cascaded solution for long-form SimulST through the use of adaptive "black-box" policies. We explore relaxations of these policies to achieve better quality-latency trade-offs. Compared to last year, we participate on all language directions. In addition to this, for the En$\rightarrow${De, It, Zh} directions we also participate in this year's new context track employing a combination of ASR word-boosting and a RAG mechanism of offline pre-translated exemplars to guide generation and enrich our system with domain-specific context. Finally, we provide a detailed latency analysis of our system. Compared to last year, results on the MCIF En$\rightarrow$De test set shows a substantial quality improvement of +5.82 XCOMET-XL. Our context track processing further improves performance by +1.03.

</details>


### [9] [Are you speaking my languages? On spoken language adherence in multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17281)
*Hyungwon Kim,Kandarp Joshi,Lillian Zhou,Pavel Golik,Petar Aleksic*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper addresses the problem of LLM-based ASR systems misidentifying output languages, proposing soft prompting to hint at spoken languages without rigid constraints. It introduces a new metric for language adherence violations and compares three mitigation strategies: zero-shot prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and Chain-of-Thought reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based multilingual ASR systems often suffer from language misidentification during transcription, which degrades fidelity and harms downstream applications. Existing solutions either sacrifice flexibility or code-switching capability. The authors aim to preserve these capabilities while improving language adherence.

Method: The authors formally define the language adherence problem and propose a novel metric to quantify violations. They then evaluate three strategies: (1) zero-shot prompting for robust guidance under uncertainty, (2) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to improve prompt adherence, and (3) Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to enforce adherence during decoding. A comparative analysis is conducted across multiple languages.

Result: A comparative analysis across multiple languages shows the effectiveness of each strategy in reducing language violations while maintaining overall ASR performance. Trade-offs are identified to guide strategy selection under varying compute constraints.

Conclusion: Soft prompting is an effective middle ground for improving language adherence in multilingual LLM-based ASR without sacrificing code-switching flexibility. The choice among zero-shot prompting, SFT, and CoT should be guided by compute constraints and the specific accuracy-flexibility trade-offs required.

Abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM) based Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) enables seamless multilingual use, models often misidentify the output language, compromising transcription fidelity and downstream application quality. To preserve flexibility and code-switching capabilities, we propose a soft prompting approach that hints at potential spoken languages without strictly constraining the output. We formally define this challenge as a lack of language adherence, introduce a novel metric to quantify violations, and evaluate three mitigation strategies: (1) zero-shot prompting for robust guidance under uncertainty, (2) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to improve prompt adherence, and (3) Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to enforce adherence during decoding. We present a comparative analysis of these methods across multiple languages, evaluating effectiveness in reducing the language violation while maintaining overall ASR performance. Finally, we discuss trade-offs to guide strategy selection under various compute constraints.

</details>


### [10] [HistoRAG: Embedding Historical Methodology in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Through Critical Technical Practice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18103)
*Noah J. Kim-Baumann,Torsten Hiltmann*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HistoRAG adapts retrieval-augmented generation for historical research by introducing temporal windowing, separated retrieval/generation, and LLM-as-judge evaluation, addressing how standard RAG's factual QA orientation conflicts with historiographical practice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RAG architectures and evaluation paradigms are built for factual question-answering, embedding assumptions that conflict with interpretive disciplines like history. The authors identify specific deficiencies: era-specific vocabulary causes zero retrieval across time periods, vector similarity correlates weakly with relevance judgments, and keyword vs. semantic retrieval surface disjoint source pools.

Method: The authors propose HistoRAG with three core interventions: (1) separated retrieval and generation to decouple source discovery from interpretation; (2) temporal windowing to enforce balanced source representation across research periods; (3) LLM-as-judge evaluation for transparent, contestable relevance judgments. They evaluate on SPIEGELragged, a corpus of 102,189 Der Spiegel articles (1950–1979), and introduce Zwischentexte as intermediate interpretive proposals.

Result: Each intervention addresses a measurable deficiency: 1950s terminology retrieves zero chunks using 1970s terms (motivating windowing); vector similarity and LLM relevance correlate at only Spearman ρ=0.275 (motivating post-retrieval evaluation); keyword and semantic retrieval surface largely disjoint sources (motivating complementary retrieval layers under shared LLM filtering).

Conclusion: HistoRAG demonstrates how domain-specific epistemological commitments can be translated into architectural design decisions for RAG systems, offering a transferable model for other interpretive disciplines working with large corpora.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is the prevailing architecture for grounding language model outputs in external evidence, yet its dominant evaluation paradigms and default configurations remain oriented toward factual question-answering. For interpretive disciplines such as historical studies, RAG embeds assumptions that conflict with scholarly practice. We introduce HistoRAG, a framework that translates historiographical principles into concrete architectural interventions. Separated retrieval and generation decouples source discovery from interpretation, temporal windowing enforces balanced source representation across the research period as a methodological requirement of historical inquiry, and LLM-as-judge evaluation makes relevance judgments transparent and contestable. We evaluate these interventions using SPIEGELragged, applied to 102,189 articles from Der Spiegel (1950-1979). Each intervention addresses a measurable deficiency in standard RAG: era-specific vocabulary retrieves zero chunks from the 1950s when using 1970s terminology, evidence of the temporal skew that motivates windowing; vector similarity and LLM-assessed relevance correlate only weakly (Spearman rho = 0.275), motivating post-retrieval evaluation; and keyword-based and semantic retrieval surface largely disjoint source pools, motivating an architecture in which both operate as complementary retrieval layers under a shared LLM evaluation filter. We also introduce the concept of Zwischentexte (intermediate texts that function as interpretive proposals rather than findings) as a framework for responsible integration of LLM-generated text into scholarly practice. The architecture offers a model for how domain-specific epistemological commitments can be translated into RAG design decisions, and may transfer to other interpretive disciplines working with large corpora.

</details>


### [11] [Examining the Limits of Word2Vec with Toki Pona](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17299)
*Daniel Zhenhan Huang,Hongchen Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study tests Word2Vec on Toki Pona (~130 words), finding that distributional patterns matter more than lexicon size. Non-core tokens (named entities, loanwords) draw similar words closer in vector space without disrupting overall semantic structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Word2Vec has been validated almost exclusively on languages with large vocabularies. The authors aim to test whether it can capture semantic relationships in an extremely reduced lexicon (~130 words) and investigate the rarely-studied effect of "linguistic noise" (non-core tokens like named entities and loanwords) on embedding quality.

Method: A corpus of 1.4M sentences (7.95M tokens) was sourced from the Toki Pona community (~23% contain non-Toki Pona tokens). Two Word2Vec models were trained: one retaining incidental tokens, one filtering them out. Evaluation used (1) word proximity to semantic category centroids, (2) automated silhouette scores via agglomerative clustering, and (3) qualitative analysis with representational similarity matrices compared against English.

Result: Non-core tokens do not affect the relative structure of learned embeddings but draw similar words closer together in vector space. Word2Vec's effectiveness depends more on distributional patterns than lexicon size, even at this extreme lower bound.

Conclusion: Word2Vec remains effective at capturing semantic relationships even with ~130 words, and the presence of sparse non-core vocabulary acts as a beneficial signal that tightens semantic clusters rather than introducing harmful noise.

Abstract: Word2Vec's effectiveness at generating semantic embeddings has been widely validated, yet it has been tested almost exclusively on languages with large vocabulary inventories. This study examines whether Word2Vec can successfully capture semantic relationships within an extremely reduced vocabulary using data from Toki Pona, a constructed language with approximately 130 words. We sourced 1.4 million sentences (7.95 million tokens) from the Toki Pona community for training. Approximately 23% of sentences in the corpus contain non-Toki Pona tokens such as named entities, loanwords, and neologisms. To investigate whether this linguistic noise enhances or hinders performance -- a topic rarely addressed in word embedding literature -- we trained two distinct models: one retaining these incidental tokens and another filtering them out completely. Evaluation was conducted using quantitative methods measuring word proximity to semantic category centroids, automated silhouette scores via agglomerative clustering, and qualitative analysis utilizing representational similarity matrices compared against English. The results indicate that while sparse, non-core tokens do not affect the relative structure of the learned embeddings, they actually draw similar words closer together in the vector space. Importantly, Word2Vec's effectiveness depends more on distributional patterns than lexicon size even at this extreme lower bound.

</details>


### [12] [Do Large Language Models Always Tell The Same Stories?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17350)
*Thennal DK,Hans Ole Hatzel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs produce stories that are systematically more similar to each other than human-written stories, with frontier models converging on a "mean" narrative that lacks collective diversity. Common mitigation strategies like negative prompting and temperature scaling fail to address this homogeneity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs can generate high-quality prose, it remains unclear whether they can produce truly diverse outputs. This work addresses the contested question of LLM output diversity, specifically in the domain of narrative generation.

Method: The authors employ a contrastive framework using human-written stories and prompts from r/WritingPrompts. They collect narrative similarity judgments across 10 representative LLMs using both human evaluations and three automatic annotation methods (likely embedding-based, model-based, and lexical similarity metrics). They also test mitigation strategies: negative prompting and temperature scaling.

Result: A consistent trend emerges: LLM-generated narratives are significantly more similar to each other than human-written stories. Frontier models converge on a "mean" generic narrative that approximates individual human stories but lacks the collective diversity of human authors. Negative prompting and temperature scaling fail to meaningfully reduce this homogeneity.

Conclusion: Current LLMs exhibit a fundamental diversity limitation in narrative generation, producing homogenized outputs that fail to capture the range of human storytelling. Standard decoding interventions are insufficient to bridge this diversity gap, highlighting a significant open problem for creative language generation.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled the generation of high-quality prose, yet the question of whether these models are capable of generating diverse outputs remains contested. In this work, we investigate the diversity of LLM-generated stories through the framework of narrative similarity. Using a contrastive framework and a dataset of human-written stories and prompts from r/WritingPrompts, we collect narrative similarity judgments across 10 representative LLMs, utilizing both human evaluations and three different automatic annotation methods. Our findings reveal a consistent trend: LLM-generated narratives are consistently more similar to each other than human-written stories are. We demonstrate that frontier models in particular converge on a ``mean'' generic narrative that approximates individual human stories but lacks the collective diversity of human authors. Finally, we show that common mitigation strategies, including negative prompting and temperature scaling, fail to meaningfully address this homogeneity.

</details>


### [13] [Translating the Untranslatable: An Operationalizable Ontology for Untranslatability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17354)
*Jacob Bremerman,Brihi Joshi,Hirona Arai,Xiang Ren,Jonathan May*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces a structured ontology of untranslatability and compensation strategies, operationalized into a multilingual dataset, to study how meaning can be conveyed when one-to-one translation equivalence is impossible. Human evaluations reveal a consistent preference for the Annotation strategy (explanatory context), laying groundwork for strategy-informed machine translation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Untranslatability is well-studied in linguistics but largely ignored in NLP. As MT systems improve, their residual errors increasingly stem from cases where meaning cannot be directly preserved across languages. The authors aim to systematically characterize untranslatability and develop compensation strategies that can inform better MT behavior in such contexts.

Method: The authors first construct a structured ontology of untranslatability types and a taxonomy of compensation strategies — specific techniques for conveying meaning when direct equivalence fails. This framework is then operationalized into a multilingual dataset consisting of untranslatable sentences paired with strategy-based translations. Human preference studies are conducted to evaluate translation quality across different compensation strategies.

Result: Human preference studies show that translation quality varies significantly depending on the compensation strategy employed. Outputs incorporating the Annotation strategy — which adds explanatory context — are consistently preferred over other approaches.

Conclusion: The proposed ontology, taxonomy, and dataset establish a foundation for systematically studying untranslatability in NLP and for developing MT systems capable of strategy-informed translation that better handles linguistically irreducible meaning gaps.

Abstract: Untranslatability, cases where meaning cannot be directly preserved across languages, is well-studied in linguistics but underexplored in NLP. As machine translation (MT) systems improve on standard benchmarks, their limitations increasingly concentrate in such cases, where translation cannot be reduced to one-to-one equivalence. We introduce a structured ontology of untranslatability along with a taxonomy of compensation strategies, which are specific techniques to convey meaning under these untranslatable circumstances. We operationalize this framework into a multilingual dataset of untranslatable sentences paired with strategy-based translations, enabling controlled analysis of translation behavior. Initial human preference studies suggest that translation quality depends on the strategy used, with consistent preferences for outputs that include explanatory context, known as the Annotation compensation strategy. Our framework and dataset provide a foundation for studying and modeling strategy-informed machine translation.

</details>


### [14] [Implicit vs. Explicit Prompting Strategies for LVLMs in Referential Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17372)
*Peter Zeng,Amie J. Paige,Weiling Li,Susan E. Brennan,Owen Rambow,Cameron R. Jones*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper reconciles contradictory findings on whether LVLMs can coordinate efficient referring expressions by showing that explicit prompting enables such coordination, while implicit prompts reveal a failure to infer communicative efficiency — highlighting a key human-AI communication gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Two recent studies (Jones et al. 2026; Zeng et al. 2026) reached opposite conclusions about LVLMs' ability to coordinate efficient referring expressions. The authors aim to resolve this contradiction by isolating whether task differences or prompting style accounts for the divergent results.

Method: The authors controlled for task differences between the two prior studies while systematically comparing their prompting styles (explicit vs. implicit). They replicated the coordination experiments under controlled conditions to determine which factor drives the contradictory findings.

Result: LVLMs can successfully coordinate efficient referring expressions when explicitly prompted to do so, confirming that other task differences are not the cause of divergence. However, the same models fail to infer the need for communicative efficiency from more implicit prompts.

Conclusion: The contradictory conclusions stem from differences in prompting style rather than task design. More fundamentally, the results reveal a critical distinction: while LVLMs can execute efficient communication when instructed, they lack the pragmatic inferential capacity that humans naturally employ, underscoring a significant gap between human and AI communicative competence.

Abstract: Two recent studies (Jones et al. (2026); Zeng et al. (2026)) reach apparently contradictory conclusions about whether LVLMs can coordinate on efficient referring expressions. We control for task differences between the studies while directly comparing their prompting styles. We replicate the finding that models can coordinate efficient referring expressions when explicitly prompted to do so, suggesting that other task differences are not responsible for divergent results. However, we also find that the same models fail to infer the need for communicative efficiency from a more implicit prompt, highlighting critical differences between how humans and AI systems communicate.

</details>


### [15] [NarrativeWorldBench: A Frontier-Saturated Benchmark and a Latent World Model for Long-Horizon Co-Creative Audio Drama](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17391)
*Logan Mann,Abdur Rahman,Mohammad Saifullah,Taaha Kazi,Vasu Sharma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Long-form audio drama narratives (200-800 episodes) cause frontier LLMs to fail dramatically. The authors benchmark 21 models, introduce NarrativeWorldBench (9 narrative metrics, 5 horizons, 4 Indic languages), and propose N-VSSM — a Narrative Variational State-Space Model using a Mamba-2 backbone with a 256D latent world state. N-VSSM outperforms all closed-frontier systems at 4× lower compute, maintains plot-beat F1 ≥ 0.84 across all horizons, and is preferred by professional authors 71% of the time over Claude Opus 4.5.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frontier LLMs exhibit catastrophic degradation in long-horizon narrative consistency, particularly for serialized audio dramas spanning hundreds of episodes. Existing models cannot maintain coherent plot structure beyond short contexts, creating a gap for structured world-state approaches.

Method: The authors benchmark 21 models across classical, fine-tuned, open-frontier, closed-frontier, and reasoning tiers on NarrativeWorldBench, which measures 9 narrative-structure metrics at horizons {10, 20, 50, 100, 200} in English and four Indic languages. They then introduce N-VSSM: a Mamba-2–based variational state-space model that maintains a 256-dimensional latent world state via an event-conditioned posterior and an 8B-parameter decoder. A Cultural Transfer Function is trained to improve cross-lingual narrative fidelity. A within-subjects study with 12 professional authors (240 trials) compares N-VSSM against Claude Opus 4.5 on long-arc consistency and controllability.

Result: All closed-frontier systems saturate at plot-beat F1 ∈ [0.78, 0.81] and collapse by ~−0.20 F1 at horizon h=200. N-VSSM holds plot-beat F1 ≥ 0.84 across all horizons at 4× lower compute. The Cultural Transfer Function improves cross-language fidelity by +0.20 to +0.23 Likert points. In the writer study, N-VSSM is preferred 71% of the time for long-arc consistency and rated +1.3 Likert points higher on controllability versus Claude Opus 4.5.

Conclusion: Explicit structured world-state models like N-VSSM dramatically outperform general-purpose frontier LLMs on long-horizon narrative generation, suggesting that architectural inductive biases for state persistence are essential for serialized creative content. The cross-lingual cultural transfer results further indicate that language-agnostic latent representations can improve narrative fidelity across languages.

Abstract: Long-form serialized audio drama, with arcs that run for 200 to 800 episodes, is a major creative medium and a setting where frontier large language models (LLMs) fail. We benchmark 21 models, spanning classical, fine-tuned, open-frontier, closed-frontier, and reasoning tiers, on a uniform set of structural narrative metrics. All closed-frontier systems saturate at a plot-beat F1 in the band [0.78, 0.81] and collapse by about -0.20 F1 at horizon h=200. We introduce NarrativeWorldBench, an open benchmark of nine narrative-structure metrics evaluated across horizons h in {10, 20, 50, 100, 200}, with cross-lingual evaluation across four Indic languages (Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi). We introduce N-VSSM, a Narrative Variational State-Space Model that maintains a structured 256-dimensional latent world state over more than 200 episodes via a Mamba-2 backbone with an event-conditioned posterior and an 8B decoder. N-VSSM holds plot-beat F1 >= 0.84 across all horizons at 4x lower compute than the closed-frontier band. A learned Cultural Transfer Function lifts cross-language fidelity by +0.20 to +0.23 Likert points. In a within-subjects writer study (n = 12 professional authors, 240 trials), N-VSSM is preferred over Claude Opus 4.5 on long-arc consistency 71% of the time and rated +1.3 Likert points higher on controllability.

</details>


### [16] [MODE-RAG: Manifold Outlier Diagnosis and Energy-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17449)
*Zehang Wei,Jiaxin Dai,Jiamin Yan,Xiang Xiang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MODE-RAG is a Multi-Agent system that uses Variational Free Energy and internal attention states to dynamically gate interventions in Multimodal RAG, employing MCTS for causal reasoning and logit perturbations to reduce hallucinations and sycophancy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal RAG systems are highly susceptible to cross-modal hallucinations, causal fabrications, and sycophancy. Existing mitigation methods face an intervention paradox: static rules disrupt accurate outputs, while unguided reasoning allows mismatches to cascade into logical fabrications.

Method: MODE-RAG is a Multi-Agent system featuring five stage-specific agents. It uses Variational Free Energy (VFE) and internal attention states to dynamically gate interventions for high-risk queries. MCTS is integrated for rigorous causal derivation, and logit perturbations penalize sycophancy. Dedicated Correction and Overseer agents handle formatting stability and post-hoc factual verification. Evaluation uses ModeVent, a challenging subset of the MultiVent dataset.

Result: Extensive experiments show that MODE-RAG effectively reduces hallucination rates and logical fabrication, significantly improving the robustness of M-RAG systems.

Conclusion: The proposed MODE-RAG framework, grounded in VFE-driven dynamic intervention and multi-agent coordination, successfully mitigates key failure modes in M-RAG, offering a more robust and reliable approach for multimodal retrieval-augmented generation.

Abstract: While Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (M-RAG) enhances Large Vision-Language Models, it remains highly susceptible to cross-modal hallucinations, causal fabrications, and sycophancy. Furthermore, existing mitigation pipelines often face an intervention paradox: static rules tend to unnecessarily disrupt accurate generations, whereas leaving the multi-modal reasoning completely unguided allows existing mismatches to cascade into severe logical fabrications. To quantify and mitigate these hallucinations, we propose a Multi-Agent system, MODE-RAG, driven by Variational Free Energy (VFE) and internal attention states to dynamically gate interventions. High-risk queries are routed to five stage-specific agents, integrating Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for rigorous causal derivation and logit perturbations to penalize sycophancy. Dedicated Correction and Overseer agents ensure formatting stability and perform post-hoc factual verification. To objectively evaluate our approach, we introduce ModeVent, a challenging subset derived from the MultiVent dataset. Extensive experiments indicate that our system effectively reduces hallucination rates and logical fabrication, significantly improving the robustness of M-RAG systems.

</details>


### [17] [AIPatient Arena: EHR-grounded evaluation of large language models in end-to-end clinical consultation workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17474)
*Jiahui Niu,Huizi Yu,Wenkong Wang,Guangxin Dai,Jingxian He,Xiang Li,Zhiying Liang,Xinxin Lin,Kent CY So,Bryan YP Yan,Yun Kwok Wing,Yanqiu Xing,Xin Ma,Lizhou Fan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AIPatient Arena is an EHR-grounded, multi-turn evaluation framework that assesses LLMs across 8 clinical competence dimensions. While LLMs excel at questioning skills and ethical conduct, they show persistent weaknesses in handling ambiguity, information coverage, and diagnostic reasoning. The framework reveals that final-answer accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating clinical readiness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing medical LLM evaluations are static, single-turn, and outcome-based, failing to capture the sequential, uncertain, and interactive nature of real clinical consultations. There is a need for a workflow-oriented, process-based evaluation that reflects how models gather, interpret, and communicate information throughout a consultation.

Method: The authors propose AIPatient Arena, which integrates EHR data into patient-specific knowledge graphs to enable multi-turn physician-patient interactions. The framework evaluates LLMs across eight dimensions: questioning skills (QS), ethical/professional conduct (ET), clarity/transparency of explanations (EX), information integration (II), medication safety/justification (MS), handling of ambiguous responses (HR), information coverage (IC), and diagnostic accuracy/reasoning (Dx). Evaluation was conducted on a primary cohort of 437 patients and two out-of-distribution validation cohorts (119 and 67 patients).

Result: LLMs scored highest in QS (4.43–4.99/5), ET (4.38–4.93/5), and EX (3.80–4.72/5). Moderate performance in II (3.19–4.21/5) and MS (3.13–3.78/5). Weakest in HR (2.57–3.32/5), IC (2.08–3.02/5), and Dx (2.63–3.55/5). Recurrent failures included repetitive questioning, omission of past medical history, and inadequate uncertainty handling. Richer conversational context improved diagnostic reasoning but provided limited gains in treatment planning.

Conclusion: Final-answer accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating clinical readiness. Process-based, workflow-oriented assessment is essential. AIPatient Arena provides a robust EHR-grounded framework for pre-deployment evaluation of medical LLMs, highlighting the importance of assessing how models gather, interpret, and communicate information throughout the consultation process.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for use in clinical consultation tasks, yet most medical evaluations remain static, single-turn, or narrowly outcome-based, limiting their ability to reflect the sequential, uncertain, and interactive nature of real-world care. Here, we propose AIPatient Arena, an EHRs-grounded evaluation framework for assessing the clinical utility of LLMs across eight dimensions of clinical competence. The framework integrates EHR data into patient-specific knowledge graphs, enabling multi-turn physician-patient interactions. We applied AIPatient Arena on a primary cohort of 437 patients and two out-of-distribution validation cohorts of 119 and 67 patients. We observe that LLMs performed well in medical interview questioning skills (QS; mean scores, 4.43-4.99/5), ethical and professional conduct (ET; 4.38-4.93/5), and clarity and transparency of clinical explanations (EX; 3.80-4.72/5). Performance was moderate in information integration (II; 3.19-4.21/5) and medication safety and justification (MS; 3.13-3.78/5), but persistent weaknesses were observed in handling of ambiguous patient responses (HR; 2.57-3.32/5), information coverage (IC; 2.08-3.02/5), and diagnostic accuracy and reasoning (Dx; 2.63-3.55/5). Process-based evaluation revealed recurrent interaction failures, including repetitive questioning, omission of past medical history, and inadequate handling of uncertainty. Richer conversational context improved diagnostic reasoning but yielded limited gains in treatment planning. These findings indicate that final-answer accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating clinical readiness and highlight the importance of assessing how models gather, interpret, and communicate information throughout a consultation. AIPatient Arena provides an EHR-grounded framework for workflow-oriented pre-deployment evaluation of medical LLMs.

</details>


### [18] [Decoding Hidden Deception in Reasoning LLMs: Activation Explainers for Deception Auditing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17478)
*Kexin Chen,Yi Liu,Haonan Zhang,Yanhui Li,Xinyu Deng,Dongxia Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: STATEWITNESS is an activation explainer that decodes hidden states from LLMs into natural-language explanations and structured reports for deception auditing, achieving 0.916 mean AUROC (11.6% improvement over black-box monitors and 25.0% over activation probes) across seven deception datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deception monitoring methods either analyze visible text transcripts or produce scalar probe scores from internal representations, but both offer little inspectable evidence explaining why a response is deemed suspicious. This lack of interpretability hinders trust and human oversight in safety-critical deployments.

Method: A separate decoder model reads the hidden states of a target reasoning LLM and generates natural-language answers to queries or structured reports about the internal activations. The system is evaluated on two target LLMs across seven deception datasets, comparing against black-box text monitors and activation-probe baselines under a unified evaluation protocol. Ensemble methods combining STATEWITNESS with existing monitors are also tested.

Result: STATEWITNESS achieves 0.916 mean AUROC, outperforming the best black-box text monitor by 11.6% and the best activation-probe baseline by 25.0%. In threshold ensembles, it reduces missed deceptive examples. The decoder additionally provides query-level answers, schema-based reports, and token- or sentence-level evidence traces suitable for human inspection.

Conclusion: The authors position STATEWITNESS as a building block for broader interpretability and alignment tooling, emphasizing its dual value as both a high-performance deception detector and an inspectable interface that produces human-readable evidence for auditing decisions.

Abstract: As LLMs acquire stronger reasoning capabilities, deceptive behavior becomes an increasingly serious safety concern. Existing deception monitors either score visible transcripts or derive scalar probe scores from representation vectors, leaving little inspectable evidence about why a response is suspicious. We introduce STATEWITNESS, an activation explainer for deception auditing. A separate decoder reads a target model's hidden states, then answers natural-language queries or emits structured reports about them. We evaluate STATEWITNESS on two target reasoning LLMs across seven deception datasets. STATEWITNESS reaches 0.916 mean AUROC, a relative gain of 11.6% over the best black-box text monitor and 25.0% over the best activation-probe baseline under the same evaluation protocol. When combined with existing monitors, STATEWITNESS reduces missed deceptive examples in simple threshold ensembles. Beyond scalar detection, the decoder returns query-level answers, schema reports, and token- or sentence-level evidence traces for human inspection. We view this interface as a potential building block for broader interpretability and alignment tools.

</details>


### [19] [Evaluating Second-Order Bias of LLMs Through Epistemic Entitlement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17506)
*Ramaravind Kommiya Mothilal,Terry Jingchen Zhang,Raiyan Ahmed,Zhijing Jin,Shion Guha,Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces "second-order bias" — bias in how LLMs judge whether content is biased, rather than bias in what they generate. Using entitlement epistemology, the authors design a logical reasoning task where LLMs must determine to whom a biased text is acceptable, then measure whether models infer demographics without sufficient support. Results show LLM judgments systematically vary across target groups, bypass safety guardrails, and reflect implicit social maps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current bias evaluations focus on first-order bias (whether LLMs generate biased content), but as LLMs are increasingly deployed as judges of bias in content moderation and evaluation pipelines, their judgments may exhibit subtler "second-order" social biases. Existing methods do not systematically capture how models evaluate biased content, necessitating a new framework and measurement approach.

Method: The authors ground their work in entitlement epistemology, conceptualizing bias as misplaced foundational knowledge shaping rational inquiry. From this, they derive a logical reasoning task: LLMs must judge to whom a biased text would be acceptable or unacceptable. They develop two metrics — (1) how biased LLM judges are in inferring target demographics without sufficient textual support, and (2) how these inferences vary across different groups targeted by biased texts. Both open and closed models are evaluated.

Result: The reasoning task successfully evades safety guardrails by surfacing bias in model judgment. Model judgments vary systematically across target groups, reflect implicit social maps (models' internal representations of social hierarchies), and show that models remain triggered by demographic labels. This reveals second-order bias patterns that first-order evaluations miss.

Conclusion: The findings demonstrate the need for evaluating LLM bias specifically in judgment tasks, beyond generation-focused assessments. The work calls for more theoretically grounded approaches to bias evaluation in NLP, and the authors release their code and model responses to facilitate further research.

Abstract: Evaluations of social bias in LLMs largely focus on whether models generate or imply biased content. However, as LLMs are increasingly used as judges of bias, they may exhibit social biases in subtler ways in how they evaluate biased content, which current methods do not systematically capture. We call this second-order bias: social bias in an LLM's judgment about social bias, which we evaluate through a novel, philosophically grounded reasoning task. Drawing on entitlement epistemology, we conceptualize bias as misplaced foundational knowledge that shapes an agent's rational inquiry, and derive a logical reasoning task for LLMs to judge to whom a biased text is acceptable or non-acceptable. We develop two simple metrics to measure how biased LLM judges are in inferring demographics for acceptability without sufficient support, and how these inferences vary across groups targeted by biased texts. Evaluating open and closed models, we find that our task evades safety guardrails by surfacing bias in model judgment. It varies systematically across target groups, reflects implicit social maps, and shows how models are still triggered by demographic labels. Our work points to the need for LLM bias evaluation in judgment tasks and broadly, for more theoretically grounded approaches to bias evaluation in NLP. We release our code and model responses at https://github.com/uofthcdslab/second-order-bias.

</details>


### [20] [Scaling Enterprise Agent Routing: Degradation, Diagnosis, and Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17519)
*Kellen Gillespie,Robyn Perry*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: As LLM tool catalogs scale to hundreds of tools across many agents, single-step routing accuracy degrades significantly due to both retrieval and confusion gaps. Embedding-based shortlisting recovers 10–17pp F1 in production.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production LLM assistants increasingly route user requests to large, growing catalogs of specialized tools, but the impact of catalog scale on routing accuracy is not well understood.

Method: The authors study single-step routing on a production enterprise assistant with a 110-agent, 584-tool catalog. They evaluate three frontier models across 10–110 agents, decompose degradation via an oracle analysis into retrieval and confusion gaps, and test embedding-based shortlisting as a mitigation. A production annotation study with 1,435 human-labeled utterances (three annotators) validates findings on real traffic.

Result: Routing F1 on under-specified requests drops 16–23pp across models when scaling from 10 to 110 agents. Oracle analysis shows the retrieval gap accounts for part of the loss; even with perfect retrieval, the oracle ceiling drops 10pp (confusion gap). Embedding-based shortlisting recovers +10–11pp F1 at full scale. The production annotation study confirms +10–17pp recovery on real traffic, though absolute performance is 10–15pp lower than offline.

Conclusion: Tool catalog scale substantially degrades routing accuracy through both retrieval failures and increased model confusion. Embedding-based shortlisting is an effective, model- and provider-agnostic mitigation that significantly recovers lost performance in production settings.

Abstract: Production LLM assistants route user requests to growing libraries of specialized tools, but how does routing accuracy degrade as the catalog scales? We study single-step routing on a 110-agent, 584-tool catalog from a deployed enterprise productivity assistant, evaluating three frontier models from 10 to 110 agents. Routing F1 on under-specified requests drops 16--23 percentage points across models. An oracle analysis decomposes the degradation into a \emph{retrieval} gap (the model cannot surface the right tool) and a \emph{confusion} gap (even with perfect retrieval, the oracle ceiling drops 10pp). Embedding-based shortlisting recovers +10--11pp F1 at full scale across all three models and two providers. A production annotation study (1,435 human-labeled utterances, three annotators) confirms the recovery on real traffic at +10--17pp despite 10--15pp lower absolute performance.

</details>


### [21] [An expressivity analysis of hierarchical modelling in deep transformers via bounded-depth grammars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17522)
*Vinoth Nandakumar,Qiang Qu,Pramod Thebe,Sakshi Khachariya,Tongliang Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper provides a theoretical construction showing that deep transformers with positional attention can represent bounded-depth context-free grammars, with depth scaling linearly in grammar depth and width scaling quadratically in production rules. The construction supports the "linear representation hypothesis" by encoding grammatical states as linearly separable subspaces in the residual stream.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the widespread belief that deep transformers derive power from hierarchical representations—capturing syntax locally in early layers and clause-level dependencies in later layers—there is little rigorous theory demonstrating *how* transformers actually represent such hierarchical structure. This work aims to fill that gap.

Method: The authors adopt the formal lens of bounded-depth, non-recursive context-free grammars. They explicitly construct deep transformers with positional attention, where transformer depth grows linearly with grammar depth, neuron count scales with the number of derivation-tree shapes, and quadratically with production rule count. The construction encodes abstract grammatical states into low-dimensional, linearly separable subspaces within the residual stream.

Result: The construction demonstrates that deep transformers provably possess the structural capacity to represent hierarchical grammatical structure. Specifically, grammatical states are encoded as linearly separable representations in the residual stream, providing formal support for the linear representation hypothesis. The depth requirement is linear in grammar depth, and width scales quadratically in production rules.

Conclusion: Deep transformers have the theoretical capacity to encode hierarchical syntactic structure, with the residual stream serving as a medium for linearly separable grammatical state representations. This bridges the gap between empirical observations of hierarchical processing in language models and formal expressiveness theory.

Abstract: Deep neural networks are widely believed to derive their expressive power from their ability to form \textbf{hierarchical representations}, capturing progressively more abstract and compositional features across layers. In language modeling, \textbf{transformers} have emerged as the dominant architecture, with early layers capturing local syntactic patterns and later layers encoding more complex clause-level dependencies. While this intuition has shaped model design, there remains a lack of rigorous theoretical work demonstrating \textbf{how} deep transformers represent such hierarchical structures. In this work, we analyze the expressiveness of deep transformer models through the formal lens of bounded-depth, non-recursive context-free grammars. For this class of grammars, we explicitly construct transformers with positional attention whose depth grows linearly with grammar depth, while the neuron count scales with the number of derivation-tree shapes and quadratically with the number of production rules. Our theoretical results support the linear representation hypothesis by demonstrating that these architectures possess the structural capacity to encode abstract grammatical states into low-dimensional, linearly separable subspaces within the residual stream.

</details>


### [22] [Evaluating Large Language Models Abilities for Addressee, Turn-change, and Next Speaker Prediction in Meetings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17542)
*Ryo Fukuda,Takatomo Kano,Siddhant Arora,Marc Delcroix,Naohiro Tawara,Atsunori Ogawa,Yuya Chiba,Atsushi Ando,William Chen,Shinji Watanabe*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs were evaluated on three turn-taking tasks in multi-party conversations. Text-based LLMs surpassed supervised models and humans on next speaker prediction without domain training or audio-visual input. Multimodal LLMs improved addressee detection and turn-change prediction but still underperformed humans, revealing difficulty in leveraging raw audio-visual signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To systematically investigate how well large language models, including multimodal variants, can handle turn-taking phenomena in multimodal multi-party conversations—a core challenge for conversational AI that involves coordinating who speaks when and to whom.

Method: An evaluation framework was constructed covering three tasks: addressee detection, turn-change prediction, and next speaker prediction. The authors compared supervised task-specific models, text-based LLMs, multimodal LLMs (MM-LLMs), and human subjects using the AMI meeting corpus. Ablation analyses were conducted to isolate the contribution of conversational context, and error patterns were compared between humans and LLMs.

Result: Text-based LLMs outperformed both supervised models and humans on next speaker prediction despite no target-domain training and no audio/visual access. MM-LLMs outperformed text-only LLMs on addressee detection and turn-change prediction but remained below human performance. Conversational context proved critical, especially for next speaker prediction. Human and LLM prediction patterns were similar, with both struggling during frequent turn-change intervals.

Conclusion: LLMs exhibit strong latent competence for turn-taking, particularly next speaker prediction driven by conversational context, but current multimodal LLMs still cannot effectively exploit raw audio-visual signals to match human-level performance on other turn-taking tasks.

Abstract: We investigate turn-taking in multimodal multi-party conversations using large language models (LLMs). We construct an evaluation framework for three tasks: addressee detection, turn-change prediction, and next speaker prediction. We compare supervised models trained for these tasks, text-based LLMs, multimodal LLMs (MM-LLMs), and human subjects. Experiments on the AMI corpus showed that LLMs outperformed supervised models and humans in next speaker prediction, despite not being trained on the target domain and without access to audio or visual information. An MM-LLM performed better than text-based LLMs on addressee detection and turn-change prediction but remained below human performance, indicating difficulty leveraging raw audio-visual signals. Ablation analyses revealed that conversational context was critical, particularly for next speaker prediction. We observed that human and LLM prediction patterns were similar, and intervals with frequent turn changes were difficult for both.

</details>


### [23] [Security and Privacy Prompts in the Wild: What Users Ask LLMs and How LLMs Respond](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18062)
*Hobin Kim,Xiaoyuan Wu,Omer Akgul,Lujo Bauer,Nicolas Christin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: First large-scale study analyzing real user questions about digital security and privacy (S&P) posed to LLMs in the wild. Using 3.2M WildChat conversations, researchers identified 14,727 S&P prompts across nine categories, evaluated LLM response quality, and found commercial models outperform open-weight models but sometimes produce contradictory answers across repeated runs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior research on LLM responses to S&P questions relied on expert-authored misconceptions or FAQs rather than authentic user queries. No study had collected or analyzed the actual S&P questions users ask LLMs in real-world settings, leaving a gap in understanding user needs and LLM performance in this critical domain.

Method: Researchers drew from WildChat (3.2M real user-LLM conversations), identified 14,727 S&P prompts using keyword-based filtering, categorized them into nine S&P topic categories, performed thematic analysis on a sample of 450 prompts to characterize user question types, curated 270 advice-seeking prompts, and evaluated response quality by posing each prompt to LLMs 10 times to measure both quality and consistency across commercial and open-weight models.

Result: Commercial LLMs significantly outperformed open-weight models: GPT-5.5 provided "good enough" responses on 98% of prompts versus Llama 4 on only 47%. However, even for prompts that received high-quality responses on average, commercial models sometimes produced contradictory responses across repeated runs, posing risks of confusing or misleading users.

Conclusion: While commercial LLMs demonstrate strong capability in answering user S&P questions, their inconsistency across runs represents a significant reliability concern for security and privacy advice, where contradictory guidance could have harmful consequences for users seeking to protect themselves.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to fulfill users' information needs; users ask LLMs about the weather, pose educational questions, and consult them for legal assistance. One particularly understudied area is digital security and privacy (S&P), where users may seek LLMs' help on how to secure their online accounts or protect their computers from cyber attacks. To the best of our knowledge, no prior study has collected or analyzed the S&P questions users ask LLMs; prior research on LLM response quality relied on expert-authored S&P misconceptions or FAQs rather than user queries. Drawing from WildChat, a dataset of 3.2M user-LLM conversations collected in the wild, our study identifies 14,727 S&P prompts and categorizes them into nine categories covering a wide range of S&P topics. From the S&P prompts, we sampled 450 and performed a thematic analysis to characterize the S&P questions users ask LLMs. Separate from the thematic analysis, we curated 270 advice-seeking S&P prompts, where users ask for recommendations, guidance, or specific S&P information. We measured LLM response quality and consistency when posing the prompt to LLMs 10 times. We found that commercial LLMs outperform open-weight models (GPT 5.5 provided "good enough" responses on 98% of prompts; Llama 4 on 47%). However, among prompts that received high-quality responses on average, commercial models sometimes produce contradictory responses across runs, risking confusing or misleading users.

</details>


### [24] [The Benchmark Illusion: Pruned LLMs Can Pass Multiple Choice but Fail to Answer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17609)
*Rui Wen,Lu Sun,Jiayang Liu,Zesheng Xu,Tianshuo Cong,Zheng Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Pruned LLMs exhibit a "benchmark illusion" where they maintain high multiple-choice accuracy but fail on open-ended generation for the same questions. The correct answer is typically not erased but demoted in the output distribution, recoverable via beam search, sampling, or in-context examples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard compression benchmarks relying on multiple-choice (recognition-based) evaluation may overstate the true usability of pruned models, creating a blind spot where failures in generative settings go undetected.

Method: The authors track identical questions before and after pruning using multilingual QA tasks. They compare greedy open generation against multiple-choice scoring under high-sparsity pruning (particularly Wanda), and test recovery of correct answers through beam search, sampling, and one-shot in-context examples.

Result: Under high-sparsity pruning, models frequently commit "recognition-only errors": failing greedy generation while still selecting the correct answer in multiple-choice format. The answer is demoted—not erased—and often reappears with beam search, sampling, or a single in-context example.

Conclusion: Multiple-choice benchmarks overstate compressed LLM usability. Evaluation of compressed models must include generative assessments, not merely recognition-based metrics.

Abstract: Compressing large language models reduces memory use and inference cost, but it can also create failures that standard benchmarks miss. A pruned model may still perform well on multiple-choice evaluations, yet fail to answer the same question in open generation. We ask what pruning changes: does it erase the correct answer, or does it make the answer harder to produce as the top output?
