  We study this question with multilingual question answering, tracking the same questions before and after pruning. We find a benchmark illusion. Under high-sparsity pruning, especially Wanda, models often fail in greedy open generation while still selecting the correct answer under multiple-choice scoring. In these recognition-only errors, the answer is usually not gone, but demoted: it often reappears with beam search, sampling, or one in-context example. Overall, multiple-choice benchmarks can overstate the usability of compressed LLMs, creating an evaluation blind spot. Compressed models should be tested on what they can produce, not only on what they can recognize.

</details>


### [25] [OPD-Evolver: Cultivating Holistic Agent Evolver via On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17628)
*Guibin Zhang,Xun Xu,Yanwei Yue,Zikun Su,Wangchunshu Zhou,Xiaobin Hu,Shuicheng Yan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OPD-Evolver is a slow-fast co-evolution framework that trains agents to self-evolve through on-policy self-distillation over a four-level memory hierarchy, enabling reading, using, writing, and maintaining reusable knowledge. It outperforms prior memory systems and training-based methods, with a 9B model rivaling much larger counterparts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory-augmented agents can store and retrieve experiences but lack the integrated competence to selectively use, act on, write reusable knowledge from, and maintain a growing memory repository. Retaining experience is not equivalent to learning how to evolve through it.

Method: OPD-Evolver employs a slow-fast co-evolution framework with on-policy self-distillation. The fast loop operates a four-level memory hierarchy for test-time evolution (read, use, write, maintain). The slow loop uses outcome-calibrated memory attribution and privileged hindsight to distill these four abilities into a deployable policy.

Result: OPD-Evolver surpasses memory systems like ReasoningBank by up to 11.5% and training-based methods like Skill0 by ~5.8%. The 9B variant (OPD-Evolver-9B) challenges much larger models such as Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and Step-3.5-Flash.

Conclusion: OPD-Evolver demonstrates that distilling memory management and high-value experience selection into a policy moves beyond memory-augmented agents toward genuinely qualified agent evolvers, enabling smaller models to rival giant counterparts.

Abstract: Memory has become a standard substrate for self-evolving agents, yet retaining experience is not the same as learning how to evolve through it. Existing memory agents can store trajectories, retrieve reflections, or accumulate skills, but often lack the holistic competence to select useful experience, act on it, write reusable knowledge, and maintain a growing repository. We introduce OPD-Evolver, a slow-fast co-evolution framework that cultivates such an agent evolver through on-policy self-distillation. In the fast loop, OPD-Evolver interacts with a four-level memory hierarchy to read, use, write, and maintain experience for rapid test-time evolution. In the slow loop, outcome-calibrated memory attribution and privileged hindsight distill these four abilities into the deployable policy. Across multi-domain benchmarks, OPD-Evolver surpasses memory systems such as ReasoningBank by up to 11.5%, and training-based methods such as Skill0 by ~5.8%. Further analysis shows that OPD-Evolver internalizes high-value experience and memory management, enabling OPD-Evolver-9B to challenge giant counterparts such as Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and Step-3.5-Flash, pointing beyond memory-augmented agents toward genuinely qualified agent evolvers.

</details>


### [26] [Prompt Perturbation for Reliable LLM Evaluation over Comparison Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17634)
*Dong Huang,Jianbo Sun,Pengkun Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a prompt perturbation framework to reduce intransitivity (cyclic preferences, tie inconsistencies) in pairwise LLM evaluation by filtering out structurally inconsistent comparison patterns using graph-level consistency checks before ranking aggregation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pairwise LLM evaluation for open-ended tasks suffers from intransitivity: comparison outcomes often contain cycles (A > B > C > A) and tie-related contradictions, making leaderboards unstable and difficult to interpret. Existing methods lack explicit structural consistency enforcement.

Method: A prompt perturbation framework: (1) generate perturbed variants of each evaluation prompt; (2) construct comparison graphs from the resulting pairwise judgments; (3) identify and filter out structurally inconsistent comparison patterns at the graph level; (4) apply standard ranking methods (e.g., Elo, Bradley-Terry) to the filtered comparisons. Graph-level structural consistency is explicitly incorporated before ranking aggregation.

Result: The framework provides a simple and principled mechanism to reduce cyclic inconsistencies and tie-related contradictions, leading to more reliable and interpretable LLM rankings. (Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.)

Conclusion: Incorporating graph-level structural consistency into the evaluation pipeline before ranking aggregation effectively mitigates intransitivity in pairwise LLM evaluation, improving leaderboard stability and interpretability without complex interventions.

Abstract: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) is important for understanding their capabilities, comparing competing systems, and supporting the deployment of reliable models in practice. For open-ended tasks, pairwise evaluation has become a popular paradigm, in which two responses to the same prompt are compared and the resulting judgments are aggregated into an overall ranking. A central challenge of this paradigm is intransitivity: the induced comparison outcomes may fail to support any coherent global ranking. For example, one may observe cyclic preferences such as $A \succ B \succ C \succ A$, or inconsistencies involving ties such as $A \equiv B\equiv C\neq A$. Such contradictions make the resulting leaderboard unstable and challenging to interpret. In this paper, we propose a prompt perturbation framework for improving the consistency of pairwise LLM evaluation. Our approach generates perturbed variants of each prompt, uses the resulting comparison graphs to identify and filter out structurally inconsistent comparison patterns, and then applies standard ranking methods to the filtered comparisons. A key feature of the proposed framework is that graph-level structural consistency is incorporated explicitly into the evaluation pipeline before ranking aggregation. This provides a simple and principled way to reduce cyclic inconsistencies and improve the reliability of LLM rankings.

</details>


### [27] [From Trainee to Trainer: LLM-Designed Training Environment for RL with Multi-Agent Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17682)
*Chao Chen,Chengzu Li,Zhiwei Li,Yinhong Liu,Zhijiang Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes an "LLM-as-Environment-Engineer" framework where the RL policy model itself automatically analyzes failure trajectories and proposes modifications to the training environment configuration for the next stage, eliminating manual heuristic tuning. They also introduce MAPF-FrozenLake, a configurable testbed, and demonstrate that a Qwen3-4B backbone outperforms larger proprietary models and fixed-environment baselines, with the current RL checkpoint proving a better environment engineer than the base model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning pipelines for LLM training currently require practitioners to manually redesign environments between stages using heuristic inference about which configurations will best improve the policy. This manual process is inefficient and suboptimal, motivating an automated approach to environment redesign.

Method: The authors propose the LLM-as-Environment-Engineer framework: the current policy model receives structured summaries of policy behavior, failure cases, and environment statistics, then proposes modifications to the next-stage training environment configuration. They introduce MAPF-FrozenLake, a controllable testbed with a generator exposing multi-dimensional environment configurations, for benchmarking environment redesign. Experiments use Qwen3-4B as the backbone and compare against larger proprietary models (GPT, Gemini) and fixed-environment baselines. Ablations analyze which contextual information is most critical for effective redesign.

Result: The Qwen3-4B-based framework achieves the strongest aggregate performance, outperforming larger proprietary LLMs (GPT, Gemini) and fixed-environment training baselines. Successful environment updates rely on failure evidence and preserving configurations that already work. The current RL checkpoint serves as a better environment engineer than the original base model, suggesting policy learning improves the model's diagnostic ability for its own weaknesses.

Conclusion: Automated environment engineering by the policy model itself is not only feasible but outperforms both manual baselines and larger proprietary models. The finding that RL training improves self-diagnosis ability has implications for building more autonomous and self-improving LLM training pipelines.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning pipelines for Large Language Model (LLM) training often rely on manually redesigned environments between stages, requiring practitioners to heuristically infer which configuration will best improve the current policy. To automate this process, we propose the LLM-as-Environment-Engineer framework in which the current policy model analyzes failure trajectories together with contextual information and proposes modifications to the next-stage training environment configuration. We also introduce MAPF-FrozenLake, a controllable testbed whose generator exposes multi-dimensional environment configurations, making it suitable for studying and benchmarking environment redesign. On this testbed, we condition the environment engineer on structured summaries of policy behavior, failure cases, and environment statistics, from which it produces the configuration for the next training stage. With Qwen3-4B as the backbone, our framework achieves the strongest aggregate performance on our benchmarks, outperforming larger proprietary LLMs (e.g., GPT, Gemini) and fixed-environment training baselines. We further analyze which forms of context are most effective, finding that successful environment updates rely on failure evidence and preserve configurations that already work. Interestingly, the current RL checkpoint serves as a better environment engineer than the original base model, suggesting that policy learning improves the model's ability to diagnose its remaining weaknesses.

</details>


### [28] [Bridging Functional Correctness and Runtime Efficiency Gaps in LLM-Based Code Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17683)
*Longhui Zhang,Jiahao Wang,Chenhao Hu,Bingyu Liang,Jing Li,Min Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SwiftTrans is a two-stage code translation framework that improves both functional correctness and runtime efficiency of LLM-translated programs by generating diverse translation candidates via parallel in-context learning, then selecting the optimal one through explicit difference comparison.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based code translation systems focus heavily on functional correctness but neglect runtime efficiency. Preliminary experiments show LLM-translated programs are often slower than human-written ones, and prompt engineering alone cannot fix this. With Moore's law slowing, runtime efficiency is increasingly critical.

Method: SwiftTrans has two stages: (1) Multi-Perspective Exploration using MpTranslator with parallel in-context learning and Hierarchical Guidance to generate diverse translation candidates; (2) Difference-Aware Selection using DiffSelector with Ordinal Guidance to explicitly compare inter-translation differences and pick the optimal candidate. The authors also extend CodeNet and F2SBench benchmarks and introduce SwiftBench for runtime evaluation.

Result: SwiftTrans achieves consistent improvements in both correctness and runtime efficiency across all three benchmarks (extended CodeNet, extended F2SBench, and the new SwiftBench).

Conclusion: Runtime efficiency is an underexplored dimension in LLM-based code translation. SwiftTrans demonstrates that a multi-perspective generation plus difference-aware selection paradigm, augmented with hierarchical and ordinal guidance, can effectively address both correctness and efficiency simultaneously.

Abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have greatly advanced the functional correctness of automated code translation systems, the runtime efficiency of translated programs has received comparatively little attention. With the waning of Moore's law, runtime efficiency has become increasingly important for program quality, alongside functional correctness. Our preliminary study reveals that LLM-translated programs often run slower than human-written ones, and this issue cannot be remedied through prompt engineering alone. Therefore, our work proposes SwiftTrans, a code translation framework comprising two key stages: (1) Multi-Perspective Exploration, where MpTranslator leverages parallel in-context learning (ICL) to generate diverse translation candidates; and (2) Difference-Aware Selection, where DiffSelector identifies the optimal candidate by explicitly comparing differences between translations. We further introduce Hierarchical Guidance for MpTranslator and Ordinal Guidance for DiffSelector, enabling LLMs to better adapt to these two core components. To support the evaluation of runtime efficiency in translated programs, we extend existing benchmarks, CodeNet and F2SBench, and introduce a new benchmark, SwiftBench. Experimental results across all three benchmarks show that SwiftTrans achieves consistent improvements in both correctness and runtime efficiency.

</details>


### [29] [SuCo: Sufficiency-guided Continuous Adaptive Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17687)
*Jiahao Wang,Bingyu Liang,Chenhao Hu,Longhui Zhang,Xuebo Liu,Min zhang,Jing Li,Xuelong Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Minimal Sufficient CoT (MSC) — the shortest reasoning prefix needed for a correct answer — and proposes SuCo, a two-stage framework (MFT + SAPO) that trains models to generate concise yet adequate reasoning, improving both accuracy and efficiency across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large Reasoning Models waste computational resources by generating excessively long Chain-of-Thought even for simple queries. Existing solutions use rigid discrete modes or fixed budgets, lacking a principled criterion for when reasoning is "enough."

Method: The authors first define Minimal Sufficient CoT (MSC) as the shortest CoT prefix yielding a correct answer. They then propose SuCo: Stage 1 (MSC-Aligned Fine-Tuning) constructs MSC data using problem-adaptive sufficiency thresholds and fine-tunes the model; Stage 2 (Sufficiency-Aware Policy Optimization) applies RL with dynamic complexity tracking and sufficiency-aware rewards that penalize both over-thinking and under-thinking.

Result: Empirically, MSC reduces reasoning tokens while improving accuracy across difficulty levels. SuCo achieves consistent gains in both accuracy and reasoning efficiency on mathematics, code, and science benchmarks.

Conclusion: SuCo provides a principled, continuous approach to adaptive reasoning control, demonstrating that models can learn to generate reasoning that is both minimal and sufficient, outperforming discrete or fixed-budget baselines.

Abstract: Despite remarkable performance on complex tasks, Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) often generate excessively long Chain-of-Thoughts (CoT), inflating computational costs even for simple queries. Existing efforts to mitigate this inefficiency typically rely on discrete reasoning modes or fixed budget tiers, lacking a principled criterion of when reasoning is sufficient. In this work, we introduce Minimal Sufficient CoT (MSC), defined as the shortest prefix of a CoT trajectory which is adequate for producing the correct answer. We empirically show that MSC not only reduces reasoning tokens, but also improves accuracy across difficulty levels. Building on MSC, we propose Sufficiency-guided Continuous Adaptive Reasoning (SuCo), a two-stage training framework for autonomous reasoning control along a continuous spectrum. In stage 1, MSC-Aligned Fine-Tuning (MFT) constructs MSC data using problem-adaptive sufficiency thresholds that naturally scale with question difficulty, then fine-tunes the model to internalize concise yet sufficient reasoning patterns. In stage 2, Sufficiency-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO) further optimizes the model through reinforcement learning with dynamic complexity tracking and sufficiency-aware rewards that penalize both over- and under-thinking. Extensive experiments across mathematics, code, and science benchmarks show that SuCo consistently achieves improvements in both accuracy and reasoning efficiency.

</details>


### [30] [LLMs Infer Cultural Context but Fail to Apply It When Responding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17688)
*Yisong Miao,Jian Zhu,Vered Shwartz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs exhibit cultural knowledge but fail to spontaneously adapt responses to users' cultural conventions (e.g., measurement units, time/quantity expressions) unless explicitly prompted, and their priors are not culture-neutral, often aligning with the model's origin country.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work established that LLMs overrepresent Western cultures while marginalizing others. This paper investigates whether this cultural bias impairs models' ability to generate culturally adapted responses—specifically, whether models can infer a user's cultural background and appropriately adjust their use of local measurement units and subjective linguistic conventions.

Method: The authors introduce CAPRI (Cultural and Pragmatic Response Inference), a dataset of conversations with systematically varying levels of cultural cues. They evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs on two dimensions: (1) use of local measurement units based on perceived cultural background, and (2) adaptation to culture-dependent interpretations of time and quantity expressions. Experiments test both spontaneous adaptation and explicitly prompted sequential task performance.

Result: LLMs can infer cultural background and recall relevant conventions, but often fail to utilize this information for cultural adaptation without explicit sequential prompting. Adaptation improves as cultural cues accumulate; however, model priors are not culture-neutral and sometimes align with the model's country of origin rather than the user's cultural context.

Conclusion: CAPRI serves as a benchmark resource for narrowing the gap between cultural knowledge and culturally adaptive language generation, highlighting that current LLMs possess but underutilize cultural awareness in pragmatic response generation.

Abstract: Recent work has shown that LLMs overrepresent dominant cultures, particularly Western ones, while marginalizing others. We investigate whether this affects models' ability to generate culturally adapted responses by evaluating their use of local measurement units based on the user's perceived cultural background. We introduce Cultural and Pragmatic Response Inference (CAPRI), a dataset of conversations with varying levels of cultural cues. Experiments with state-of-the-art LLMs show that models can infer cultural background and recall relevant conventions, but often fail to utilize the information to adapt their answers to the relevant cultural conventions, unless explicitly prompted to perform the tasks sequentially. We further evaluate adaptation to the interpretation of time and quantity expressions, two subjective language grounding dimensions that are affected by culture. We find that models increasingly adapt their answers as cultural cues accumulate, but their priors are not culture-neutral, sometimes aligning with the model's country of origin. Overall, CAPRI provides a resource for future research aimed at narrowing the gap between cultural knowledge and culturally adaptive language generation.

</details>


### [31] [The Slop Paradox: How Synthetic Standardization Erodes Clinical Uncertainty and Cross-Modal Alignment in AI-Rewritten Radiology Reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17791)
*Samar Ansari*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLM rewriting of radiology reports causes a "slop paradox": EHR summarization erases clinical entities and hedging language but preserves image-text alignment, while standardization and teaching-case rewrites preserve more entities but severely degrade cross-modal alignment. The rewriting task type, not clinical content rarity, drives degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-assisted clinical documentation tools increasingly use LLMs to rewrite radiology reports, but the information degradation these rewrites introduce—particularly for downstream multimodal AI training—has not been systematically measured.

Method: Controlled experiment using 450 chest X-ray reports from the Indiana University dataset. Three realistic LLM rewriting tasks applied: (1) EHR summarization, (2) standardized rewriting, (3) teaching case preparation. Degradation measured along three axes: entity erosion via medical NER, hedging collapse (loss of uncertainty language), and cross-modal alignment degradation via BiomedCLIP image-text similarity. Nine rare-vs-common pathology comparisons tested with multiple-comparison correction.

Result: EHR summarization eroded 51.4% of clinical entities and 43.7% of hedging language but caused only a 2.5% drop in image-text alignment. Standardized rewriting and teaching case preparation preserved more entities (26.8% and 29.3% eroded, respectively) but caused 14.9–16.5% alignment drops—6–7× worse than EHR summarization. Rare pathologies were not preferentially degraded; no rare-vs-common difference survived correction.

Conclusion: The "slop paradox" shows that cleaner-looking clinical text for multimodal training paradoxically pulls representations away from associated images. Task type, not clinical content, is the dominant degradation driver. This has direct implications for multimodal medical AI dataset construction and governance of AI-assisted clinical documentation pipelines.

Abstract: AI-assisted clinical documentation tools increasingly summarize, standardize, and reformat radiology reports using large language models (LLMs). We present a controlled measurement of the resulting information degradation. Using 450 chest X-ray reports from the Indiana University dataset, we generate synthetic versions via three realistic LLM rewriting tasks: EHR summarization, standardized rewriting, and teaching case preparation. We measure entity erosion (via medical NER), hedging collapse (loss of clinical uncertainty language), and cross-modal alignment degradation (via BiomedCLIP image-text similarity). Our central finding is a dissociation between information loss and cross-modal fidelity. EHR summarization is the most destructive at the content level, eroding 51.4% of clinical entities and 43.7% of hedging language, yet it preserves image-text alignment almost entirely (a 2.5% drop). The two tasks meant to produce cleaner training data, standardized rewriting and teaching case preparation, do the reverse: they preserve more entities (26.8% and 29.3% eroded) but cause 14.9-16.5% alignment drops, six to seven times those of EHR summarization. We term this the slop paradox: rewriting that makes clinical text look cleaner for multimodal training is precisely what pulls it away from the image. Contrary to our pre-specified hypothesis, rare pathologies were not preferentially degraded: across nine rare-versus-common comparisons, no difference survived multiple-comparison correction, and nominal differences ran in the opposite direction (common > rare), so contamination is invisible to condition-specific monitoring. The dominant determinant of degradation is the type of AI rewriting task, not the clinical content. These findings bear on multimodal medical AI dataset construction and the governance of AI-assisted clinical documentation.

</details>


### [32] [Improving low-resource ASR using bilingual fine-tuning with language identification: a cross-linguistic evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17820)
*Reihaneh Amooie,Yun Hao,Wietse de Vries,Jelske Dijkstra,Matt Coler,Martijn Wieling*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Bilingual fine-tuning for low-resource ASR is investigated across nine diverse language pairs. The method uses prepended language identification tokens during training, with joint language and transcription prediction at inference. Results show that bilingual fine-tuning helps when language ID accuracy is high; when it is low, providing the language token at inference improves ASR performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Low-resource languages suffer from limited training data for ASR. The authors aim to determine whether bilingual fine-tuning — training a single model on two languages simultaneously — can improve ASR performance for such languages, and under what conditions this approach is effective.

Method: Bilingual fine-tuning is applied to ASR models across nine linguistically and geographically diverse language pairs. During training, each input text is prepended with a language identification token to distinguish the two languages. At inference, the model jointly predicts both the language label and the transcription from speech input alone. A follow-up experiment provides the language ID token at both training and inference to assess the impact when language identification is unreliable.

Result: Bilingual fine-tuning yields ASR gains when language identification accuracy is high. When language identification performance is low, ASR quality degrades. Providing the language ID token at inference in these low-accuracy scenarios helps recover and improve ASR performance.

Conclusion: Bilingual fine-tuning is a viable strategy for low-resource ASR, but its success hinges on accurate language identification. In scenarios where the model struggles to identify the language, explicitly supplying the language ID token at inference serves as an effective remedy.

Abstract: This study explores how bilingual fine-tuning affects automatic speech recognition (ASR) in low-resource languages. We evaluate this method across nine linguistically and geographically diverse language pairs, covering a range of language families and writing systems. To distinguish the two languages, during training, we pre-pend each input text with a language identification token. At inference, the model jointly predicts both the language and transcription from the speech input alone. As texts for which the language is incorrectly determined show low ASR performance, we also conduct a follow-up experiment in which the language identification token is provided both during training and inference. Our results show that bilingual fine-tuning can be beneficial when language identification accuracy is high, and that in cases where language identification performance is low, including the language identification token at inference helps to improve ASR performance.

</details>


### [33] [When Multiple Scripts Matter: Evaluating ASR in Clinical Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17826)
*Jean Seo,Minkyu Kim,Jeonguk Lee,Jisoo Jung,Wooseok Han,Eunho Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MultiClin is a clinical ASR benchmark that addresses multiscript variability in non-English medical speech recognition by providing multiscript-aware evaluation, demonstrating that conventional metrics unfairly penalize valid orthographic variants, and showing that script-unified training yields optimal ASR performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard ASR evaluation uses string-matching metrics that treat valid orthographic variants of the same clinical term as errors, underestimating real-world performance in non-English clinical settings where multiscript variability is common.

Method: The authors introduce MultiClin, a benchmark dataset for clinical ASR with multiple valid orthographic references per utterance. They evaluate diverse ASR models using both conventional single-reference and multiscript-aware metrics, and systematically study the effect of script consistency ratios during training on model convergence, orthographic entropy, and final performance.

Result: Multiscript-aware evaluation yields fairer, higher performance estimates than single-reference scoring. Inconsistent script mappings during training increase orthographic uncertainty and impair convergence; a 50% mapping ratio produces maximal entropy. Script-unified training consistently achieves the best ASR performance.

Conclusion: Adopting multiscript-aware evaluation and maintaining script consistency during training are critical for reliable clinical ASR in multilingual, multiscript environments. The publicly released dataset and code aim to facilitate further research in this direction.

Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) in non-English clinical settings is challenged by multiscript variability, where the same term may appear in multiple valid orthographic forms. Conventional string-matching evaluation metrics often underestimate ASR performance by treating orthographic variants as errors. To address this issue, we introduce MultiClin, a clinical ASR benchmark designed to evaluate robustness to multiscript variability. Experiments across diverse ASR models show that multiscript-aware evaluation provides a fairer assessment of recognition quality than conventional single-reference evaluation. We further investigate the impact of script consistency during training and find that inconsistent script mappings increase orthographic uncertainty and hinder model convergence, with a balanced 50% mapping ratio producing the highest entropy. In contrast, script unification consistently yields the best ASR performance. Our dataset and code are publicly available at: https://github.com/aitrics-ronaldo/Interspeech_MultiClin.

</details>


### [34] [Perceptual compensation for tonal context in self-supervised speech models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17835)
*James Kirby,Ioana Krehan,Michele Gubian*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study investigates whether wav2vec2.0 models exhibit compensation for tonal coarticulation in Mandarin Chinese, finding that purely self-supervised pre-training yields no evidence of such phonological compensation, while probing classifiers on fine-tuned models show partial but incomplete compensation compared to human listeners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether self-supervised speech models like wav2vec2.0 spontaneously acquire phonological abstraction—specifically compensation for tonal context effects in Mandarin—without explicit supervised training, thereby testing claims that linguistic structure emerges from pre-training alone.

Method: A pseudo-replication of a human perceptual compensation experiment on Mandarin tone coarticulation. The authors compared two wav2vec2.0 variants—a purely self-supervised pre-trained model and one fine-tuned for Mandarin ASR—using (1) cosine similarity of embeddings across tonal contexts and (2) linear probing classifiers trained to categorize tones on isolated syllables, testing for human-like compensation patterns.

Result: No evidence of tonal compensation was found in embedding similarities of the purely pre-trained model. Probing classifiers showed some compensation effects and expected layer-wise improvements in tone categorization, but failed to replicate human performance on isolated test syllables. Compensation emerged only partially and only in the fine-tuned model.

Conclusion: Supervised fine-tuning objectives may be necessary to encourage abstraction of certain types of phonological regularities. Purely self-supervised pre-training appears insufficient for inducing human-like compensation for tonal coarticulation, challenging claims that linguistic structure robustly emerges without supervision.

Abstract: This study examines the extent to which the wav2vec2.0 architecture exhibits evidence of compensation for phonological context. We conducted a pseudo-replication of a perceptional compensation experiment on Mandarin Chinese tones, and compared the embedding similarities and probing classifier outputs between a purely self-supervised pre-trained model and a model fine-tuned for Mandarin ASR. No evidence of compensation was found in the embedding similarities of the purely pre-trained model. Probing classifiers showed some evidence of compensation in addition to the expected layer-wise improvements in categorization, but failed to replicate human performance on isolated test syllables. Our findings contrast with previous reports of sensitivity to phonological structure emerging through pre-training alone, and suggest that supervised objectives may be necessary to encourage the abstraction of at least some types of phonological regularities.

</details>


### [35] [Environment-Grounded Automated Prompt Optimization for LLM Game Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17838)
*Rean Clive Fernandes,Lukas Fehring,Theresa Eimer,Marius Lindauer,Matthias Feurer*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes an automated prompt optimization framework for LLM agents that uses a multi-agent architecture (goal-conditioned descriptor + action selector) refined through an evolutionary loop with a behavior analyzer and mutator, achieving up to 72.5% success on tasks where baseline RobustCoTAgent scores 0%, all without model fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents in interactive environments are highly sensitive to prompt design, yet prompt engineering remains a manual, task-specific, and labor-intensive process. There is a need for automated methods to optimize prompts without requiring model weight updates or extensive human supervision.

Method: The framework decomposes the observation-to-action pipeline into two specialized agents: a goal-conditioned descriptor agent and an action selection agent. Prompts for both are iteratively refined through an LLM-driven evolutionary loop. A behavior analyzer attributes episode outcomes (success/failure) to specific prompt components, and a mutator proposes targeted prompt revisions, which are then validated through environment rollouts. The approach is evaluated on all five BabyAI tasks in the BALROG benchmark against the RobustCoTAgent baseline.

Result: The optimization pipeline consistently improves performance across all five BabyAI tasks under both plain and guided prompt initializations. Most notably, on the PutNext task—a multi-step coordination task where RobustCoTAgent achieves 0% success—the optimized framework reaches up to 72.5% success rate using the same underlying LLM.

Conclusion: A multi-agent architecture combined with automatic prompt optimization can significantly enhance LLM agent performance in interactive environments without requiring fine-tuning or extensive human supervision, suggesting this is a viable and scalable alternative to manual prompt engineering.

Abstract: LLM agents in interactive environments are highly sensitive to their prompts, yet prompt engineering remains a manual, task-specific process. We introduce an automated prompt optimization framework for LLM agents that decomposes the observation-to-action pipeline into a goal-conditioned descriptor agent and an action selection agent, and iteratively refines each module's prompt through an LLM-driven evolutionary loop guided by environment returns. We propose a behavior analyzer to attribute episode outcomes to specific prompt components, and a mutator to propose targeted revisions to the prompt, before validating them through environment rollouts. We evaluate on all five BabyAI tasks in the BALROG benchmark, comparing our pipeline against BALROG's RobustCoTAgent under both plain and guided prompt initializations. Optimization improves performance consistently across tasks and conditions, without requiring updates to the model weights. On PutNext, a multi-step coordination task where the RobustCoTAgent achieves 0% success, our framework reaches up to 72.5% success rate using the same underlying LLM with optimized prompts. These results suggest that a multi-agent framework, combined with automatic prompt optimization, enhances LLMs without the need for fine-tuning or extensive human supervision.

</details>


### [36] [GameCraft-Bench: Can Agents Build Playable Games End-to-End in a Real Game Engine?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17861)
*Tongxu Luo,Rongsheng Wang,Jiaxi Bi,Chenming Xu,Zhengyang Tang,Jianlong Chen,Juhao Liang,Ke Ji,Shuqi Guo,Yuhao Du,Fan Bu,Wenyu Du,Xiaotong Zhang,Kyle Li,Shaobo Wang,Linfeng Zhang,Yuxuan Liu,Xin Lai,Chenxin Li,Yiduo Guo,Zhexin Zhang,Xinyuan Wang,Tianyi Bai,Ziniu Li,Benyou Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GameCraft-Bench formalizes end-to-end game generation as producing complete, playable game artifacts from natural-language specs within the Godot engine. It introduces an interaction-grounded evaluation framework with three desiderata: Engine Grounding, Artifact Completeness, and Interactive Verification. The benchmark comprises 140 tasks across 15 game families. Frontier coding agents score below 42%, revealing that while mechanics are often recognizable, agents fail at content sufficiency, visual feedback, and coherent presentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing coding benchmarks focus on isolated scripts rather than end-to-end game production within a game engine, where scripts, scenes, assets, rendering, and runtime interactions must cohere. There is no standardized framework for evaluating whether an agent can produce a complete, playable game artifact from a specification.

Method: The authors formalize end-to-end game generation and propose three evaluation desiderata: (1) Engine Grounding — the agent must operate within the constraints of a real game engine (Godot); (2) Artifact Completeness — the output must be a full, runnable game project; (3) Interactive Verification — evaluation must assess observable player-game interaction, not just static code. They instantiate this via GameCraft-Bench (140 Godot tasks, 15 game families) using replayed gameplay demonstrations and rubric-guided multimodal judging.

Result: The strongest frontier coding agent achieves only 41.46% on the benchmark; most agents score below 40%. Agents can often implement recognizable game mechanics but struggle with delivering sufficient content, functional visual feedback, and coherent overall presentation.

Conclusion: End-to-end game generation remains a highly challenging open problem for current coding agents. The bottleneck is not in isolated mechanic implementation but in producing complete, visually coherent, content-rich playable games. The proposed interaction-grounded evaluation framework provides a rigorous foundation for future progress.

Abstract: Game generation is an emerging application of coding agents, requiring models to transform natural-language specifications into playable interactive systems. Unlike traditional coding tasks, game generation takes place within a game engine, where scripts, scenes, assets, rendering, and runtime interactions must jointly produce coherent gameplay. We formalize end-to-end game generation as the problem of producing a complete game artifact that realizes a specification through observable player-game interaction in a target environment. We argue that evaluating this setting requires three desiderata: Engine Grounding, Artifact Completeness, and Interactive Verification. We propose an interaction-grounded evaluation framework that assesses executable gameplay through replayed demonstrations and rubric-guided multimodal judging. We instantiate this framework as GameCraft-Bench, a benchmark comprising 140 Godot tasks across 15 game families. Evaluations of frontier coding agents show that end-to-end game generation remains highly challenging: the strongest agent achieves only 41.46%, and most agents score below 40%. Further analysis reveals that while agents often implement recognizable mechanics, they struggle to deliver complete games with sufficient content, functional visual feedback, and coherent presentation. See https://tongxuluo.github.io/gamecraft-bench-website for demos, code, and data.

</details>


### [37] [Dynamic Rollout Editing for Reducing Overthinking in RL-Trained Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17890)
*Zihao Wei,Wenjie Shi,Liang Pang,Jingcheng Deng,Shicheng Xu,Shasha Guo,Zenghao Duan,Jiahao Liu,Jingang Wang,Huawei Shen,Xueqi Cheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GRPO-style RL training for LLMs can amplify "overthinking" — unnecessary reasoning after answers are found — due to sequence-level credit assignment. The authors propose Dynamic Rollout Editing (DRE), which edits post-answer reasoning in successful trajectories during training to suppress this feedback loop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In GRPO-based RL post-training, sequence-level credit assignment cannot distinguish the useful reasoning prefix that reaches a correct answer from the superfluous continuation (overthinking). An initial slight imbalance where successful trajectories overthink more than unsuccessful ones can spiral into severe overthinking during training, degrading efficiency without improving accuracy.

Method: Dynamic Rollout Editing (DRE) identifies when a correct answer first emerges within a successful trajectory, preserves the verified prefix (solution-reaching reasoning), truncates or edits the remaining overthinking portion, and places the edited trajectory in the same RL group to weaken the preference signal for unnecessary continuation — all without penalizing the productive reasoning needed to reach the answer.

Result: DRE effectively mitigates overthinking during GRPO training. Experiments across diverse tasks demonstrate that DRE reduces unnecessary reasoning while maintaining or improving task performance.

Conclusion: Overthinking is a training-time credit-assignment problem in GRPO-style RL, not merely a decoding issue. DRE provides a principled intervention that breaks the overthinking feedback loop by editing successful rollouts during training, yielding more concise reasoning without sacrificing accuracy.

Abstract: Long-form chain-of-thought reasoning can improve LLM performance on complex tasks, but models often continue generating unnecessary reasoning after a correct answer has emerged. We refer to this behavior as overthinking. We study this phenomenon from the perspective of GRPO-style reinforcement learning (RL) post-training, framing it as a training-time credit-assignment problem rather than merely a decoding-time stopping problem. In rollouts sampled at the onset of GRPO training, we observe that successful trajectories can exhibit a slightly higher degree of overthinking than unsuccessful trajectories for the same prompts. This early imbalance provides a starting point for an undesirable feedback loop: because GRPO assigns sequence-level credit, it cannot distinguish the solution-reaching prefix from the unnecessary continuation that lengthens a successful trajectory. Both receive positive update signal, allowing the initial imbalance to grow into more severe overthinking during training. To address this issue, we introduce Dynamic Rollout Editing (DRE), a training-time intervention for successful trajectories that continue thinking after answer emergence. DRE preserves the accepted verified prefix, edits the remaining thinking, and prefers the edited trajectory within the same RL group, weakening the preference signal for unnecessary thinking without penalizing the reasoning needed to reach the answer. Experiments across diverse tasks show the effectiveness of DRE.

</details>


### [38] [ChLogic: Evaluating Robustness of Logical Reasoning in Chinese Expressions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17905)
*Peixian Zhou,Yuxu Chen,Chaorui Zhang,Wei Han,Bo Bai,Xueyan Niu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ChLogic is a bilingual logical reasoning benchmark revealing that LLMs exhibit a persistent English-Chinese performance gap when identical logical structures are expressed in different surface forms. Back-translation effects are mixed, highlighting the interplay of surface realization, translation artifacts, and model-specific behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs excel at English logical reasoning benchmarks, it is unclear whether this ability generalizes across languages, particularly when the same latent logical structure is expressed in Chinese with diverse surface realizations. No existing benchmark systematically tests this cross-lingual logical robustness.

Method: The authors construct ChLogic, an English-Chinese aligned benchmark derived from formal logical templates with three subsets: (1) General aligned set (60 General Propositions, 9 template families), (2) Difficult aligned set (40 Difficult Problems), and (3) Chinese-only set (15 language-specific phenomenon types). Each aligned item pairs one English reference with five Chinese realizations. Experiments are conducted on Qwen3, Ministral, and GLM models, including back-translation from standard Chinese to English to isolate surface-form vs. latent-logic effects.

Result: All tested models show a persistent English-Chinese performance gap across both General and Difficult aligned sets. Back-translation into English often improves performance on the General aligned set, but produces mixed results on the Difficult aligned set — Qwen3-32B and GLM-5.1 perform worse after translation, suggesting that translation artifacts and model-specific behaviors jointly influence reasoning.

Conclusion: Chinese surface realization, translation artifacts, and model-specific characteristics all contribute to performance degradation in multilingual logical reasoning. ChLogic serves as an effective stress test for evaluating cross-lingual reasoning robustness in LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models perform increasingly well on standardized logical reasoning benchmarks, but whether this ability remains robust beyond English is unclear. We introduce ChLogic, an English--Chinese aligned benchmark that tests whether models preserve logical reasoning performance when the same latent logical structure is expressed in English and diverse Chinese surface realizations. Built from formal logical templates, the benchmark contains three data sets: (i) the General aligned set, derived from 60 General Propositions across nine template families; (ii) the Difficult aligned set, derived from 40 Difficult Problems; and (iii) the Chinese-only set, covering 15 language-specific phenomenon types. Each aligned item pairs one English reference expression with five Chinese realizations. Experiments on Qwen3, Ministral, and GLM models reveal a persistent English--Chinese performance gap. Back-translation from standard Chinese into English often improves performance on the General aligned set, but produces mixed effects on the Difficult aligned set, where Qwen3-32B and GLM-5.1 perform worse after translation. These results indicate that Chinese surface realization, translation artifacts, and model-specific behavior jointly affect multilingual logical reasoning. Overall, ChLogic provides a useful stress test for the robustness of multilingual reasoning.

</details>


### [39] [Learning task-specific subspaces via interventional post-training of speech foundation models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17967)
*Jack Cox,Jon Barker*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a post-training refinement method using interventional contrastive learning to disentangle speech foundation model representations into separate content and speaker subspaces, improving out-of-domain speaker verification and keyword spotting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speech foundation models encode salient speech variables (e.g., content, speaker identity) in a distributed, entangled manner, whereas downstream tasks typically require only a subset of this variability. Disentangling these representations would enable more effective use for specific tasks.

Method: A post-training refinement approach using interventional contrastive learning with an interventional dataset and a multi-part contrastive loss. This learns a transformation mapping from the entangled representation space of pre-trained speech foundation models into separate content and speaker subspaces.

Result: The method yields improved out-of-domain speaker verification performance and provides evidence that speaker and content information are effectively separated across the learned subspaces. Gains are also observed on keyword spotting tasks.

Conclusion: Interventional contrastive learning applied as a post-training step successfully disentangles speech representations, enabling better task-specific performance without retraining the foundation model.

Abstract: Speech foundation models, pre-trained on large corpora of unlabelled speech data, produce general-purpose representations which are useful across tasks. However, these representations encode information about salient speech variables in a distributed manner, while downstream speech tasks rely on only some of this variability. In this work, we propose a post-training refinement approach using interventional contrastive learning. By leveraging an interventional dataset and multi-part contrastive loss, we learn a transformation from the entangled representation space of speech foundation models into separate content and speaker subspaces. We evaluate the learnt representations on speaker verification and keyword spotting tasks, showing improved out-of-domain speaker verification performance and evidence that speaker and content information are separated across the learned subspaces.

</details>


### [40] [Fine-tuning LLMs for Passive Depression Severity Estimation from AI Mental Health Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17973)
*Olivier Tieleman,Ziyi Zhu,Ting Su,Samuel J. Bell,Thomas D. Hull,Caitlin A. Stamatis*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A fine-tuned Qwen3.5-27B model predicts PHQ-9 depression scores directly from AI mental health app conversation transcripts, achieving strong performance (MAE=2.6, r=0.80, AUC=0.91) using pseudolabel augmentation with Claude Opus, enabling passive symptom monitoring without self-report questionnaires.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world PHQ-9 completion rates are low, introducing response bias and systematic missingness in depression monitoring. A passive approach inferring depression severity from routinely generated conversational data could bridge this gap, enabling continuous, unbiased symptom tracking without burdening users.

Method: A Qwen3.5-27B backbone is fine-tuned with a regression head to predict PHQ-9 total scores from conversation transcripts. The training data combines 3,111 ground-truth labels with pseudolabels generated by Claude Opus (a reasoning model) and iteratively trained intermediate models, yielding a dataset of 6,283 users. Evaluation uses MAE, RMSE, Pearson r, and AUC at the PHQ-9 ≥ 10 clinical threshold on an 842-user held-out test set.

Result: The best model achieves MAE=2.6, RMSE=4.0, Pearson r=0.80, and AUC=0.91 at PHQ-9 ≥ 10. AUC exceeds 0.87 across all severity thresholds from PHQ-9 ≥ 3 to ≥ 24, indicating robust performance across the full clinical spectrum.

Conclusion: Passive depression severity inference from conversational text is feasible and clinically viable, opening the door to continuous, unobtrusive symptom monitoring in AI mental health platforms without requiring users to complete self-report measures.

Abstract: Depression is the leading cause of disability worldwide, and early detection of symptom change is essential for timely intervention. Validated instruments such as the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) support symptom monitoring at scale, but real-world completion rates are low, introducing response bias and systematic missingness. Passive approaches that infer severity from routinely generated data could close this gap. We address this by predicting PHQ-9 total scores directly from transcripts of conversations between users and an AI mental health application, requiring only conversation text and no additional clinical data. We fine-tune a Qwen3.5-27B backbone with a regression head, augment 3,111 ground-truth labels with pseudolabels generated by a reasoning model (Claude Opus) and iteratively trained intermediate models, for a combined dataset of 6,283 users. On a held-out test set of 842 users, our best model achieves MAE = 2.6, RMSE = 4.0, Pearson r = 0.80, and AUC = 0.91 at the PHQ-9 >= 10 clinical threshold. We also find AUC > 0.87 at every severity threshold from PHQ-9 >= 3 to PHQ-9 >= 24, demonstrating that the model captures depression severity across the full clinical spectrum. This work opens the door to passive, continuous symptom monitoring in AI mental health platforms, without requiring users to complete self-report measures.

</details>


### [41] [VoidPadding: Let [VOID] Handle Padding in Masked Diffusion Language Models so that [EOS] Can Focus on Semantic Termination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17999)
*Chunyu Liu,Zhengyang Fan,Kaisen Yang,Alex Lamb*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: VoidPadding decouples the dual role of [EOS] as both terminator and padding token in masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) by introducing a dedicated [VOID] token for padding, improving reasoning benchmarks by +17.84 points and reducing decoding cost by 55.7% on Dream-7B-Instruct.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In MDLMs that generate via iterative denoising of a masked canvas, [EOS] tokens serve dual roles: semantic termination signal and padding filler. Under large-block decoding, this causes [EOS] overflow—excessive early termination—degrading output quality. The authors aim to disentangle these two functions.

Method: VoidPadding introduces a new [VOID] token exclusively for padding the preallocated response canvas during instruction tuning, while [EOS] is reserved solely as a semantic terminator. During inference, the learned [EOS] signal triggers early stopping, and the learned [VOID] signal drives adaptive expansion of the response canvas.

Result: On Dream-7B-Instruct, VoidPadding improves block-size-averaged four-task mean across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks by +17.84 points over the original model and +6.95 points over RainbowPadding, while reducing decoding NFE (number of function evaluations) by 55.7% on average.

Conclusion: Decoupling the termination and padding roles via dedicated tokens substantially improves both generation quality and inference efficiency in MDLMs. The approach enables reliable early stopping and adaptive canvas expansion, offering a simple yet effective fix for a fundamental design flaw in current MDLM instruction tuning pipelines.

Abstract: MDLMs generate text by denoising a preallocated masked response canvas, making response-length modeling central to instruction tuning. Existing MDLMs often inherit the autoregressive convention of using repeated \texttt{[EOS]} tokens for padding during instruction tuning, giving \texttt{[EOS]} a dual role as both a semantic terminator and a padding token. We show that this dual role is a root cause of \texttt{[EOS]} overflow under large-block decoding. To decouple these roles, we propose VoidPadding, which introduces \texttt{[VOID]} for padding and reserves \texttt{[EOS]} for termination. During inference, the learned \texttt{[EOS]} signal enables early stopping, while the learned \texttt{[VOID]} signal guides adaptive response canvas expansion. On Dream-7B-Instruct, VoidPadding improves the block-size-averaged four-task mean across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks by \(+17.84\) points over the original model and \(+6.95\) points over RainbowPadding, while reducing decoding NFE by 55.7\% on average. Code is available at https://github.com/Haru-LCY/VoidPadding.

</details>


### [42] [When English Isn't the Best Teacher: Source Language Effects in Cross-Lingual In-Context Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18033)
*Fred Philippy,Siwen Guo,Jacques Klein,Tegawendé F. Bissyandé*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper empirically investigates whether insights from supervised fine-tuning for cross-lingual transfer hold in In-Context Learning (ICL), finding they do not, and proposes alternative heuristics for selecting source languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The shift from supervised fine-tuning to few-shot ICL in multilingual NLP has occurred without rigorous evaluation of whether established cross-lingual transfer principles (e.g., data availability, linguistic similarity) remain valid. The authors aim to fill this gap and determine how to effectively choose source languages for cross-lingual ICL.

Method: A broad empirical study spanning seven tasks, six models, and a typologically diverse set of languages. The authors also analyze "language confusion" — a key obstacle in generative cross-lingual ICL where models mix or misattribute languages during generation.

Result: Conventional fine-tuning-based expectations do not consistently apply in the ICL regime. Language confusion emerges as a significant barrier for generative tasks in cross-lingual ICL.

Conclusion: Alternative heuristics beyond linguistic similarity and data availability are needed for selecting source languages in cross-lingual ICL. Fine-tuning insights do not directly transfer to the ICL paradigm.

Abstract: Cross-lingual transfer in multilingual NLP has been widely explored in supervised fine-tuning contexts, where factors like data availability and linguistic similarity largely determine transfer quality. As the field shifts toward few-shot In-Context Learning (ICL), it is often presumed that insights from fine-tuning carry over unchanged. Yet this assumption has not been rigorously evaluated, leaving open the question of how to choose source languages for cross-lingual ICL. We conduct a broad empirical study of cross-lingual transfer in ICL spanning seven tasks, six models, and a typologically diverse set of languages. We further analyze language confusion, a key obstacle for generative tasks in cross-lingual ICL. Our results show that conventional fine-tuning-based expectations do not consistently apply in the ICL regime and point to alternative heuristics for selecting source languages effectively.

</details>


### [43] [Compositional Skill Routing for LLM Agents: Decompose, Retrieve, and Compose](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18051)
*Xueping Gao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SkillWeaver introduces a decompose-retrieve-compose framework for compositional skill routing, where complex queries are broken into sub-tasks, matched to skills via a bi-encoder retriever, and assembled into executable DAG plans. A novel Iterative Skill-Aware Decomposition (SAD) feedback loop significantly boosts decomposition accuracy. The accompanying CompSkillBench benchmark contains 300 queries over 2,209 MCP skills across 24 categories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world LLM agent tasks require composing multiple external skills rather than selecting a single one. Existing approaches lack a systematic framework for decomposing complex queries, retrieving relevant skills for each sub-task, and composing them into coherent executable plans — a gap the authors formalize as the Compositional Skill Routing problem.

Method: SkillWeaver is a three-stage framework: (1) an LLM-based task decomposer that breaks queries into atomic sub-tasks; (2) a bi-encoder skill retriever with FAISS indexing for efficient skill lookup; and (3) a dependency-aware DAG planner that assembles sub-task skills into an executable plan. The key innovation is Iterative Skill-Aware Decomposition (SAD), a retrieval-augmented feedback loop that iteratively refines decomposition by aligning sub-tasks with actually available skills. Evaluation uses CompSkillBench, a benchmark of 300 compositional queries over 2,209 real MCP server skills spanning 24 functional categories.

Result: Standard LLM decomposition achieves only 34.2% category recall at the step level, identifying decomposition quality as the critical bottleneck. SAD improves decomposition accuracy from 51.0% to 67.7% (+32.7%, Wilcoxon p < 10^-6) in a single iteration. DA-conditioned analysis shows correct granularity (DA=1) lifts CatR@1 from 34% to 41%. SkillWeaver reduces context window consumption by over 99%. Transfer experiments demonstrate +35.6% relative DA gain even when target categories are absent from the retrieval pool.

Conclusion: Task decomposition quality is the primary bottleneck in compositional skill routing. The SAD feedback mechanism effectively addresses this by aligning decomposition with the skill library. SkillWeaver dramatically reduces context overhead while generalizing to unseen skill categories, demonstrating practical viability for real-world LLM agent systems.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external skills -- reusable tool specifications -- but real-world tasks often require composing multiple skills, not just selecting one. We formalize this as the Compositional Skill Routing problem: given a complex user query and a large skill library, decompose the query into atomic sub-tasks, retrieve the appropriate skill for each sub-task, and compose an executable plan. We present SkillWeaver, a decompose-retrieve-compose framework combining an LLM task decomposer, a bi-encoder skill retriever with FAISS indexing, and a dependency-aware DAG planner. To support evaluation, we introduce CompSkillBench, a benchmark of 300 compositional queries over 2,209 real MCP server skills spanning 24 functional categories, sourced from the public MCP ecosystem. Our experiments reveal that task decomposition quality is the primary bottleneck: standard LLM decomposition reaches only 34.2% category recall at the step level. To address this, we propose Iterative Skill-Aware Decomposition (SAD), a retrieval-augmented feedback loop that iteratively aligns decomposition with available skills. SAD improves decomposition accuracy from 51.0% to 67.7% (+32.7%, Wilcoxon p < 10^-6) in a single iteration; DA-conditioned analysis confirms that correct granularity is the prerequisite for effective retrieval (CatR@1 rises from 34% to 41% when DA=1). SkillWeaver reduces context window consumption by over 99%, and transfer experiments confirm generalization (+35.6% relative DA gain even when target categories are absent from the retrieval pool).

</details>


### [44] [ConSA: Controllable Sparsity in Hybrid Attention via Learnable Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18056)
*Yao Chen,Yinqi Yang,Junyuan Shang,Xiangzhao Hao,Simeng Zhang,Yilong Chen,Tingwen Liu,Shuohuan Wang,Dianhai Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ConSA learns optimal allocation of full attention (FA) vs. sliding-window attention (SWA) in hybrid LLM architectures using L0 regularization with augmented Lagrangian constraints, outperforming hand-crafted baselines and revealing that SWA concentrates in bottom layers while FA clusters in contiguous middle-layer blocks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hybrid FA/SWA architectures rely on hand-crafted rules or post-hoc heuristics for allocating attention types, with limited understanding of the underlying attention behaviors that should drive these design choices.

Method: ConSA uses L0 regularization to learn binary masks that select FA or SWA per attention unit, combined with an augmented Lagrangian constraint to enforce a user-specified sparsity target at either layer-wise or KV-head-wise granularity.

Result: Learned allocations consistently beat rule-based baselines on 0.6B and 1.7B LLMs; KV-head-wise allocation outperforms layer-wise; SWA concentrates in bottom layers with FA forming contiguous blocks in middle layers rather than interleaved patterns, and this structure persists across scales, sparsity levels, and granularities.

Conclusion: The learned allocation patterns reveal a fine-grained spectrum of intrinsic attention behaviors that diverges from standard interleaved designs, suggesting that principled, sparsity-controllable FA/SWA assignment can improve inference efficiency in LLMs.

Abstract: Hybrid architectures combining full attention (FA) and sliding-window attention (SWA) are a promising paradigm for efficient LLM inference. However, existing methods typically rely on hand-crafted rules or simple post-hoc heuristics for FA/SWA allocation and offer limited analysis of the attention behaviors underlying these designs. We propose Controllable Sparsity in Hybrid Attention (ConSA), a framework that learns optimal FA/SWA assignment under a user-specified sparsity target. ConSA employs L0 regularization to learn binary masks selecting between FA and SWA for each attention unit, while an augmented Lagrangian constraint enforces the target sparsity at either layer or KV-head granularity. We evaluate ConSA on two LLMs at the 0.6B and 1.7B scales. Learned allocations consistently outperform rule-based baselines, with KV-head-wise allocation yielding clear gains over layer-wise allocation. The learned patterns place SWA in the bottom layers and concentrate FA into contiguous middle-layer blocks, diverging from evenly interleaved patterns in rule-based methods. This structure persists across model scales, sparsity levels, and allocation granularities, revealing a fine-grained spectrum of intrinsic attention behaviors that underlies the learned allocation.

</details>


### [45] [Unintended Effects of Geographic Conditioning in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18124)
*Naz Col,David M. Chan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Even with neutral prompts, LLMs exposed to user location metadata systematically leak region-specific geographic references, increasing up to 793× over baseline. The mere presence of a location field—even with "Unknown"—triggers leakage, revealing a structural conditioning effect independent of actual geographic content.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern conversational AI systems routinely use user metadata (e.g., location) to personalize responses, but the unintended regional biases this introduces are poorly understood. The authors aim to quantify and characterize "location leakage"—the phenomenon where models generate geographic references even when prompts are geographically neutral.

Method: The authors design experiments across two task types: creative writing and open-ended Q&A. They systematically vary user location metadata (including real locations and the placeholder "Unknown") and measure the frequency of region-specific geographic references in model outputs against a no-metadata baseline. Multiple state-of-the-art LLMs are tested, including Llama 3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Claude Sonnet 4.6.

Result: Location leakage spikes dramatically: Llama 3.1-8B jumps from 0.04% (baseline) to 31.7% with location metadata (793× increase); Qwen3-8B reaches 21.3% and Claude Sonnet 4.6 reaches 8.8%. Critically, even replacing the location with "Unknown" still elevates leakage up to 72× above baseline, demonstrating that the structural presence of the user profile frame alone acts as a conditioning signal.

Conclusion: Location metadata introduces substantial unintended regional bias in LLM outputs, even with neutral prompts. The discovery of structural conditioning—where the mere frame of a user profile triggers geographic leakage—reveals a deeper, previously unrecognized mechanism of bias that persists independent of actual location content.

Abstract: Modern conversational AI systems frequently rely on user metadata to localize responses, yet the unintended regional biases introduced by this hidden context remain poorly understood. In this work, we evaluate location leakage: the phenomenon where a model generates geographic references despite receiving a geographically neutral user prompt. Across both creative writing and open-ended Q&A prompts, even state-of-the-art LLMs systematically favor region-specific outputs when exposed to location metadata, with leakage spiking by up to 793 times above baseline (e.g., from 0.04% to 31.7% for Llama 3.1-8B, and 21.3% and 8.8% for Qwen3-8B and Claude Sonnet 4.6, respectively). Our analysis further shows a novel structural conditioning effect: replacing the injected location with the placeholder "Unknown" still elevates leakage by up to 72 times above baseline, demonstrating that the user profile frame itself, independent of any geographic content, acts as a generative conditioning signal.

</details>


### [46] [Learning from the Self-future: On-policy Self-distillation for dLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18195)
*Yifu Luo,Zeyu Chen,Haoyu Wang,Xinhao Hu,Yuxuan Zhang,Zhizhou Sha,Shiwei Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: d-OPSD adapts on-policy self-distillation to diffusion LLMs by replacing autoregressive prefix conditioning with suffix-based "self future-experience" conditioning and shifting from token-level to step-level supervision, achieving strong reasoning performance with ~10% of RLVR's optimization steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) methods are designed exclusively for autoregressive LLMs, relying on left-to-right prefix conditioning and token-level KL divergence. These design choices are fundamentally incompatible with diffusion LLMs (dLLMs), which generate tokens in arbitrary order through iterative denoising. The lack of an OPSD framework for dLLMs motivates this work.

Method: d-OPSD introduces two key innovations: (1) Self-teacher construction using self-generated answers as suffix conditioning rather than prefix conditioning, allowing the student to learn from its own future outputs; (2) Step-level supervision that aligns the distillation loss with the iterative denoising steps of dLLMs, replacing token-level divergence. The method is evaluated against RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards) and SFT baselines across four reasoning benchmarks.

Result: d-OPSD consistently outperforms both RLVR and SFT baselines across four reasoning benchmarks. Notably, it demonstrates superior sample efficiency, requiring only approximately 10% of the optimization steps needed by RLVR to achieve better performance.

Conclusion: d-OPSD is the first OPSD framework successfully adapted to diffusion LLMs, overcoming fundamental architectural conflicts. It establishes a promising and sample-efficient pathway for post-training dLLMs.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models (LLMs), yet its application to diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) remains unexplored. Existing OPSD methods are inherently autoregressive-centric. They inject privileged information via left-to-right prefix conditioning with token-level divergence supervision, a design that fundamentally conflicts with the arbitraryorder generation of dLLMs. We introduce d-OPSD, the first OPSD framework tailored for dLLMs. Our approach makes two core contributions. First, we reframe self-teacher construction by using self-generated answers as suffix conditioning, enabling the student model to learn from "self future-experience" rather than privileged prefixes. Second, we shift supervision from token-level to step-level, aligning training with the iterative denoising process of dLLMs. Experiments across four reasoning benchmarks show that d-OPSD consistently outperforms RLVR and SFT baselines with superior sample efficiency, requiring only around 10% of the optimization steps by RLVR and opening a promising pathway for dLLM posttraining. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/d-OPSD.

</details>


### [47] [RubricsTree: Scalable and Evolving Open-Ended Evaluation of Personal Health Agents across Health Memory and Medical Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18203)
*Weizhi Zhang,Zechen Li,Hamid Palangi,Ben Graef,A. Ali Heydari,Simon A. Lee,Salman Rahman,Ray Luo,Zeinab Esmaeilpour,Erik Schenck,Chloe Zhang,Yamin Li,Menglian Zhou,Philip S. Yu,Daniel McDuff,Lindsey Sunden,Mark Malhotra,Shwetak Patel,Ahmed A. Metwally*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RubricsTree introduces a scalable evaluation framework for LLM-based personal health agents, using a hierarchical taxonomy of 100+ clinically-verifiable Boolean rubrics curated by medical experts. It employs an adaptive router to activate relevant rubrics per query, achieving expert-aligned, auditable evaluation at scale, and demonstrates significant gains in model performance when used for optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-powered personal health agents face a critical evaluation bottleneck: physician annotation is reliable but prohibitively expensive and unscalable, while LLM-as-a-judge approaches are scalable but suffer from subjectivity, inconsistency, and clinical misalignment. A solution combining the reliability of expert evaluation with the scalability of automated methods is needed for clinical deployment.

Method: RubricsTree features (1) a hierarchical taxonomy of 100+ atomic, Boolean, clinically-verifiable rubrics developed through iterative human-in-the-loop curation with an expert physician panel, informed by 4,000 real user queries; and (2) a context-aware adaptive router that selectively activates only the relevant auto-weighted rubric subset for each query, enabling high-throughput evaluation. The framework was also tested as structured instructions, text feedback, and training rewards for downstream model optimization.

Result: RubricsTree substantially outperforms a strong large-scale evaluation baseline in expert alignment on open-ended queries, reliably penalizes contextually degraded responses, and yields up to ~66% relative gains on HealthBench when used for performance optimization across Gemini, GPT, and Qwen model families.

Conclusion: RubricsTree provides a scalable, auditable, and evolving evaluation infrastructure suitable for continuous optimization of product-level personal healthcare AI, bridging the gap between expert reliability and automated scalability.

Abstract: The LLM-empowered personal health agents with user health (sensor) metrics have offered a promising pathway to alleviate global disparities in healthcare access. However, large-scale clinical deployment remains constrained by an open-ended evaluation bottleneck: physician annotation is reliable but costly and unscalable, while LLM-as-a-judge evaluators are scalable but subjective, inconsistent, and sometimes clinically misaligned. We introduce RubricsTree, a scalable evaluation framework with an expert-aligned hierarchical taxonomy of over 100 atomic, clinically-verifiable Boolean rubrics, evolving from the insights of 4,000 real user queries through an iterative human-in-the-loop curation protocol with an expertise panel led by an experienced physician. A context-aware adaptive router activates only the relevant auto-weighted rubric subset per query, providing the throughput needed for scalable evaluation with expert-aligned quality. Through a systematic meta-evaluation, we show that RubricsTree (i) substantially exceeds a strong large-scale evaluation baseline in expert alignment on challenging open-ended queries; (ii) reliably penalizes contextually degraded responses; and (iii) when used as structured instructions, text feedback, or training rewards for performance optimization, yields up to ~66% relative gains on HealthBench for Gemini, GPT, and Qwen model families. RubricsTree thus provides a scalable, auditable, and evolving evaluation infrastructure required for the continuous optimization of product-level personal healthcare AI.

</details>


### [48] [Analyzing and Encoding the Al-Mawrid Arabic-English Dictionary with the ISO Language Markup Framework and TEI Lex-0](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18205)
*Diaa Fayed,Laurent Romary*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents a systematic methodology for retro-digitizing the Al-Mawrid Arabic-English dictionary into a standardized computational lexicon using ISO LMF and TEI Lex-0 standards, achieving 91% parsing accuracy and demonstrating high precision/recall for lexical feature extraction, while critically examining TEI Lex-0 limitations for Arabic-specific phenomena and exploring LLOD integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a significant gap in Arabic lexical infrastructure, particularly the lack of machine-tractable, standardized computational lexicons derived from legacy print dictionaries. Existing Arabic lexical resources are limited, and 20th-century bilingual dictionaries like Al-Mawrid suffer from structural ambiguities and punctuation inconsistencies that impede computational use.

Method: The methodology employs a dual-standard framework aligning ISO Lexical Markup Framework (LMF) with TEI Lex-0 guidelines. An editorial view is applied to the dictionary's macro- and microstructure to resolve structural ambiguities. The approach is empirically grounded in lexical knowledge density analysis using a representative sample (the letter Ayn, 4.6% of total volume). Information extraction rules are quantitatively evaluated for synonyms and morpho-semantic features. A scalable prefix-based referencing system is established for potential LLOD integration.

Result: Structural parsing accuracy reached 91%. Information extraction achieved 85% precision and 98% recall for synonyms, and 88% precision for other morpho-semantic features. The methodology produced an interoperable, machine-tractable lexical resource with a reproducible retro-digitization workflow.

Conclusion: The dual-standard LMF/TEI Lex-0 approach effectively transforms legacy bilingual dictionaries into standardized computational lexicons. However, TEI Lex-0 exhibits limitations in modeling Arabic-specific phenomena such as implicit open-set semantic relations and scattered morphological cues. The prefix-based referencing system enables future LLOD integration, making the resource suitable for Arabic NLP and Digital Humanities applications.

Abstract: This paper presents a robust methodology for the systematic digitization and encoding of the Al-Mawrid Arabic-English dictionary, transforming it from a legacy print resource into a standardized computational lexicon. Addressing a significant gap in Arabic lexical infrastructure, the study adopts a dual-standard framing that aligns the ISO Lexical Markup Framework (LMF) with the Text Encoding Initiative TEI Lex-0 guidelines. By applying an editorial view to the dictionary's macro- and microstructure, the research resolves the structural ambiguities and punctuation inconsistencies typical of 20th-century bilingual dictionaries.
