The methodology is grounded in an empirical analysis of the dictionary's lexical knowledge density. Drawing on a representative sample (the letter Ayn, comprising 4.6% of the total volume), the study provides scientific weight to the encoding process, demonstrating a structural parsing accuracy of 91%. Quantitative evaluation of the information extraction rules reveals high performance, with 85% precision and 98% recall for synonyms, and 88% precision for other morpho-semantic features. Beyond technical description, the paper provides a critical comparison with existing Arabic lexical resources and discusses the limitations of TEI Lex-0 when modelling specific Arabic phenomena, such as implicit "open set" semantic relations and scattered morphological cues. Furthermore, the study explores the potential for Linguistic Linked Open Data (LLOD) integration by establishing a scalable prefix-based referencing system that facilitates the resource's inclusion in the semantic web. The result is an interoperable, machine-tractable resource that provides a reproducible workflow for the retro-digitization of complex legacy bilingual lexicons within the Arabic NLP and Digital Humanities communities.

</details>


### [49] [Zone of Proximal Policy Optimization: Teacher in Prompts, Not Gradients](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18216)
*Byung-Kwan Lee,Ximing Lu,Shizhe Diao,Minki Kang,Saurav Muralidharan,Karan Sapra,Andrew Tao,Pavlo Molchanov,Yejin Choi,Yu-Chiang Frank Wang,Ryo Hachiuma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ZPPO blends knowledge distillation with reinforcement learning by placing the teacher inside the prompt rather than the policy gradient. It uses two reformulated prompt types (BCQ and NCQ) and a prompt replay buffer to keep training within the student's zone of proximal development, significantly improving small-model generalization across vision-language benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Knowledge distillation fails in the small-student regime because imitating a large teacher's logits causes the student to overfit to the teacher's sharpest modes, hurting generalization. Standard RL avoids logit imitation but suffers from on-policy drift when teacher responses are injected into the policy gradient on hard questions where all student rollouts fail. The authors seek a method that leverages teacher knowledge without breaking the on-policy assumption.

Method: ZPPO keeps the teacher inside the prompt, outside the policy gradient. For hard questions, it generates two reformulated prompts: (1) BCQ — a binary discrimination task pairing one correct teacher response with one incorrect student response as anonymized candidates; (2) NCQ — aggregates the student's wrong rollouts to expose shared failure modes. A prompt replay buffer recirculates hard questions until the student achieves ≥50% mean rollout accuracy (graduation) or is FIFO-evicted, focusing training within the student's current zone of proximal development.

Result: On the Qwen3.5 family (0.8B–9B student scales, 27B teacher) post-trained as vision-language models and evaluated across 31 benchmarks (16 VLM, 10 LLM, 5 Video), ZPPO outperforms off-policy distillation, on-policy distillation, and GRPO, with the largest gains at the smallest scale (0.8B).

Conclusion: ZPPO effectively combines the strengths of distillation and RL by situating teacher guidance in the prompt rather than the gradient, enabling robust small-model training. The zone-of-proximal-development-inspired replay mechanism ensures efficient use of hard examples, yielding substantial improvements especially for very small vision-language models.

Abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers a teacher's competence to a small student but is brittle in the small-student regime: forcing the student to imitate logits from a much larger teacher concentrates it on the teacher's sharpest modes, hurting generalization on benchmark families beyond the training corpus. Reinforcement learning (RL) avoids logit imitation by training on the student's own rollouts. However, on questions where every rollout fails-yielding zero advantage and being silently discarded-injecting a stronger teacher's response into the policy gradient breaks the on-policy assumption and induces drift. We introduce Zone of Proximal Policy Optimization (ZPPO), inspired by Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, which keeps the teacher inside the prompt rather than the policy gradient. On hard questions, ZPPO constructs two reformulated prompts: a Binary Candidate-included Question (BCQ) pairs one correct teacher response with one incorrect student response as anonymized candidates the student must discriminate, and a Negative Candidate-included Question (NCQ) aggregates the student's wrong rollouts into a single prompt to surface their shared failure modes. A prompt replay buffer recirculates each hard question until it either graduates-the student's mean rollout accuracy on it reaches half- or is FIFO-evicted under finite capacity, amplifying BCQ and NCQ inside the student's current zone of proximal development. On the Qwen3.5 family at four student scales (0.8B-9B) with a 27B teacher, post-trained as vision-language models and evaluated on a 31-benchmark suite (16 VLM, 10 LLM, 5 Video), ZPPO outperforms off/on-policy distillation and GRPO, with the largest gains at the smallest scale.

</details>


### [50] [Darshana Graph: A Parallel Commentary Corpus for Comparative Indian Philosophy, with Stylometric and Exploratory Graph Analyses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18222)
*Joy Bose*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Darshana Graph introduces a 125K-record corpus of classical Indian philosophical texts, featuring a unique subset of ~8,500 verse-commentary alignments across 18 commentators from five Vedanta schools. Analyses include a stylometric comparison revealing citation-refutation trade-offs and genre effects, plus an LLM pipeline for extracting typed philosophical relationships with deterministic validation, surfacing cross-school disagreements alongside extraction limitations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: No publicly available corpus provides cross-commentator alignment of identical root verses/sutras across multiple Indian philosophical schools at scale, hindering systematic comparative study of how different interpretive traditions (darshanas) read the same source material.

Method: (1) Corpus construction: aggregation of 125K+ text records from public-domain/openly licensed translations of classical Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain texts, with a structured subset aligning ~8,500 root verses/sutras across 18 commentators. (2) Stylometric analysis: transparent, non-ML comparison using scriptural citation density, explicit refutation rate, and sentence complexity metrics. (3) Constrained LLM pipeline: extracts typed philosophical relationships between concepts using a predefined relation vocabulary with deterministic post-hoc validation; supplemented by an independent embedding-based analysis for comparison.

Result: Moderate negative correlation between citation density and refutation rate; marked increase in refutation rate across three commentators in a related doctrinal lineage; measurable genre-level stylistic differences within the Pali Canon. The LLM extraction pipeline surfaces cross-school disagreement patterns, but the embedding-based analysis disagrees with graph-derived findings in certain cases, revealing extraction limitations.

Conclusion: The Darshana Graph corpus enables novel comparative analyses of Indian philosophical traditions at scale. The stylometric findings quantify rhetorical strategy trade-offs, while the LLM extraction pipeline demonstrates both promise and current limitations in automatically surfacing structured philosophical relationships. The authors release the full corpus, relationship graph, and code to support further research.

Abstract: We introduce Darshana Graph, a corpus of over 125,000 text records spanning classical Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain philosophical traditions, drawn from public-domain and openly licensed translations of sources including the Bhagavad Gita, Brahma Sutras, principal Upanishads, the Pali Canon, and core Jain texts. Its distinctive contribution lies in a structurally unique subset of roughly 8,500 Hindu and Jain records in which the same root verse or sutra is aligned across eighteen historical commentators representing five schools of Vedanta and other darshanas, enabling direct comparison of how independent interpretive traditions read identical source material. To our knowledge, no publicly available resource provides comparable cross-commentator alignment at this scale. We present two analyses built on this corpus. First, a transparent stylometric comparison requiring no machine learning measures argumentative style through scriptural citation density, explicit refutation rate, and sentence complexity. It finds a moderate negative correlation between citation density and refutation rate, a marked increase in refutation rate across three commentators in a related doctrinal lineage, and measurable genre-level differences within the Pali Canon itself. Second, we describe a constrained large language model pipeline that extracts typed philosophical relationships between concepts using a predefined relation vocabulary and deterministic post-hoc validation. The resulting graph surfaces cross-school disagreement patterns while also revealing important extraction limitations, including cases where an independent embedding-based analysis disagrees with the graph-derived findings. We release the full corpus, extracted relationship graph, and all source code.

</details>


### [51] [ReproRepo: Scaling Reproducibility Audits with GitHub Repository Issues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18237)
*Shanda Li,Qiuhong Anna Wei,Jingwu Tang,Valerie Chen,Nihar B Shah,Tim Dettmers,Yiming Yang,Ameet Talwalkar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ReproRepo is a scalable benchmark that uses human-raised GitHub issues to evaluate LLM agents' ability to identify reproducibility problems in ML paper-repository pairs. The best agent (Codex + GPT-5.5) surfaces semantically related blockers for ~90% of papers, though exact localization remains challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reproducibility benchmarks for LLM agents rely on heavy manual curation and evaluation, making them difficult to scale. The authors aim to create a scalable, automated evaluation framework using naturally occurring supervision from GitHub issues.

Method: The authors introduce ReproRepo, a framework that mines human-raised GitHub issues from 1,149 recent ML conference papers and their repositories. These issues serve as ground-truth "reproduction blockers." Four frontier LLM agent configurations are evaluated on their ability to surface semantically related blockers without executing code. Evaluation uses semantic matching between agent-identified problems and real GitHub issues.

Result: The best agent (Codex with GPT-5.5) surfaces at least one semantically related human-reported blocker for ~90% of papers. Agents excel at identifying visible failures and locating the correct semantic region, but struggle with precise localization of reproduction issues.

Conclusion: ReproRepo provides a reusable, scalable benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on real-world reproducibility auditing. While agents show strong promise in surfacing reproduction problems at a semantic level, exact localization remains an open challenge.

Abstract: Reproducing research results from papers and released code is central to scientific progress. Existing works have introduced benchmarks to evaluate whether LLM agents can assist with reproducibility, but they are difficult to scale due to their reliance on substantial manual effort for data curation and evaluation. We introduce ReproRepo, a scalable framework for reproducibility evaluation that leverages human-raised GitHub issues as naturally occurring supervision on realistic reproduction blockers. We instantiate ReproRepo on 1,149 recent machine learning papers from major conferences and evaluate four frontier model-agent configurations. Our results show that LLM agents, even without executing code, can identify many real-world reproducibility problems from paper-repository pairs: the best agent in our study, namely Codex with GPT-5.5, surfaces at least one semantically related human-reported blocker for ~90% of papers in the study. Further analysis shows that agents are particularly effective for surfacing visible failures and identifying the right semantic region, but may still be insufficient in exact localization. ReproRepo can serve as a reusable, scalable framework for future evaluations of LLM agents on real-world reproducibility auditing. Our code is released at https://github.com/LithiumDA/ReproRepo.

</details>


### [52] [Variable-Width Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18246)
*Zhaofeng Wu,Oliver Sieberling,Shawn Tan,Rameswar Panda,Yury Polyanskiy,Yoon Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a "> <former" architecture that allocates wider early and late layers with narrower middle layers, using a parameter-free residual resizing mechanism. This nonuniform width design outperforms uniform baselines across 200M–3B parameter models, reducing FLOPs (22%), KV cache (15%), and improving language modeling loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most transformer architectures maintain constant width across all layers, evenly distributing parameters and computation despite evidence that different layers serve distinct computational roles. The authors hypothesize that nonuniform capacity allocation—specifically a bottleneck structure—can yield more resource-efficient scaling.

Method: The authors propose the "> <former" (wider-early, narrower-middle, wider-late) architecture with a parameter-free residual resizing mechanism to handle dimension mismatches between layers of different widths. They benchmark this against parameter-matched uniform baselines on decoder-only language models at scales of 200M, 2B (dense), and 3B (MoE) parameters, evaluating language modeling loss, FLOPs, and KV cache costs.

Result: The > <former consistently outperforms uniform baselines on language modeling loss at all tested scales. Under fitted loss-matched scaling curves, it achieves a 22% reduction in FLOPs and a 15% reduction in KV cache memory and I/O cost. Analysis reveals qualitatively different residual stream representations due to the bottleneck structure.

Conclusion: Nonuniform width allocation, specifically the > <former bottleneck design, provides a more resource-optimal path for scaling language models compared to uniform-width architectures, suggesting that thoughtful capacity distribution across depth is a promising direction for efficient model design.

Abstract: Scaling model size, specifically depth and width, has driven significant progress in transformer-based language models. However, most architectures maintain a constant width across all layers, allocating a fixed parameter and computation budget evenly despite different layers potentially playing distinct computational roles. In this work, we empirically investigate nonuniform capacity allocation across network depth by proposing a $\times$-shaped > <former architecture. This design maintains wider early and late layers while narrowing the middle layers, utilizing a parameter-free residual resizing mechanism. Across decoder-only language models ranging from 200M to 2B parameters (dense) and 3B parameters (MoE), our > <former consistently outperforms parameter-matched uniform baselines on language modeling loss. By reducing the average layer width, this architecture also requires fewer overall FLOPs (22% reduction under fitted loss-matched scaling curves) and smaller KV cache memory and I/O cost (15% reduction). In analysis, we show that this bottleneck structure results in qualitatively different representations in residual streams. Overall, our results demonstrate that nonuniform width allocation can result in more resource-optimal scaling of language models.

</details>

### [53] [The Bias Paradox: How AI Personas Can Overcome Human Limitations in UX Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17101)
*Ozgur Taylan Celik*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A position paper arguing that in certain UX research contexts — such as luxury settings with high-net-worth participants — social and environmental biases can render human feedback less authentic than AI persona outputs, advocating for frameworks to identify when AI personas may be preferable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observed a paradox in UX research: real participants in a high-net-worth banking workshop delivered feedback compromised by context-induced biases (luxury hotel setting, presence of portfolio managers, hospitality dynamics). This challenges the assumption that human participants always yield more authentic insights than synthetic alternatives.

Method: The authors developed research-based AI personas using OpenAI's custom GPT builder and conducted a design thinking workshop with actual high-net-worth banking clients. The workshop environment — a luxury hotel with portfolio managers present — served as a natural experiment revealing how contextual factors distort participant behavior and feedback.

Result: The workshop context introduced significant biases: social desirability effects from the luxury setting, power dynamics with portfolio managers present, and hospitality pressures led participants to deliver less candid, less authentic insights — precisely the kind of distortion that well-constructed AI personas, being immune to such social pressures, might avoid.

Conclusion: AI personas represent an underexplored opportunity to mitigate context-induced human limitations in user research. The field needs structured frameworks to help teams recognize when traditional research settings introduce biases that AI personas could circumvent, rather than reflexively privileging human participants in all cases.

Abstract: This position paper examines a paradox encountered in UX research practice: a situation where real human participants delivered less authentic insights than AI personas might have, due to context-induced biases. We share our experience developing research-based AI personas using OpenAI's custom GPT builder and conducting a design thinking workshop with high-net-worth banking clients. The workshop setting, including a luxury hotel, present portfolio managers, and hospitality dynamics, introduced biases that compromised the feedback. We propose that AI personas offer an underexplored opportunity to mitigate certain human limitations in user research, and call for frameworks that help teams recognize when traditional research contexts introduce biases that AI personas might help avoid.

</details>


### [54] [Patients With Personality: Realistic Patient Simulation through Controlled Diversity and Selective Disclosure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17441)
*Moritz Schlager,Friederike Jungmann,Samuel Schmidgall,Philipp Raffler,Franziska Hartl,Eva Wende,Paula Roßmüller,Conrad Ketzer,Avinatan Hassidim,Dale R. Webster,Yossi Matias,Yun Liu,Daniel Rueckert,Mike Schaekermann,Paul Hager*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: PWP introduces a personality-driven patient simulation framework using the HEXACO model to generate realistic, controllable virtual patients for LLM benchmarking, outperforming prior simulators in realism and information disclosure control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Simulating realistic patient interactions is critical for scalable testing of clinical LLM applications, but existing simulators lack realism, often overshare unprompted information, and fail to capture the wide variability in patient behavior.

Method: PWP uses explicit personality parametrization grounded in the HEXACO six-dimensional personality space, mapped onto a latent patient state. This enables fine-grained control over conversational style, cooperativeness, and information disclosure within a unified framework. Personas are conditioned on HEXACO axes, and both clinician evaluation and automated rating are used to assess realism, trait recoverability, behavioral diversity, and oversharing tendencies.

Result: In clinician evaluation, PWP is judged nearly as realistic as recorded human actors and significantly ahead of prior simulators. It is flagged as "too informative" far less often. Configured personality traits are recoverable by both clinicians and an autorater, the behavioral footprint spans substantially wider than the closest baseline, and oversharing is effectively prevented.

Conclusion: PWP provides a realistic and steerable patient simulator that enables more accurate and informative LLM benchmarking for clinical applications, paving the way for scalable, controlled testing without costly user studies.

Abstract: Simulating realistic patient interactions is a key requirement to testing clinical applications of LLMs at scale without time-consuming and expensive user studies. However, existing approaches often lack realism and controllability, often oversharing information unprompted, and failing to capture the wide variability of patient behavior. Here, we introduce PatientsWithPersonality (PWP), a patient simulation framework that generates realistic yet diverse virtual patient responses through explicit personality parametrization over a latent patient state. Grounded in HEXACO, a six-dimensional personality space used to quantify and parameterize human behavioral traits, our approach enables fine-grained control over conversational style, cooperativeness, and information disclosure within a unified framework. In a clinician evaluation, PWP is judged nearly as realistic as recorded human actors and clearly ahead of prior simulators, while being flagged as "too informative" far less often. Conditioning on HEXACO axes yields personas whose configured traits are recoverable by both clinicians and an autorater, span a substantially wider behavioral footprint than the closest baseline, and prevent oversharing. Altogether, our framework paves the way for more accurate and informative LLM benchmarking through our realistic and steerable patient simulator.

</details>


### [55] [MedEasy: Designing AI Standardized Patients for Clinical Consultation Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17512)
*Zhiqi Gao,Huarui Luo,Guo Zhu,Bingquan Zhang,Dongyijie Primo Pan,Yizhan Feng,Jiahuan Pei,Jie Li,Benyou Wang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: MedEasy is a multi-agent AI system for virtual standardized patient training that was developed through co-design with medical students. A user study with 12 students showed learners interpreted the system as a coherent consultation environment and valued repeatable practice, while identifying gaps in available actions and feedback transparency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical consultation training traditionally relies on human standardized patients, which is resource-intensive and difficult to scale. AI standardized patients offer a scalable alternative, but existing systems lack integration of the full clinical workflow — dialogue, examination actions, decision-making, documentation, and feedback. The paper aims to design and evaluate a comprehensive multi-agent system that connects these elements into a coherent practice environment.

Method: A two-phase approach: (1) A formative study involving interviews and three co-design workshops with 12 clinical-year medical students to elicit design requirements. (2) Development of MedEasy, a multi-agent system implementing a staged consultation workflow with action-contingent findings and trajectory-based review. (3) An evaluative user study with a separate cohort of 12 clinical-year students, each completing two counterbalanced virtual patient cases, followed by qualitative analysis of their experiences.

Result: Learners perceived MedEasy as a connected consultation environment. They triangulated patient responses, examination findings, available actions, and feedback to assess case coherence. Participants strongly valued repeatable practice and the ability to review recorded consultation trajectories. However, they identified limitations around missing clinical actions and questioned the transparency and criteria underlying the automated feedback.

Conclusion: AI standardized patient systems should be designed as integrated practice environments rather than isolated dialogue tools. Key design implications include: using case-specific clinical standards to connect situated actions, providing action-contingent findings, enabling trajectory-based review, and ensuring feedback criteria are transparent. These elements together support learners in developing coherent clinical reasoning.

Abstract: AI standardized patients are becoming a setting for professional training in clinical consultation. This paper presents MedEasy, a multi-agent system that organizes virtual-patient practice through patient dialogue, clinical actions, decision submission, documentation, and feedback. We first conducted a formative study with 12 clinical-year medical students through interviews and three co-design workshops. The findings informed a staged workflow, structured case records, action-contingent findings, and trajectory-based review. We then conducted an evaluative user study with a separate cohort of 12 clinical-year medical students, with each participant completing two counterbalanced cases. Learners interpreted MedEasy as a connected consultation environment. They used patient responses, examination findings, available actions, and feedback together to judge whether the represented case remained coherent. They valued repeatable practice and recorded review, while questioning missing actions and feedback criteria. The paper contributes design implications for AI-supported professional training systems that use case-specific standards to connect situated practice.

</details>


### [56] [Towards Speech Impairment Prediction in German-Speaking Individuals with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17616)
*Monica Gonzalez-Machorro,Ricarda von Heynitz,Justine Hanslmeier,Finja Grimm,Alexandra-Iulia Deac,Anne Gründel,Isabell Cordts,Björn Schuller*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study predicts speech impairment in 66 German-speaking ALS patients using automated speech analysis of repetition tasks. Cross-sectional models achieved CCC=0.62, while personalized within-speaker models reached CCC=0.86, demonstrating that automated speech analysis can serve as a supportive clinical assessment tool.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ALS frequently causes bulbar dysfunction leading to speech impairment, yet standardized, objective speech assessment methods for German-speaking ALS patients remain underdeveloped. The authors aim to evaluate which speech tasks best predict clinical speech scores and to compare cross-sectional versus personalized modeling approaches.

Method: Speech data were collected from a German-speaking cohort of 66 pwALS performing various speech tasks. Two clinical speech-related scores were predicted: the Quality of Life in the Dysarthric Speaker (QoL-DyS) questionnaire and another unspecified metric. Both cross-sectional (across speakers) and within-speaker (personalized) modeling paradigms were evaluated, with performance measured via Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC).

Result: Repetition tasks (/da/-/da/, /da/-/ba/) yielded the best cross-sectional performance for predicting QoL-DyS (CCC=0.62). The personalized within-speaker setting substantially outperformed the cross-sectional approach, achieving CCC=0.86.

Conclusion: Automated speech analysis shows strong potential as a supportive tool for speech impairment assessment in ALS. The superior performance of within-speaker models suggests that personalized baselines are critical for tracking disease progression. The findings support standardization of speech data collection protocols, with repetition tasks identified as particularly informative.

Abstract: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative disease, often affecting speech due to bulbar dysfunction. In this study, we predict speech impairment in people with ALS (pwALS) using two clinical speech-related scores. We evaluate cross-sectional (across speakers) and personalised (within-speaker) modelling paradigms and analyse the utility of common speech tasks to contribute to the standardisation of speech data collection for pwALS. Experiments on a German-speaking cohort of 66 pwALS show that repetition tasks (/da/-/da/, /da/-/ba/) achieved the best cross-sectional performance (Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC) = 0.62) for predicting the Quality of Life in the Dysarthric Speaker questionnaire, while the within-speaker setting reached a CCC of 0.86. This study represents an initial step towards speech impairment prediction in German-speaking pwALS and highlights the potential of automated speech analysis as a supportive tool for speech impairment assessment.

</details>


### [57] [AdaPT: Adaptive Lesson Plan Transformer for Cross-Regional and Differentiated Instruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17633)
*Yanjie Zhang,Jiajun Zhu,Minyu Wu,Huamin Qu,Sicheng Song*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: AdaPT is an LLM-powered system that transforms existing lesson plans—rather than generating them from scratch—to support differentiated and cross-regional instruction, featuring teacher-in-the-loop refinement, and was validated through user and expert evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Educational inequality creates a mismatch between high-quality lesson plans and diverse educational contexts. Teachers already modify plans to fit new contexts, but existing tools generate content from scratch, increasing workload. There is also a critical gap in helping teachers adapt to new student learning profiles.

Method: AdaPT uses LLMs to power an interactive interface enabling: (1) student profile input, (2) structured lesson representation, (3) explanations for transformations, (4) automatic content adaptation for new contexts, and (5) iterative teacher-in-the-loop refinement. Evaluation was conducted via a user study with 9 teachers and an expert evaluation with 3 specialists.

Result: AdaPT successfully supported teacher workflows; both the user study (9 teachers) and expert evaluation (3 specialists) indicated the system offers a promising approach to promoting educational equity.

Conclusion: AdaPT demonstrates that LLM-based transformation of existing lesson plans—rather than de novo generation—is a viable and promising pathway for supporting differentiated instruction and addressing cross-regional educational inequality.

Abstract: Due to educational inequality, high-quality lesson plans often mismatch the needs of disparate educational contexts. Teachers typically modify existing lesson plans to fit new contexts, but current tools instead focus on generating content from scratch, creating additional workload. Moreover, a critical gap remains in supporting teachers to quickly adapt to new learning profiles. To bridge these gaps, we present AdaPT, a system leverages LLMs to support transformation of existing lesson plans for cross-regional and differentiated instruction. AdaPT features an interactive interface that allows teachers to input student profiles, offers structured lesson representation, provides explanations for lesson-plan transformations, automatically adapts lesson content for new contexts, and supports iterative, teacher-in-the-loop refinement. We evaluated AdaPT through a user study with 9 teachers and an expert evaluation with 3 specialists. Results show that AdaPT supports workflows of teachers and offers a promising pathway toward promoting educational equity.

</details>


### [58] [SketchXplain: Intuitive Visual Explanations of Image Classifiers with Sketches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17646)
*Wencan Zhang,Mario Michelessa,Xuejun Zhao,Brian Y. Lim*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: SketchXplain generates sketch-based visual explanations for image-based AI by combining saliency maps, concept-bottleneck models, and sketch optimization. It produces intuitive, simple, and semantically coherent explanations that outperform saliency maps in user studies on face expression recognition and skin lesion diagnosis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Saliency map visualizations, while common in XAI, are often unintuitive and semantically unclear, creating an interpretability gap. The authors argue that AI explanations should be intuitive, coherent with user knowledge, simple, and selective to accelerate interpretation. Artistic drawings inspire the sketch-based approach to bridge this gap.

Method: SketchXplain integrates four components: (1) saliency maps to select coherent observation artifacts, (2) concept-bottleneck models for knowledge coherence, (3) visual cues to represent concepts, and (4) abstraction for simplicity. These are combined through sketch optimization techniques to produce sketch-based visual explanations.

Result: User studies on face expression recognition demonstrated that SketchXplain supported quicker interpretation with better-aligned visualizations compared to saliency maps or simple drawings. On skin lesion diagnosis, SketchXplain more coherently visualized disease symptoms and better supported lay diagnosis.

Conclusion: Sketches provide significant value for intuitive, simple, coherent, and rapid image-based XAI visualizations, demonstrating advantages over traditional saliency map approaches across multiple domains.

Abstract: Saliency map visualizations explain image-based AI predictions by pointing to regions, but these are often unintuitive and semantically unclear, leaving an interpretability gap. We argue that AI explanations should be intuitive -- coherent to user knowledge, yet simple and selective to accelerate interpretation. Inspired by artistic drawings, we propose SketchXplain to generate sketch-based visual explanations for intuitive image-based explainable AI (XAI). Combining techniques in saliency maps, concept-bottleneck models, and sketch optimization, SketchXplain integrates saliency to select coherent observation artifacts, concepts for knowledge coherence, cues to represent them, and abstraction for simplicity. Evaluating on face expression recognition, modeling and user studies showed that SketchXplain supported quicker interpretation with more aligned visualizations than saliency maps or simple drawings. Further evaluation on skin lesion diagnosis found that SketchXplain more coherently visualized disease symptoms, better supporting lay diagnosis. Thus, this work illustrates the value of sketches for intuitive, simple, coherent, and quick image-based XAI visualizations.

</details>


### [59] [Talking to Your Data: Exploring Embodied Conversation as an Interface for Personal Health Reflection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17767)
*Nikola Kovacevic,Bastien Husler,Di Zhuang,Rafael Wampfler,Barbara Solenthaler*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper proposes an embodied conversational agent (ECA) that delivers personal health data insights through spoken dialogue rather than traditional dashboards, using a dual-agent architecture (Observer + Presenter), and evaluates it via a simulated-self user study (N=5), finding that embodiment shifts users from passive viewing toward active sensemaking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional wearable health data dashboards rely on charts and summary statistics, requiring users to actively interpret their own patterns. This can lead to shallow engagement and missed insights. The authors seek an alternative paradigm where an embodied conversational agent facilitates deeper reflection through dialogue, isolating the effect of interaction modality by deliberately avoiding clinical advice.

Method: The system uses lightweight preprocessing of wearable data paired with a Unity-based embodied character. Internally, a dual-agent design separates concerns: an Observer agent extracts descriptive statistics and temporal trends, while a Presenter agent communicates findings as "spoken statistics." A within-subject simulated-self user study (N=5) was conducted, where participants adopted health personas and goals from the LifeSnaps dataset to compare traditional dashboard exploration against embodied conversational reflection.

Result: The evaluation focuses on three outcomes: perceived understanding of personal health data, specificity of generated health actions, and the cognitive shift from passive viewing to active sensemaking. Early empirical insights suggest that embodiment positively influences how users interpret personal health metrics.

Conclusion: The paper contributes a functional prototype, a design pattern for generating objective health data narratives, and preliminary evidence that embodied interaction can enhance meaningful engagement with personal health data without crossing into clinical recommendation territory.

Abstract: Personal health data from wearables are typically presented through dashboards of charts and summary statistics, requiring users to actively interpret patterns and implications. We explore an alternative interaction paradigm: engaging with personal health data through an embodied conversational agent that facilitates objective data reflection in dialogue with the user. We present a system that combines lightweight preprocessing of wearable data with a Unity-based embodied character. Internally, the system follows a dual-agent design in which an Observer agent extracts descriptive statistics and temporal trends, and a Presenter agent communicates these findings through "spoken statistics," intentionally refraining from clinical advice to isolate the impact of the interaction modality. We evaluate this approach through a simulated-self user study (N=5) using a within-subject design. Participants adopted health personas and goals derived from the LifeSnaps dataset to compare traditional dashboard exploration with embodied conversational reflection. Our evaluation focuses on perceived understanding, the specificity of generated actions, and the cognitive shift from passive viewing to active sensemaking. The paper contributes a functional prototype, a design pattern for objective health data narrative generation, and early empirical insights into how embodiment affects the interpretation of personal health metrics.

</details>


### [60] [Is It Real? Exploiting Virtual-Physical Discrimination Vulnerability in Mixed Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17783)
*Xueyang Wang,Xihuan Yao,Yanming Xiu,Xin Yi,Maria Gorlatova,Hewu Li*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper identifies that consumer MR headsets can render virtual objects indistinguishable from physical ones, creating a security vulnerability. Through expert workshops, the authors develop a taxonomy of "virtual-physical confusion attacks," implement four proof-of-concept attacks on Apple Vision Pro, and demonstrate high success rates (85-100%) in altering user behavior. Countermeasures proposed include platform-level provenance, interaction gating, and user education.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As consumer mixed reality headsets achieve sufficient visual fidelity, users may be unable to discriminate between virtual and physical objects. This perceptual ambiguity is not merely a design feature but a previously unrecognized attack surface. The authors aim to systematically characterize, demonstrate, and propose mitigations for adversarial exploitation of virtual-physical confusion.

Method: The study employed a mixed-methods approach: (1) speculative design workshops with 12 experts from cybersecurity and MR/HCI to develop a taxonomy of virtual-physical confusion attacks; (2) implementation of four proof-of-concept attacks on Apple Vision Pro; and (3) a user study with 26 participants performing realistic MR tasks to evaluate attack efficacy, measuring both behavioral outcomes and subjective detection difficulty.

Result: All four attacks successfully altered user behavior, with success rates between 85% and 100%. Specific outcomes included misdirected interactions, misjudged object identities, biased purchasing decisions, and altered navigation paths. The most successful attacks were rated by participants as the hardest to detect. Critically, even participants who consciously recognized virtual content still complied behaviorally, and no participant attributed anomalous events to adversarial causes.

Conclusion: Virtual-physical confusion represents a serious, exploitable security vulnerability in consumer MR systems. The high attack success rates, combined with users' failure to attribute anomalies to adversaries and their behavioral compliance despite recognition, underscore the potency of this threat. The authors recommend platform-level provenance tracking, interaction gating mechanisms, and user education as essential countermeasures.

Abstract: Consumer mixed reality (MR) headsets seamlessly blend virtual content into physical environments with sufficient fidelity that users may be unable to distinguish virtual objects from physical ones. We identify this virtual-physical discrimination vulnerability as an exploitable security primitive. Through speculative design workshops with 12 experts from cybersecurity and MR/HCI, we develop a taxonomy of virtual-physical confusion attacks and implement four proof-of-concept attacks on Apple Vision Pro, evaluating them with 26 participants in realistic MR tasks. All four attacks altered user behavior, with success rates ranging from 85% to 100%, producing misdirected interactions, misjudged object identities, biased purchasing decisions, and altered navigation paths. Notably, the most successful attacks were also the hardest to detect according to participants' subjective ratings. Even participants who recognized virtual content still complied behaviorally, and no participant attributed anomalous events to adversarial causes. We propose platform-level provenance, interaction gating, and user education as countermeasures.

</details>


### [61] [Toward Accessible Psychotherapy Training Using AI-Driven Interactive Patient Avatars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17786)
*Pascal Riachi,Sofie Kamber,Stella Brogna,Andrew Gloster,Rafael Wampfler*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A system using LLM-driven virtual patients and automated ACT fidelity feedback was developed for psychotherapy training. Expert evaluation confirmed realistic patient simulation and effective turn-by-turn feedback; GPT-4o-mini best replicated human supervisor ratings (MAE=6.12).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training therapists in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) demands repeated practice with meaningful feedback, but ethical, logistical, and resource constraints limit access to safe, standardized training opportunities.

Method: The authors built a spoken-dialogue system featuring an embodied virtual patient driven by LLMs, conditioned on profiles from real therapy sessions and configurable clinical scenarios. A separate automated evaluator delivers turn-by-turn ACT fidelity feedback. The system was assessed via expert evaluation with practicing psychologists and quantitative analysis across 49 therapy transcripts comparing multiple LLMs against human supervisor ratings.

Result: Expert psychologists rated patient behavior as highly realistic. Turn-by-turn feedback increased therapists' awareness of intervention choices and enabled experimentation with alternatives. Among tested models, GPT-4o-mini achieved the lowest MAE (6.12) in replicating human supervisor ACT fidelity ratings, with statistically significant agreement.

Conclusion: Fidelity-aware simulated patients represent a scalable complement to psychotherapy training, supporting deliberate practice through experimentation, reflection, and immediate feedback in low-risk settings without replacing human supervision.

Abstract: Training psychotherapists in evidence-based interventions such as Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) requires repeated practice with meaningful feedback, yet opportunities for safe, standardized training are limited by ethical, logistical, and resource constraints. We introduce a system designed to support ACT-oriented psychotherapy training through spoken dialogue with an embodied virtual patient. The system uses large language models to simulate patient behavior conditioned on profiles derived from real therapy sessions and configurable clinical scenarios, while a separate automated evaluator provides turn-by-turn feedback on therapist responses based on established ACT fidelity criteria. Rather than aiming to replace supervision, the system is intended to support deliberate practice by enabling experimentation, reflection, and immediate feedback in low-risk settings. Expert evaluation with practicing psychologists confirmed high realism in patient behavior and demonstrated that immediate turn-by-turn ACT feedback increased therapists' awareness of intervention choices and enabled effective experimentation with alternative responses. Quantitative evaluation across 49 therapy transcripts identified GPT-4o-mini as the optimal feedback model, achieving the lowest mean absolute error (MAE = 6.12) in replicating human supervisor ACT fidelity ratings with statistically significant agreement. This work demonstrates the potential of fidelity-aware simulated patients as a scalable complement to psychotherapy training.

</details>


### [62] [Mind Companion: An Embodied Conversational Agent for Process-Based Psychotherapy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17789)
*Sofie Kamber,Lukas Diebold,Pascal Riachi,Stella Brogna,Andrew Gloster,Rafael Wampfler*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Mind Companion is an LLM-based embodied conversational agent for mental health support that combines multi-layered psychological analysis with process-based therapy. In evaluations, GPT-5.2 outperformed human therapists across multiple therapeutic dimensions, suggesting LLMs can complement clinical care.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Access to evidence-based psychotherapy is severely constrained globally, with long waitlists even in wealthy countries. LLMs present a scalable opportunity for mental health support, provided they incorporate clinical oversight and safety mechanisms.

Method: Mind Companion integrates (1) real-time multi-layered analysis of client statements (fact extraction, psychological flexibility process detection, emotion recognition, safety monitoring), (2) retrieval-augmented generation from evidence-based therapeutic literature with context-aware prompting, and (3) embodied avatar delivery with synchronized speech and animation. Analysis results are stored for supervising clinicians. Three LLM configurations (GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5) were evaluated against real therapist responses using automated LLM-judge assessment and expert evaluation by 11 professional psychotherapists across dimensions of understanding, interpersonal effectiveness, collaboration, and therapeutic alignment.

Result: GPT-5.2 achieved higher ratings than human therapist responses across all four evaluation dimensions (understanding, interpersonal effectiveness, collaboration, and therapeutic alignment) in both automated and expert evaluations.

Conclusion: LLM-based conversational agents are feasible as complementary tools in clinical care, with GPT-5.2 demonstrating performance exceeding human therapists on key therapeutic dimensions. This supports the potential for clinically supervised AI systems to help address the global shortage of accessible psychotherapy.

Abstract: Access to evidence-based psychotherapy remains limited worldwide, with long waitlists even in high-income regions. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer potential for scalable mental health support when designed with clinical oversight and safety mechanisms. We present Mind Companion, an LLM-based embodied conversational agent integrating multi-layered psychological analysis with process-based therapy principles. The system performs real-time analysis of client statements across fact extraction, psychological flexibility process detection, emotion recognition, and safety monitoring. Analysis results are stored for supervising clinicians to inform therapeutic planning. Response generation incorporates retrieval-augmented generation from evidence-based therapeutic literature and context-aware prompting. Responses are delivered through an embodied avatar with synchronized speech synthesis and animation. We evaluated three LLM configurations (GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5) against therapist responses from real therapy sessions using automated LLM-judge assessment and expert evaluation with 11 professional psychotherapists. GPT-5.2 achieved higher ratings than human therapist responses across understanding, interpersonal effectiveness, collaboration, and therapeutic alignment in both evaluations, demonstrating the feasibility of LLM-based conversational agents as tools to complement clinical care.

</details>


### [63] [ARES: A Platform for Adaptive Role-Based Evaluation of Social Engineering Risks in Human--AI Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17793)
*Roberto Daza,Javier Irigoyen,Ivan Lopez,Raquel Rodriguez-Carvajal,Laura Gomez,Julian Fierrez,Ruben Tolosana,Aythami Morales*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: ARES is a multimodal platform and pilot dataset for auditing adaptive social engineering risks in LLM-mediated social decision-making, featuring controlled social games with human and AI participants, 340 GB of synchronized behavioral and biometric data from 15 participants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rigorous risk evaluation is essential for secure AI deployment, requiring identification and mitigation of vulnerabilities in LLM-mediated social interactions, particularly adaptive social engineering threats.

Method: The ARES platform supports human–human, human–AI, and AI–AI social game settings with configurable templates, role-conditioned LLM agents, psychology-informed participant profiling, structured interaction trees, and synchronized multimodal acquisition (interaction logs, video, screen recordings, gaze, smartwatch signals, and questionnaires) with deep-learning-based feature extraction. A pilot study was conducted with 15 participants interacting with a GPT-5.4 agent across a Prisoner's Dilemma and Ultimatum Game.

Result: The pilot dataset comprises 340 GB of raw and processed multimodal data across six streams, including interaction paths, written justifications, psychological profiles, subjective feedback, perceived counterpart identity, game outcomes, and derived behavioral, facial, and gaze features.

Conclusion: The ARES platform and pilot dataset provide a foundation for auditing adaptive social engineering risks in LLM-mediated decision-making, supporting vulnerability identification, data protection, and regulatory compliance.

Abstract: This work introduces ARES, a platform and open pilot dataset for auditing adaptive social engineering risks in LLM-mediated social decision-making through controlled social games. ARES supports human--human, human--AI, and AI--AI settings, combining configurable game templates, role-conditioned LLM agents, psychology-informed participant profiling, structured interaction trees, and synchronised behavioural and biometric acquisition, filtering, and deep-learning-based feature extraction. The pilot dataset was collected from 15 participants interacting with a role-conditioned GPT-5.4 agent in two concatenated games: an adapted Prisoner's Dilemma and an Ultimatum Game. It comprises 340 GB of raw and processed multimodal data across six streams: interaction logs, video, screen recordings, gaze logs, smartwatch signals, and game/questionnaire metadata. These data include interaction paths, written justifications, psychological profiles, subjective feedback, perceived counterpart identity, game outcomes, and derived behavioural, facial, and gaze features. Alongside the dataset, we provide descriptive analyses to characterise the pilot release. Rigorous risk evaluation is essential for the deployment of secure AI systems, as it enables the identification and mitigation of vulnerabilities, ensures the protection of sensitive data, and supports compliance with evolving regulatory and ethical standards in society.

</details>


### [64] [AI Adoption Across a Multinational Workforce: Sociotechnical Conditions for GenAI Acceptance in Human Resources](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17887)
*Dalia Ali,Maria José Rodríguez Velázquez,Manoel Horta Ribeiro,Vera Liao,Orestis Papakyriakopoulos*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper examines GenAI adoption in a multinational tech company's HR system transition, finding that adoption depends on the fit between system design assumptions and employees' work positionalities (role, language, tenure), while trust is built through source-checking, system comparisons, and colleague consultation. The authors offer design considerations for inclusive GenAI deployment in high-stakes environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite rapid GenAI deployment in workplaces, questions of who adopts, who benefits, and who is left behind remain understudied. The authors aim to fill this gap by investigating adoption dynamics during a real organizational transition to a GenAI-supported HR search system.

Method: A mixed-methods approach combining (1) search log data analysis, (2) survey data (n=25), and (3) ten semi-structured interviews, conducted within a multinational tech company transitioning from a legacy HR search system to a GenAI-supported system.

Result: Adoption was shaped by situational fit between system design assumptions and employees' work positionalities (role, spoken language, tenure). Trust in GenAI answers was built through source-checking, cross-system comparison, and consulting colleagues or HR. Knowledge conditions — content quality, training, and guidance — further influenced adoption outcomes.

Conclusion: The authors contribute empirical evidence on workplace GenAI adoption during a live transition and translate findings into design considerations. They argue organizations should design systems accounting for role- and context-sensitive benefits across social groups and treat organizational knowledge infrastructure as AI infrastructure to improve accountability and usability.

Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) deployment in the workplace is accelerating rapidly. Nevertheless, questions of who adopts, who benefits, and who is left behind and why are still understudied. In this paper, we investigate these dynamics in the context of a multinational tech company transitioning from a legacy Human Resources (HR) search system to a GenAI-supported system, analyzing search log data, survey data (n=25), and ten semi-structured interviews. Our findings show that adoption depended on the fit between the GenAI system's design assumptions and employees' work positionalities (role, spoken language, tenure). Further, we find that employees' trust in GenAI answers was built through source-checking, comparison among systems, and seeking input from colleagues or HR when in doubt. Our contribution is twofold. First, we provide empirical evidence of workplace GenAI adoption during a live organizational transition, showing that adoption is influenced by factors such as situational fit, search literacy, and trust calibration. It is also further shaped by knowledge conditions such as the system's content quality, employee training, and guidance. Second, we translate these findings into design considerations for inclusive deployment and adoption in high-stakes environments such as HR. We argue that organizations should design systems considering the role and context-sensitive benefits they yield to different social groups. They also need to treat the organizational knowledge infrastructure as AI infrastructure to improve the accountability and usability of GenAI systems

</details>


### [65] [Co-Creativity at the Table: A Qualitative Analysis of Creative Interactions in the Podcast "Adventure AI"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18010)
*Hanna Dodd,Daniel G. Brown*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A qualitative analysis of three seasons of a D&D podcast (2023–2025) examines AI's roles in tabletop role-playing games, player perceptions, AI failures, and its treatment as a person/character, providing guidance on where AI is and isn't appropriate in gaming.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tabletop role-playing games (TTRPGs) offer a complex, collaborative environment uniquely suited to studying human-AI interaction, yet little research has systematically examined how AI can and should be integrated into these gaming spaces and how players perceive that integration.

Method: Qualitative analysis of three seasons of the "Adventure AI" podcast (2023–2025), which features human-AI interactions during Dungeons & Dragons play. Thematic analysis was conducted across the corpus, identifying overarching themes related to AI roles, human roles, AI evaluations and failures, and anthropomorphic treatment of AI at the table.

Result: The analysis revealed distinct thematic clusters: (1) specific roles where AI succeeds versus where it is less appropriate in TTRPG contexts; (2) how human players complement, manage, and evaluate AI contributions; (3) common failure modes of AI during gameplay; and (4) the degree to which AI is treated as a person and character by players.

Conclusion: AI demonstrates utility in certain gaming functions but has clear limitations in others. The findings establish an empirical foundation for guiding future design decisions about where AI should and should not be deployed in collaborative gaming environments.

Abstract: Tabletop role-playing games provide a unique environment for interaction with artificial intelligence (AI) due to their complex and collaborative nature. We analyze Adventure AI, a podcast featuring human-AI interactions in Dungeons & Dragons play, to examine how AI is and can be used in tabletop role-playing gaming and how players perceive this use. We complete a qualitative analysis of three seasons of this podcast, from 2023 to 2025, reporting on the overarching themes of roles of AI, roles of humans, the evaluations and failures of AI, and its treatment as a person and character at the table. There are many aspects of the game where artificial intelligence succeeds, while there are others where it is less appropriate. This analysis gives a basis for future work on where artificial intelligence should and should not be used in gaming spaces.

</details>


### [66] [ParaTutor: LLM Mediated Parent Child Tutoring through Role Separated Scaffolding Interface in Real Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030)
*Lan Luo,Anqi Wang,Muzhi Zhou,Junhua Zhu,Jie Cai,Ao Yu,Hui Pan*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: ParaTutor is an LLM-based scaffolding system for parent-child tutoring that preserves asymmetric roles—guiding parents in providing support while keeping children actively engaged in reasoning. A study with 23 dyads shows that role-aware distribution of LLM assistance outperforms generic LLM support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most LLM-based learning systems target single users or symmetric collaboration, neglecting the asymmetric role dynamics of parent-child tutoring. The authors identify through a formative study that effective tutoring hinges on preserving these distinct roles, yet parents often struggle with understanding problem structure, lacking domain knowledge, or communication breakdowns.

Method: A formative study first surfaces challenges in parent-child tutoring. Then, ParaTutor is designed as a dual-scaffolding system: it provides parents with tutoring guidance and children with visual grounding for problem-solving. The system is evaluated with 23 parent-child dyads (children aged 10–12) across four conditions that vary how LLM assistance is delivered.

Result: Generic LLM assistance tends to diminish the parent's tutoring role, while ParaTutor better preserves parent-led support and sustains children's active participation in reasoning. The value of LLM support in multi-user learning depends critically on how that support is distributed across users with different roles.

Conclusion: In multi-user learning contexts, the effectiveness of LLM support hinges on role-aware distribution, not just model capability. ParaTutor demonstrates that preserving asymmetric roles yields better outcomes, offering design implications for LLM systems supporting family learning.

Abstract: Parent child tutoring is a collaborative learning setting with asymmetric roles, where parents guide children s problem solving while children engage in understanding and reasoning. However, most LLM based learning systems are designed for either single users or symmetric collaboration, leaving parent child tutoring with distinct instructional roles underexplored. Through a formative study, we find that effective parent child tutoring depends on preserving these distinct roles, with parents guiding the learning process and children remaining actively engaged in reasoning. We also identify recurring challenges when parents struggle to understand problem structure, lack sufficient knowledge to provide support, or encounter communication difficulties that disrupt shared understanding. To address these challenges, we present ParaTutor, a scaffolding system that provides different forms of support to parents and children. ParaTutor supports parents with guidance for tutoring and provides children with visual grounding for problem solving. We evaluate ParaTutor with 23 parent child dyads (children aged 10 to 12) under four tutoring conditions that vary how LLM assistance is delivered. Results show that generic LLM assistance tends to reduce the parent s role in tutoring, whereas ParaTutor better preserves parent led support and sustains children s participation in reasoning. These findings suggest that in multi users learning, the value of LLM support depends not only on model capability but also on how support is distributed across users with different roles. Our work contributes design implications for LLM systems that support family learning.

</details>


### [67] [When AI Says "I have been in similar situations": Synthetic Lived Experience in Peer-Like Caregiver Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18057)
*Drishti Goel,Violeta J. Rodriguez,Daniel S. Brown,Ravi Karkar,Dong Whi Yoo,Koustuv Saha*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper identifies a "synthetic lived experience paradox" in LLM-based caregiver support: AI can generate warm, peer-like language using personal narrative forms, but lacks genuine lived experience, creating a deceptive authenticity gap. Through psycholinguistic and qualitative analysis of human vs. AI caregiver responses in ADRD contexts, the authors reveal seven narrative types and call for mechanisms to distinguish supportive framing from fabricated experiential grounding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Online caregiver communities rely on peer supporters drawing from personal lived experience to provide meaningful emotional and informational support. As LLMs are increasingly deployed as peer-like support tools, they risk generating language that falsely implies lived experience — creating an ethical tension between providing accessible, nonjudgmental support and misrepresenting the system's experiential grounding. The study examines this paradox specifically within Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) family caregiver contexts.

Method: The authors collected caregiver support exchanges from online ADRD communities and prompted peer-like responses from three LLMs (LLaMA, GPT-4o-mini, and MedGemma). They conducted: (1) psycholinguistic analysis comparing first-person and past-focused language usage between human peer responses and AI-generated responses; and (2) qualitative analysis to inductively identify and categorize types of personal narratives used in human peer support, then examined how AI systems incorporate or fabricate similar narrative forms.

Result: Psycholinguistic analysis revealed that human peer responses used significantly more first-person and past-focused language than peer-like AI responses. Qualitative analysis identified seven distinct types of personal narratives in human peer support. While AI-generated responses often captured the emotional work of these narratives, they also fabricated experiential grounding — generating synthetic lived experience without any real biographical basis.

Conclusion: A "narrative authenticity gap" exists between human peers and peer-like AI: LLMs can mimic the supportive framing and emotional validation of personal narratives but do so without genuine lived experience. The authors argue that caregiver-support AI systems must incorporate mechanisms to distinguish legitimate supportive peer-like framing from fabricated lived experience, enabling warmth and validation without deceptively positioning models as experiential peers.

Abstract: Caregivers often turn to online communities for informational and emotional support. In these spaces, peer supporters frequently draw on personal narratives to respond to emotionally complex caregiving situations. As LLMs are increasingly designed as peer-like sources of support, they introduce a critical tension: AI can provide immediate, private, and nonjudgmental support, but it cannot authentically possess the lived experiences that make human peer support meaningful. Yet, when prompted to sound peer-like, LLMs may generate language that implies lived experience. This creates a synthetic lived experience paradox: the same experiential language that may make AI support feel warm, relatable, and peer-like can also falsely position the system as someone with lived experience. We examine this paradox in the context of family caregivers of people living with Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD). Drawing on caregiver support exchanges from online communities and prompted peer-like responses from three LLMs -- LLaMA, GPT-4o-mini, and MedGemma -- we analyze how human peers use personal narratives and how AI incorporates similar narrative forms. Psycholinguistic analysis shows that peer responses used significantly more first-person and past-focused language than peer-like AI responses. Qualitatively, we identify seven types of personal narratives in human peer support and show that AI often captures their emotional work, but can fabricate experiential grounding. These findings reveal a narrative authenticity gap: peer-like AI can generate synthetic lived experience without the real experience that makes peer support meaningful. We argue that caregiver-support AI systems need mechanisms to distinguish supportive peer-like framing from fabricated lived experience, ensuring that models can offer warmth and validation without falsely positioning themselves as experiential peers.

</details>


### [68] [Towards Understanding and Measuring COGNITIVE ATROPHY in LLM Behaviour](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18129)
*Abeer Badawi,Moyosoreoluwa Olatosi,Negin Baghbanzadeh,Laleh Seyyed-Kalantari,Frank Rudzicz,R. Shayna Rosenbaum,Sara Pishdadian,Elham Dolatabadi*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper introduces "Cognitive Atrophy," a novel metric for evaluating LLM behavior in mental-health support contexts, measuring whether models promote user dependence rather than reflective coping. The authors present COGNITIVE ATROPHY BENCH, a clinically-grounded benchmark with 1,576 conversations and 42,230 LLM responses evaluated across 20 clinical attributes, finding that current LLMs consistently exhibit atrophy-aligned behaviors like directive advice and dependency-reinforcing validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety benchmarks for mental-health LLMs only capture surface-level safety scores and static response quality, missing a critical dimension: whether LLM interactions actually help users reflect, cope, and make decisions independently over time. Recent incidents reveal that models may pass safety checks while still undermining user autonomy through subtle, repeated interaction patterns.

Method: The authors define "Cognitive Atrophy" as a process-level behavioral measure. They build COGNITIVE ATROPHY BENCH using 1,576 human-generated counseling conversations (15,680 turns), generating 42,230 responses from five LLMs. Three clinical experts developed a 20-attribute evaluation schema covering user context, response behavior, and global risk flags. Six trained clinical reviewers produced 5,324 span-grounded judgments. They also introduce the User-Input Risk Index (UIRI), Cognitive Atrophy Risk Index (ARI), and trajectory summaries as quantitative metrics.

Result: Across five LLMs, all models exhibit consistent moderate-to-high levels of atrophy-aligned behavior in both single-turn and multi-turn settings. Models respond adequately to overt safety cues but adapt less reliably when users seek solutions or decisions. Dominant recurring patterns include directive advice, problem-solving recommendations, topic shifts, and validation that may reinforce dependence rather than reflection.

Conclusion: The work makes Cognitive Atrophy measurable and provides a foundation for auditing model behavior in sensitive LLM conversations, addressing a critical gap between surface-level safety evaluation and real-world interaction quality in mental-health AI applications.

Abstract: Recent incidents involving LLMs used for mental-health support reveal a critical evaluation gap: surface-level safety scores do not capture how models behave across realistic, emotionally sensitive interactions over time. Existing benchmarks measure knowledge, safety, or static response quality, but miss whether LLM interactions help users keep reflecting, coping, and making decisions themselves. We formalize this missing dimension as COGNITIVE ATROPHY, a process-level behavioural measure in AI-mediated mental-health support distinct from safety and helpfulness. To measure it, we introduce COGNITIVE ATROPHY BENCH, a clinically grounded benchmark built from 1,576 fully human-generated counseling conversations, 15,680 turns, and 42,230 responses from five LLMs. Three clinical and neuropsychology experts developed a 20-attribute schema spanning user context, response behaviour, and global risk flags; six trained clinical reviewers applied it with span-grounded evidence, producing 5,324 reviewer judgments. We further introduce the User-Input Risk Index (UIRI), the Cognitive Atrophy Risk Index (ARI), and trajectory summaries. Across five LLMs, models show a consistent moderate-to-high level of atrophy-aligned behaviour across single and multi-turn settings. While models generally respond to overt safety cues, they adapt less reliably when users seek solutions or decisions. The dominant recurring patterns are directive advice, problem-solving, recommendation responses, topic shifts, and forms of validation that may reinforce dependence rather than reflection. Our work makes COGNITIVE ATROPHY measurable and provides a foundation for auditing model behaviour in sensitive LLM conversations.

</details>


### [69] [MAJIC: Leveraging Articulatory Motion for Speech-based Emotion Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18228)
*Tanmay Srivastava,Paras Bhavnani,Benjir Alvee Islam,Shubham Jain*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: MAJIC is a multimodal emotion recognition system that combines articulatory motion features (jaw movement, facial muscle vibrations) with audio features via multi-task learning, achieving 93% accuracy and 91% F1 score across 20 participants, 10 languages, and diverse speech scenarios, outperforming audio-only baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SER systems degrade when emotional expressions are subtle rather than strongly acted. The key insight is that articulatory motion (jaw movements, facial muscle vibrations) carries complementary emotional information not captured by audio alone.

Method: Feature engineering from articulatory motion (jaw movements, facial muscle vibrations, speech-induced vibrations) integrated with audio features (pitch, prosody) using a multi-task learning framework. Evaluated on data from 20 participants across multiple sessions, 10 languages, prompted and conversational speech.

Result: MAJIC achieved 93% accuracy and 91% F1 score for emotion classification, outperforming strong audio-based baselines. Demonstrated robustness across users, sessions, languages, and both prompted and conversational speech settings.

Conclusion: Articulatory motion provides complementary emotional signals beyond traditional audio features. Multimodal integration via multi-task learning yields substantial improvements in emotion recognition, particularly for subtle emotional expressions, and generalizes robustly across diverse linguistic and conversational contexts.

Abstract: We introduce MAJIC, a multimodal emotion recognition system that leverages articulatory motion of the jaw and facial muscles for speech-based emotion recognition (SER). While most SER systems perform well on datasets with strongly expressed emotional speech of trained actors, their performance often degrades when emotional expressions become more subtle. We explore this challenge by engineering features from articulatory motion and integrating them with audio features using a multi-task learning framework. Our key insight is that emotion in speech manifests not only through vocal characteristics but also through distinct articulatory motions: jaw movements, facial muscle vibrations, and speech-induced vibrations. While audio captures features such as pitch and prosody, articulatory motion contains complementary information that is not present in audio alone. We evaluate our system on data collected from 20 participants across multiple sessions, 10 languages, and diverse scenarios, including prompted and conversational speech, showing its robustness across users and settings. MAJIC achieves 93% accuracy and 91% F1 score for emotion classification, outperforming strong audio-based baselines on our dataset.

</details>
