### [70] [Intermittent Strategic Cooperation of Two Selfish Agents on Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17216)
*Itay Shedlezki,Noa Agmon*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: This paper formalizes intermittent strategic cooperation between two self-interested agents as a shortest-path game on graphs (IC2PP), where agents can optionally cooperate at specific nodes to reduce travel times. It characterizes the structure of Pure Nash Equilibria, proves existence of at least one PNE in every instance, provides a polynomial-time enumeration algorithm, and studies bargaining-based coordination mechanisms for equilibrium selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cooperation between self-interested agents in path-planning scenarios is strategically fragile — agents may deviate at any point. Understanding when and how stable cooperation can emerge, and what forms it must take, is both theoretically important and practically relevant for multi-agent systems.

Method: The problem is modeled as a 2-player game (IC2PP) on graphs with individual targets and optional cooperation nodes. The authors characterize the structural properties of PNE joint strategies, prove PNE existence for all instances, and develop a polynomial-time algorithm to enumerate all relevant PNEs. For cases with multiple equilibria, they employ bargaining-theoretic selection concepts to compare outcomes empirically along dimensions of individual travel time and social welfare.

Result: Stable cooperation in IC2PP must follow a highly constrained structural form. At least one PNE exists in every instance, and all relevant PNEs can be enumerated in polynomial time. Empirical comparison using bargaining-theoretic coordination mechanisms reveals trade-offs between individual travel times and social welfare across equilibria.

Conclusion: Strategic cooperation in space- and time-constrained two-agent path planning is viable but requires adherence to strict structural conditions for stability. The guaranteed existence of PNEs and the ability to enumerate them efficiently opens the door to practical coordination mechanisms grounded in bargaining theory.

Abstract: We study strategic space- and time-constrained cooperation between two self-interested agents through the Intermittent Strategic Cooperation-Based Two-Agent Path Planning (IC2PP) problem, a shortest-path game on graphs in which agents navigate toward individual targets while optionally cooperating at specific nodes to reduce their own travel times. Although such cooperation can strictly benefit both agents, it is strategically fragile: agents may deviate at any point along their paths. Modeled as a 2-player game, we characterize the structure of Pure Nash Equilibrium (PNE) joint strategies in IC2PP, and show that stable cooperation must follow a highly constrained form. We further prove that at least one PNE exists in every instance of IC2PP, and present a polynomial-time algorithm for enumerating all relevant PNEs. When multiple equilibria arise, we study coordination mechanisms based on bargaining-theoretic selection concepts and empirically compare equilibrium outcomes in terms of individual travel times and social welfare.

</details>


### [71] [Trustworthy Self-Composable Big-Data-as-a-Service: An LLM-Orchestrated Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Data Engineering, AutoML, MLOps Deployment, and Drift-Aware Lifecycle Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17915)
*Aueaphum Aueawatthanaphisut,Badri Raj Lamichhane*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: A multi-agent LLM-orchestrated BDaaS framework is proposed that decomposes the full data science lifecycle into specialized agents with artifact governance, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and drift-aware feedback loops. Evaluation with tabular benchmarks shows competitive predictive performance while improving lifecycle reliability over manual ML, AutoML-only, and single-agent LLM baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based data science agents and AutoML systems operate on isolated workflow stages (ingestion, cleaning, modeling, etc.) and lack support for lifecycle-level orchestration, artifact governance, human oversight, and drift-aware adaptation required by production BDaaS platforms.

Method: The authors design a self-composable BDaaS architecture decomposing the lifecycle into specialized agents (data ingestion, data cleaning, feature engineering, AutoML training, model evaluation, MLOps deployment, monitoring, drift detection) coordinated by a central LLM orchestration layer. The layer validates outputs, manages workflow context, and enables dynamic composition. The system incorporates shared artifact governance, reproducibility support, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and drift-aware feedback loops. A prototype is evaluated on controlled tabular benchmark datasets with missing values, categorical variables, outliers, class imbalance, and simulated covariate drift, compared against manual ML, AutoML-only, and single-agent LLM baselines.

Result: The multi-agent BDaaS pipeline achieves competitive predictive performance while demonstrating improved lifecycle-level reliability across workflow completion, artifact traceability, deployment readiness, reproducibility, and drift recovery compared to all baselines.

Conclusion: LLM-orchestrated multi-agent systems can extend conventional AutoML toward trustworthy, adaptive, and production-oriented BDaaS lifecycle automation, bridging the gap between isolated workflow automation and end-to-end platform requirements.

Abstract: Big-Data-as-a-Service (BDaaS) platforms require re liable automation across data ingestion, cleaning, feature engi neering, model development, deployment, and post-deployment monitoring. However, existing LLM-based data science agents and AutoML systems mainly focus on isolated workflow stages, leaving limited support for lifecycle-level orchestration, artifact governance, human oversight, and drift-aware adaptation. This paper proposes a trustworthy self-composable BDaaS frame work based on LLM-orchestrated multi-agent collaboration. The proposed architecture decomposes the BDaaS lifecycle into specialized agents for data ingestion, data cleaning, feature engineering, AutoML training, model evaluation, MLOps de ployment, monitoring, and drift detection. A central LLM or chestration layer coordinates agent execution, validates interme diate outputs, manages workflow context, and enables dynamic workflow composition. The framework also incorporates shared artifact governance, reproducibility support, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and drift-aware feedback loops. A prototype-based evaluation is conducted using controlled tabular benchmark datasets with missing values, categorical variables, outliers, class imbalance, and simulated covariate drift. Compared with manual ML, AutoML-only, and single-agent LLM baselines, the pro posed multi-agent BDaaS pipeline achieves competitive predictive performance while improving lifecycle-level reliability, including workflow completion, artifact traceability, deployment readiness, reproducibility, and drift recovery. The results suggest that LLM-orchestrated multi-agent systems can extend conventional AutoML toward trustworthy, adaptive, and production-oriented BDaaS lifecycle automation.

</details>


### [72] [A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Strategy Synthesis for Strategic Logics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17962)
*Marco Aruta,Vadim Malvone,Aniello Murano,Domenico Parente,Luca Rizzuti*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: A neuro-symbolic framework uses LLMs as strategy-generation oracles paired with formal MAS model checkers in a generate-and-certify architecture, achieving 92% accuracy on a new NatATL strategy-synthesis dataset of 4211 instances.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Strategic ability logics like ATL offer rigorous reasoning for MAS but suffer from high computational costs in strategy synthesis, limiting practical adoption.

Method: A generate-and-certify neuro-symbolic architecture where an LLM (Qwen3-32B) proposes candidate strategies that are then formally validated by a standard MAS model checker for bounded strategic reasoning in NatATL. Only certified strategies are accepted.

Result: The certified pipeline achieves 92% accuracy on strategy-synthesis outcomes, evaluated on a newly introduced benchmark dataset of 4211 NatATL strategy-synthesis instances.

Conclusion: Neuro-symbolic integration via LLM-guided strategy generation with formal verification effectively navigates large combinatorial strategy spaces while preserving soundness, offering a practical path forward for strategic reasoning in MAS.

Abstract: Reasoning about what agents can achieve through strategic interaction is a core challenge in Multi-Agent Systems (MAS). Logics for strategic ability, such as ATL, provide rigorous methods, but their adoption is often hindered by the computational cost of strategy synthesis. We introduce a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates large language models (LLMs) into the model-checking pipeline for MAS. The LLM acts as a strategy-generation oracle, proposing candidate strategies that are then formally validated by a standard MAS model checker. This generate-and-certify architecture uses LLM guidance to navigate large combinatorial strategy spaces while preserving formal soundness: generated strategies are accepted only when certified by the verifier. We instantiate the framework for bounded strategic reasoning in NatATL and introduce the first NatATL strategy-synthesis dataset, consisting of 4211 instances. Experiments with an open-weight Qwen3-32B model show that our certified pipeline achieves 92\% accuracy on strategy-synthesis outcomes.

</details>


### [73] [Intelligence Entropy Principle and the ADE Stability Engineering Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18065)
*Dexing Liu*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Proposes the Intelligence Entropy Principle to explain nonlinear degradation in production LLM-driven multi-agent systems, formalized via an entropy growth equation; introduces the ADE four-layer framework and Elastic Organization morphology, achieving dramatic reductions in channel fracture and system death probability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM-driven multi-agent systems move from laboratory to production environments, they exhibit nonlinear degradation behaviors that are poorly understood and lack principled mitigation frameworks. Current approaches fail to systematically characterize or prevent the spontaneous drift toward disorder in such systems.

Method: 1) Intelligence Entropy Principle: formalizes system entropy as S(t) = S0 * exp(alpha*t/Cm), where Cm is a model capability coefficient. 2) Lyapunov stability analysis yields the stabilization condition lambda > alpha/Cm. 3) ADE (Agent Delivery Engineering) four-layer framework: L1 Physical Laws, L2 System Architecture, L3 Agent Coordination, L4 User Adaptation, comprising 23 core components. 4) Five-Layer Disorder Taxonomy for failure classification. 5) Elastic Organization as a novel MAS morphology. Validated via 100K-scale experiments and 33.6 days of production monitoring.

Result: Channel fracture rate reduced from 69–98% to near 0%. System death probability reduced below 0.02% over the monitoring period.

Conclusion: The Intelligence Entropy Principle provides a theoretically grounded explanation for MAS degradation in production. The ADE framework, combined with the Five-Layer Disorder Taxonomy and Elastic Organization morphology, offers an effective engineering methodology for stabilizing LLM-driven multi-agent systems at scale.

Abstract: As LLM-driven multi-agent systems (MAS) transition from lab to production, system behavior exhibits nonlinear degradation. We introduce the Intelligence Entropy Principle: probability-driven systems spontaneously drift toward disorder, formalized as S(t) = S0 * exp(alpha*t/Cm), where Cm is a model capability coefficient we propose. Lyapunov analysis yields the stabilization condition lambda > alpha/Cm. We construct the ADE (Agent Delivery Engineering) four-layer framework (L1 Physical Laws through L4 User Adaptation) with 23 core components. Validation spans 100K-scale experiments and 33.6 days of production monitoring. We propose a Five-Layer Disorder Taxonomy unifying failures under structural collapse, and present Elastic Organization as an original MAS morphology. Results: channel fracture reduced from 69-98% to near 0%; system death probability below 0.02%.

</details>


### [74] [On the Reliability of Networks of AI Agents: Density Evolution, Stopping Sets, and Architecture Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18121)
*Ehsan Aghazadeh,Hossein Pishro-Nik*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: This paper models multi-agent AI systems as message-passing on sparse factor graphs inspired by LDPC codes, extending density evolution to handle nonlinear Boolean verifier nodes and three distinct erasure-type failure modes, yielding threshold predictions for when such systems succeed or fail.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern AI systems increasingly rely on ensembles of imperfect agents (proposers, verifiers, aggregators) that empirically outperform single models, yet there is little theoretical understanding of why they work or when they break. The authors seek to provide a rigorous framework for analyzing reliability and failure propagation in such collaborative architectures.

Method: The system is modeled as message-passing on a sparse, role-typed factor graph where check nodes are noisy Boolean verifiers. Three failure modes are modeled as erasures (agent abstention, verifier null output, lost messages). Check agents apply a logical-forcing rule (specializing to XOR, AND, OR, implication, Horn constraints). The authors prove a density-evolution theorem for asymptotic unresolved-subclaim fraction on random architectures, with extensions to deterministic locally tree-like sequences, and derive finite-length and converse results.

Result: A density-evolution theorem is proven predicting the asymptotic fraction of unresolved subclaims. The XOR specialization recovers classical LDPC density evolution on the BEC. The AND case reveals an asymmetry between positive and negative verifier certificates. The three failure modes do not collapse to a single effective channel, necessitating new threshold and converse analyses distinct from standard LDPC theory.

Conclusion: The framework provides a principled way to analyze reliability thresholds in multi-agent AI systems, exposing distinct failure propagation dynamics due to nonlinear, value-asymmetric verifier functions and multiple erasure modes—insights not obtainable by direct reuse of classical coding-theoretic tools.

Abstract: Modern AI systems increasingly solve a task not with a single model call but with several imperfect agents working together: some propose pieces of a solution, others verify them, and the results are combined. These systems often outperform any single model, yet it is rarely clear why they succeed or when they will fail. We model such a system as message passing on a sparse graph, the structure that underlies low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, and extend the density-evolution machinery of coding theory to this richer setting. In our model a task is a set of coupled binary subclaims, and an agent architecture is a sparse, role-typed factor graph whose check nodes are noisy Boolean verifier nodes, each computing a local Boolean function of the subclaims it touches. Three distinct failure modes, all modeled as erasures (an agent abstaining, a verifier returning no usable output, and a message lost between two agents), propagate as the agents exchange set-valued messages. The check agents combine these messages by a single logical-forcing rule that specializes to XOR, AND, OR, implication, and Horn constraints. This is more than a relabeling of LDPC theory: the verifier functions are nonlinear and value-asymmetric, and the three failure modes do not reduce to a single effective channel, so they require new threshold, finite-length, and converse results rather than a direct reuse of parity-check density evolution. We prove a density-evolution theorem that predicts the asymptotic fraction of unresolved subclaims on random role-typed architectures, with an extension to deterministic, locally tree-like graph sequences. The XOR case recovers the classical LDPC recursion on the binary erasure channel (BEC); the AND case exposes an asymmetry between positive and negative verifier certificates.

</details>
