### [75] [On the Memorization Behavior of LLMs in Generative Recommendation: Observations, Implications, and Training Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17276)
*Sunwoo Kim,Sunkyung Lee,Clark Mingxuan Ju,Donald Loveland,Bhuvesh Kumar,Kijung Shin,Neil Shah,Liam Collins*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: LLMs fine-tuned for generative recommendation heavily rely on one-hop memorization rather than leveraging pretrained knowledge. The paper proposes IIRG, a training strategy that teaches LLMs collaborative (multi-hop co-occurrence) and semantic relations, yielding significant gains especially for users whose target items are not reachable via simple memorization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based generative recommendation methods overlook LLMs' tendency to memorize training data. The authors investigate whether LLM gains over traditional GR baselines stem from genuine generalization or merely from one-hop memorization—recommending direct successors of training items. They find most gains are attributable to memorization, motivating a method to teach LLMs richer relational signals.

Method: The authors propose IIRG (presumably "Item-Item Relation Generation"), a training strategy with two components: (1) collaborative relations from multi-hop item co-occurrences in user interaction sequences, and (2) semantic relations among thematically similar items. These signals are incorporated into LLM fine-tuning beyond standard next-item prediction.

Result: LLMs exhibit more one-hop memorization than non-LLM GR models, with the majority of their performance gains concentrated on users whose target items are predictable via one-hop transitions. IIRG significantly outperforms standard next-item prediction training, with especially large improvements on users whose test items are not covered by training-time one-hop transitions.

Conclusion: LLM-based GR models suffer from a memorization-over-generalization problem. Teaching LLMs to capture both collaborative (multi-hop) and semantic item-item relations via IIRG effectively mitigates this issue, enabling better utilization of pretrained knowledge for users requiring deeper relational reasoning.

Abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) has emerged as a promising direction for recommender systems. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been increasingly adopted for GR, as their rich pretrained knowledge is expected to help them generalize beyond common user behavior patterns that traditional memorization-oriented baselines can capture. However, existing LLM-based GR works largely ignore LLMs' well-known tendency to memorize, which, if present in LLMs fine-tuned for GR, would restrict their utilization of pretrained knowledge. In this work, we investigate this concern by examining one-hop memorization, where a model recommends items that are direct successors of items in the training data. We show that LLMs do this more than non-LLM-based GR models-in fact, the vast majority of their gains over GR baselines are actually on users whose target items can be predicted through one-hop memorization. We intuit that improving performance on the remaining users requires LLMs to learn richer item-item relations beyond one-hop transitions. To achieve this, we propose IIRG, a novel training strategy that teaches LLMs to capture: (1) collaborative relations derived from item co-occurrences across multiple hops in user sequences, and (2) semantic relations among items with similar themes, both of which can serve as useful recommendation signals. We show that IIRG significantly improves over LLMs trained solely with standard next-item prediction, with especially large gains for users whose test items are not covered by train-time one-hop transitions.

</details>


### [76] [RSRank: Learning Relevance from Representational Shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17468)
*Archit Gupta,Sai Sundaresan,Debabrata Mahapatra*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a reranking method based on representational shift (RS)—the change in a query's internal LM representation when conditioned on a document. By aligning a candidate document's RS with that of an oracle document-set, the method produces calibrated relevance scores with a natural zero threshold, outperforming SOTA rerankers without heuristic tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing rerankers suffer from two key limitations: (1) reliance on heuristic thresholds for filtering relevant vs. irrelevant documents, and (2) use of LM logit signals (designed for next-token prediction) for relevance scoring, which is not their intended purpose. A principled, calibration-free relevance signal is needed.

Method: The authors identify representational shift (RS)—the difference in a query's internal representation before and after conditioning on a document—as a principled relevance signal. They show that alignment between a candidate document's RS and an oracle document-set's RS robustly indicates relevance. A lightweight training framework learns projections that map RS to calibrated relevance scores, with a natural zero threshold separating relevant from irrelevant content, eliminating heuristic tuning.

Result: The method achieves gains over state-of-the-art rerankers across diverse retrieval datasets, delivering superior filtering performance without requiring heuristic threshold tuning.

Conclusion: Representational shift provides a principled, well-calibrated signal for document relevance in RAG pipelines, enabling effective reranking with a natural zero threshold and outperforming existing approaches that rely on logit-based scoring and heuristic filtering.

Abstract: As enterprises deploy RAG-based systems to provide grounded responses to user queries, reranking has become a critical component for the final filtering step that separates relevant from distracting or irrelevant documents. Existing rerankers often rely on heuristic thresholds to achieve optimal filtering. Moreover, for relevance scoring, state-of-the-art methods use a language model's logit signals, which are designed for next-token prediction, not for assessing relevance. To address these limitations, we identify a principled signal for relevance: the representational shift (RS) induced in a query's internal state when conditioned on a document. We observe that the alignment between (a) RS induced by a candidate document and (b) RS induced by an oracle document-set provides a robust indicator of relevance. Building on this insight, we introduce a lightweight training framework that learns projections mapping RS to calibrated relevance scores. Our training objectives naturally filter irrelevant content at a zero threshold, reducing dependence on heuristic tuning. Across diverse retrieval datasets, our method delivers gains over SOTA rerankers.

</details>


### [77] [Temporal Preference Optimization for Unsupervised Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17664)
*HyunJin Kim,Jaejun Shim,Young Jin Kim,JinYeong Bak*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: TPOUR introduces Temporal Retrieval Preference Optimization (TRPO), a preference-learning method that guides unsupervised dense retrievers to favor temporally aligned documents without needing explicit timestamps, using interpolation in learned time embeddings to generalize to unseen periods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unsupervised dense retrievers excel at semantic similarity but fail to capture temporal relevance, retrieving semantically correct yet temporally misaligned documents (e.g., retrieving documents about a 2024 president for a query about 2019). Existing solutions require supervised training with explicit timestamps, which are often unavailable.

Method: TPOUR employs TRPO, which reinterprets preference optimization along the temporal dimension to steer retrievers toward temporally aligned documents. It uses a learned continuous time embedding space with interpolation, enabling generalization to unseen time periods without requiring explicit timestamp supervision.

Result: TPOUR outperforms both unsupervised and supervised baselines on temporal IR benchmarks. Notably, the TPOUR Contriever model, despite being ~72.7× smaller than Qwen-Embedding-8B, achieves +4.04 (+12.15%) average nDCG@5 on explicit temporal queries and +4.98 (+15.21%) on implicit temporal queries.

Conclusion: TRPO offers an effective, scalable approach for injecting temporal alignment into unsupervised dense retrievers without requiring explicit timestamp supervision, with strong generalization to unseen time periods via interpolated time embeddings.

Abstract: Unsupervised dense retrievers offer scalability by learning semantic similarity from unlabeled documents via contrastive learning, but they struggle to capture the temporal relevance, retrieving semantically related but temporally misaligned documents-an important aspect when a document collection spans multiple time periods (e.g., retrieving documents from 2018-2025 for "Who is the president in 2019?" introduces temporal ambiguity). Existing methods rely on supervised training with explicit timestamps, which are not always feasible. We propose TPOUR (Temporal Preference Optimization for Unsupervised Retriever), which uses our novel training method Temporal Retrieval Preference Optimization (TRPO). TRPO reinterprets preference learning in the temporal dimension, guiding the retriever to favor temporally aligned documents. TPOUR further generalizes to unseen time periods via interpolation in a learned time embedding, enabling continuous temporal alignment. Experiments on temporal information retrieval (T-IR), TPOUR outperforms both unsupervised and supervised baselines. Compared to Qwen-Embedding-8B, despite being about 72.7x smaller, TPOUR Contriever improves average nDCG@5 by +4.04 (+12.15%) on explicit and +4.98 (+15.21%) on implicit queries. We provide our code at https://github.com/agwaBom/TPOUR.

</details>


### [78] [Do Generative Recommenders Deepen the Information Cocoon? A Closed-Loop Simulation with LLM-powered User Simulators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17707)
*Jiyuan Yang,Gengxin Sun,Mengqi Zhang,Lingjie Wang,Yuanzi Li,Hongxi Cui,Xin Xin,Pengjie Ren*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper introduces RecLoop, a closed-loop simulation framework to study whether generative recommenders (using Semantic IDs) deepen information cocoons compared to traditional sequential recommenders. Results show generative recommenders maintain broader exposure diversity but can still induce SID-space concentration, with cocoon severity depending on tokenization strategy and model scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While information cocoons are well-studied in traditional recommendation, their formation in generative recommendation—where items are represented as Semantic ID sequences rather than atomic IDs—remains unexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically comparing how generative vs. traditional recommenders behave under repeated feedback loops.

Method: The authors propose RecLoop, a closed-loop simulation framework with LLM-driven user agents. They compare two generative recommenders and two traditional sequential baselines on two Amazon datasets across multiple feedback cycles. Beyond standard exposure-level metrics, they introduce "Code-Space Structural Cocoon," a model-level metric measuring concentration in the generated SID space.

Result: Generative recommenders are less prone to exposure-level cocoon formation than traditional baselines, preserving broader diversity and slowing cross-user homogenization. However, feedback loops still induce SID-space concentration. Collaborative-signal tokenization produces stronger cocoon effects than semantic tokenization, while larger models maintain greater code-space diversity and better retain access to niche content.

Conclusion: Information cocoons in generative recommendation are shaped not only by recommendation behavior but also by item tokenization strategy and model capacity. These factors must be considered when designing generative recommender systems to mitigate cocoon formation.

Abstract: Recommender systems alleviate information overload, yet repeated feedback between recommendations and user interactions can reinforce existing preferences and narrow users' exposure, forming information cocoons. While this phenomenon has been widely studied in traditional sequential recommendation, its impact on generative recommendation remains unclear. By replacing atomic item IDs with Semantic ID (SID) sequences, generative recommenders introduce a different recommendation mechanism whose role in information cocoon formation is not yet understood. To investigate whether generative recommenders deepen information cocoons, we propose \textsc{RecLoop}, a closed-loop simulation framework with LLM-driven user agents. We compare two generative recommenders and two traditional sequential baselines on two Amazon datasets across multiple feedback cycles. In addition to standard exposure-level metrics, we introduce \emph{Code-Space Structural Cocoon}, a model-level metric that measures concentration in the generated SID space. Experimental results show that generative recommenders are generally less prone to exposure-level cocoon formation than traditional baselines, preserving broader exposure diversity and slowing cross-user homogenization. However, feedback loops can still induce concentration within the generated SID space. We further find that cocoon severity depends strongly on tokenization strategy and model scale: collaborative-signal tokenization produces stronger cocoon effects than semantic tokenization, whereas larger models maintain greater code-space diversity and better retain access to niche content. These findings suggest that information cocoons in generative recommendation are shaped not only by recommendation behavior, but also by item tokenization and model capacity. Our code is available at https://github.com/Dregen-Yor/RecLoop.

</details>


### [79] [Understanding and Debugging Failures in N-Gram-Based Generative Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17721)
*Richard Takacs,Adrian Bracher,Svitlana Vakulenko*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper investigates failure modes in Generative Retrieval (GR), proposes a taxonomy of GR failure modes, empirically analyzes ngram-based methods (SEAL, MINDER) revealing issues like ambiguous docids and low identifier diversity, and introduces a web-based tool for visualizing and diagnosing GR failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative Retrieval is a promising paradigm where language models directly generate document identifiers for retrieval, but it introduces distinct failure mechanisms that are not well understood. Understanding these failure modes is critical for improving GR system robustness and reliability.

Method: The authors (1) construct a taxonomy of GR failure modes from literature review; (2) empirically evaluate two ngram-based GR methods — SEAL and MINDER — to identify common failure patterns such as ambiguous docids, low identifier diversity, and disproportionate impact of specific identifiers; (3) develop a web-based tool for interactive analysis of generated ngrams and their ranking contributions.

Result: The empirical analysis reveals three key failure patterns in ngram-based GR: ambiguous document identifiers that map to multiple documents, low diversity among generated identifiers, and certain identifiers having a disproportionately large influence on final rankings, degrading retrieval quality.

Conclusion: Generative Retrieval systems, while promising, suffer from systematic failure modes that can be taxonomized and empirically characterized. The introduced visualization tool enables the IR community to diagnose these failures, facilitating more robust GR system design.

Abstract: Generative Retrieval (GR) is an emerging Information Retrieval (IR) paradigm that is motivated by increasingly capable language models. In GR, a model directly generates identifiers for relevant documents. While these systems offer unique advantages, they also introduce distinct failure mechanisms. We explore these failure modes in three contributions: (1) We present a taxonomy of GR failure modes based on GR literature. (2) We empirically investigate failure in a subset of GR: ngram-based methods, more specifically, SEAL and MINDER. Our analysis reveals common issues, such as ambiguous docids, low identifier diversity, and the disproportionate impact of specific identifiers. (3) We introduce a new web-based tool that helps the IR community analyze generated ngrams and their respective contribution to the final ranking, providing an intuitive interface to identify where such GR methods go wrong.

</details>


### [80] [Non-negative Elastic Net Decoding for Information Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17910)
*Koki Okajima,Yasutoshi Ida,Tsukasa Yoshida,Yasuaki Nakamura*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper proposes Non-Negative elastic Net (NNN) decoding, a new retrieval paradigm that selects documents jointly as a sparse non-negative linear combination reconstructing the query embedding. Theoretically, NNN decoding strictly generalizes dense retrieval—handling every query dense retrieval can while also succeeding on queries involving correlated documents where dense retrieval fails. Experiments show consistent improvements over standard inner-product scoring, with further gains from end-to-end NNN-optimized training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense retrieval scores each document independently via inner product with the query embedding, making it oblivious to the full corpus context. This causes it to retrieve semantically similar but redundant documents, lacking diversity. The authors reframe retrieval as a joint decoding problem where documents are selected as a set, accounting for inter-document relationships across the corpus.

Method: The method, Non-Negative elastic Net (NNN) decoding, selects documents whose embeddings jointly reconstruct the query embedding via a sparse, non-negative linear combination. This is formalized as an optimization problem combining ℓ₁ and ℓ₂ regularization with non-negativity constraints. The authors also propose an end-to-end training procedure that directly optimizes embeddings for NNN decoding rather than for inner-product scoring.

Result: A theoretical separation result: for any corpus, NNN decoding handles every query that dense retrieval correctly handles, and additionally handles queries on corpora with correlated documents where dense retrieval fails. Empirically, applying NNN decoding to frozen inner-product-trained embeddings yields consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks. End-to-end NNN-optimized embeddings produce significant further gains, surpassing dense retrieval across all metrics and benchmarks.

Conclusion: NNN decoding establishes a new paradigm for leveraging dense embeddings in IR, moving beyond standard inner-product scoring to a joint decoding approach that naturally promotes diversity and handles corpus-level dependencies. The work demonstrates both theoretical superiority and practical performance gains.

Abstract: Dense retrieval has become the dominant paradigm in information retrieval, in which each document is scored against a query by the inner product of their vector embeddings, and the top-$k$ documents by score are retrieved for this query. However, since each document's score depends solely on the embedding of the query and itself, the retrieval process is oblivious to the content of the entire corpus. Therefore, dense retrieval cannot avoid selecting semantically similar documents from the corpus, which may result in a non-diverse, redundant set of retrieved documents. To this end, we approach retrieval as a joint decoding problem, in which documents are selected as a set with regard to the context of the rest of the corpus. To achieve this, we propose Non-Negative elastic Net (NNN) decoding, which selects documents whose embeddings jointly reconstruct the query embedding as a sparse non-negative linear combination.
  Our main theoretical result establishes a strict separation between dense retrieval and NNN decoding. For any corpus, every query correctly handled by dense retrieval is also handled by NNN decoding, while on corpora containing correlated documents, NNN decoding additionally handles queries that dense retrieval cannot. Experimental results indicate that applying NNN decoding to frozen embeddings trained for inner-product scoring yields consistent improvements across several benchmarks. Moreover, we introduce an end-to-end training procedure which optimizes the embeddings for NNN decoding, producing significant performance gains surpassing in all metrics and benchmarks compared to dense retrieval. Our work establishes a new paradigm for leveraging dense embeddings in information retrieval, beyond the standard practice of inner-product scoring.

</details>


### [81] [IUU+DB: Tracking Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated Fishing, Seafood Fraud, and Labor Abuse through LLM-driven Information Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18181)
*Henry Bodwell,Hong Yang,John C. Simeone,Kelvin Gorospe,Bella Sullivan,Lana Huang,Jessica Gephart,Sandy Aylesworth,Molly Masterton,Naren Ramakrishnan*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper proposes IUU+DB, an LLM-driven system that ingests heterogeneous documents to build a global incident database of illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing plus associated environmental and supply chain crimes (IUU+). It classifies incidents, extracts key entities, supports deduplication and trend analysis, and is validated as useful for research, industry risk assessment, and policy enforcement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantitative understanding of IUU fishing and broader fisheries-related crimes (IUU+) — including frequency, geography, species, actors, and illicit activity patterns — remains difficult to obtain despite its recognized threat to marine ecosystems, markets, and livelihoods. Fragmented evidence across heterogeneous sources hinders systematic analysis.

Method: The authors develop IUU+DB, a large language model (LLM) driven system that ingests heterogeneous documents, classifies whether they describe IUU+ incidents, extracts structured data elements (actors, locations, species, vessels, violations, enforcement outcomes), and supports deduplication and trend analysis to construct a global incident database.

Result: Case studies and validation demonstrate that IUU+DB effectively organizes fragmented evidence, surfaces geographic and behavioral hotspots, supports fisheries-specific academic/NGO research, assists industry source and species risk assessments, and aids government policy implementation and targeted enforcement.

Conclusion: IUU+DB provides a scalable, LLM-powered solution for systematically capturing and analyzing IUU+ incidents globally, bridging a critical data gap and serving diverse stakeholders across academia, industry, NGOs, and government.

Abstract: Illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing (IUU) traditionally refers to fishing activities that violate applicable laws or occur in areas that lack applicable laws. We propose the term IUU+ to capture a broader suite of fisheries sector environmental and associated supply chain trade-related crimes and behaviors. Although IUU+ activity is widely recognized as a serious threat to marine ecosystems, markets, and livelihoods, a quantitative understanding of these incidents, e.g., their frequency, geography, species, actors, and patterns in the type of illicit activity, remains difficult to obtain. We propose IUU+DB, a large language model driven system for building a global incident database of IUU+ activity. The system ingests heterogeneous documents, classifies whether they describe relevant incidents, extracts key data elements such as actors, locations, species, vessels, violations, and enforcement outcomes, and supports deduplication and trend analysis. Case studies and validation results show that IUU+DB can help organize fragmented evidence, surface geographic and behavioral hotspots, support fisheries-domain specific research in academia and non-government organizations, assist source and species risk assessments for industry, and provide support for policy implementation and targeted enforcement efforts to government agencies.

</details>


<div id='cs.SE'></div>

# cs.SE [[Back]](#toc)

### [82] [LogCopilot: Automating Log Aggregation Analysis through Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17094)
*Senyu Xie,Chenxi Zhang,Tong Zhou,Jiacheng Liu,Xiaoyu Hong,Qingshan Li,Xin Peng*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LogCopilot is an LLM-based framework that automates log aggregation analysis by translating natural language instructions into LogQL queries, using a hierarchical knowledge base and tool calling, achieving 76.8% average accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual writing of DSL queries (e.g., LogQL) for log aggregation systems like Grafana Loki and ELK is time-consuming and labor-intensive, requiring deep knowledge of both the query language syntax and the log contents. There is a need for automated log analysis from natural language instructions.

Method: LogCopilot leverages large language models (LLMs) with two key components: (1) a hierarchical knowledge base that represents and retrieves key knowledge from logs, and (2) a tool-calling mechanism that generates and executes LogQL queries to perform automated log aggregation analysis based on natural language instructions.

Result: Evaluated on four log datasets, LogCopilot achieves an average accuracy of 76.8%, outperforming baseline approaches, and demonstrates effectiveness specifically in LogQL query generation.

Conclusion: LogCopilot effectively automates log aggregation analysis by combining LLMs with structured knowledge retrieval and query generation, significantly reducing the manual effort required for log analysis tasks.

Abstract: Logs record the runtime behavior of software and are widely used in various tasks such as debugging, testing, and fault diagnosis. With the increase in system size and complexity, log analysis has gradually become a challenging task. Current industrial systems typically use log aggregation systems such as Grafana Loki and ELK to simplify the log collection and analysis process. Engineers write queries using the DSL query language provided by these systems can complete a variety of log analysis tasks. However, writing these queries is often time-consuming and labor-intensive, as it requires engineers to have a thorough understanding of the DSL syntax and the detailed information contained in the logs. To address these challenges, this paper proposes LogCopilot, an automated log aggregation analysis framework based on large language models (LLMs). LogCopilot accepts natural language log analysis instructions and accomplishes automated log analysis through knowledge retrieval and tool calling. LogCopilot constructs a hierarchical knowledge base to represent and provide key knowledge in logs. And it achieves automated log aggregation analysis by generating and executing LogQL queries. The evaluation based on four log datasets confirm the effectiveness of LogCopilot, which achieves an average accuracy of 76.8% and outperforms baseline approaches. Moreover, experiment results shows that LogCopilot is effective in LogQL query generation.

</details>


### [83] [Software Delegation Contracts: Measuring Reviewability in AI Coding-Agent Work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17099)
*Vincent Schmalbach*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A controlled pilot study on 64 AI coding agent runs found that explicit software delegation contracts did not improve task correctness (all runs passed acceptance tests) but significantly improved reviewability—enhancing evidence sufficiency, reducing reviewer ambiguity, and eliciting artifacts like known-limitations sections and checklists—at a cost of +13% tokens and +38% time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work introduced the concept of a "software delegation contract" (covering task, authority, work package, and acceptance context) as a unit of analysis for delegated AI coding work, but had not empirically measured its effects. The authors aimed to test whether such contracts improve task outcomes or reviewability.

Method: A dependency-free TypeScript API task environment was built with seeded defects and documentation gaps. Ten tasks across five families were authored. 64 agent runs were executed across two model tiers under three conditions: (1) realistic issue-style prompt, (2) explicit delegation contract, (3) contract with a required evidence bundle. Each run was scored using hidden acceptance tests, mutation checks, and scope analysis. Three independent condition-blinded model-based reviewers assessed each run using a fixed rubric, yielding 192 reviews.

Result: All 64 runs passed hidden acceptance checks with zero scope violations—contracts did not improve objective outcomes. However, contracts significantly improved reviewability: evidence sufficiency improved in 22/30 paired comparisons (none worsened, +0.83 on 5-point scale, p<0.0001, Cliff's delta=0.66); reviewer ambiguity decreased (p=0.035). Key artifacts (changed-file lists, known-limitations, residual-risk sections, reviewer checklists) appeared mostly or only when demanded by contract. Contracts cost +13% agent tokens and +38% wall-clock time, with larger effects for the weaker model tier.

Conclusion: On small, self-contained tasks, delegation contracts buy reviewability rather than correctness. The primary benefit is making AI-generated code submissions easier and more reliable to review, not improving the functional quality of the code itself.

Abstract: AI coding agents increasingly accept assigned software tasks, modify repositories under bounded authority, and return work packages for review. Prior work proposed the software delegation contract, covering the task, authority, returned work package, and acceptance context, as the unit of analysis for delegated coding work, but did not measure its effects. This paper reports a controlled pilot study of explicit delegation contracts for coding agents. We built a dependency-free TypeScript API task environment with seeded defects and documentation gaps, authored ten tasks across five families, and ran 64 agent executions across two model tiers under three conditions: a realistic issue-style prompt, an explicit delegation contract, and a contract with a required evidence bundle. Each run was scored with hidden acceptance tests, mutation checks, and scope analysis, then reviewed by three independent condition-blinded model-based reviewers using a fixed rubric, for 192 reviews. Explicit contracts did not improve objective task outcomes: all 64 runs passed hidden acceptance checks, with zero scope violations. They did improve reviewability. Evidence sufficiency improved in 22 of 30 paired comparisons and worsened in none (+0.83 on a 5-point scale, p < 0.0001, Cliff's delta = 0.66); reviewer ambiguity decreased (p = 0.035); changed-file lists, known-limitations sections, residual-risk sections, and reviewer checklists appeared mostly or only when demanded by the contract. Contracts cost +13% agent tokens and +38% wall-clock time, with larger effects for the weaker model tier. On these small tasks, delegation contracts bought reviewability rather than correctness.

</details>


### [84] [Cluster-Aware Dual-Level Test Specification Generation for Large-Scale Automotive Software Requirements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17197)
*Hazem Ayman,Menna Sedik,Kareem Mostafa,Mahmoud Soliman,Samer Saber,Ibrahim Habib*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An automated three-stage pipeline ("Cluster-then-Summarize") uses sentence-transformers, UMAP, HDBSCAN clustering, and map-reduce summarization to generate Automotive SPICE SWE.6-compliant test specifications at scale, preserving inter-requirement dependencies while overcoming LLM context-window limits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual generation of Automotive SPICE SWE.6 test specifications doesn't scale to thousands of requirements (consuming weeks of effort). Standard LLM approaches fail because processing requirements individually loses inter-requirement dependencies, while batch processing exceeds context-window limits, causing incomplete integration coverage and redundant tests.

Method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) Requirement embedding via sentence transformers, then dimensionality reduction with UMAP and density-based clustering with HDBSCAN, using an automatic minimum cluster size selection based on combined Silhouette and Calinski-Harabasz scores. (2) Multi-level map-reduce summarization that distills clusters into concise, domain-conformant descriptions retaining quantitative thresholds and safety integrity levels. (3) Test specification generation at two levels — individual requirement verification and cluster-level integration tests — with a nearby-cluster context mechanism for bounded cross-feature awareness, grounded via Retrieval-Augmented Generation on ISO 26262 and ASPICE standards.

Result: On automotive requirement datasets of varying scale, the cluster-aware approach improves integration test coverage and maintains summarization fidelity compared to baselines, while scaling efficiently to thousands of requirements.

Conclusion: The Cluster-then-Summarize pipeline effectively addresses the scalability and dependency-awareness limitations of LLM-based test specification generation for automotive systems, enabling SPICE-compliant automation at industrial scale.

Abstract: Generating test specifications that satisfy Automotive SPICE SWE.6 requirements becomes increasingly challenging and time-consuming as projects scale to thousands of requirements. Because this manual process often consumes weeks of engineering effort, automation becomes a critical necessity. However, standard Large Language Model (LLM) approaches struggle at scale: processing requirements individually discards vital inter-requirement dependencies, while feeding entire corpora at once exceeds context-window limits, leading to incomplete integration coverage and redundant test cases. This paper presents a novel "Cluster-then-Summarize" pipeline that addresses these limitations through three-stages. Requirements are embedded using sentence transformers and grouped using UMAP dimensionality reduction followed by HDBSCAN density-based clustering. This grouping utilizes an automatic minimum cluster size selection driven by a quality criterion combining normalized Silhouette and Calinski-Harabasz scores. A multi-level map-reduce summarization algorithm then distills each cluster into concise, domain-conformant descriptions while preserving quantitative thresholds and safety integrity levels. The pipeline exploits the derived cluster topology to generate test specifications at two levels: individual requirement verification and cluster-level integration tests that verify cross-requirement feature behavior. A nearby-cluster context mechanism provides bounded cross-feature awareness during each LLM call, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation grounds all outputs in ISO 26262 and ASPICE standards. Evaluation on automotive requirement datasets of varying scale demonstrates that the cluster-aware approach improves integration test coverage and maintains summarization fidelity compared to baseline methods while scaling efficiently to thousands of requirements.

</details>


### [85] [Trust-Aware Multi-Agent Traceability: Confidence-Calibrated Knowledge Graphs for Consistent Software Artifact Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17203)
*Mohamed Essam,Kareem Wael,Azza Hassan,Ahmed Haitham,Mahmoud Soliman,Samer Saber,Ibrahim Habib*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A trust-aware coordination framework using a shared knowledge graph with calibrated confidence scores prevents error propagation in multi-agent software engineering pipelines. Validated on an automotive case study, ablation shows confidence calibration is essential.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent AI pipelines for software engineering suffer from error propagation when upstream agents pass low-confidence decisions to downstream agents, creating orphaned requirements, contradictory links, and compliance gaps — particularly dangerous in safety-critical domains.

Method: A trust-aware coordination framework built on a shared knowledge graph acting as both semantic memory and coordination surface. It features: (1) a two-stage traceability link prediction pipeline (embedding-based retrieval + LLM-based multi-criteria analysis), (2) a traceability seeding mechanism comparing derivation-time vs. validation-time confidence, and (3) a consistency protocol with confidence threshold gating, confidence divergence detection, and conflict resolution.

Result: Evaluated on an automotive software engineering case study, measuring link prediction calibration, protocol effectiveness, threshold sensitivity, and traceability seeding impact. Ablation studies confirmed that confidence calibration is essential for effective pipeline coordination.

Conclusion: Confidence-calibrated coordination via a shared knowledge graph is a viable and necessary approach to mitigating error propagation in multi-agent software engineering pipelines, with particular relevance to safety-critical systems.

Abstract: Multi-agent AI systems are increasingly used to automate software engineering tasks including requirements analysis, architecture design, test generation, and traceability linking. When these agents operate as a sequential pipeline over shared software artifacts, errors and low-confidence decisions made by upstream agents propagate to downstream stages, producing orphaned requirements, contradictory links, and compliance gaps that pose significant risks in safety-critical domains. We propose a trust-aware coordination framework where a shared knowledge graph serves as both centralized semantic memory and a coordination surface through which agents assess and build upon each other's contributions using calibrated confidence scores. Our approach introduces a two-stage traceability link prediction pipeline combining embedding-based retrieval with LLM-based multi-criteria analysis, a traceability seeding mechanism that enables comparison between derivation-time and validation-time confidence, and a consistency protocol governing pipeline interactions through confidence threshold gating, confidence divergence detection, and conflict resolution. We evaluate on an automotive software engineering case study measuring link prediction calibration, protocol effectiveness, threshold sensitivity, and the impact of traceability seeding. Ablation studies confirm that confidence calibration is essential for effective pipeline coordination.

</details>


### [86] [Supporting the Adoption of Privacy-Enhancing Technologies through Requirements Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17387)
*Oleksandr Kosenkov,Vadym Honcharenko,Abhinava Singh,Volodymyr Spirin,Danica Vranjanin*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: PETs adoption remains limited despite decades of research and industry support. This paper applies a requirements engineering (RE)-driven perspective to examine adoption challenges across multiple stakeholder groups (developers, integrators, adopters) and disciplinary viewpoints (engineering, law, business), arguing that RE can systematically reconcile these perspectives to facilitate practical PET adoption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite substantial research, regulatory backing, and industry interest, the practical adoption of privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs) in software engineering remains stubbornly limited. Recurring challenges—technical complexity, insufficient training—persist unresolved, motivating the need for a fresh, cross-disciplinary diagnostic approach.

Method: The authors adopt an industrial challenge paper approach, applying a requirements engineering (RE)-driven analytical lens. They examine PET adoption challenges across three stakeholder groups (PET developers, integrators, and adopters) and three disciplinary perspectives (engineering, law, and business), arguing that RE provides the mechanisms to explicitly specify and coordinate these viewpoints.

Result: The analysis reveals that adoption impediments arise from neglecting any one of the three complementary viewpoints. Engineering challenges (e.g., architectural impact), business concerns (e.g., cost–benefit implications), and legal considerations (e.g., regulatory compliance contribution) are interdependent. Failure in any domain can cascade into implementation failure. Explicit RE-driven specification enables meaningful cross-stakeholder coordination.

Conclusion: RE can serve as a facilitating framework for PET adoption by systematically addressing engineering, business, and legal viewpoints in an integrated manner. Explicitly specifying these concerns within RE processes enables stakeholders to coordinate effectively, resolve persistent adoption barriers, and realize the benefits of PETs in practice.

Abstract: In recent decades, privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs) have been recognized as a means of meeting regulatory and user privacy requirements in software systems that process personal data. Despite substantial research efforts, support from regulators, contributions by large technology companies such as Google and Microsoft, and growing interest among software practitioners, the practical adoption of PETs remains limited. Existing research consistently identifies recurring challenges to PETs adoption in SE, such as technical complexity and insufficient training. Despite ongoing research efforts, these challenges largely remain unresolved in practice.
  In this industrial challenge paper, we apply a practical, requirements engineering (RE)-driven perspective to examine challenges to PET adoption across multiple stakeholder groups (PET developers, integrators, and adopters) as well as across different disciplinary perspectives (engineering, law, and business).
  We argue that RE can facilitate the adoption of PETs by systematically addressing each of the complementary engineering, business, and legal viewpoints on privacy. Neglecting challenges in any of these viewpoints (e.g., the impact of PETs on software architecture, their business implications, and their contribution to regulatory compliance) can increase the impediments or even lead to implementation failure. In practice, explicit specification of these viewpoints within RE can enable meaningful coordination among stakeholders to more effectively realize the benefits of PETs in software engineering.

</details>


### [87] [OmniDroneX: An LLM-Assisted Holistic Drone-as-a-Service Ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17510)
*I-Ling Yen,Akeem Mohammed,Farokh Bastani,San-Yih Hwang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: OmniDroneX proposes a unified Drone-as-a-Service ecosystem that transforms UAVs from fixed-function platforms into dynamically composable entities via a vendor-agnostic interface (libUAV), a physical-service abstraction model (PT-SOA), and pervasive integration of large language models (LLMs) for automated service composition, workflow generation, and natural-language mission specification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current UAV deployments suffer from gaps in systems research, with drones operating as fixed-function platforms that lack dynamic composability, interoperability, and integration with external infrastructures, limiting scalability and adaptability in complex environments.

Method: The authors propose the OmniDroneX architecture built on two core components: (1) libUAV, a unified vendor-agnostic interface bridging low-level physical primitives with high-level mission intent, and (2) PT-SOA, a formal physical-service abstraction model. LLMs are applied across multiple architectural layers to identify/formalize primitive device functions, support automated service composition and workflow generation, and enable interactive natural-language mission specification. The framework incorporates six composition techniques: physical layer, spatiotemporal, functional, collaborative, exception-aware, and QoS-based service compositions.

Result: The paper is a systems/architecture proposal paper; the abstract describes architectural features and capabilities but does not report quantitative experimental results. The claimed contributions are the design of a scalable, resilient, self-evolving UAV ecosystem framework with LLM-driven automation across the service composition stack.

Conclusion: OmniDroneX establishes a foundation for next-generation UAV ecosystems that are scalable, resilient, and self-evolving, enabling drones to operate as dynamically composable service entities in complex and dynamic environments.

Abstract: Despite rapid advances in UAV technologies, current deployments remain limited due to several gaps in UAV systems research. To address these challenges, we propose OmniDroneX, a unified Drone-as-a-Service ecosystem, in which drones are transitioned from fixed function platforms into dynamically composable entities that can be integrated with external infrastructures to offer omni-capabilities. OmniDroneX bridges low-level physical primitives with high-level mission intent through a unified vendor-agnostic interface (libUAV) and a formal physical-service abstraction model (PT-SOA). A core innovation is the diverse application of large language models (LLMs) across multiple layers of the OmniDroneX architecture. LLMs are used to assist in identifying and formalizing primitive device functions and abstract service definitions, supporting automated service composition and workflow generation, and enabling interactive, natural-language mission specification and refinement. OmniDroneX also incorporates important categories of composition techniques that are essential in dynamic UAV systems, including physical layer composition for drone capability augmentation, as well as spatiotemporal, functional, collaborative, exception-aware, and QoS-based service compositions. Collectively, these features allow OmniDroneX to serve as a foundation for scalable, resilient, and self-evolving UAV ecosystems operating in complex and dynamic environments.

</details>


### [88] [Unlocking LLM Code Correction with Iterative Feedback Loops](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17514)
*Le Zhang,Suresh Kothari*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates how well LLMs can iteratively refine their own code using compiler and testcase feedback, comparing reasoning vs. non-reasoning models across two languages, and finds that reasoning models leverage feedback more effectively while syntactic/runtime errors are easier to fix than logical failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing code generation benchmarks evaluate only single-attempt accuracy, ignoring the iterative, feedback-driven refinement process that mirrors real-world software development. There is a gap in understanding how LLMs respond to execution feedback (compiler errors, test failures) across multiple rectification cycles.

Method: The authors construct an iterative refinement framework where four LLMs (spanning reasoning and non-reasoning architectures) generate code for real-world programming problems in two languages. After each attempt, models receive compiler error messages and testcase feedback, then re-generate code. Novel metrics are introduced to categorize failure types (syntactic, runtime, logical/algorithmic), track rectification patterns, and quantify improvement trajectories across iterations.

Result: Reasoning models consistently improve over successive iterations and substantially outperform non-reasoning models in leveraging execution feedback. Syntactic and runtime errors prove far more tractable for LLMs to rectify than logical or algorithmic failures, which remain stubbornly difficult to resolve even with iterative feedback.

Conclusion: Iterative refinement with execution feedback significantly enhances LLM code generation quality, but model architecture matters — reasoning models benefit far more. Feedback loops are practically valuable, yet fundamental limitations persist for deep algorithmic errors, highlighting areas needing further advancement.

Abstract: Large Language Models have shown remarkable capabilities in code generation. However, most existing evaluations focus only on single-attempt accuracy and overlook the iterative refinement process that is central to real-world programming. This study presents a systematic investigation of LLMs' ability to rectify their own code through execution feedback. Using real-world programming problems across four models and two major programming languages, this study evaluates performance using iterative refinement framework where LLMs receive compiler error messages and testcase feedback after each attempt. This study introduces metrics to evaluate code failures, analyze rectification patterns, and compare the effectiveness of reasoning and non-reasoning models, offering actionable insights into both the understanding and practical application of feedback loops in LLM-driven code generation systems. Results show that reasoning models consistently improve over iterations, substantially outperforming non-reasoning models in leveraging feedback, while syntactic and runtime errors are far more tractable than logical or algorithmic failures.

</details>


### [89] [Understanding LLMs in Title-Abstract Screening: From Disagreements to Recommendations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17588)
*Mika Mäntylä,Patricia Matsubara,Katia Romero Felizardo,Miikka Kuutila,Marco Gerosa,Savio de Sousa Sampaio,Tayana Conte,Igor Steinmacher*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper qualitatively investigates why LLMs fail in title-abstract screening for systematic reviews, identifying recurring failure patterns (boundary ambiguity, keyword overemphasis, incorrect topic inference) and proposing actionable recommendations for practitioners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior studies on LLM-assisted title-abstract screening in systematic reviews report mixed accuracy but neglect the reliability question—specifically, *how and why* LLMs produce disagreements with human screeners. Understanding failure modes is essential before LLMs can be responsibly deployed in high-stakes evidence synthesis workflows.

Method: The authors conducted a qualitative analysis of human-LLM disagreements across six software engineering systematic reviews encompassing over 1,000 primary studies. Papers were screened independently by human experts and LLMs in zero-shot mode. Disagreement cases were then systematically examined to identify recurring causal patterns. Quantitative agreement was measured via Cohen's Kappa (range: 0.52–0.77).

Result: Three recurring failure modes were identified: (1) boundary ambiguity in key terminology leading to inconsistent inclusion/exclusion decisions, (2) keyword overemphasization where LLMs overweight surface-level lexical matches while missing semantic nuance, and (3) incorrect topic inference where LLMs misjudge the actual subject of a paper. Kappa values across the six SRs ranged from 0.52 (moderate) to 0.77 (substantial agreement).

Conclusion: LLM-based screening failures are systematic rather than random, making them diagnosable and potentially mitigable. Recommendations include: validating semantic understanding prior to deployment, employing multiple LLMs for cross-validation, and concentrating human validation efforts on borderline cases. The authors call for future empirical validation of these recommendations and the development of community-wide normative guidelines for LLM use in systematic reviews.

Abstract: Several studies have examined the use of large language models (LLMs) for title-abstract screening in systematic reviews (SRs), reporting mixed accuracy. However, questions of reliability remain largely unaddressed. In this study, we go beyond quantitative LLM-human agreement metrics and qualitatively investigate how and why LLMs fail. We also propose actionable recommendations. We analyzed disagreements between LLMs and researchers across six software engineering SRs and over 1,000 primary study papers. For each SR, papers were screened independently by human experts and LLMs in zero-shot mode, resulting in Kappa values ranging from 0.52 to 0.77. Qualitative analysis suggests that human-LLM disagreement results from recurring, identifiable causes, such as boundary ambiguity in key terms, keyword overemphasization, and incorrect topic inference. Based on these findings, we propose recommendations such as validating semantic understanding before deployment, running multiple LLMs, and focusing validation efforts on borderline cases. Future studies are needed to validate the impact of our recommendations, and community efforts are needed to develop normative guidelines on LLM usage in SRs.

</details>


### [90] [Why Model Credibility Isn't Enough: -Rethinking Trust in Simulation Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17593)
*Romain Barbedienne,Adeline Lanugue,Rim Kaddah,Julien Silande,Anthony Levillain,Cedric Leclerc,Maxime Hayet,Boussaad Soualmi,Cristian Maxim*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper surveys methods for assessing the credibility of simulation architectures based on the credibility of their constituent models, comparing sensitivity analysis, expert qualitative analysis, explainable AI, and network-based approaches against criteria such as rigor, generalization, and resource requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While individual simulation model credibility has been extensively studied, simulation systems are typically composed of multiple models within an architecture. The core open question is whether and how the credibility of an entire simulation architecture can be derived from or assessed based on the credibility of its component models — a problem the paper identifies as "assembly credibility."

Method: The paper conducts a survey and comparative analysis of four methodological approaches: (1) sensitivity analysis techniques, (2) qualitative assessment by domain experts, (3) explainability methods from AI (XAI), and (4) network-based approaches. Each approach is evaluated against defined criteria including rigor, generalization capability, and resource requirements to reveal respective strengths and weaknesses.

Result: The paper delivers a structured overview of the state of the art in assembly credibility, along with a comparative assessment matrix that maps each approach's performance against the evaluation criteria, exposing trade-offs between methodological rigor, generalizability, and practical resource constraints.

Conclusion: No single approach definitively solves the assembly credibility problem; each exhibits distinct strengths and weaknesses. The paper implies that hybrid or context-dependent strategies may be necessary, and it highlights gaps warranting further research in the compositional assessment of simulation credibility.

Abstract: Credibility of a simulation model is an important topic. Several approaches try to quantify the credibility of simulation. However, models are mostly assembled within a simulation architecture. Can the credibility of a simulation architecture be assessed based on the credibility of the models that comprise it? This paper aims to address this issue by providing an overview of the current state of the art in the field of assembly credibility. It will compare sensitivity analysis techniques, qualitative analysis by experts, explainability in AI, and networks. Finally, an assessment of the proposed approaches, based on criteria such as rigor, generalization, and resource requirements, will reveal the strengths and weaknesses of each approach.

</details>


### [91] [PracRepair: LLM-Empowered Automated Program Repair Inspired by Human-Like Debugging Practices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17612)
*Yu Cheng,Zhongxin Liu,Zhenchang Xing,Chao Ni,Qing Huang,Xiaoxue Ren*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: PracRepair is an LLM-based automated program repair framework that mimics human debugging by constructing dynamic context from failing executions, performing question-driven failure diagnosis, and iteratively refining patches using validation diagnostics. It significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on Defects4J and real-world bug datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based APR approaches underutilize dynamic information — specifically failure-execution dynamics and patch-validation dynamics. Failure traces are large and noisy, static-dynamic context lacks self-explanation, and validation feedback is typically too coarse-grained, limiting repair effectiveness.

Method: PracRepair introduces three key components: (1) on-demand construction of static-dynamic context from buggy programs and failure executions; (2) question-driven failure diagnosis that formulates explicit repair hypotheses; and (3) iterative patch refinement using validation diagnostics and trace-level behavioral change analysis.

Result: On Defects4J V1.2 and V2.0, PracRepair with GPT-3.5 fixes 139 and 136 bugs respectively; with GPT-4o, performance rises to 162 and 171 bugs. It also achieves state-of-the-art results on the RWB (Real-World Bugs) benchmark across multiple foundation models.

Conclusion: Leveraging rich dynamic execution information through a human-like debugging workflow — diagnosis, hypothesis formulation, and iterative refinement — enables LLMs to substantially improve automated program repair, outperforming static- and retrieval-based approaches across multiple benchmarks and model tiers.

Abstract: As software systems grow in scale and complexity, debugging and repair remain costly and time-consuming. Large language models (LLMs) have advanced automated program repair (APR), but existing LLM-based APR approaches still largely rely on static or retrieved context, error messages, and coarse-grained validation outcomes. As a result, they underutilize dynamic information for failure understanding and repair, including failure-execution dynamics and patch-validation dynamics. Effectively leveraging such information, however, is challenging: failure-execution traces are large and noisy, raw static-dynamic context is not self-explanatory, and patch-validation dynamics are often reduced to coarse feedback. To address these challenges, we propose \textsc{PracRepair}, a fully automated LLM-based APR framework inspired by human-like debugging practices. \textsc{PracRepair} constructs an on-demand static-dynamic context from buggy programs and failure executions, performs question-driven failure diagnosis to formulate explicit repair hypotheses, and iteratively refines candidate patches using validation diagnostics and trace-level behavioral changes. Experimental results on Defects4J V1.2 and V2.0 show that \textsc{PracRepair} consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Specifically, under GPT-3.5, \textsc{PracRepair} correctly fixes 139/136 bugs on Defects4J V1.2/V2.0, while under GPT-4o it further improves to 162/171. Moreover, \textsc{PracRepair} generalizes effectively to RWB (Real-World Bugs), achieving the best performance across multiple foundation models.

</details>


### [92] [FacProcessTwin: An LLM-Based System for Process Twin Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17666)
*Yash Pulse,Yong-Bin Kang,Abhik Banerjee,Prem Prakash Jayaraman*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: FacProcessTwin uses an LLM to automatically build process twins from plant documentation and operator input, drastically reducing development time (1/6 of manual) while maintaining high accuracy (95.2% F1). A human-in-the-loop mechanism ensures safety-critical data bindings are correct by deferring to operators in ambiguous cases, eliminating mis-bindings that a fully automated baseline would produce.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Process twins offer whole-process visibility and efficiency gains beyond asset-based digital twins, but developing them is prohibitively costly — requiring detailed modeling of process steps, equipment settings, product-specific parameters, and process variations, followed by binding to live operational data. The goal is to reduce this development burden using LLMs while ensuring safety-critical correctness through human oversight.

Method: FacProcessTwin takes process documentation and natural-language operator input, then uses a large language model to (1) generate a complete process model encompassing process steps, equipment, product settings, and variations, and (2) automatically bind those steps to live operational data. The result is rendered as an interactive process diagram where operators can monitor decisions and intervene at safety-critical binding steps — particularly when the system faces ambiguity — constituting a human-in-the-loop governance framework.

Result: Evaluated on a real-world case study at an Australian food manufacturer with 16 production process flows (spanning chilled, frozen, and aseptic shelf-stable categories with intra-product variations), FacProcessTwin achieved a mean F1 of 95.2% against ground truth for model generation and reduced development time to roughly one-sixth of manual effort. In safety-critical binding, a single-pass baseline mis-bound 75% of ambiguous tags, whereas FacProcessTwin's deferral mechanism eliminated all such errors.

Conclusion: LLM-driven generation of process twins is both feasible and effective, dramatically accelerating deployment while maintaining high fidelity. Crucially, human-in-the-loop governance is essential for safety-critical binding decisions where full automation fails; deferring to operators at points of ambiguity ensures correctness without sacrificing the overall efficiency gains.

Abstract: Process twins provide real-time representations of entire production processes. By capturing how process steps interact, rather than monitoring a single machine in isolation as an asset-based digital twin does, they have the potential to drive efficiency gains across the whole process. However, developing a process twin is costly. It requires accurately modelling the entire production process: its process steps, the equipment and product-specific settings each step uses, and its process variations. The resulting model must then be bound to live operational data. We present FacProcessTwin, a system that leverages a large language model (LLM) to reduce this development time, building a process twin from a plant's process documentation and natural-language input from an operator. FacProcessTwin generates this complete process model and then automatically binds its process steps to live operational data. The generated model and its data bindings are rendered as an interactive process diagram through which manufacturing personnel can monitor and correct the system's autonomous decisions, such as resolving uncertainty at safety-critical binding steps. We evaluate FacProcessTwin through a real-world case study of an Australian food manufacturer, covering 16 production process flows that span chilled, frozen, and aseptic shelf-stable product categories and include process variations within the same product. The results show that FacProcessTwin generates these process models accurately (a mean F1 of 95.2% against ground truth) and builds each twin in roughly a sixth of the manual time. Its human-in-the-loop governance then keeps the safety-critical bindings correct: at ambiguous tags where a single-pass baseline silently mis-binds 75.0% of the time, FacProcessTwin defers to the operator and mis-binds none.

</details>


### [93] [Position: Coding Benchmarks Are Misaligned with Agentic Software Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17799)
*Maria I. Gorinova,Macey Baker,Amy Heineike,Maksim Shaposhnikov,Rob Willoughby,Dru Knox*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Current coding benchmarks are misaligned with agentic software engineering because they collapse model, harness, and environment into a single end-to-end score, conflating distinct system components and penalizing valid alternative solutions while offering no component-level signal for iteration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents have become dominant in software engineering, but existing benchmarks were designed for a pre-agent era and treat the entire system (model + harness + environment) as a monolithic black box. This prevents meaningful diagnosis and iterative improvement of individual components.

Method: The paper presents a conceptual critique rather than an empirical method. It identifies and discusses three symptoms of benchmark misalignment: (1) conflation of model and harness in scores, (2) single-reference grading that penalizes valid alternative solutions, and (3) absence of component-level feedback signals.

Result: The analysis reveals that any component — models, harnesses, contexts, environments, or feedback signals — can shift benchmark scores by margins comparable to differences between adjacent model generations, making it impossible to attribute performance gains to specific improvements.

Conclusion: The field needs new benchmarking paradigms that disentangle the model from the rest of the agentic harness, support multi-reference or functional grading, and provide fine-grained component-level signals to enable principled iteration in coding agent development.

Abstract: Coding agents have become a major mode of software engineering, but the benchmarks we use to compare them were designed in a pre-agent era: they collapse model, harness, and environment into a single end-to-end score, typically computed against one reference solution, with no component-level signal for iteration. We argue that current coding benchmarks are misaligned with agentic software engineering. A coding agent in practice is not a model: it is a system harness -- a composite of models, harnesses, contexts, environments, and feedback signals, any one of which can move the benchmark score by margins comparable to those between adjacent model generations. We discuss three symptoms: (i) benchmark scores conflate the model with the rest of the harness; (ii) grading against a single reference solution penalises equally valid alternatives; and (iii) the absence of signal at the level of individual harness components makes the end-to-end system score difficult to iterate on.

</details>


### [94] [A Framework for Evaluating Agentic Skills at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17819)
*Maksim Shaposhnikov,Nicolas Fortuin,Simon Stipcich,Maria I. Gorinova,Amy Heineike,Rob Willoughby*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Presents an evaluation framework for assessing individual LLM agent skills, applies it to 500 real-world skills with 1,000 tasks, and benchmarks 19 model configurations (proprietary and open-source), revealing wide variance in instruction adherence and significant behavioral shifts when skills are provided.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent skills are rapidly adopted in industry as reusable knowledge artifacts for LLM agents, but cross-domain impact, performance across diverse model types, and a principled methodology for evaluating individual skills remain unexplored.

Method: An evaluation framework enabling skill authors to construct realistic tasks that rigorously assess skill-specific aspects. Applied at scale: 500 real-world skills → 1,000 derived tasks with instruction-following and goal-completion scoring rubrics. Benchmarked 19 agent-model configurations (both proprietary and open-source) on these tasks.

Result: Models exhibit wide variance in adherence to skill-encoded instructions, producing substantial differences in performance gains. Providing access to a skill significantly alters model behavior compared to no-skill baselines, demonstrating skills as a mechanism for encoding opinionated workflows.

Conclusion: The evaluation framework and dataset fill a methodological gap in skill assessment. Skills are a powerful mechanism for shaping LLM agent behavior, and the released dataset supports future research on agent skills.

Abstract: Agent skills -- structured, reusable knowledge artifacts that augment LLM agent capabilities -- have been rapidly adopted in industry, yet their cross-domain impact and use across commercial and open-source models remain under-studied, and no reusable methodology exists for evaluating an individual skill. In this work, we present an evaluation framework that lets a skill author construct realistic tasks to rigorously assess the aspects of a skill that matter most to them, and that estimates skill utility by solving those tasks. Further, we apply our evaluation approach at scale to 500 real-world skills, generating 1,000 tasks derived from the skills' content, along with instruction-following and goal-completion scoring rubrics. Using these metrics, we evaluate how 19 agent-model configurations, both proprietary and open-source, perform on the tasks. Our results show that models vary widely in how closely they adhere to the instructions encoded in skills, leading to substantial differences in their performance gains. Furthermore, we show that access to a skill significantly changes model behavior compared to the no-skill setup, providing an essential mechanism for encoding opinionated workflows into LLM agents. We release our evaluation dataset to support future work on agent skills.

</details>


### [95] [Planning to Hammer: Difficulty-Aware Decomposition for Automating Rocq Proofs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17981)
*Ning Zhang,Nongyu Di,Zenan Li,Yuan Yao,Xiaoxing Ma*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Quarry is a proof synthesis framework that combines LLM-based high-level proof planning with CoqHammer's local goal-solving. It uses an LLM to propose proof decompositions with sublemmas, ranks them via a hammer-solvability difficulty model, and recursively discharges sublemmas within a budget, achieving 7–13% improvement over baselines on Rocq benchmarks under a 10-minute wall-clock constraint.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-generated code demands rigorous formal verification, but producing machine-checked proofs in interactive theorem provers like Rocq remains a bottleneck. Existing approaches are polarized: LLMs excel at high-level proof strategy but lack local rigor, while automated tactics like CoqHammer reliably solve local goals but lack long-range planning. Neither approach alone suffices for complex proofs, motivating a hybrid framework that combines their complementary strengths.

Method: Quarry separates proof planning from proof execution. The LLM proposes multiple proof decompositions with arbitrarily complex sublemmas, which are type-checked in Rocq with sublemmas temporarily admitted. A proof-state-based difficulty model estimates hammer solvability and ranks candidate decompositions. Quarry then recursively proves sublemmas within a bounded budget, transforming long proofs into sequences of hammer-solvable obligations. The system is implemented on SerAPI and CoqHammer and evaluated with frontier LLMs across multiple Rocq benchmarks.

Result: Under a uniform 10-minute wall-clock budget, Quarry improved over the strongest baseline by 7% to 13% in proof success rate across three Rocq benchmarks. The planning-based decomposition with solvability-aware ranking substantially improved automation while maintaining predictable cost.

Conclusion: Reliable proof automation can be achieved by coordinating neural planning (LLMs) with symbolic execution (hammer tactics), rather than attempting to replace either. The planning-decomposition paradigm with solvability-aware ranking offers a practical path toward scalable, predictable formal verification.

Abstract: As AI-generated code proliferates, formal verification, particularly through interactive theorem provers such as Rocq and Isabelle, becomes increasingly important for ensuring software correctness. However, producing machine-checked proofs in such provers remains a bottleneck. Existing solutions bring complementary strengths to proof automation: large language models (LLMs) can propose high-level proof strategies but lack local rigor, while automated tactics such as CoqHammer can reliably discharge many local goals but lack long-range planning capabilities. To combine the best of both worlds, we present Quarry, a planning-based proof synthesis framework that separates proof planning from proof execution. Specifically, Quarry asks an LLM to actively propose multiple proof decompositions with arbitrary sublemmas, type-checks them in Rocq under temporarily admitted sublemmas, and ranks candidates using a proof-state-based difficulty model that estimates hammer solvability. It then recursively proves sublemmas within a bounded budget, effectively turning long proofs into sequences of hammer-solvable obligations. We implement Quarry on top of SerAPI and CoqHammer and evaluate it using multiple frontier LLMs across multiple benchmarks. The experimental results show that planning-based decomposition with solvability-aware ranking substantially improves automation while maintaining predictable cost. Under a uniform 10-minute wall-clock budget, Quarry improves over the strongest baseline by 7% to 13% in success rate across three Rocq benchmarks. These results demonstrate that reliable proof automation can be achieved by coordinating neural planning with symbolic execution rather than replacing either.

</details>


### [96] [All Smoke, No Alarm: Oracle Signals in Agent-Authored Test Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18168)
*Dipayan Banik,Kowshik Chowdhury,Shazibul Islam Shamim*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Analyzed 86,156 test-file patches from 33,596 agent-authored PRs across 2,807 GitHub repos. Found 80.2% of test patches contain weak or no explicit oracle signals. Strong oracles significantly improve merge likelihood (OR=1.28, p<0.001), yet raw test-file counts substantially overestimate verification strength.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI coding agents generate massive volumes of test code in open-source PRs (932,000+ agent-authored PRs across 116,000+ repos), but whether these test files contain meaningful verification logic (oracles) is unknown. Test-file presence is commonly used as a quality gate, yet files without assertions inflate perceived verification strength, creating a false sense of test adequacy.

Method: Empirical study of 86,156 test-file patches from 33,596 agent-authored PRs across 2,807 GitHub repositories, generated by five coding agents (OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Cursor, Claude Code). Qualitative analysis of 384 stratified patches produced a syntactic taxonomy of 8 oracle signal categories. This taxonomy was then applied at scale to classify all patches, followed by regression analysis linking oracle strength to merge outcomes and review effort, controlling for agent, PR size, repository popularity, task type, and language.

Result: 80.2% of test patches contain weak or no explicit oracle signals. While raw merge rates are lower for strong-oracle PRs, regression analysis adjusting for confounders shows strong oracles significantly improve merge likelihood (OR=1.28, p<0.001). Test file counts substantially overestimate actual verification strength.

Conclusion: Practitioners should not rely on test-file presence alone as a quality signal for agent-authored code. Oracle-aware quality checks provide a more accurate assessment of verification strength. Strong oracles are positively associated with merge acceptance after controlling for confounding factors.

Abstract: Software practitioners increasingly use AI coding agents that generate test code alongside production code in open source pull requests (PRs). Recent studies report more than 932,000 agent-authored PRs across more than 116,000 repositories, yet whether their test files contain meaningful verification logic remains underexplored. Test files lacking explicit assertions execute code without verifying behavior, so quality gates based on test-file presence overestimate verification strength. The goal of this paper is to help practitioners assess the verification strength of agent-authored patches by characterizing oracle signals and their link to merge outcomes and review effort. We conduct an empirical study of 86,156 test-file patches from 33,596 agent-authored PRs across 2,807 GitHub repositories produced by five coding agents: OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Cursor, and Claude Code. A qualitative analysis of 384 stratified patches informs a syntactic taxonomy of eight oracle signal categories. Applied at scale, 80.2% of test patches contain weak or no explicit oracle signals. While raw merge rates are lower for strong-oracle PRs, a regression analysis adjusting for agent, PR size, repository popularity, task type, and language shows strong oracles significantly improve merge likelihood (OR = 1.28, p < 0.001). Our findings suggest that test file counts substantially overestimate verification strength and that practitioners can adopt oracle-aware quality checks to more accurately evaluate agent-authored contributions.

</details>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [97] [Correct When Paired, Wrong When Split: Decoupling and Editing Modality-Specific Neurons in MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17057)
*Tingchao Fu,Wenkai Wang,Fanxiao Li,Huadong Zhang,Jinhong Zhang,Dayang Li,Yunyun Dong,Renyang Liu,Wei Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Current knowledge editing methods for MLLMs suffer from "editing decoupling failure": updated knowledge triggers correctly on multimodal inputs but reverts to outdated facts on unimodal inputs. The authors attribute this to knowledge being distributed across modality-specific pathways and propose DECODE, a method that disentangles and targets modality-specific neuron groups for consistent editing across all input modalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing knowledge editing paradigms for MLLMs exhibit a critical underexplored problem — editing decoupling failure — where edited knowledge is only accessible via multimodal (text-image) queries but fails when the same inputs are presented unimodally. This reveals a fundamental gap in how knowledge is stored and updated in MLLMs.

Method: The authors first conduct empirical analysis showing that entity knowledge in MLLMs is distributed across disentangled modality-specific pathways rather than stored as a unified representation. Based on this insight, they propose DECODE, which explicitly disentangles and localizes modality-specific neuron groups associated with targeted knowledge, enabling edits to propagate effectively to both multimodal and unimodal circuits.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that DECODE consistently achieves effective knowledge updates across different modality triggers (multimodal and unimodal), successfully mitigating editing decoupling failures compared to current paradigms.
