Conclusion: Knowledge in MLLMs is modality-disenangled rather than unified, causing editing decoupling failure. DECODE addresses this by targeting modality-specific neuron groups, enabling robust and consistent knowledge updates irrespective of input modality.

Abstract: Although Knowledge Editing provides an efficient mechanism for updating the knowledge of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), we find that current paradigms still suffer from an important yet remain underexplored issue : editing decoupling failure, where entity-related knowledge can be updated when the model is triggered by multimodal inputs (text--image query pairs), however, it often reverts to outdated pre-edit facts when the paired inputs are split into unimodal ones. Our in-depth empirical analysis reveals that the entity knowledge in MLLMs is not stored as a unified representation, but is instead distributed across disentangled modality-specific pathways. As a result, updates biased toward multimodal queries fail to propagate effectively to unimodal circuits. To bridge this gap, we propose DECODE, which explicitly disentangles and localizes modality-specific neuron groups for targeted knowledge. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DECODE consistently achieves effective knowledge updates under different modality triggers, thereby mitigating editing decoupling failures.

</details>


### [98] [Diagnosing and Repairing Shape-Prior Shortcuts in Long-Range Single-Shot Fringe Projection Profilometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17093)
*Adam Haroon,Anush Lakshman,Cody Fleming,Beiwen Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A mechanistic interpretability and conformal uncertainty quantification study reveals that a UNet baseline for long-range single-shot fringe projection profilometry solves the task via object-boundary shape priors rather than fringe-phase decoding. Architecturally constraining the network to output wrapped phase (PhiCalNet) reduces object MAE 3.3×. MI and UQ converge on the same failure locus: ±π wrap discontinuities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-range (standoff >1 m) single-shot fringe projection profilometry remains largely unaddressed due to three challenges: (1) inverse-square intensity falloff degrades fringe SNR and ground truth quality, (2) the single-shot problem is ill-posed without fringe-order information from a single image, and (3) existing learning-based architectures have not been studied mechanistically to understand how they actually solve the task.

Method: A diagnose-repair-verify framework is employed. First, a photorealistic synthetic benchmark (15,600 fringe images, 50 objects at 1.5–2.1 m) is constructed. Three MI probes (linear probing, Grad-CAM, flat-plane out-of-distribution test) diagnose that the UNet baseline relies on object-boundary shape priors. The repair is PhiCalNet: it outputs wrapped phase instead of depth and applies a fixed differentiable calibration layer mapping phase to depth, architecturally removing the shape-prior shortcut. A physics-informed soft-penalty loss on a depth-regressing network is tested as a control. Conformal UQ provides pixel-wise uncertainty, and both diagnostics are compared for convergence.

Result: The UNet baseline achieves 14.54 mm object MAE. All three MI probes converge: the network uses shape priors, not fringe-phase decoding. A physics-informed loss alone yields no measurable gain. PhiCalNet reduces object MAE 3.3× to 4.46 mm, with residual error concentrated at ±π wrap discontinuities (0.103% of pixels). Conformal UQ confirms: rejecting the top 5% of object pixels by snapshot disagreement cuts PhiCalNet RMSE by 64% (20.6→7.4 mm) versus only 3.5% for the baseline.

Conclusion: MI and UQ converge on the same physical failure locus, validating both as complementary diagnostics. Architectural constraints (outputting wrapped phase with a fixed calibration layer) are more effective than soft physics-informed loss penalties for preventing shape-prior shortcuts. The residual error is a physically interpretable wrap-discontinuity problem, opening a clear path for future improvement.

Abstract: Learning-based single-shot fringe projection profilometry (FPP) has been studied mostly at close range. The long-range regime (standoff beyond 1 m) remains largely unaddressed: inverse-square intensity falloff lowers fringe signal-to-noise ratio and degrades physical ground truth, the single-shot problem is ill-posed because fringe-order information is absent from one image, and these architectures have not been studied mechanistically. We present a diagnose-repair-verify study using mechanistic interpretability (MI) and conformal uncertainty quantification (UQ) as convergent diagnostics: they agree on one physical failure locus, driving and verifying an architectural repair. On a photorealistic synthetic benchmark (15,600 fringe images, 50 objects at 1.5-2.1 m), a best UNet baseline reaches 14.54 mm object mean absolute error (MAE). Three probes (linear probing, Grad-CAM, flat-plane out-of-distribution test) converge: the baseline solves the task via object-boundary shape priors rather than fringe-phase decoding. We repair this with PhiCalNet, which outputs wrapped phase rather than depth and applies a fixed differentiable calibration layer mapping phase to depth, removing the shape-prior solution from the hypothesis space architecturally rather than by a loss penalty. A physics-informed loss that enforces the same physics as a soft penalty on a depth-regressing network yields no measurable gain, isolating the architecture as the operative factor. PhiCalNet reduces object MAE 3.3x to 4.46 mm; the residual is carried by 0.103% of pixels at the +/-pi wrap discontinuity. Pixel-wise conformal UQ confirms the diagnosis: rejecting the top 5% of object pixels by snapshot disagreement cuts PhiCalNet RMSE by 64% (20.6->7.4 mm) versus 3.5% for the baseline. MI and UQ converge on the same failure locus.

</details>


### [99] [Informative Missingness to Generate Irregular Clinical Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17106)
*Hadi Mehdizavareh,Gabriele Santangelo,Giovanna Nicora,Simon Lebech Cichosz,Arianna Dagliati,Arijit Khan,Riccardo Bellazzi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A diffusion-based generative model (extending TimeDiff) jointly learns continuous lab values and discrete observation patterns from irregularly sampled EHR data, demonstrating that synthetic trajectories preserve clinically meaningful dependencies between patient physiology and missingness under MNAR conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In EHR data, the absence of a lab test is not random but reflects clinicians' decisions and patient physiology (informative missingness under MNAR). Most prior work treats missingness as a preprocessing artifact rather than modeling it directly. The authors argue that joint modeling of lab values and observation patterns is essential for generating realistic clinical time series and for future clinical foundation models.

Method: The method extends the TimeDiff diffusion framework with complementary diffusion objectives: one for continuous lab values and another for discrete missingness indicators. Chart times are aligned into 4-hour intervals and admissions segmented into 7-day windows. Each trajectory pairs a lab value with a corresponding observation indicator. Standard transformations and normalization stabilize training. The approach is evaluated on the DACMI benchmark derived from MIMIC-III.

Result: Generated data closely match real patient trajectories across individual lab distributions and joint value-missingness embeddings, demonstrating that the diffusion model captures clinically meaningful dependencies between physiology and testing behavior under MNAR-like missingness.

Conclusion: The model can serve as an initial component toward clinical foundation models by producing synthetic priors that preserve key physiology-missingness relationships. This motivates subsequent training of Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) that leverage informative missingness, planned as future work.

Abstract: Laboratory tests in electronic health records are collected irregularly, and the absence of a test order can be as informative as the measurement itself. Such missingness reflects clinicians' decisions and patient physiology, making it important to model it directly rather than treat it as a preprocessing artifact. Here we present a diffusion-based approach for generating clinical time series that jointly models laboratory values and their observation patterns using the public Data Analytics Challenge on Missing Data Imputation (DACMI) benchmark derived from MIMIC-III. To preserve realistic sampling, we align chart times into 4-hour intervals and segment admissions into 7-day windows, producing trajectories that pair each lab value with a corresponding observation indicator. Standard transformations and normalization are applied to stabilize training. Our method extends the TimeDiff framework to learn continuous lab values and discrete missingness patterns through complementary diffusion objectives. Experiments show that the generated data closely match real patient trajectories across individual lab distributions and joint value-missingness embeddings, demonstrating that diffusion models can capture clinically meaningful dependencies between patient physiology and clinicians' testing behavior under MNAR-like (missing-not-at-random) missingness. These preliminary results indicate that our model can serve as an initial component toward developing clinical foundation models. By producing synthetic priors that preserve key physiology-missingness relationships, this work motivates the subsequent training of Prior-Data Fitted Networks capable of leveraging informative missingness, which we will investigate in the extended work.

</details>


### [100] [Models Take Notes at Prefill: KV Cache Can Be Editable and Composable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17107)
*Bojie Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Prefix caching is fragile because a single changed field invalidates the entire downstream cache. This paper shows that in transformer KV caches, the model writes "conclusions" onto downstream tokens during prefill, and the field's own key/value vectors contribute under 1% to decisions. This insight enables (1) editable caching via an appended erratum and (2) composable caching via position-portable skill splicing, achieving up to 14.9× lower latency while maintaining decision identity with full recompute.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard prefix caching fails when even one field in a shared prefix changes, forcing full recomputation of the KV cache. Simply overwriting the changed field's vectors while reusing the rest also fails because the model acts on stale downstream information. The authors aim to understand *why* this happens and leverage that understanding to build efficient, editable, and composable KV cache mechanisms.

Method: The authors first establish causality across four model families: during prefill, the model writes the field-conditioned conclusion onto *downstream* tokens (not the field itself), with the field's own key/value driving under 1% of the decision. They reframe the KV cache as a "notebook of memoized conclusions." From this, they derive two mechanisms: (1) editable caching — appending a salient erratum to amend downstream notes, recovering decisions with chain-of-thought at ~1% compute cost; (2) composable caching — position-portable notes that can be RoPE-repositioned and spliced into any context. The approach is validated across scale, quantization, MoE, multimodal models, and attention variants via small adapters. A unified edit+compose agent is benchmarked in online vLLM, maintaining 98.5% prefix cache hit-rate and cutting p90 TTFT by 53–398×.

Result: Editing with chain-of-thought achieves 1.00 decision recovery at 8B scale using ~1% compute. Composable skill splicing yields logit cosine similarity of 0.90–0.999 against full recompute across twelve models, at O(L) rather than O(L²) time-to-first-token. The unified agent remains decision-identical to recompute at up to 14.9× lower latency. In online vLLM benchmarks, the approach maintains 98.5% prefix cache hit-rate, cutting p90 TTFT by 53–398×.

Conclusion: The KV cache behaves as a notebook of memoized conclusions where downstream tokens, not the field itself, carry decision-critical information. This enables lightweight, append-only editability and composability that composes naturally with production prefix caching, dramatically reducing latency without sacrificing decision fidelity. The method generalizes broadly across model architectures, scales, and modalities.

Abstract: Prefix caching reuses prefill only across an exactly shared prefix, so one changed field invalidates the entire downstream cache. Yet overwriting the field's own key/value vectors and reusing the rest leaves the model acting on the old value. The reason, established causally across four model families: at prefill the model has already written the field-conditioned conclusion onto downstream notes; the field's own key/value drives under 1% of the decision. Read as a notebook of memoized conclusions, two capabilities follow. (1) It is editable. A salient erratum amends the notes; and with chain-of-thought, editing the field alone recovers the decision (1.00 at 8B, ~1% compute), while without CoT it is ignored. (2) It is composable. The notes are position-portable, so a precompiled skill can be RoPE-repositioned and spliced into any context, indistinguishable from full recompute (logit cosine 0.90-0.999, twelve models) at O(L) rather than O(L^2) time-to-first-token. A unified edit+compose agent stays decision-identical to recompute at up to 14.9x lower latency. The approach applies to any per-token attention KV cache, validated across scale, quantization, Mixture-of-Experts, and multimodal caches, and extends to several attention variants through small adapters. Because the erratum is append-only, it composes with production prefix caching: in an online vLLM benchmark it keeps the prefix cache-aligned (98.5% hit-rate), cutting p90 time-to-first-token by 53-398x.

</details>


### [101] [Verified Detection and Prevention of Concurrency Anomalies in Multi-Agent Large Language Model Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17182)
*Sajjad Khan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper formalizes four concurrency anomalies in multi-agent LLM systems (stale-generation, phantom-tool, causal-cascade, tool-effect reordering) as analogues of classical database isolation anomalies. It presents the first machine-checked consistency hierarchy (L0–L4) with mechanically verified detectors, implemented and verified in three Rust runtimes, and reproduces real-world bugs in ByteDance's deer-flow and LangGraph's ToolNode.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems share mutable state across agents via memory stores, vector indices, and tool registries under long-running read-generate-write operations. Without proper concurrency control, these systems suffer from isolation anomalies that corrupt agent reasoning and action sequencing. The authors aim to formally characterize these anomalies and construct a verified consistency hierarchy analogous to classical database isolation levels.

Method: The authors model multi-agent LLM sharing as long-running read-generate-write operations under deterministic-generation semantics, enforced by durable-execution engines via deterministic replay. They formalize four concurrency anomalies in TLA+ with TLC-generated counter-examples, produce an exclusion lattice over the anomalies, and mechanically verify a maximal chain L0 ⊊ L1 ⊊ L2 ⊊ L3 ⊊ L4 within this lattice. A development of 274 Verus obligations (zero assume, zero admit) proves anomaly detectors sound and complete. Three Rust runtimes realize L0–L1 (pessimistic locking, serializable snapshot isolation, default-SI), with L2–L4 verified via dependency-free prevention twins. Real-world bugs are reproduced and fixed: a silent lost update in ByteDance's deer-flow (L0→L1 refinement) and tool-effect reordering in LangGraph's ToolNode (L3 commit-order sequencer).

Result: All four anomalies are mechanically demonstrated as realizable and strictly separable along the L0–L4 chain. The verified detectors are proven sound and complete against TLA+ specifications. Prevention twins for L2 (A3), L3 (A6), and L4 (A2) show 0/1000 anomalies versus 1000/1000 in unmodified runtimes. L2 runs live across three model families, preventing A3 in all 120 retracted sessions. The deer-flow lost update and LangGraph ToolNode reordering are both reproduced and corrected with verified refinements.

Conclusion: The contribution is the first machine-checked consistency hierarchy for multi-agent LLM runtimes, with mechanically verified detectors, runtime refinements, and realizability artifacts. The phenomena and lattice themselves are classical, recasting database isolation anomalies in the new context of LLM agent systems. The work demonstrates that formal methods (TLA+, Verus, deterministic replay) can provide rigorous concurrency guarantees for emerging multi-agent architectures.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems share state through memory stores, vector indices, and tool registries. We model such sharing as long-running read-generate-write operations under deterministic-generation semantics -- the regime durable-execution engines enforce by deterministic replay -- and formalize four concurrency anomalies in TLA+: stale-generation, phantom-tool, causal-cascade, and tool-effect reordering, structural analogues of classical isolation anomalies, each with a TLC counter-example. The exclusion lattice over these anomalies is trivial; the contribution is the mechanically verified realizability and strict separation of one maximal chain within it, $L_0 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq L_4$, to our knowledge the first machine-checked consistency hierarchy for such runtimes. A development of 274 Verus obligations (zero assume, zero admit; trust base: two structural axioms and a mutex correspondence) proves the detectors sound and complete against the specifications and each runtime its avoidance set. Three deployed Rust runtimes realize L0-L1 (pessimistic locking, serializable snapshot isolation, default-SI), each verified against stale-generation and refined to its state machine; L2-L4 are exec-mode-verified with dependency-free prevention twins (A3, A6, A2: 0/1000 versus 1000/1000), and L2 is run live across three model families (A3 prevented in all 120 retracted sessions). We reproduce a silent lost update in ByteDance's deer-flow, formalizing its fix as a verified $L_0 \to L_1$ refinement, and exhibit tool-effect reordering in LangGraph's ToolNode on unmodified output, removed by an L3 commit-order sequencer. The verified detector, refinements, and realizability artifacts are the contribution; the phenomena and lattice are classical.

</details>


### [102] [The Critical Role of Model Selection in Causal Inference: A Comparative Analysis of Classification Models within the InferBERT Framework for Pharmacovigilance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17113)
*Csaba Kiss,Roland Molontay,Gabriele Pergola*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study evaluates model choice within the InferBERT causal ADE detection framework, finding that domain-specific pre-training (BioBERT) outperforms both simpler baselines (XGBoost) and larger LLMs (Med-LLaMA), with calibration having mixed effects on causal discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Distinguishing causal adverse drug events from spurious correlations is a central pharmacovigilance challenge. The InferBERT framework relies on an underlying classification model, but the optimal model choice — simpler classifiers, domain-specific transformers, or scaled-up LLMs — remains unexamined.

Method: A comparative study on two benchmarks (AILF and TRAM) evaluating four models: XGBoost, ALBERT, BioBERT, and Med-LLaMA. Performance assessed via 5-fold cross-validation repeated over 20 runs, measuring accuracy, Expected Calibration Error (ECE) before/after isotonic regression, and Jaccard concordance of causal terms with PRR, ROR, and EBGM pharmacovigilance signals. Statistical significance tested via paired t-tests.

Result: BioBERT achieved the highest accuracy on both datasets. Med-LLaMA underperformed despite its larger scale and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Domain-specific pre-training proved decisive. Post-hoc calibration (isotonic regression) improved ECE but produced mixed effects on accuracy and causal discovery. BioBERT also yielded the strongest concordance with traditional pharmacovigilance signals.

Conclusion: Domain-specific pre-training provides a clear and consistent advantage over both simpler baselines and larger LLMs for computational pharmacovigilance. Investing in manageable, domain-aware models is more effective than simply scaling model size.

Abstract: Distinguishing causal adverse drug events (ADEs) from spurious correlations remains a central challenge in pharmacovigilance. The InferBERT framework integrates transformer models with Do-calculus, but its success hinges on the underlying classification model. This study evaluates the impact of model choice in InferBERT, assessing whether simpler models suffice, if domain-specific pre-training helps, whether scaling to LLMs improves causal detection, and the effect of post-hoc calibration. We performed a comparative study on two benchmarks: Analgesics-induced Acute Liver Failure (AILF) and Tramadol-related Mortalities (TRAM). Four models were evaluated-XGBoost (baseline), ALBERT (original InferBERT), BioBERT (biomedical transformer), and Med-LLaMA (medical LLM)-using 5-fold cross-validation repeated over 20 runs. We measured accuracy, Expected Calibration Error (ECE) pre- and post-isotonic regression, and Jaccard concordance of causal terms with PRR, ROR, and EBGM; significance was tested with paired t-tests. BioBERT achieved the highest accuracy on both datasets, while Med-LLaMA underperformed despite its size and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Domain-specific pre-training was decisive. Calibration improved ECE but had mixed effects on accuracy and causal discovery. BioBERT's superiority also yielded the strongest concordance with traditional pharmacovigilance signals. These results show that domain-specific pre-training provides a clear advantage over simpler baselines and larger LLMs. Investing in manageable, domain-aware models is more effective for computational pharmacovigilance than simply scaling model size.

</details>


### [103] [Probing, Fusion, and Trustworthiness: A Systematic Evaluation of Foundation Model Representations for Multimodal Cancer Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17115)
*Jingyu Hu,Giuseppe Tripodi,Reed Naidoo,Sarah F. McGough,Tapabrata Chakraborti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates foundation model (FM) representations for computational pathology across two commercial cohorts, benchmarking unimodal and multimodal (whole-slide images + transcriptomics) performance on out-of-distribution data. It finds that image and omics representations are complementary, multimodal fusion helps when no single modality dominates, and conformal prediction enables trustworthy uncertainty quantification where true diagnoses are often recoverable within prediction sets despite point-prediction failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation models are increasingly used as feature extractors for medical data, but their generalizability under distribution shift—particularly on real-world commercial datasets—remains underexplored. There is also limited understanding of whether multimodal fusion of image and transcriptomic representations yields consistent gains and whether uncertainty-aware inference (conformal prediction) can enhance clinical trustworthiness.

Method: The authors benchmark five foundation models on eight downstream classification tasks using two in-house oncology cohorts (IH-BC for breast cancer, IH-NSCLC for lung cancer). They evaluate unimodal probing performance for whole-slide image and transcriptomic modalities separately, then compare three image-omics fusion strategies using paired representations. Trustworthiness is assessed via conformal prediction, examining whether true diagnoses fall within prediction sets when point predictions fail.

Result: FM-based representations achieve competitive performance under distribution shift. Image and omics modalities carry complementary predictive signals. Multimodal fusion yields gains primarily when neither single modality dominates. Conformal prediction shows that in most cases where point predictions are incorrect, the true diagnosis remains recoverable within the prediction set, supporting uncertainty-aware inference for clinical decision support.

Conclusion: FM representations generalize reasonably to out-of-distribution clinical data. Multimodal fusion is beneficial but context-dependent, and conformal prediction provides a practical framework for trustworthy, uncertainty-aware clinical inference by maintaining coverage even when point estimates fail.

Abstract: Foundation models (FMs) have emerged as powerful representation extractors for medical data, yet their generalizability to datasets under distribution shift remains underexplored. This work systematically evaluates FM-based representations on a suite of computational pathology tasks across two real-world commercial cohorts, IH-BC and IH-NSCLC, drawn from the licensed in-house (IH) oncology dataset. The analysis focuses on two modalities, whole-slide images and transcriptomic profiles, drawn from the IH multimodal data. We first benchmark unimodal probing performance across five FMs on eight downstream classification tasks, and find that image and omics representations carry complementary predictive signals. Then we investigate whether multimodal fusion can yield additional gains over unimodal baselines by comparing three image-omics fusion strategies built on paired representations. The trustworthiness of selected unimodal and multimodal pipelines is further assessed through conformal prediction. Our results show that FM representations achieve competitive performance on out-of-distribution data and that multimodal fusion helps mainly when no single modality dominates the signal. Conformal prediction reveals that in the majority of cases where a point prediction fails, the true diagnosis remains recoverable within the prediction set, reinforcing the value of uncertainty-aware inference for clinical support.

</details>


### [104] [MODE: Modality-Decomposed Expert-Level Mixed-Precision Quantization for MoE Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17118)
*Yuanteng Chen,Peisong Wang,Zhilei Liu,Nanxin Zeng,Yuantian Shao,Shiqiang Lang,Tao Liu,Chuangyi Li,Qinghao Hu,Gang Li,Jing Liu,Jian Cheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MODE is a modality-decomposed expert-level mixed-precision quantization framework for MoE-MLLMs that corrects biases in expert importance estimation by separating vision/text modality frequencies, denoising redundant vision tokens, and incorporating modality-specific quantization sensitivity into an ILP-based bit-width assignment, achieving <2.9% performance loss at W3A16.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing expert-level mixed-precision quantization methods for MoE-LLMs degrade significantly on MoE-MLLMs due to two overlooked biases: (1) cross-modal bias where vision tokens numerically dominate expert selection frequency, masking text-critical experts; (2) intra-vision bias where redundant vision tokens skew frequency statistics, obscuring experts critical for informative visual content.

Method: MODE proposes a three-component framework: (1) modality-decomposed expert selection frequency that separately tracks vision and text token routing; (2) denoised visual frequency obtained by filtering redundant vision tokens; (3) modality-specific quantization sensitivity as a complementary signal. These signals are integrated into an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) formulation to assign per-expert bit-widths under a given memory budget.

Result: MODE limits average performance loss to within 2.9% at W3A16, with larger gains at the extreme 2-bit setting. It consistently outperforms prior expert-level mixed-precision quantization methods across various MoE-MLLM architectures.

Conclusion: Decomposing expert importance by modality and removing redundant visual tokens are critical for effective quantization of MoE-MLLMs. MODE demonstrates that modality-aware mixed-precision allocation significantly mitigates the degradation observed when directly applying MoE-LLM quantization techniques to multimodal settings.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts Multimodal Large Language Models (MoE-MLLMs) offer remarkable performance but incur prohibitive GPU memory costs, making compression essential. Among PTQ methods, expert-level mixed-precision quantization has proven effective for MoE-LLMs, yet suffers notable degradation on MoE-MLLMs due to two overlooked biases in expert importance estimation. (1) At the cross-modal level, the numerical dominance of vision tokens causes expert selection frequency to be dominated by vision tokens, masking experts that are critical to the text modality; (2) at the intra-vision level, the large proportion of redundant vision tokens further skew frequency statistics, obscuring experts critical for informative visual content. To bridge gaps, we propose MODE, a modality-decomposed expert-level mixed-precision quantization framework for MoE-MLLMs that decomposes expert selection frequency by modality, filters redundant vision tokens to obtain denoised visual frequency, and further evaluates quantization sensitivity per modality as a complementary signal to frequency-based estimation. These signals are integrated into an Integer Linear Programming formulation to assign per-expert bit-widths under a given budget. Extensive experiments show that MODE is particularly well-suited for MoE-MLLMs, limiting average performance loss to within 2.9% at W3A16, with larger gains at the extreme 2-bit setting.

</details>


### [105] [Noise-Driven Escape from Metastable Phases explains Grokking in Deep Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17120)
*Ibrahim Talha Ersoy,Karoline Wiesner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Linear DNNs exhibit first-order L2 phase transitions where metastable states trap networks via energy barriers. Grokking—the delayed onset of generalization—is explained as hysteresis-driven escapes from these metastable states, with escape times following Arrhenius scaling. The number of metastable states equals the number of singular values in the data covariance, and the mechanism likely extends to nonlinear DNNs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite DNNs' strong generalization ability, the origin of "grokking"—an abrupt, delayed generalization after prolonged overfitting—remains poorly understood. The authors aim to provide a mechanistic explanation rooted in phase transition physics.

Method: The authors analyze linear DNNs under L2 regularization, framing grokking as hysteresis in first-order phase transitions. They engineer deliberate trapping by tuning L2 strength, study SGD-noise-driven escapes across energy barriers, measure escape times against Arrhenius scaling, and reproduce grokking curves via sparse sub-sampling across two orders of magnitude in escape time. The analysis links metastable states to singular values of the data covariance matrix.

Result: Grokking-like delayed convergence is reproduced across two orders of magnitude in escape time. Escape times follow Arrhenius scaling with respect to energy barrier height. The canonical grokking curve (test error eventually approaching training error) is reproduced via sparse sub-sampling. The number of metastable states matches the number of learnable features, one per singular value of the data covariance, suggesting hysteresis potential grows with task complexity. Preliminary evidence indicates the mechanism also operates in nonlinear DNNs.

Conclusion: Grokking is consistent with hysteresis in first-order L2 phase transitions. Metastable trapping, with barrier escapes driven by SGD noise and obeying Arrhenius scaling, provides a unified mechanistic picture. This framework offers routes toward more efficient learning schemes and explains why complex tasks exhibit greater training instability.

Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) exhibit first order phase transitions under variations of the L2 regularization strength, with each transition marking the onset of a new learnable feature. Below a critical regularization strength, all features are in principle learnable, but coexisting metastable states, separated by energy barriers, can trap the network and impede convergence. A strength of DNNs is their ability to generalize. But many open questions remain, among them the origin of so called grokking: the abrupt, delayed onset of generalization after prolonged apparent overfitting. We show for linear DNNs that grokking is consistent with hysteresis in first-order L2 phase transitions: using L2 regularization to engineer deliberate trapping, we demonstrate that a model in a low-accuracy metastable state escapes only when SGD noise drives it across an energy barrier, with escape times following Arrhenius scaling. We reproduce grokking-like delayed convergence across two orders of magnitude in escape time by deliberately trapping models in metastable phases. Using sparse sub-sampling we also reproduce the canonical grokking curve where test error eventually approaches the final training error. Our work suggests that the number of metastable states equals the number of learnable features -- one per singular value of the data covariance -- the potential for hysteresis grows naturally with task complexity. We provide evidence that the same mechanism likely operates in general nonlinear DNNs. Our results provide routes toward more efficient learning schemes.

</details>


### [106] [Towards Fast GNN Surrogates for CO2 Migration in Complex Geological Formations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17180)
*Rodrigo S. Luna,Thiago H. N. Coelho,Luiz S. L. Neto,Roberto M. Velho,Adriano M. A. Cortes,Renato N. Elias,Alexandre G. Evsukoff,Fernando A. Rochinha,Mauricio Araya-Polo,Herve Gross,Alvaro L. G. A. Coutinho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A graph neural network surrogate model with anisotropic message-passing is proposed for forecasting CO₂ plume migration in geological storage, evaluated on the SPE11A benchmark with strong predictive performance over extended horizons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate forecasting of CO₂ plume migration in complex geological formations is computationally expensive with traditional physics-based simulators. A data-driven surrogate that captures key multiphase flow physics—including sharp interfaces, advection, and convective mixing—can dramatically accelerate predictions while maintaining fidelity.

Method: The geological domain is represented as a graph where nodes are computational cells and edges encode transmissibility-based interactions with geometric attributes. An anisotropic message-passing mechanism uses geometry-conditioned edge embeddings to bias message aggregation toward physically relevant transport directions, capturing directional transport from grid geometry, permeability contrasts, and heterogeneity. Temporal evolution is modeled via an autoregressive residual formulation in latent space with multi-step supervision.

Result: The model produces competitive forecasts of gas saturation and liquid-phase density on the SPE11A benchmark, with cumulative errors remaining moderate over extended forecasting horizons.

Conclusion: The proposed end-to-end graph neural surrogate effectively reproduces key physical behaviors of CO₂ plume migration, offering a promising computationally efficient alternative for long-term monitoring and forecasting in geological carbon storage applications.

Abstract: This chapter discusses how a data-driven machine learning approach can reproduce key aspects of the physical behavior of multiphase flows in complex geological formations. We propose an end-to-end graph neural surrogate tailored to CO$_2$ plume migration forecasting in geological storage. The method is evaluated on the SPE11A benchmark, a well-known industry test case designed to assess CO$_2$ storage scenarios and characterized by sharp gas-water interfaces, strong advective transport, and rapid convective mixing with fingering development. The benchmark is reformulated as a graph in which nodes represent computational cells and edges encode transmissibility-based interactions enriched with geometric attributes. Directional transport arising from grid geometry, permeability contrasts, and geological heterogeneity is captured through an anisotropic message-passing mechanism, where interaction weights are computed via geometry-conditioned edge embeddings, biasing message aggregation toward physically relevant transport directions. Temporal evolution is modeled in latent space using an autoregressive residual formulation trained with multi-step supervision. The proposed model produces competitive forecasts of gas saturation and liquid-phase density, which are key indicators for CO$_2$ storage monitoring, with cumulative errors that remain moderate over extended forecasting horizons.

</details>


### [107] [Finsler Geometry, Graph Neural Networks, and You](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17185)
*T. Mitchell Roddenberry,Richard G. Baraniuk*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes Finslerian graph neural networks (FGNNs) that generalize beyond isotropic Laplace-Beltrami operators by using discrete estimates of the Finsler Laplacian on point clouds, with proven convergence guarantees, enabling recovery of geometry underlying nonlinear diffusion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard graph neural networks based on the graph Laplacian approximate the Laplace-Beltrami operator, which is inherently isotropic and cannot capture direction-dependent (anisotropic) geometric information. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by introducing a nonlinear, anisotropic alternative grounded in Finsler geometry.

Method: The authors construct discrete estimates of the Finsler Laplacian on point clouds sampled from a manifold and mathematically prove pointwise convergence to the true continuum operator as sample size increases. They then reformulate this discrete operator as a graph neural network layer, yielding a family of Finslerian GNNs explicitly constrained to encode Finsler geometric structure.

Result: The discrete Finsler Laplacian estimates are proven to converge to the true manifold operator. Empirically, Finslerian GNNs successfully recover the underlying geometry of nonlinear diffusion equations in practice, demonstrating their capacity to model anisotropic phenomena.

Conclusion: Finslerian graph neural networks provide a principled, provably convergent framework for incorporating anisotropic, nonlinear geometric structure into graph learning, extending the expressivity of Laplacian-based GNNs beyond isotropic regimes.

Abstract: Graph neural network architectures based on the graph Laplacian approximate the Laplace-Beltrami operator, thus limiting their application to isotropic operators. As a nonlinear alternative to the Laplace-Beltrami operator, we consider estimates of the Finsler Laplacian on point clouds sampled from a manifold. We prove that these discrete estimates converge to the true operator on the manifold as the number of point samples grows. Moreover, we show that this operator can be expressed as a graph neural network layer, which we use to define a family of Finslerian graph neural networks constrained to express Finsler geometry. We show that Finslerian graph neural networks recover the geometry underlying nonlinear diffusion equations in practice.

</details>


### [108] [Constrained Diffusion Models with Primal-Dual Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17192)
*Samar Hadou,Yigit Berkay Uslu,Alejandro Ribeiro*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PDI is a novel method for constrained diffusion sampling that jointly infers the optimal distribution and its dual variable during reverse diffusion. A single dual-conditioned score network is trained over the Gibbs family, and dual ascent updates use denoised sample constraint violations. Convergence is proven, with applications in Gaussian mixtures, wireless allocation, and portfolio management.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Constrained sampling problems with average constraints—prevalent in wireless resource allocation, portfolio management, and other domains—typically require estimating the optimal dual multiplier before sampling and freezing it during generation. This decoupled approach is suboptimal because it cannot adapt to distributional shifts during inference. The authors seek a principled method that jointly solves for the optimal primal distribution and its parametrizing dual variable throughout the sampling process.

Method: The paper formalizes constrained sampling in the Lagrangian dual domain, where the optimal distribution is a Gibbs distribution indexed by the optimal dual variable. The proposed Primal-Dual Inference (PDI) framework alternates within each reverse diffusion step: (1) denoising using the score field conditioned on the current dual multiplier, and (2) updating the multiplier via dual ascent using the estimated constraint violation of the denoised samples. A single dual-conditioned score network is trained over the entire family of Gibbs distributions induced by dual variables encountered during inference, enabling conditional score evaluation without retraining. Theoretical analysis proves that the time-averaged dual variables converge to a neighborhood of the dual optimum and bounds the terminal distribution error due to residual dual mismatch using schedule-dependent stability factors.

Result: PDI is evaluated on three tasks: constrained sampling from a mixture of Gaussians (synthetic), wireless resource allocation, and portfolio management. The method effectively satisfies average constraints while generating high-quality samples. The theoretical convergence guarantees are validated empirically, showing that dual variables stabilize near the optimum and the terminal distribution closely approximates the target Gibbs distribution.

Conclusion: PDI provides a unified, theoretically grounded approach for constrained diffusion sampling under average constraints. By jointly inferring the primal distribution and dual variable, it avoids the suboptimality of frozen dual estimates. The dual-conditioned score network and dual ascent update scheme are both practical and provably convergent, making the method applicable to real-world constrained generation tasks.

Abstract: This paper develops constrained diffusion models with primal-dual inference (PDI) to sample from optimal distributions of entropy-regularized optimization problems with \emph{average} constraints. We formalize constrained sampling in the Lagrangian dual domain, where the optimal distribution takes the form of a Gibbs distribution indexed by the optimal dual variable. Rather than estimating this dual multiplier before sampling and freezing it throughout generation, PDI jointly infers the optimal primal distribution and its parametrizing dual variable. Each reverse diffusion step denoises using the score field associated with the current multiplier and then updates the multiplier through dual ascent using the estimated constraint violation of the denoised samples. To enable this conditional score field, we train a single dual-conditioned score network over the family of Gibbs distributions induced by the dual variables encountered during inference. We prove that the time average of the dual variables generated along the inference trajectory converges to a neighborhood of the dual optimum and bound the effect of residual dual mismatch on the terminal distribution through schedule-dependent stability factors. We evaluate PDI on constrained sampling from a mixture of Gaussians, wireless resource allocation, and portfolio management.

</details>


### [109] [PowerOPD: Stabilizing On-Policy Distillation with Bounded Power Transformation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17199)
*Anhao Zhao,Junlong Tong,Yingqi Fan,Ping Nie,Wenjie Li,Xiaoyu Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) suffers from high-variance gradients due to an unbounded log-ratio reward. The authors propose PowerOPD, which uses Box-Cox power transformations to create bounded, sign-consistent rewards, achieving significant gains in accuracy, stability, and efficiency over vanilla OPD, post-hoc stabilization, and full-vocabulary OPD.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vanilla on-policy distillation uses a single-sample Monte Carlo estimator with a log-ratio reward that is unbounded, causing high-variance gradients, sample inefficiency, unstable generation, and a large performance gap relative to exact full-vocabulary OPD. Existing post-hoc stabilization methods are insufficient because they operate after the distortion has already occurred.

Method: PowerOPD replaces the unbounded log-ratio reward with a family of natively bounded, sign-consistent reward functions derived from the Box-Cox power transformation, parameterized by α > 0. The standard log-ratio emerges as the degenerate α → 0 limit. This transformation is applied directly in the reward formulation, preventing high-variance gradients at the source rather than attempting post-hoc correction.

Result: Across six math reasoning benchmarks with four Qwen3 teacher-student pairs, PowerOPD achieves Avg@8/Pass@8 gains: +6.37/+5.71 over vanilla OPD, +3.01/+3.54 over post-hoc stabilization, and +2.59/+8.90 over full-vocabulary OPD. It also reduces wall-clock time by 59.2% and peak GPU memory by 23.1%. Larger α improves accuracy, shortens responses, and keeps gradient norms >3,000× smaller than vanilla OPD.

Conclusion: PowerOPD demonstrates that natively bounding the reward function via Box-Cox transformation effectively resolves the training pathologies of standard OPD, yielding substantial improvements in performance, stability, and computational efficiency. The approach outperforms both post-hoc stabilization and the exact full-vocabulary baseline while being significantly cheaper to run.

Abstract: Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) for large language models estimates the reverse-KL objective using student-sampled tokens, yielding an unbiased single-sample Monte Carlo estimator that avoids vocabulary-wide computation. However, we show that this estimator suffers from severe training pathologies in practice: sample inefficiency, unstable generation dynamics, and a substantial performance gap compared to exact full-vocabulary OPD. Reward-level diagnosis traces these pathologies to the log-ratio reward, which is unbounded by construction, producing extremely high-variance gradients concentrated at early positions and persisting throughout training; standard post-hoc scaling fail as they operate only after this distortion occurs. To solve this problem, we propose PowerOPD: a family of natively bounded, sign-consistent rewards from the Box-Cox power transformation, parameterized by alpha > 0, of which the log-ratio is the degenerate alpha -> 0 limit. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks and four Qwen3 teacher-student pairs, PowerOPD achieves benchmark-averaged Avg@8/Pass@8 gains of up to +6.37/+5.71 over vanilla OPD, +3.01/+3.54 over post-hoc stabilization, and +2.59/+8.90 over full-vocabulary OPD, while reducing wall-clock time by 59.2% and peak GPU memory by 23.1%. Larger alpha generally improves accuracy, consistently shortens responses, and keeps gradient norms more than 3,000x smaller than vanilla OPD.

</details>


### [110] [Sum-of-Squares Degree Barriers for the Reweighted-Hinge Method in Robust Halfspace Learning: A Christoffel-Function Characterization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17215)
*Xiaoyu Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes that the Christoffel function of the clean marginal distribution precisely quantifies the maximal corruption an adversary can hide from degree-bounded outlier-removal certificates. It uses this "resolution principle" to derive three results for robustly learning γ-margin halfspaces: a margin-degree tradeoff, a degree-2 barrier where error is stuck at η^{1/2}, and a degree-2t algorithm achieving error η^{1-1/2t} that is provably tight.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Outlier-removal certificates in robust learning rely on low-degree moment tests, but adversaries can exploit the blind spot where corrupt data mimics clean data in its low-degree moments. The paper seeks to characterize this blind spot exactly, providing a principled understanding of the limits of the Sum-of-Squares (SoS) certificate method for robust halfspace learning under malicious noise.

Method: The paper identifies the Christoffel function λ_{t+1}(c) of the clean marginal as the exact maximal corruption mass concealable at center c from a degree-2t SoS certificate. This "resolution principle" is applied within the reweighted-hinge framework. A weighted-Chebyshev reduction relates degree thresholds to geometric parameters (|c|/s). The analysis yields explicit constructions demonstrating lower bounds and an algorithm tracing the η^{1-1/2t} error frontier.

Result: Three main consequences: (1) A margin-degree tradeoff: certifying the dense pancake to error ε requires SoS degree Ω(log(1/ε)) or margin Ω(√(log(1/ε))/√d). (2) A degree-2 outlier barrier: an explicit instance where degree-2 certificates are stuck at error η^{1/2}, while degree 4 escapes — showing the method's breakdown is due to degree, not analysis. (3) A degree-2t algorithm achieving error η^{1-1/2t}, recovering Shen (2025) at t=1, with an explicit constant gain capped by pancake density and proven unimprovable via the degree-2 barrier.

Conclusion: The Christoffel function serves as the fundamental organizing principle for understanding the resolution limits of bounded-degree outlier-removal certificates. The results explain why existing SoS-based robust learning methods face inherent degree-dependent barriers, and the derived tradeoffs and lower bounds are tight, delineating precisely what is and is not achievable by the certificate method.

Abstract: A certificate that removes outliers sees the data only through its low-degree moments, and an adversary exploits exactly this, hiding corruption where the clean data already looks typical, in the blind spot no bounded-degree test resolves. That blind spot turns out to have an exact size: the Christoffel function of the clean marginal, the very quantity modern data analysis thresholds to detect outliers, here read from the adversary's side as the corruption a bounded-degree certificate cannot remove. We turn this inversion into the organizing principle of the reweighted-hinge approach to robustly learning $γ$-margin halfspaces under malicious noise (Shen, 2025; Zeng and Shen, 2025): the governing resource is the Sum-of-Squares degree of the outlier-removal certificate, and the resolution principle states that the maximal corruption mass which can hide at a center $c$ from a degree-$2t$ certificate is exactly the Christoffel function $λ_{t+1}(c)$ of the clean marginal. Three consequences follow, all against the certificate method (not information-theoretic). A margin-degree tradeoff: certifying the dense pancake to error $ε$ costs SoS degree $Ω(\log(1/ε))$ or margin $Ω(\sqrt{\log(1/ε)}/\sqrt{d})$, explaining why the $\log(1/ε)$ margin Shen (2025) records is forced, with a weighted-Chebyshev reduction making the threshold $2t=Θ((|c|/s)^2)$ tight modulo one classical weighted-extremal estimate. A degree-$2$ outlier barrier: the resolution principle realized as an explicit instance on which degree $2$ is stuck at $η^{1/2}$ while degree $4$ escapes, locating the method's small breakdown rate in the degree, not the analysis. And a degree-$2t$ algorithm tracing the frontier $η^{1-1/2t}$ (recovering Shen (2025) at $t=1$), whose gain is an explicit constant, capped by the pancake density and shown unimprovable by the degree-$2$ barrier.

</details>


### [111] [Rift: A Conflict Signature for Deception in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17229)
*Petr Nyoma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies an internal "conflict signature" in transformer models that distinguishes deliberate lying (knowing the truth but outputting falsehoods) from honest mistakes. By comparing sleeper agents with naive liars producing identical wrong outputs, the authors find deceptive forward passes exhibit 2.1–2.3× higher residual rank. This signature enables 100% lie detection accuracy across multiple architectures, transfers zero-shot across model families and languages, is robust to strategic concealment, but is read-only (detectable, not injectable).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard behavioral evaluation cannot distinguish a model that deliberately lies (knowing the truth) from one making honest errors, posing a fundamental challenge for ELK (Eliciting Latent Knowledge). The authors investigate whether internal model representations carry a detectable signature of this knowledge conflict — the tension between what a model knows and what it outputs — that would allow identifying deception without relying on output correctness alone.

Method: The key experimental design is a controlled contrast: "sleeper agents" (models trained honestly but triggered to lie, thus possessing knowledge conflict) versus "naive liars" (models fine-tuned exclusively on wrong answers, no honest training, thus no conflict). Both produce identical incorrect outputs, isolating the effect of knowledge conflict from mere incorrectness. The authors measure residual stream rank (dimensional complexity), use basis-free relative representations for cross-model transfer, train linear probes for deception detection, and test robustness across: multiple architectures (GPT-2, Qwen2.5, Phi-3-mini), strategic self-constructed lies, active concealment, length-controlled settings, and cross-lingual transfer (5 languages). They also test injectability (can the signature be artificially inserted?) and document six negative results.

Result: Deceptive passes show 2.1–2.3× higher residual rank than naive-liar passes, enabling 100% lie identification accuracy across GPT-2 small/medium (three seeds) and three instruct models. On Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B and Phi-3-mini, instructed deception raised residual rank on every tested fact (18/18, 40/40, 34/34). On Phi-3, lies separated perfectly from both honest answers and hallucinations (AUC 1.0, Wilcoxon p≈6e-11). The signature survived strategic self-constructed deception (AUC 1.0), active concealment (AUC 1.0), and length-controlled replication (20/20, AUC 1.0, p≈1e-6). Zero-shot cross-family probe transfer achieved mean AUC 0.933, surviving simultaneous architecture and format changes (AUC 0.821), and transferred across five languages (AUC 1.000, length-controlled). The signature is read-only: detectable but not injectable (0/8 both directions).

Conclusion: Deliberate deception in language models leaves a robust, detectable internal signature rooted in knowledge conflict — the tension between known truth and output falsehood — that manifests as elevated residual rank. This signature generalizes impressively across models, languages, and deceptive strategies, offering a potential pathway for ELK and lie detection beyond behavioral evaluation. However, its read-only nature (undetectable via injection) suggests it is a genuine emergent phenomenon of knowledge conflict rather than an easily manipulable artifact, though the documented honest limitations and negative results warrant caution about real-world deployability.

Abstract: A model that lies while knowing the truth is the central case ELK cannot handle with behavioral evaluation alone. We ask whether such deception leaves an internal signature distinguishing it from honest error. Our key move is a control for wrongness: we contrast a sleeper agent (knows the truth, lies on trigger) against a naive liar (fine-tuned to emit the same wrong answers with no honest training). Both produce identical wrong outputs; any difference is about knowledge conflict, not incorrectness. We find deceptive forward passes carry a conflict signature - 2.1-2.3x higher residual rank than naive-liar passes on the same wrong answer - strong enough to identify which of two responses is the lie with 100% accuracy and no labels, across GPT-2 small/medium (three seeds) and three instruct models. Across Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B and Phi-3-mini, instructed deception raises residual rank on every tested fact (18/18, 40/40, 34/34); on Phi-3, lies separate perfectly from both honest answers and hallucinations (AUC 1.0, Wilcoxon p~6e-11). The signature survives strategic self-constructed deception (model invents its own lie, AUC 1.0), active concealment attempts (AUC 1.0), and length-controlled replication (20/20, AUC 1.0, p~1e-6). Using basis-free relative representations, a probe trained on one model family detects deception in two other families zero-shot (mean AUC 0.933), surviving simultaneous architecture and format change (AUC 0.821), and transfers across five languages (AUC 1.000, length-controlled). The signature is read-only: detectable but not injectable (0/8 both directions). Honest limitations and six negative experiments are documented in full.

</details>


### [112] [Uncertainty Quantification of Engineering Structures by Polynomial Chaos Expansion and Multivariate Active Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17233)
*Qitian Lu,Jafar Jafari-Asl,Panagiotis Spyridis,Lukas Novak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an adaptive sequential sampling method for building polynomial chaos expansion surrogate models that handle multiple quantities of interest simultaneously, balancing exploration and aggregated variance exploitation across all outputs to improve accuracy, stability, and statistical estimation over Latin Hypercube Sampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A single experimental design often inadequately represents all outputs when different QoIs exhibit varying input sensitivities. While separate sampling per output is possible, it increases cost and ignores inter-output correlations. Hence, a unified sequential sampling strategy that leverages shared information across outputs is needed.

Method: The authors generalize an adaptive sequential sampling approach for vector-valued QoIs within polynomial chaos expansion surrogates. New samples are iteratively selected from a candidate pool based on each candidate's local contribution to output variance. The selection criterion balances distance-based exploration of the input space with exploitation of aggregated variance information across all outputs.

Result: Numerical experiments on engineering problems show the proposed method outperforms non-sequential Latin Hypercube Sampling in surrogate accuracy, stability, and reliability of second-order statistics estimation.

Conclusion: The generalized adaptive sequential sampling strategy effectively constructs multi-output PCE surrogates with superior accuracy and statistical fidelity compared to one-shot space-filling designs, without incurring the cost of separate per-output sampling.

Abstract: In many engineering applications, a single high-fidelity model produces multiple quantities of interest (QoIs) under the same input parameters, e.g. finite element models of complex physical systems. To alleviate the high computational cost of direct model evaluations, surrogate models are widely used to construct efficient approximations of model responses. Naturally, the accuracy of surrogates strongly depends on the quality of the experimental design (ED). However, a single ED may not provide an adequate representation for all outputs simultaneously, especially when different outputs exhibit varying sensitivities to the input variables. A straightforward solution is to perform separate sampling for each output, but this results in increased sampling complexity and computational cost. From a statistical perspective, such an approach also ignores potential correlations among all outputs and may compromise data consistency. To address this issue, an adaptive sequential sampling method for constructing polynomial chaos expansion surrogate models is generalized for vector valued QoIs. The method sequentially selects new samples from a candidate pool based on their local contribution to the output variance, while balancing distance-based exploration of the input space and exploitation of aggregated variance information across all outputs. Its performance is compared with non-sequential Latin Hypercube Sampling through several numerical examples from engineering problems. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed strategy improves both surrogate accuracy and stability, and provides a more reliable estimation of second-order statistics.

</details>


### [113] [Rethinking Groups in Critic-Free RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17250)
*Yihong Wu,Liheng Ma,Lingfeng Xiao,Muzhi Li,Xinyu Wang,Yingxue Zhang,Jian-Yun Nie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Current critic-free RL methods for LLMs rely on grouped rollouts for baseline estimation, causing data inefficiency and synchronization overhead. The authors identify that the group's core function is preventing false penalties on negative samples, and propose negative token filtering to enable stable single-rollout training with comparable or better performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing critic-free RL methods (e.g., GRPO) require generating multiple rollouts per question to compute advantage baselines, which introduces three problems: (1) data inefficiency from redundant generations, (2) synchronization barriers from waiting for all rollouts to complete, and (3) inflexibility with structured or multi-turn rollouts. The goal is to eliminate the need for grouped rollouts while preserving training stability.

Method: The authors first analyze the role of group-based baseline estimation and find its primary function is preventing false penalties — where correctly reasoned but unlucky negative samples get penalized due to noisy reward signals. Building on this insight, they propose negative token filtering (NTF): during single-rollout training, when computing advantage, tokens from negative samples (incorrect final answers) that are not clearly responsible for the failure are masked from the loss, preventing them from receiving misleading penalty gradients. This is applied to two batch-level advantage methods (Reinforce with Leave-One-Out baseline and Batch Advantage), enabling stable single-rollout training.

Result: The proposed negative token filtering with single-rollout training achieves: (1) comparable performance to group-based methods (GRPO) on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, and (2) stronger performance on agentic/multi-turn tasks where structured rollouts make group-based methods less applicable.

Conclusion: The group mechanism in critic-free RL for LLMs primarily serves to prevent false penalties rather than merely estimate baselines. Negative token filtering effectively replicates this protective function in single-rollout settings, enabling more data-efficient, flexible training without synchronization overhead, while maintaining or surpassing group-based performance.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a central paradigm for post-training large language models. Existing critic-free RL methods typically generate a group of rollouts for the same question to estimate value baselines for advantage computation. However, this design suffers from data inefficiency, group synchronization barriers, and inflexibility with structured rollouts. In this work, we revisit the role of the ``group'' and show that its underlying function is not merely to estimate baselines but to prevent false penalties on negative samples. Building on this insight, we propose negative token filtering, a simple and effective strategy that enables stable single-rollout training. We apply it to two batch-level advantage methods, achieving comparable performance on reasoning tasks and stronger performance on agentic tasks relative to group-based RL techniques.

</details>


### [114] [ProCUA-SFT Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17321)
*Jaehun Jung,Ximing Lu,Brandon Cui,Muhammad Khalifa,Shaokun Zhang,Hao Zhang,Jin Xu,Amala Sanjay Deshmukh,Karan Sapra,Andrew Tao,Yejin Choi,Jan Kautz,Mingjie Liu,Yi Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ProCUA-SFT is a 3.1M-sample supervised fine-tuning dataset for computer-use agents, automatically distilled from 93K synthetic trajectories. Fine-tuning UI-TARS 7B on it achieves 45.0% on OSWorld, dramatically outperforming the AgentNet baseline which causes negative transfer (8-10%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing human-collected CUA training data like AgentNet (22.5K trajectories) causes negative transfer when used for supervised fine-tuning—UI-TARS 7B's OSWorld success rate drops from 26.3% to 8-10%. This motivates the need for larger-scale, higher-quality synthetic trajectory data that better aligns with inference-time conditions.

Method: A fully automated pipeline where a single VLM (Kimi-K2.5) serves as goal generator, precondition judge, and trajectory executor. The pipeline: (i) synthesizes grounded tasks on live desktops seeded with real-world content (912 spreadsheets, ~10K presentations, multi-app OSWorld configs) across 2,484 application combinations; (ii) verifies task feasibility via binary precondition checking before rollout; (iii) expands each trajectory into step-prefix samples that exactly reproduce inference-time context layout.

Result: Fine-tuning UI-TARS 7B on ProCUA-SFT for one epoch yields 45.0% on OSWorld—an 18.7 percentage-point improvement over the base model and over 35% above AgentNet-trained counterparts. A ProCUA subset was incorporated into Nemotron 3 Nano Omni's training data.

Conclusion: Synthetic, automatically verified trajectory data at scale (3.1M step-level samples) enables substantial positive transfer for CUA fine-tuning, overcoming the negative transfer problem of smaller human-collected datasets. Using a single VLM for all stages eliminates planner-actor capability gaps, and step-prefix sample construction ensures alignment with inference-time conditions.

Abstract: Training computer-use agents (CUAs) -- models that interact with graphical desktops through screenshots and keyboard/mouse actions -- requires large-scale, diverse trajectory data collected in full desktop environments. The largest public resource, AgentNet (22.5K human trajectories), leads to negative transfer when used for supervised fine-tuning (SFT): continuing training UI-TARS 7B on AgentNet causes OSWorld success rate to fall from 26.3% to 8-10%. We present ProCUA-SFT, a dataset of 3.1M step-level SFT samples distilled from 93K synthetic trajectories across 2,484 application combinations. The dataset is produced by a fully automated pipeline that (i) synthesizes grounded tasks on live desktops seeded with real-world content -- 912 spreadsheets from SpreadsheetBench, approximately 10K permissively-licensed presentations from Zenodo10K, and multi-application OSWorld configs -- and (ii) verifies each task's feasibility through binary precondition checking before rollout. A single VLM (Kimi-K2.5) serves as goal generator, precondition judge, and trajectory executor, eliminating planner-actor capability gaps. Each trajectory is expanded into step-prefix samples that exactly reproduce the context layout seen at inference time. Fine-tuning UI-TARS 7B on ProCUA-SFT for one epoch yields 45.0% on OSWorld -- an 18.7 percentage-point improvement over the base model and over 35% above AgentNet-trained counterparts. A subset of ProCUA was incorporated into the training data for the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model, contributing to its computer-use capabilities.

</details>


### [115] [Decision-Driven Geosteering Under Uncertainty: A Unified Framework for Sequential Decision Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17331)
*Hibat Errahmen Djecta,Sergey Alyaev,Kristian Fossum,Reidar B. Bratvold,Ressi Bonti Muhammad,Apoorv Srivastava*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A geosteering framework that combines particle filtering for uncertainty quantification with reinforcement learning for sequential decision-making, evaluated across three policies (ADP, Deep Q-learning, Dual DRL) under realistic industrial simulation conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional geosteering relies on deterministic trajectory correction with limited explicit handling of geological uncertainty ahead of the drill bit. The authors aim to bridge this gap by enabling belief-informed control—where decisions are made under a probabilistic representation of the subsurface—and to compare multiple decision-making paradigms under identical uncertainty representations and operational constraints.

Method: The framework tightly couples a particle filter (PF) for probabilistic subsurface interpretation with value-based reinforcement learning policies. Three decision-making strategies are evaluated under the same PF belief representation: (1) Approximate Dynamic Programming (ADP) for interpretable control, (2) Deep Q-learning as a baseline, and (3) a Dual Deep RL architecture with a target Q-network for training stability and a dueling (value/advantage) decomposition for Q-value parameterization. Evaluation goes beyond final placement accuracy to include stability-oriented metrics (steering smoothness over time). Validation is performed via an API integration with an industrial geosteering simulator under realistic measurement noise and drilling constraints.

Result: The paper provides a controlled, high-fidelity comparison across all three policies using identical geological realizations, reward definitions, and operational limits. Results are assessed not only on final well placement but also on steering smoothness metrics that capture how policies behave dynamically as geological uncertainty evolves during drilling.

Conclusion: Belief-informed decision-making via PF-coupled RL offers a principled approach to geosteering under uncertainty. The comparative evaluation demonstrates that policy architecture choices meaningfully impact both placement performance and operational steering quality. The dueling Dual DRL architecture provides a stable and effective policy, while ADP offers interpretability. The framework establishes a reproducible benchmark for uncertainty-aware sequential decision-making in geosteering.

Abstract: Geosteering requires navigating a well trajectory through an unknown geological configuration, while sequentially updating decisions based on indirect measurements acquired during drilling. This work presents an uncertainty-aware geosteering framework that tightly integrates particle filtering for probabilistic subsurface interpretation with value-based reinforcement learning for sequential decision-making. Geological uncertainty ahead of the drill bit is represented explicitly through a particle filter (PF), enabling belief-informed control rather than deterministic trajectory correction.
  The framework couples PF belief updates with belief-informed decision policies and evaluates three decision-making options that operate under identical uncertainty representations: an interpretable Approximate Dynamic Programming (ADP) scheme, a Deep Q-learning baseline, and a Dual Deep Reinforcement Learning (Dual DRL) architecture trained with a target Q-network scheme for stability, using a dueling (value/advantage) decomposition for Q-value parameterization. Beyond final placement performance, we assess policy behavior using stability-oriented metrics that quantify steering smoothness over time, providing additional operational insight into how decision policies respond as uncertainty evolves.
  The framework is integrated with an API for validation within an industrial geosteering simulator under realistic measurement noise and drilling constraints. Using identical geological realizations, operational limits, and reward definitions across methods, the experiments provide a controlled and high-fidelity evaluation of how alternative decision policies behave throughout the drilling process, rather than evaluating performance solely from the final well trajectory.

</details>


### [116] [Counterfactual Optimization of Baseball Pitch Sequences and Estimation of Its Impact on Season-Level Statistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17345)
*Ryota Takamido,Hiroki Nakamoto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study uses a Transformer-based counterfactual analysis on MLB Statcast data to show that optimizing both setup and final pitches in a sequence can substantially improve season-level pitching performance (e.g., >1.0 K/9), providing quantitative evidence for the strategic value of pitch sequencing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior research on pitch sequencing has focused narrowly on optimizing only the final pitch of a plate appearance, overlooking the role of preceding setup pitches and their cumulative, season-level effects on pitcher performance.

Method: A Transformer-based model was trained on MLB Statcast data to predict in-play and swing-out outcomes. Counterfactual sequences were generated by substituting final or setup pitches (type and location) while holding context constant. Optimal counterfactuals minimized predicted in-play probability, and regression models linked these model outputs to seasonal statistics to estimate expected performance gains.

Result: Optimizing both final and setup pitches yielded substantial projected season-level improvements, including gains exceeding 1.0 in K/9. Additional insights included velocity-band-specific effective locations, the critical role of pitch command, and expanded pitch-selection options via middle-velocity pitches.

Conclusion: Pitch sequencing — encompassing both setup and final pitches — is quantitatively validated as a strategically important factor in pitcher performance, with meaningful season-level implications.

Abstract: Although pitch sequencing is a central topic in baseball analytics, previous studies have primarily focused on optimizing the final pitch within a single plate appearance, leaving the role of preceding setup pitches and their impact on long-term season-level performance insufficiently examined. To address these issues, this study conducted counterfactual analyses using MLB Statcast data. A Transformer-based machine-learning model was trained to predict whether a target pitch would result in an in-play outcome or swing-out. Counterfactual pitch sequences were then generated by replacing either the final pitch or the preceding setup pitch with alternative pitch types and locations while keeping the surrounding contextual information fixed. Optimal counterfactual selections were defined as those that minimized the predicted in-play probability, and their expected effects on pitchers' seasonal statistics were estimated using regression models linking model outputs to season statistics. The results suggest that the optimization of both final and setup pitches may substantially influence season-level performance, including improvements of more than 1.0 in K/9. The analyses also provided several practical insights, including velocity-band-specific effective locations, the importance of pitch commands, and the expansion of pitch-selection options through middle-velocity pitches. These findings quantitatively support the strategic importance of pitch sequencing in baseball.

</details>


### [117] [MM++: Unsupervised Scale-Invariant Multilayer OOD Detection via Top-K Gated Feature Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17352)
*Rahim Hossain,Md Tawheedul Islam Bhuian,Md Farhan Shadiq,Kyoung-Don Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MM++ is a fully unsupervised, post-hoc, scale-invariant OOD detection framework that fuses discriminative intermediate layers (selected via entropy density drops) with terminal representations in a Ledoit-Wolf regularized joint feature space to capture cross-layer correlations for robust near- and far-OOD detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing OOD detection methods face a trade-off between scale invariance and hierarchical expressivity. Scale-invariant approaches lose rich intermediate representations, while multi-layer methods suffer from early-layer noise. The authors aim to resolve this by constructing a principled joint feature space that is both scale-invariant and hierarchically expressive.

Method: MM++ operates in three stages: (1) Entropy density drop measurement to identify discriminative intermediate layers that mark semantic compression boundaries, filtering out noisy early layers. (2) Fusion of selected layers with the terminal representation into a unified feature space to capture latent cross-layer correlations. (3) Ledoit-Wolf regularized tied covariance matrix estimation to stabilize the joint space, enabling reliable Mahalanobis distance-based OOD scoring — all without auxiliary OOD data, fine-tuning, or architectural changes.

Result: MM++ delivers robust OOD detection performance across distinct architectures for both near-OOD and far-OOD scenarios, demonstrating the effectiveness of the regularized joint feature space approach compared to single-layer or unregularized multi-layer alternatives.

Conclusion: By fusing entropy-density-selected intermediate layers with terminal features under Ledoit-Wolf regularization, MM++ successfully bridges scale invariance and hierarchical expressivity, offering a practical, plug-and-play OOD detection solution requiring no additional training data or model modifications.

Abstract: We introduce MM++ (Multilayer Mahalanobis++), a fully unsupervised, strictly post-hoc, and scale-invariant framework for Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection. To address the trade-off between scale invariance and hierarchical expressivity, MM++ constructs a principled joint feature space. It first identifies discriminative intermediate layers by measuring entropy density drops, which mark the boundaries of sharp semantic compression. By fusing these selected layers with the terminal representation, the framework captures latent cross-layer correlations while mitigating early-layer noise. Crucially, a Ledoit-Wolf regularized tied covariance matrix stabilizes this unified space, enabling reliable distance estimation. Requiring no auxiliary OOD data, classifier fine-tuning, or architectural modifications, MM++ delivers robust performance across distinct architectures for both near- and far-OOD detection.

</details>


### [118] [When the Next Step Is Not One Step: Distribution-Aware Execution Modeling for Concurrent Go Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17508)
*Kaviru Hapuarachchi*

Main category: cs.LG
