TL;DR: Fine-tuning a 7B model on empirical distributions of concurrent program traces (KL objective) improves next-step prediction accuracy and calibration over single-label cross-entropy training, outperforming zero-shot Gemini 3.5 Flash.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Concurrent programs exhibit nondeterministic scheduling, meaning the same trace prefix can yield multiple valid next events. Training against a single label forces the model to guess one outcome of a random process, which is suboptimal. The authors leverage this nondeterminism as a training signal rather than a nuisance.

Method: Run each concurrent program many times to collect empirical distributions of next events from identical trace prefixes. Fine-tune a 7B parameter model to match these distributions using a KL-divergence objective (distribution training), compared against standard cross-entropy. Additionally, derive a formal goroutine-leak signature for select-blocked goroutines where P(GoUnblock)=0 by scheduler semantics. Evaluation uses 798 held-out predictions from real production Go bugs (CockroachDB, Kubernetes, gRPC, etcd).

Result: Distribution training on fewer than 1,000 traces achieves 36.2% accuracy, surpassing zero-shot Gemini 3.5 Flash (34.8%) and the non-fine-tuned base model (28.6%). Distribution training matches cross-entropy on accuracy (35.8% vs. 36.2%) while reducing Expected Calibration Error from 0.205 to 0.169.

Conclusion: Using nondeterminism as a training signal via distribution matching is effective for concurrent program trace prediction. KL-based training improves calibration without sacrificing accuracy, and formal scheduler-semantic signatures can certify certain goroutine-leak conditions. Dataset, adapters, and tooling are publicly released.

Abstract: Training a model to predict the next step in a concurrent program is harder than it looks: two runs of the same program from the same trace prefix can produce different next events, both valid, because the scheduler is nondeterministic. A model trained against a single label is learning to guess one outcome of a random process. We turn this around and use the nondeterminism as a training signal. We run each program many times, aggregate the observed next events into an empirical distribution, and fine-tune a 7B model to match that distribution with a KL objective. On 798 held-out predictions drawn from real production Go bugs (CockroachDB, Kubernetes, gRPC, etcd), fine-tuning on fewer than a thousand traces reaches 36.2% accuracy, ahead of Gemini 3.5 Flash used zero-shot (34.8%) and the same model without fine-tuning (28.6%). Distribution training matches cross-entropy on accuracy (35.8% vs. 36.2%) while reducing Expected Calibration Error from 0.205 to 0.169. We also derive a formal goroutine-leak signature for a class of select-blocked goroutines where P(GoUnblock)=0 holds by scheduler semantics, not by learning. We release the dataset, trained adapters, and all tooling.

</details>


### [119] [Performance-Driven Environment Abstraction with Multi-Timescale Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17377)
*Yue Guan,Dipankar Maity,Panagiotis Tsiotras*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a performance-driven approach to environment abstraction for large MDPs, where state aggregation is optimized directly for decision quality rather than preserving geometric structure. The authors derive a performance guarantee that decouples value-function approximation error from action-sharing loss, and propose a multi-timescale RL algorithm that jointly learns a policy and a tree-structured abstraction, adaptively refining or coarsening state partitions based on Q-value discrepancies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard environment abstractions in large MDPs often prioritize preserving geometric or topological fidelity, which does not necessarily translate to good decision-making performance. The authors aim to design abstractions that directly optimize decision quality, addressing the gap between representational accuracy and downstream policy performance.

Method: The authors model abstraction as a controlled approximation via state-space aggregation, where all states within an aggregated cluster share a common action distribution. For a fixed partition, they derive a performance bound that separates value-function approximation error from action-sharing-induced loss. Building on this analysis, they propose a multi-timescale RL framework that jointly adapts the policy and a tree-structured abstraction, using Q-value discrepancies to drive region refinement and coarsening, thereby balancing performance against abstraction complexity.

Result: Empirical evaluations show substantial state-space compression, improved sample efficiency, and faster replanning compared to actor-critic baselines, validating that performance-driven abstraction yields practical gains in large MDP settings.

Conclusion: Performance-driven abstraction that directly optimizes decision quality, rather than preserving structural fidelity, leads to more efficient and effective decision-making in large MDPs. The proposed tree-structured, Q-discrepancy-guided refinement approach successfully balances policy performance with abstraction size.

Abstract: We study performance-driven environment abstraction for decision-making in large Markov decision processes. Rather than preserving geometric or topological structure, we seek abstractions that directly optimize decision quality. We model abstraction as a controlled approximation obtained by aggregating the state space and enforcing a shared action distribution within each aggregated state. For a fixed partition, we establish a performance guarantee that separates value-function approximation error from the loss introduced by action sharing. Guided by this analysis, we develop a multi-timescale reinforcement learning framework that jointly adapts the policy and a tree-structured environment abstraction. The resulting algorithm refines and coarsens regions of the state space based on Q-value discrepancies, balancing performance against abstraction size and complexity. Empirical results demonstrate substantial state compression, improved sample efficiency, and faster replanning compared to actor-critic baselines.

</details>


### [120] [The Discrete-Log Clock: How a Transformer Learns Modular Multiplication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17399)
*Huu Danh Nguyen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Prior work found dense Fourier spectra in transformers trained on modular multiplication. The authors show this density is an artifact of using the wrong basis — the additive DFT. Using the multiplicative character transform (the natural basis for the multiplicative group), the spectrum becomes highly sparse, revealing that transformers learn a "Discrete-Log Clock" algorithm that reduces multiplication to addition in discrete-log space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reconcile the apparent discrepancy between modular addition (sparse Fourier structure, interpretable "Clock" algorithm) and modular multiplication (dense Fourier spectrum, seemingly uninterpretable). The hypothesis: the dense spectrum is an artifact of applying the additive Fourier transform to a problem with multiplicative algebraic structure.

Method: The authors train a small transformer on modular multiplication (a·b mod 113) until grokking. Instead of the standard additive DFT, they apply the multiplicative character transform (decomposing functions on (ℤ/pℤ)* into irreducible representations). They analyze the embedding spectrum in this basis using the Gini coefficient as a sparsity measure, examine MLP neuron tuning to multiplicative frequencies, and visualize neuron activations reordered by the discrete logarithm.

Result: The multiplicative character transform reveals a highly sparse spectrum (Gini 0.58 vs. 0.07 in additive basis) with only 4 key frequencies. 96.9% of MLP neurons are tuned to a single multiplicative frequency. Neuron activation heatmaps show clean 2D-periodic structure when reordered by discrete logarithm. This demonstrates the "Discrete-Log Clock" algorithm: the transformer maps inputs to discrete-log space, reducing multiplication to addition.

Conclusion: Matching the analysis basis to the algebraic structure of the task is essential for mechanistic interpretability. Standard tools (additive DFT) see noise where the correct basis (multiplicative character transform) reveals clean, interpretable structure. The methodology generalizes beyond multiplication to any task with known algebraic structure.

Abstract: When small transformers grok modular multiplication, prior work reports that the learned embedding has a "dense" Fourier spectrum requiring all frequencies. This contrasts with modular addition, where only a sparse set of key frequencies suffices. We show this density is an artifact of analyzing in the wrong basis. The natural Fourier transform for multiplication is not the standard additive DFT but the multiplicative character transform, which decomposes functions on the multiplicative group $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^*$ into its irreducible representations. Applying this transform to a grokked transformer trained on $a \cdot b \bmod 113$, we find the embedding spectrum becomes highly sparse (Gini coefficient 0.58 vs. 0.07 in the additive basis) with only 4 key frequencies carrying significant energy. Furthermore, 96.9% of MLP neurons are cleanly tuned to a single multiplicative frequency, and neuron activation heatmaps reveal 2D-periodic structure when reordered by the discrete logarithm. These results demonstrate the transformer reduces multiplication to addition in discrete-log space, implementing a "Discrete-Log Clock" algorithm analogous to Nanda et al.'s Clock algorithm for addition. The methodology generalizes: matching the analysis basis to the algebraic structure of the task reveals interpretable structure where standard tools see noise.

</details>


### [121] [Discrete Autoregressive Transformer for Generative Mechanism Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17409)
*Anar Nurizada,Anurag Purwar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A decoder-only transformer with VAE latent conditioning generates planar linkage mechanisms (4-, 6-, 8-bar) whose coupler curves match target trajectories, achieving strong geometric accuracy on a corpus of over one million mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Planar path synthesis maps a desired trajectory to linkage mechanisms, but the mapping is inherently one-to-many across different topologies (four-, six-, eight-bar). Traditional methods lack a unified generative framework that can produce diverse, accurate mechanism families across multiple topology types without dataset retrieval.

Method: Joint coordinates are uniformly quantized to tokens. A decoder-only transformer conditioned on a VAE latent of the target curve and an explicit mechanism-type token generates mechanisms autoregressively. Training uses token cross-entropy plus a Gaussian-smoothed bin auxiliary loss preserving ordinal structure. At inference, a bounded latent-noise schedule decodes all mechanism types at each noise level, retaining the top five candidates by geometric error. A latent k-NN baseline also conditions on training-set neighbor latents in VAE space.

Result: On held-out tests, aggregate mean Chamfer distance is 0.0132 and mean DTW is 0.153. The latent k-NN baseline achieves matched-topology mean Chamfer distance 0.0071 and mean DTW 0.117 using the same decoder.

Conclusion: The proposed conditional autoregressive formulation successfully generates diverse, accurate linkage families across multiple topologies for planar path synthesis, with the latent k-NN variant offering further accuracy gains by leveraging training-set neighbor latents.

Abstract: Planar path synthesis requires mechanisms whose coupler curves match a prescribed trajectory; the mapping from curve to linkage is inherently one-to-many across four-, six-, and eight-bar topologies. We address this design problem with simulation-grounded evaluation on a curated corpus of over one million mechanisms, reporting Chamfer distance and dynamic time warping after forward kinematics and geometric alignment. We formulate synthesis as conditional autoregressive sequence modeling: joint coordinates are uniformly quantized to tokens and generated by a decoder-only transformer with a variational-autoencoder (VAE) latent of the target curve and an explicit mechanism-type token. Training combines token cross-entropy with a Gaussian-smoothed bin auxiliary loss that respects ordinal structure among bins. At inference, a bounded latent-noise schedule decodes all mechanism types at each noise level; we retain the top five candidates by geometric error, yielding diverse accurate families without dataset lookup. On held-out tests, aggregate mean Chamfer distance is $0.0132$ and mean dynamic time warping is $0.153$; a latent $k$-nearest-neighbor baseline that conditions on training-set neighbor latents in VAE space achieves matched-topology mean Chamfer distance $0.0071$ and mean dynamic time warping $0.117$ using the same decoder.

</details>


### [122] [Amortized Probabilistic Retrieval of Atmospheric CO2 from OCO-2 Spectra Using Deep Learning with Laplace Approximations and Normalizing Flows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17413)
*Alejandro Calle-Saldarriaga,Felix Jimenez,Jack Grosskreuz,Jiazheng Wang,Jonathan Hobbs,Matthias Katzfuss*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A deep learning framework using multi-branch neural networks with Laplace approximations and normalizing flows achieves faster, more accurate, and better-calibrated uncertainty-quantified CO2 column retrieval from simulated OCO-2 spectra compared to operational full-physics algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current operational retrieval algorithms for NASA's OCO-2 are computationally expensive and fail to properly quantify uncertainties. There is a need for fast, accurate methods that can handle the massive data streams from satellite-based CO2 monitoring while providing reliable uncertainty estimates.

Method: A multi-branch neural network encodes spectral bands from a high-fidelity OCO-2 simulation dataset (designed for uncertainty quantification and incorporating realistic forward model errors). Two scalable uncertainty quantification methods are employed: Laplace approximations for efficient Gaussian posteriors and normalizing flows for capturing non-Gaussian, asymmetric posterior distributions. The model estimates either the full CO2 column posterior or summary statistics thereof.

Result: The framework demonstrates five key advantages over operational full-physics solvers: (1) orders-of-magnitude faster amortized inference; (2) robustness to model error via training on simulations with explicit model discrepancies; (3) superior point estimate accuracy; (4) better-calibrated uncertainty estimates; and (5) successful modeling of complex, non-Gaussian posteriors via normalizing flows.

Conclusion: Simulation-based deep learning is a viable path toward next-generation operational processing systems for satellite-based greenhouse gas monitoring, offering simultaneous improvements in speed, accuracy, and uncertainty quantification.

Abstract: Space-based monitoring of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) is essential for constraining the global carbon budget. NASA's Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 (OCO-2) estimates column-averaged dry-air mole fractions of CO2 (XCO2) using high-resolution spectra. However, current operational retrieval algorithms are computationally expensive and do not properly quantify uncertainties. We present a novel deep learning framework that addresses these challenges. Due to the difficulties of ground-truth data for real satellite observations, we develop and validate our approach using a high-fidelity simulation dataset. This dataset, created to support OCO-2 uncertainty quantification (UQ), incorporates realistic forward model errors. Our architecture encodes spectral bands using a multi-branch neural network and estimates posteriors of the full CO2 column or desired summaries thereof using two scalable UQ methods: Laplace approximations and normalizing flows. Our approach has five key advantages relative to operational "full-physics" solvers: (1) Amortization: Inference is orders of magnitude faster, enabling real-time processing of massive data streams; (2) Model error robustness: By training on simulations that explicitly include model discrepancies, our method accounts for systematic errors often neglected by standard inversions; (3) Point estimate accuracy: We achieve superior predictive accuracy compared to baseline methods; (4) Improved UQ: The probabilistic outputs yield better-calibrated uncertainty estimates; and (5) Non-Gaussian posteriors: When utilizing normalizing flows, our framework successfully models complex, asymmetric posterior distributions, overcoming the limitations of the Gaussian assumption. These results suggest that simulation-based deep learning is a viable path toward next-generation operational processing systems.

</details>


### [123] [Memory-Efficient Meta-Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Safety-Critical Control in Adversarial Spacecraft Proximity Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17414)
*Alejandro Posadas-Nava,Richard Linares,Minduli Wijayatunga*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates optimal combinations of recurrent network architectures (LSTM, GRU, Mamba) and RL algorithms (PPO, SAC) for learning ICCBF class-𝒦 functions via meta-RL to achieve safe, fuel-efficient autonomous spacecraft RPO, including under adversarial target behavior. Mamba with PPO yields the best results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous spacecraft RPO demands controllers that are both provably safe under actuation constraints and fuel-efficient. Prior work used meta-RL to learn class-𝒦 functions for ICCBFs, but the optimal choice of network architecture and training algorithm for this task remains unexplored, especially under adversarial conditions where the target spacecraft acts uncooperatively to degrade chaser safety.

Method: The authors extend a meta-RL-based ICCBF framework by systematically comparing three recurrent architectures — LSTM, GRU, and the state space model Mamba — combined with two policy optimization algorithms: PPO and SAC. Performance is evaluated on RPO tasks in both cooperative scenarios and adversarial scenarios where the target behaves to worsen chaser safety. Metrics include task completion, safety (constraint satisfaction), and fuel expenditure.

Result: Mamba paired with PPO achieves superior performance across all tested scenarios — cooperative and uncooperative — delivering the best trade-off among task completion rate, safety guarantees, and fuel savings compared to LSTM and GRU architectures under either PPO or SAC.

Conclusion: State space models like Mamba, when combined with PPO, offer a particularly effective approach for meta-RL-based tuning of ICCBF class-𝒦 functions in safety-critical spacecraft RPO, outperforming traditional RNN architectures even under adversarial disturbances.

Abstract: Autonomous spacecraft rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) require controllers that guarantee safety under thrust constraints while minimizing fuel expenditure. Input-constrained control barrier functions (ICCBFs) provide a control method for nonlinear systems with actuation constraints that construct a forward-invariant safe set. Previous work has shown that learning class-$\mathcal{K}$ functions defining the ICCBF recursion via meta reinforcement learning (meta-RL) yields a robust, non-greedy approach to safety-critical control in RPO. This paper extends that framework further by investigating the performance of three recurrent network architectures (Long Short Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), Selective State Space Model (Mamba)) and two training algorithms (Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Soft Actor Critic (SAC)) to identify the best setup for tuning ICCBF class-K functions via meta-RL. In addition to cooperative test cases, performance is evaluated in the presence of adversarial behavior where the target spacecraft behaves in a way that worsens the safety of the chaser spacecraft. Results indicate that state space models such as Mamba when used with PPO achieve superior task completion, safety, and fuel-savings compared to other architectures, across all cooperative and uncooperative scenarios tested.

</details>


### [124] [Generalization Guarantees for Multi-Input Neural Operator Learning in Sobolev Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17419)
*Yahong Yang,Zecheng Zhang,Wei Zhu,Wenjing Liao,Hao Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper derives approximation and generalization error bounds for multi-input neural operators measured in Sobolev norms, where multiple input functions may live on different domains with distinct dimensions and regularities. The rates explicitly decompose the contribution of each input, exhibit a log-log/log complexity dependence, and provide a unified framework applicable to PDE-based operator learning with Sobolev training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard operator learning typically handles a single input function. Real-world PDE and scientific computing problems often involve multiple input functions defined on different domains with varying dimensions and regularities. There is a need for a rigorous theoretical framework that quantifies how each input's properties contribute to overall approximation and generalization error, especially when training with Sobolev norms.

Method: The authors extend neural operator approximation theory to the multi-input setting. They analyze the error in Sobolev norms (rather than L²), decompose the total error into contributions from each input function space, and derive explicit rates that depend on each input's dimension, Sobolev regularity, and the target Sobolev order. The analysis covers both approximation error (capacity) and generalization error (sample complexity), yielding a log-log/log-type scaling with model size.

Result: The derived error rates explicitly quantify how each input space contributes to the final bound. In the balanced regime, rates are governed by interactions among input dimensions, regularities, and Sobolev orders. Model complexity dependence retains a mild log-log/log structure, matching known single-input results. The framework supports Sobolev training and applies broadly to operator learning from PDEs and scientific computing.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a general theoretical foundation for multi-input operator learning with Sobolev error metrics. The explicit role of each input's properties in the error bounds provides practical guidance for designing architectures and training strategies. The framework unifies and extends prior single-input operator learning theory to realistic, multi-input scenarios.

Abstract: We develop approximation and generalization error estimates for multi-input neural operators, with the output error measured in Sobolev norms. In contrast to standard operator-learning settings with a single input function, our framework allows multiple input functions defined on possibly different domains, with different dimensions and Sobolev regularities. The derived rates explicitly quantify the contribution of each input space to the final error bound. In particular, in the balanced regime, the approximation and generalization rates are governed by the interaction between the input dimensions, regularities, and Sobolev orders, while the dependence on the model complexity retains a \(\log\log/\log\)-type structure. Our analysis provides a general theoretical framework for multi-input operator learning, including Sobolev training, and is applicable to operator learning problems arising from partial differential equations and scientific computing.

</details>


### [125] [MorphStrata: Layer-Specific Perturbations for Generating Morphence Students in Time-Series Moving Target Defense](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17435)
*Abhishek Bhardwaj,Arnav Doshi,Anusri Nagarajan,Thanh Quynh Nhu Ta,Mohammad Masum,Robert Chun,Jaydip Sen,Saptarshi Sengupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MorphStrata introduces a selective, layer-specific stochastic noise injection strategy for generating diverse student models in a Moving Target Defense framework, using a Transformer teacher. It achieves comparable or superior adversarial robustness against FGSM, BIM, and PGD attacks on time-series benchmarks with minimal training overhead (<1% increase over Morphence).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time-series forecasting models are vulnerable to gradient-based adversarial attacks. Existing defenses, particularly Moving Target Defense (MTD) with randomized model instances, incur prohibitive training costs and trade off robustness against bounded response and compute. There is a need for a cost-efficient MTD strategy that maintains strong adversarial robustness without excessive overhead.

Method: MorphStrata uses a Transformer backbone as the teacher model and generates student models via selective, layer-specific stochastic noise injection — randomly perturbing specific architectural blocks rather than the entire model. This creates structured heterogeneity across student ensembles tailored to different data distributions and threat models. The approach extends the prior Morphence defense. Evaluation uses FGSM, BIM, and PGD attacks across multiple epsilon values on Jena Climate, Electricity Load Diagrams, and Appliances Energy Prediction datasets, with 30 randomized trials. Pairwise L2 distance among students is also measured and correlated with defense effectiveness.

Result: MorphStrata maintains comparable adversarial RMSE across datasets and attack regimes. On the high-entropy, periodic AEP dataset, it achieves the lowest RMSE across all attacks and perturbation budgets, improving over the static baseline by up to 24.11% (FGSM) and 97.97% (BIM) at epsilon=0.5. The targeted layer selection incurs less than 1% additional training time over Morphence while yielding double-digit gains in adversarial RMSE reduction. Higher pairwise L2 distance among students correlates positively with defense effectiveness.

Conclusion: MorphStrata delivers adversarial robustness as an MTD defense at marginal cost deltas compared to existing baselines, effectively balancing robustness and computational efficiency through selective, structured stochastic perturbations.

Abstract: Time-series forecasting models remain vulnerable to gradient-based adversarial attacks while existing defense mechanisms typically incur a trade-off in robustness for bounded response and compute cost. The problem is pronounced in Moving Target Defense where maintaining multiple randomized model instances substantially exacerbates the training overhead. In this work, we introduce MorphStrata, a student generation strategy with selective, layer-specific stochastic noise injection that extends the traditional Morphence defense. MorphStrata uses a Transformer backbone as the teacher and perturbs randomly selected architectural blocks to create structured heterogeneity across student models in response to varied data distributions and threat models. We evaluate against vanilla Transformer and Morphence backbones on a suite of benchmarks including the Jena Climate, Electricity Load Diagrams, and Appliances Energy Prediction using FGSM, BIM and PGD attacks across multiple attack strengths. Across datasets and attack regimes, the proposed ensemble maintains comparable adversarial RMSE. Specifically, for high entropy, periodic datasets as in the case of the AEP data, MorphStrata achieves the lowest RMSE across all attacks and perturbation budgets, improving over the static baseline by up to 24.11% and 97.97% under FGSM and BIM respectively at an epsilon value of 0.5 over 30 randomized trials. Targeting the layers to generate MorphStrata students accounts for less than 1% increase in train-times over the Morphence MTD baseline for most of the experiments, while accounting for double digit gains in adversarial RMSE reduction. We also observe a positive correlation between higher pairwise L2 distance (among generated students) and overall defense effectiveness. In summary, MorphStrata maintains adversarial robustness as an MTD defense at marginal cost deltas when compared to existing baselines.

</details>


### [126] [Toward Controllable Catalyst Inverse Design via Large-Scale Autoregressive Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17445)
*Dong Hyeon Mok,Jonggeol Na,Seoin Back*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A conditional generative model based on the GPT architecture with a numerical embedding layer was developed for inverse design of heterogeneous catalysts. Pretrained on 133M structures and fine-tuned on ~460K optimized structures with properties, it achieved 98% structural validity and up to 4-fold improvement in screening efficiency for binding-energy-targeted catalyst discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inverse design of heterogeneous catalysts is difficult due to the structural complexity of catalyst surfaces and the vast, coupled chemical space of surface-adsorbate interactions. Conventional high-throughput screening, even when ML-accelerated, becomes inefficient as the search space grows. There is a need for generative models that can directly construct catalysts with desired target properties, bypassing exhaustive enumeration.

Method: The authors developed a conditional catalyst generative model built on the Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) architecture, augmented with a numerical embedding layer to handle both categorical properties (e.g., adsorbate type, composition) and continuous properties (e.g., binding energy) within a single autoregressive framework. The model was pretrained on 133 million catalyst structures and then fine-tuned on ~460,000 DFT-optimized structures labeled with categorical properties and binding energies for conditional generation.

Result: The model achieved 98% structural validity, 95% optimization validity, and 93% joint match rate for adsorbate type and composition. For binding energy conditioning, the match rate (~20%) was a four-fold improvement over the baseline training distribution, with generated distributions shifting systematically toward target values. This enabled a 1.5- to 4-fold improvement in screening efficiency for reaction-targeted catalyst discovery without additional fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Large-scale autoregressive pre-training combined with explicit property conditioning offers a practical and effective route toward controllable catalyst generation and accelerated catalyst discovery, demonstrating that generative models can meaningfully navigate the vast chemical space of heterogeneous catalysts.

Abstract: Inverse design of heterogeneous catalysts remains challenging because catalyst surfaces exhibit substantial structural complexity with coupled surface-adsorbate interactions across a vast chemical space that is difficult to explore efficiently through conventional screening alone. Although machine learning-based high-throughput screening has accelerated catalyst discovery, its efficiency inevitably declines as the search space grows, motivating the development of generative models that can directly construct catalysts with target properties. Here, we present a conditional catalyst generative model based on the Generative Pretrained Transformer architecture with a numerical embedding layer that enables the generation of catalyst structures conditioned on both categorical and continuous properties within a single autoregressive framework. The model was pretrained on 133 million catalyst structures and subsequently fine-tuned on approximately 460,000 optimized structures with associated categorical properties and binding energies for conditional generation. The resulting model achieved 98% structural validity, 95% optimization validity, and high categorical condition fidelity, with a 93 % joint match rate for adsorbate type and composition. For binding energy conditioning, the match rate of approximately 20% represents a four-fold improvement over the baseline training distribution, and the generated distributions shift systematically toward the target values, enabling a 1.5 to 4-fold improvement in screening efficiency for reaction-targeted catalyst discovery without additional fine-tuning. These results show that large-scale autoregressive pre-training, combined with explicit property conditioning, provides a practical route toward controllable catalyst generation and accelerated catalysts discovery.

</details>


### [127] [Credibility-Weighted Pricing of Autonomous Vehicle Liability Under Operational Design Domain Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17451)
*Doyeon Jang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a hierarchical Bayesian credibility framework for automated driving system insurance ratemaking, using an ODD-similarity kernel to pool sparse crash data across cities, software versions, and territories. Tested on Waymo crash data (648 crashes, 116M miles), showing partial pooling decisively outperforms no pooling, with kernel advantages detectable at ~12 deployed cities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated driving systems face a foundational ratemaking problem: sparse crash experience, shifting operational design domains (ODDs), and non-stationary risk across software releases. Traditional actuarial credibility models (e.g., Bühlmann-Straub) struggle with these dynamics, necessitating a framework that intelligently pools information across heterogeneous deployment contexts.

Method: A hierarchical Bayesian credibility framework that pools data across cities, software versions, and territories using a learned ODD-similarity kernel. The kernel captures similarity between operational design domains to inform partial pooling. The Bühlmann-Straub credibility model emerges as a limiting case. Validation uses 648 verified-engaged Waymo crashes (NHTSA Standing General Order database) against 116 million matched miles across four U.S. metropolitan areas, supplemented by power analysis.

Result: City-aggregate credibility weights range from 0.12 to 0.46, indicating moderate partial pooling. Partial pooling decisively outperforms no pooling. Power analysis reveals the learned kernel's statistical advantage becomes detectable at approximately twelve deployed cities.

Conclusion: The hierarchical Bayesian framework with ODD-similarity kernel provides a principled solution for ratemaking in automated driving systems, enabling robust risk estimation even with sparse, non-stationary data. Practical deployment at scale (~12+ cities) is necessary to fully realize the kernel's benefits.

Abstract: Automated Driving System deployments create a foundational ratemaking challenge: sparse experience, shifting operational design domains, and non-stationary risk across software releases. We propose a hierarchical Bayesian credibility framework pooling across cities, software versions, and territories via a learned ODD-similarity kernel, nesting Buhlmann-Straub as a limiting case. Demonstrated on 648 verified-engaged Waymo crashes across four U.S. metros from the NHTSA Standing General Order database against 116 million matched miles, city-aggregate credibility weights are moderate (0.12-0.46), partial pooling decisively outperforms no pooling, and a power analysis shows the learned kernel's advantage becomes detectable at approximately twelve deployed cities.

</details>


### [128] [Operator Boosting Produces Pareto-Efficient PDE Surrogates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17460)
*Lennon J. Shikhman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Operator Boosting is a stagewise residual-learning framework that constructs compact neural-operator surrogates by sequentially training tiny models on residual fields, achieving ~72–95% parameter reduction while often improving accuracy across diverse PDE benchmarks compared to full-size monolithic baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Full-size neural operators are costly to store, deploy, and evaluate in many-query scientific workflows. Rather than post-hoc compression, the authors seek a direct method to build compact yet accurate surrogates, improving the accuracy-parameter Pareto frontier.

Method: Operator Boosting begins from the empirical mean predictor in normalized output coordinates, then iteratively trains a sequence of tiny, same-family neural operators (FNO, DeepONet, CNO) on residual fields. Each correction is incorporated using validation-selected shrinkage. The framework is evaluated on 30 dataset-architecture pairs spanning 1D, 2D, and 3D PDE benchmarks from PDEBench, APEBench, and The Well.

Result: Across 30 dataset-architecture pairs, 21 showed positive mean accuracy gains and 17 had positive confidence intervals. All boosted stacks reduced trainable parameters by ~72–95%. Best-model comparisons showed empirical Pareto improvements on 7 of 10 completed PDE benchmarks, including 2D Navier-Stokes, shallow-water dynamics, Darcy flow, 1D transport/reaction, and 3D compressible Navier-Stokes.

Conclusion: Operator Boosting often improves the empirical accuracy-parameter Pareto frontier of neural PDE surrogates, though PDE- and architecture-dependent regimes exist where residual boosting fails to offset compression.

Abstract: Neural operators are widely used as surrogate solution maps for partial differential equations (PDEs), but full-size models can be costly to store, deploy, and evaluate in many-query scientific workflows. This work introduces Operator Boosting, a stagewise residual-learning framework for constructing compact neural-operator surrogates directly, rather than training a large model and compressing it afterward. Starting from the empirical mean predictor in normalized output coordinates, the method trains a sequence of tiny same-family neural operators on residual fields and incorporates each correction through validation-selected shrinkage. We instantiate the framework with Fourier neural operators (FNOs), DeepONets, and convolutional neural operators (CNOs), and compare boosted tiny stacks against full-size monolithic baselines across one-, two-, and three-dimensional PDE benchmarks from PDEBench, APEBench, and The Well. Across 30 dataset-architecture pairs, 21 show positive mean accuracy gains and 17 have positive confidence intervals, while all boosted stacks reduce trainable parameter count by approximately 72-95%. Best-model comparisons show empirical Pareto improvements on 7 of 10 completed PDE benchmarks, including two-dimensional Navier-Stokes, shallow-water dynamics, Darcy flow, one-dimensional transport and reaction systems, and three-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes. These results show that Operator Boosting often improves the empirical accuracy-parameter Pareto frontier of neural PDE surrogates, while also exposing PDE- and architecture-dependent regimes where residual boosting fails to offset compression.

</details>


### [129] [ResAware: Cross-Environment Website Fingerprinting via Resource-Privileged Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17462)
*Chongru Fan,Wei Wang,Wentao Huang,Zhenquan Ding,Jinqiao Shi,Lei Cui,Zhiyu Hao,Xiaochun Yun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ResAware proposes a resource-aware knowledge distillation framework for Website Fingerprinting that distills privileged resource-level features from a teacher model into a student model which operates solely on encrypted traffic at deployment, significantly improving cross-environment robustness against temporal drift and other real-world perturbations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Website Fingerprinting attacks degrade in real-world settings due to spatio-temporal drift, browser heterogeneity, and proxy obfuscation, because they rely exclusively on low-level traffic features that are noisy and sensitive to environmental perturbations. The core insight is that resource-level information (e.g., object sizes, types) provides richer, more stable supervisory signals that can improve robustness without expanding online observation capabilities at inference time.

Method: ResAware operates under a training-rich/inference-poor asymmetric setting. A teacher model is first trained on resource-level features (privileged information available only during training). Heterogeneous knowledge distillation then transfers this knowledge to a student model that performs inference using only encrypted traffic features. At deployment, the student model incurs zero additional cost, requiring no resource-level access.

Result: Evaluated on a large-scale dataset collected over five months from six globally distributed vantage points with 160,000+ paired samples. Under 150-day temporal drift, ResAware improved Var-CNN's F1-score from 72.77% to 81.49% and open-world TPR@1%FPR from 22.40% to 27.20%. Consistent robustness gains were demonstrated across diverse WF baselines.

Conclusion: Resource-level supervision via knowledge distillation significantly enhances WF robustness against real-world distribution shifts without requiring additional online observation capabilities, offering a practical path toward deploying reliable WF in realistic environments.

Abstract: While Website Fingerprinting (WF) attacks achieve high accuracy in controlled laboratory settings, they often degrade substantially in real-world environments due to spatio-temporal drift, browser heterogeneity, proxy obfuscation and etc. This limitation stems from their sole reliance on low-level traffic features that are noisy and highly sensitive to environmental perturbations. To address this problem, we propose \textbf{ResAware}, a cross-environment resource-aware distillation framework under a \textit{training-rich/inference-poor} asymmetric setting. Specifically, ResAware trains a teacher model on resource-level features, and then distills the resulting privileged knowledge into a student model through heterogeneous knowledge distillation. At deployment time, the student model performs inference using only encrypted traffic, incurring zero additional cost. We evaluate ResAware on a large-scale dataset collected over five months from six globally distributed vantage points, comprising more than $160{,}000$ paired samples. The results show that ResAware significantly enhances the cross-environment robustness of diverse WF baselines. Under a 150-day temporal drift, for example, ResAware improves the F1-score of Var-CNN from $72.77\%$ to $81.49\%$ and the open-world $TPR@1\%FPR$ from $22.40\%$ to $27.20\%$. Our results demonstrate that resource-level supervision improves WF robustness without expanding online observation capabilities.

</details>


### [130] [CheckMIABench: Firm Foundations For Membership Inference Attacks on Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17464)
*Jeffrey G. Wang,Jason Wang,Marvin Li,Seth Neel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a principled benchmark for evaluating membership inference attacks (MIAs) on LLMs by using training data before and after a fixed checkpoint from the same distribution, then applies it to evaluate published attacks on Pythia and OLMo models (70M–7B parameters), releasing a modular open-source library.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MIA evaluations on language models suffer from distribution shifts between member and non-member sets, undermining statistical validity. "Blind" methods with no model access can outperform published attacks, revealing flawed benchmarks. A clean, principled evaluation framework is urgently needed.

Method: The authors leverage the insight that for models with intermediate checkpoints and public training data, samples seen before a fixed training step and those seen after are drawn from the same distribution — eliminating distribution shift. They construct an MIA benchmark by treating pre-checkpoint data as members and post-checkpoint data as non-members, applying this to open-source Pythia and OLMo models (70M–7B parameters) to evaluate several published attacks.

Result: The framework enables statistically valid MIA evaluation across six published attacks on models spanning 70M to 7B parameters, avoiding the confounding effects of distribution shifts that plagued prior benchmarks.

Conclusion: The proposed benchmark provides a sound methodological foundation for MIA evaluation on LLMs. The open-sourced Pandora-LLM library facilitates reproducible and principled privacy research going forward.

Abstract: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) are a canonical way to assess a machine learning model's privacy properties. Although several attempts have been made to evaluate MIAs on language models, the extant literature has suffered numerous difficulties in constructing clean evaluations to test new techniques. In particular, subtle distribution shifts between member and non-member sets can undermine the statistical validity of MIAs; recent work has underscored this by showing that "blind" methods with no access to the underlying model can perform far better than published methods on the same benchmarks. This paper constructs a benchmark for principled evaluation of MIAs against LLMs, by leveraging the insight that training data before and after a fixed point during training are drawn from the same distribution. Therefore, all open-source models with intermediate checkpoints and public training data can be converted into MIA testbeds. We apply our framework to a half-dozen published attacks on the Pythia and OLMo family of models, from 70M to 7B parameters. To facilitate further privacy research, we open-source a modular library for designing and implementing attacks in this setting: https://github.com/safr-ai-lab/pandora_llm.

</details>


### [131] [Perron--Frobenius Operator Matching for Generative Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17465)
*Shiqi Zhang,Wuwei Wu,Jaemin Oh,Jie Chen,Xiaoning Qian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PFOM introduces a generative framework based on the Perron-Frobenius operator that unifies flow, diffusion, and jump models under operator matching. It proves KL divergence uniquely preserves equivalence between density and sample-conditioned objectives among Bregman divergences, and proposes Nesterov-accelerated training/sampling for improved stability and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing generative models (flows, diffusions, jump processes) are treated separately despite sharing underlying density evolution dynamics. The authors seek a unified operator-theoretic framework that subsumes these paradigms while enabling principled loss design and accelerated training.

Method: The paper proposes PFOM, which matches density evolution via the integral Perron-Frobenius operator. Theoretically, it proves that only KL divergence among Bregman divergences preserves equality between the density-level objective and the sample-conditioned objective, yielding a practical loss equivalent to Koopman path matching. It further develops Nesterov-accelerated schemes for both training and sampling to stabilize discretization and accelerate convergence.

Result: On Gaussian mixtures and two-moons benchmarks, PFOM demonstrates faster decrease in KL divergence, Wasserstein-2 distance, and MMD, along with improved wall-clock efficiency compared to baselines.

Conclusion: PFOM bridges operator-theoretic identification with modern generative modeling, providing a unified perspective that encompasses flow, diffusion, and jump models. The framework opens future directions toward adaptive dictionaries and high-dimensional applications.

Abstract: We introduce Perron--Frobenius Operator Matching (PFOM), a generative framework that matches density evolution via the integral PF operator, subsuming flow, diffusion, and jump models. We prove that among Bregman divergences, only Kullback--Leibler divergence preserves equality between density-level and sample-conditioned objectives, yielding a practical loss equivalent to Koopman path matching. We further develop Nesterov-accelerated training and sampling that stabilize discretization and accelerate convergence. %On Gaussian mixtures and two-moons, PFOM achieves faster KL/$W_2$/MMD decrease and improved wall-clock efficiency with empirical validation. PFOM unifies operator-theoretic identification with modern generative modeling and opens paths to adaptive dictionaries and high-dimensional applications.

</details>


### [132] [ReRAM-aware Model Finetuning addressing I-V Non-linearity and Retention Errors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17471)
*Ching-Yi Lin,Shamik Kundu,Arnab Raha,Sahil Shah*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a finetuning-based hardware-aware training algorithm for deploying DNNs on ReRAM crossbar arrays, addressing I-V non-linearity and retention errors without requiring computationally prohibitive training from scratch. The method achieves minimal accuracy degradation (e.g., <2% on MobileNetV3/ImageNet, 1-point F1 drop on SQuAD v2) on large-scale models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional von Neumann architectures face bottlenecks, and while ReRAM-based In-Memory Computing offers a promising alternative, its non-idealities (e.g., I-V non-linearity, retention errors) hinder practical deployment. Existing hardware-aware training frameworks demand training from scratch, which is computationally infeasible for modern large-scale DNNs.

Method: A finetuning-based hardware-aware training approach with two key components: (1) a range-shrunk sinh transformation to mitigate I-V non-linearity, and (2) incorporating retention errors directly into a regularization loss term during finetuning, enabling adaptation to ReRAM non-idealities with minimal training overhead.

Result: The method achieves accuracy comparable to baseline models on ResNet18 and DeiT-Tiny. On ImageNet with MobileNetV3 families, accuracy degradation is less than 2%. On the SQuAD v2 question-answering dataset, F1 score degrades by only 1 point.

Conclusion: The proposed finetuning-based framework enables robust DNN deployment on ReRAM crossbar arrays with minimal computational overhead, making hardware-aware training practical for large-scale models across vision and NLP tasks.

Abstract: Traditional CPU, GPU, and NPU architectures are increasingly limited by the von Neumann bottleneck. While In-Memory Computing (IMC) using ReRAM crossbar arrays offers a high-density, energy-efficient alternative, its practical deployment is constrained through their non-idealities. Existing hardware-aware training frameworks often require training from scratch, which is computationally prohibitive for modern large-scale models. In this work, we propose a finetuning-based hardware-aware training algorithm that enables robust DNN deployment on ReRAM with minimal training overhead. Our approach mitigates I-V non-linearity by applying a range-shrunk sinh transformation and incorporates retention errors directly into a regularization loss during the finetuning process. We evaluate our framework across models and tasks such as image classification and question-answering (QA). Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves similar accuracy on large-scale models like ResNet18 and DeiT-Tiny as the base model. In-case of ImageNet for MobileNetV3 families the technique has only less than 2% accuracy degradation. Further, applying the technique on the SQuAD v2 dataset results in only 1 point degradation of F-1 score.

</details>


### [133] [Multi-Adapter PPO: A Cross-Attention Enhanced Wavelength Selection Framework for LIBS Quantitative Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17476)
*Hao Li,Man Fung Zhuo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Multi-Adapter PPO reinforcement learning framework with cross-attention mechanisms is proposed for wavelength selection in LIBS quantitative analysis, outperforming PSO by 28.4% in comprehensive score and 45.2% in prediction accuracy on steel and coal datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LIBS quantitative analysis suffers from high-dimensional spectral data and a fundamental trade-off between prediction accuracy and feature efficiency in wavelength selection. Traditional methods like PSO struggle to capture complex spectral relationships effectively.

Method: The authors reformulate wavelength selection as a reinforcement learning problem using a Multi-Adapter Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) framework. The method employs cross-attention mechanisms and multiple specialized adapters to capture intricate spectral relationships and select informative wavelengths.

Result: The Multi-Adapter PPO framework outperforms traditional PSO by 28.4% in comprehensive score and 45.2% in prediction accuracy on steel and coal datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results while balancing accuracy and feature efficiency.

Conclusion: The proposed MAPPO framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in LIBS quantitative analysis with strong interpretability and computational efficiency. Code and dataset are publicly released.

Abstract: Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) quantitative analysis faces critical challenges in wavelength selection due to high-dimensional spectral data and the fundamental trade-off between prediction accuracy and feature efficiency. This paper presents a novel Multi-Adapter PPO framework that transforms wavelength selection into a reinforcement learning problem, leveraging cross-attention mechanisms and multiple specialized adapters to capture complex spectral relationships. Our approach outperforms traditional Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) by an average of 28.4\% in comprehensive score and 45.2\% in prediction accuracy across steel and coal datasets. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance in balancing prediction accuracy with feature efficiency, achieving state-of-the-art results in LIBS quantitative analysis while maintaining interpretability and computational efficiency. We released our code and dataset here: https://github.com/Hflying/MAPPO

</details>


### [134] [Online LLM Selection via Constrained Bandits with Time-Varying Demand](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17489)
*Yin Huang,Qingsong Liu,Jie Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper formulates LLM selection in edge-cloud systems as a constrained stochastic bandit problem with hard budget and soft latency constraints, proposes a confidence-bound-based online learning algorithm, and provides theoretical guarantees of sublinear regret and constraint violations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs deployed in edge-cloud inference systems exhibit heterogeneous and stochastic performance profiles, while task demands vary over time. Static model selection fails under these conditions. Real-world deployments impose hard monetary budgets and soft latency requirements, making online decision-making with partial feedback both critical and challenging.

Method: The problem is cast as a constrained stochastic bandit with both packing-type (hard budget) and covering-type (soft latency) constraints. The proposed algorithm uses confidence-bound estimates for unknown reward/cost/latency distributions and demand predictions to sequentially select models. It balances reward maximization with long-term constraint satisfaction using only partial feedback.

Result: The algorithm achieves sublinear regret and sublinear cumulative covering constraint violations against an offline full-information benchmark. Synthetic workload experiments demonstrate effectiveness and robustness in dynamic, resource-constrained environments.

Conclusion: The approach provides a principled online learning solution for cost- and latency-aware LLM selection in edge-cloud systems, with both theoretical backing and empirical validation.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in edge-cloud inference systems to handle diverse user tasks with heterogeneous accuracy, latency, and cost profiles. Selecting the appropriate LLM for each incoming task is critical for ensuring service quality and efficient resource utilization. However, model heterogeneity, stochastic and unknown performance characteristics, and time-varying task demands make static selection strategies inadequate. Real-world deployments often impose hard resource budgets such as monetary expenditure limits, along with soft service-level requirements such as latency guarantees. These constraints introduce additional challenges for online decision-making. We formulate this problem as a constrained stochastic bandit learning task, where the learner sequentially selects models under both packing-type (hard) and covering-type (soft) constraints, while adapting to time-varying task demand. The learner operates without access to the underlying reward, cost, or latency distributions and must rely on partial feedback. We develop a novel online learning algorithm that leverages confidence-bound estimates and demand predictions to balance reward maximization with long-term constraint satisfaction. We provide theoretical guarantees showing sublinear regret and sublinear covering constraint violations compared to an offline benchmark with full information. Experimental results on synthetic workloads demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our approach in dynamic, resource-constrained environments.

</details>


### [135] [Reconfigurable Computing Challenge: Transformer for Jet Tagging on Versal AI Engines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17500)
*Gram Koski,Sean Lipps,Zhenghua Ma,G. Abarajithan,Ryan Kastner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A reusable, open-source framework that maps quantized integer-only transformer layers (dense and multi-head attention) onto AMD Versal AI Engine tiles for low-latency jet tagging in LHC trigger systems, with automated Vitis graph code generation from Python model descriptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer models achieve high accuracy for jet tagging at the LHC, but their deployment in trigger systems is constrained by strict low-latency requirements and limited on-detector resources. There is a need to bridge the gap between model performance and hardware feasibility on FPGA-like accelerator fabrics such as the AMD Versal AI Engine.

Method: The authors implement a quantized, integer-only transformer for jet tagging, mapping dense and multi-head attention (MHA) layers onto AMD Versal AI Engine (AIE) tiles. The core contribution is a software framework that treats transformer layers as reusable, composable AIE building blocks and automatically emits Vitis graph code from a high-level Python model description.

Result: The paper presents an initial implementation demonstrating the feasibility of deploying a quantized transformer on AIE tiles. The framework successfully generates Vitis graph code from Python-level model descriptions, providing a modular foundation for further exploration of transformer acceleration on the Versal platform.

Conclusion: Mapping quantized transformers to AIE tiles is a viable path toward deploying high-performance jet taggers in low-latency LHC trigger environments. The open-source, composable framework lowers the barrier for future research and development in this area.

Abstract: Transformer-based models achieve strong performance for jet tagging at the CERN LHC, but deploying them in low-latency, resource-constrained trigger systems is challenging. We present an initial implementation of a quantized, integer-only transformer for jet tagging on the AMD Versal AI Engine (AIE), mapping dense and multi-head attention (MHA) layers to AIE tiles. The main contribution is a reusable software framework that represents transformer layers as composable AIE building blocks and automatically generates the corresponding Vitis graph code from a high-level Python model description. This framework provides a foundation for future research and is released as open-source software at https://github.com/KastnerRG/particle_transformer_aie.

</details>


### [136] [Geometry-Aware Post-Hoc Uncertainty Quantification in Operator Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17513)
*Oriol Vendrell-Gallart,Nima Negarandeh,Ramin Bostanabad*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: REEF-GP is a post-hoc uncertainty quantification framework that fits a Gaussian Process to the residuals of a frozen neural operator, using the operator's internal learned embeddings as the kernel feature space. It provides calibrated, geometry-aware uncertainty estimates competitive with deep ensembles at a fraction of the computational cost, while remaining robust under geometric distribution shifts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural operators offer fast PDE surrogates but produce deterministic predictions, limiting their utility in tasks requiring uncertainty quantification. Existing UQ methods focus on parameter uncertainty and neglect the geometry-aware representations already learned by the operator. There is a need for a practical, scalable UQ approach that leverages these intrinsic representations, especially under geometric variability.

Method: REEF-GP freezes a pretrained neural operator and fits a Gaussian Process to its prediction residuals, using the operator's internal coordinate-feature embeddings to construct the GP kernel. Key technical components include: (1) spectral-normalized projections for stability on unstructured domains, (2) heteroscedastic geometry-aware noise modeling, and (3) efficient subset-based training to avoid restrictive low-rank approximations.

Result: Evaluated across five PDE benchmarks with varying geometries, REEF-GP preserves predictive accuracy while delivering calibrated uncertainty estimates competitive with deep ensembles but at significantly lower cost. Uncertainty concentrates in physically meaningful regions (e.g., shock fronts), and the method remains robust under geometric distribution shift.

Conclusion: Accurate and scalable post-hoc UQ for neural operators can be achieved directly in their learned feature space. REEF-GP offers a practical, cost-effective alternative to parameter-centric UQ approaches by exploiting the operator's intrinsic geometry-aware representations.

Abstract: Neural operators provide fast surrogates for PDEs but their deterministic predictions limit their use in tasks requiring uncertainty quantification (UQ), especially under geometric variability. Existing approaches primarily model uncertainty in network parameters, largely overlooking the geometry-aware representations learned by the operator itself. We propose REEF-GP (Residual on Embedded Features Gaussian Process), a post-hoc UQ framework that fits a GP to the residuals of a frozen neural operator whose internal embeddings define the kernel feature space. Rather than learning a separate feature map, REEF-GP adapts the operator's intrinsic coordinate-feature representations to construct geometry-aware uncertainties. To ensure stability and scalability on unstructured domains, REEF-GP incorporates spectral-normalized projections, heteroscedastic geometry-aware noise, and efficient subset-based training that avoids restrictive low-rank approximations. Across five PDE benchmarks with varying geometries, REEF-GP preserves predictive accuracy while achieving calibrated uncertainty estimates competitive with deep ensembles but at a fraction of their cost. Our approach remains robust under geometric distribution shift, with uncertainty concentrating in physically meaningful regions (e.g., shock fronts). Our results demonstrate that accurate and scalable post-hoc UQ for neural operators can be achieved directly in their learned feature space, offering a practical alternative to parameter-centric approaches.

</details>


### [137] [FoundCause: Causal Discovery with Latent Confounders from Observational Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17516)
*Patrick Blöbaum,Krishnakumar Balasubramanian,Shiva Prasad Kasiviswanathan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FoundCause is an amortized causal discovery model trained on synthetic data that maps datasets to causal graphs in a single forward pass. It is the first amortized approach to explicitly model latent confounding and outperforms 15 baseline methods on real-world datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Causal discovery from observational data is difficult due to the need to recover both directed structure and latent confounding without experimental interventions. Existing amortized methods fail to explicitly model hidden confounders.

Method: FoundCause uses a permutation-invariant transformer encoder with alternating attention over samples and variables, statistics-conditioned attention injected with pairwise asymmetry features, a factorized decoder separating edge existence from direction, a triangular refinement module for higher-order motifs (chains, colliders), a dedicated confounder module with learnable latent tokens, and masked input representation for missing data. The model is trained entirely on synthetic data from simulated structural causal models.

Result: FoundCause outperforms 11 classical non-amortized methods (PC, GES, NOTEARS, etc.) and 4 amortized methods on 15 real-world datasets: +9.6% F1, +1.2% AUROC, and 18.9% reduction in structural Hamming distance over the strongest non-amortized baselines.

Conclusion: Amortized causal discovery with explicit latent confounder modeling and strong inductive biases (permutation invariance, statistics-conditioned attention, factorized decoding, triangular refinement) can significantly outperform both classical and existing amortized methods while requiring only a single forward pass at inference.

Abstract: Causal discovery from observational data remains challenging due to the need to recover directed structure and latent confounding without interventions. We propose FoundCause, an amortized causal discovery model trained entirely on synthetic data that maps datasets directly to causal graphs in a single forward pass. By learning from large collections of simulated structural causal models, FoundCause captures transferable statistical patterns that generalize beyond individual datasets. The architecture incorporates several key inductive biases for causal discovery. It uses a permutation-invariant transformer encoder with alternating attention over samples and variables to jointly model cross-variable dependence and per-variable distributions. Pairwise statistical features derived from classical asymmetry measures are injected through statistics-conditioned attention, guiding the model toward known causal signals. A factorized decoder separates edge existence from direction, while a triangular refinement module enables reasoning over higher-order causal motifs such as chains and colliders. In addition, a dedicated confounder module based on learnable latent tokens explicitly models hidden common causes, and the model explicitly handles missing data via its masked input representation. To our knowledge, FoundCause is the first amortized causal discovery approach to explicitly model latent confounding. FoundCause outperforms 11 classical non-amortized methods (e.g., PC, GES, NOTEARS-style optimization) and 4 amortized causal discovery methods on 15 real-world datasets, achieving +9.6% improvement in $F_1$, +1.2% in AUROC, and an 18.9% reduction in structural Hamming distance relative to the strongest non-amortized methods, while performing inference in a single forward pass.

</details>


### [138] [Learning to Refine Hidden States for Reliable LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17524)
*Chia-Hsuan Hsu,Jui-Ming Yao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReLAR is a reinforcement-guided framework that iteratively refines hidden states in LLMs before decoding, using learned controllers to adaptively determine refinement steps, improving reasoning stability and accuracy with lower inference cost than chain-of-thought methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs exhibit strong reasoning but suffer from instability in complex multi-step settings, where early hidden-state errors propagate and cause incorrect predictions. Existing explicit reasoning methods (e.g., chain-of-thought) incur high inference overhead.

Method: ReLAR maintains a compact latent reasoning state and employs two learned controllers — a depth controller and an action controller — that adaptively determine the number and direction of refinement steps. These controllers are trained via a policy gradient objective based on step-wise likelihood improvement, enabling input-dependent reasoning without generating explicit chain-of-thought tokens.

Result: ReLAR demonstrates improved accuracy, generation quality, and reasoning stability across medical, mathematical, multi-hop reasoning, and open-ended generation benchmarks, while requiring substantially lower inference overhead than explicit reasoning baselines.

Conclusion: Latent-space refinement guided by reinforcement learning offers an efficient and effective alternative to explicit chain-of-thought reasoning, addressing error propagation while maintaining computational efficiency.

Abstract: Large language models show strong reasoning ability, but their internal reasoning process can remain unstable in complex multi-step settings, where early hidden-state errors may propagate to incorrect predictions. We propose ReLAR, a reinforcement-guided latent refinement framework that iteratively updates hidden representations before decoding. ReLAR maintains a compact latent reasoning state and uses learned depth and action controllers to adaptively determine both the number and direction of refinement steps. The controllers are trained with a policy gradient objective based on step-wise likelihood improvement, enabling efficient input-dependent reasoning without explicit chain-of-thought generation. Experiments on medical, mathematical, multi-hop reasoning, and open-ended generation benchmarks show that ReLAR improves accuracy, generation quality, and reasoning stability with substantially lower inference overhead than explicit reasoning baselines.

</details>


### [139] [MGUP: A Momentum-Gradient Alignment Update Policy for Stochastic Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17526)
*Da Chang,Ganzhao Yuan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MGUP is a plug-and-play mechanism that augments momentum-based optimizers by applying larger step-sizes to a fixed proportion of parameters and smaller step-sizes to the rest, providing convergence guarantees and improved training stability for large models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing intra-layer selective update methods lack a general mechanism with both fine-grained control and theoretical convergence guarantees for training large language models.

Method: MGUP (Mixed Gradient Update Policy) selects a fixed proportion of parameters per iteration to receive larger step-sizes while the remainder receive smaller, non-zero step-sizes, and integrates seamlessly with momentum-based optimizers like AdamW, Lion, and Muon.

Result: MGUP-enhanced optimizers (MGUP-AdamW, MGUP-Lion, MGUP-Muon) achieve superior or more stable performance across MAE pretraining, LLM pretraining, and downstream fine-tuning tasks compared to base optimizers. Convergence is theoretically guaranteed for MGUP-AdamW under standard assumptions.

Conclusion: MGUP offers a principled, versatile, and theoretically grounded strategy for efficient intra-layer selective updates that accelerates and stabilizes large-scale model training.

Abstract: Efficient optimization is essential for training large language models. Although intra-layer selective updates have been explored, a general mechanism that enables fine-grained control while ensuring convergence guarantees is still lacking. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{MGUP}, a novel mechanism for selective updates. \textbf{MGUP} augments standard momentum-based optimizers by applying larger step-sizes to a selected fixed proportion of parameters in each iteration, while applying smaller, non-zero step-sizes to the rest. As a nearly {plug-and-play} module, \textbf{MGUP} seamlessly integrates with optimizers such as AdamW, Lion, and Muon. This yields powerful variants such as \textbf{MGUP-AdamW}, \textbf{MGUP-Lion}, and \textbf{MGUP-Muon}. Under standard assumptions, we provide theoretical convergence guarantees for \textbf{MGUP-AdamW} (without weight decay) in stochastic optimization. Extensive experiments across diverse tasks, including MAE pretraining, LLM pretraining, and downstream fine-tuning, demonstrate that our \textbf{MGUP}-enhanced optimizers achieve superior or more stable performance compared to their original base optimizers. We offer a principled, versatile, and theoretically grounded strategy for efficient intra-layer selective updates, accelerating and stabilizing the training of large-scale models. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MaeChd/MGUP.

</details>


### [140] [Non-negative Matrix Factorisation with Topological Regularisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17531)
*Matias de Jong van Lier,Shizuo Kaji,Keunsu Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a novel NMF framework that uses persistent homology to regularize the topology of learned basis functions, enabling the discovery of interpretable, topologically structured components across images, time series, and graph signals in a unified, threshold-free manner.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many data modalities are naturally represented as non-negative functions on structured domains, where basis quality depends on topological properties (e.g., spatial coherence, periodicity). Existing topology-incorporating methods suffer from discreteness and threshold dependence, making them incompatible with gradient-based continuous optimization.

Method: The authors employ persistent homology as a stable, threshold-free topological quantifier and design differentiable topological scores that serve as regularizers within the NMF objective function. This unifies spatially coherent, periodic, and clique-like structural priors under a single modelling language.

Result: The framework successfully learns interpretable bases that exhibit desired topological properties — spatial coherence in images, periodicity in time series, and clique-like structures in graph signals — without relying on discrete or threshold-dependent heuristics.

Conclusion: Persistent homology-based regularization provides an effective, unified approach for imposing topological priors in NMF, overcoming the limitations of discrete methods and enabling continuous optimization for interpretable basis learning across diverse data modalities.

Abstract: We investigate the learning of interpretable bases in non-negative matrix factorisation (NMF) by regularising the topology of the learned basis functions. Our approach is motivated by the observation that many data modalities can be viewed as non-negative functions on a structured domain, where the quality of a basis is intrinsically linked to its topology. However, naive methods for incorporating the topology of the support are often hindered by discreteness and threshold dependence, rendering them unsuitable for continuous optimisation. We address these challenges by employing persistent homology as a stable, threshold-free topological quantifier and by designing topological scores that integrate into the NMF objective as regularisers. The resulting framework encompasses spatially coherent image components, periodic time-series structures, and clique-like graph signals within a unified modelling language.

</details>


### [141] [Offline Preference-Based Trajectory Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17541)
*Fernando Diaz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Standard success-based evaluation of agentic systems discards partial progress, causing widespread ties (~75% of instances). The authors propose preference-based trajectory evaluation using temporal preferences over progress and time-to-return, which reduces ties to ~35% and improves discriminative power, ranking stability, and data efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline evaluation of agentic systems typically collapses trajectories to binary terminal success, discarding partial progress information. This induces widespread ties, reducing effective sample size, weakening the ability to distinguish systems, and creating substantial statistical inefficiency. The authors argue that perceived benchmark saturation may stem from poor evaluation measures rather than data or problem difficulty.

Method: Preference-based trajectory evaluation: instead of binary success/failure, trajectories are compared directly through temporal preferences — specifically, preferences over progress profiles and time-to-return profiles. This frame-level comparison captures partial progress and temporal efficiency, producing finer-grained distinctions between systems.

Result: Across diverse agentic and interactive benchmarks, standard success-based metrics produced tied comparisons on roughly 75% of instances, while trajectory-aware preferences reduced ties to roughly 35%. This yielded improved discriminative power, more stable rankings, and greater data efficiency.

Conclusion: Benchmark saturation may be partly an artifact of the evaluation measure rather than inherent data or problem limitations. Adopting trajectory-aware, preference-based evaluation can substantially improve statistical efficiency in benchmarking agentic systems.

Abstract: Offline evaluation of agentic systems often collapses trajectories to terminal success, discarding information about partial progress and inducing widespread ties, creating substantial statistical inefficiency by reducing effective sample size and weakening the ability to distinguish systems. We propose preference-based trajectory evaluation, which compares trajectories directly through temporal preferences over progress and time-to-return profiles. We find that, across diverse agentic and interactive benchmarks, standard success-based metrics produce tied comparisons on roughly 75% of instances, whereas trajectory-aware preferences reduce ties to roughly 35%, improving discriminative power, ranking stability, and data efficiency. Our results suggest that benchmark saturation, often attributed to poor data collection or problem difficulty, may also be explained by the choice of evaluation measure.

</details>


### [142] [Continuous-time Optimal Stopping through Deep Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17545)
*Cosmin Borsa,Michael Ludkovski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CARLOS is a reinforcement-learning algorithm for optimal stopping that uses an aggregate deep neural network to learn a continuous-time exercise boundary, progressively refining from coarse to fine time grids with adaptive sampling, achieving higher prices than existing Bermudan solvers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical dynamic programming for optimal stopping faces a fundamental discretization trade-off: coarse time grids undervalue the option due to too few exercise opportunities, while fine grids cause approximation errors to accumulate through backward recursion.
