The authors aim to eliminate this limitation by learning the exercise rule at arbitrarily fine time resolution.

Method: The CARLOS algorithm employs: (1) an Aggregate Deep Neural Network (ADNN) to learn a joint space-time decision boundary; (2) a progressive time-grid refinement scheme that starts from a coarse grid and incrementally increases stopping frequency while training the ADNN in parallel; and (3) an adaptive sampling strategy that concentrates training effort near the stopping boundary. The approach is inspired by reinforcement learning rather than classical backward dynamic programming.

Result: Benchmarked results demonstrate that CARLOS yields higher option prices than existing Bermudan solvers, approaching the American upper bound, while maintaining high computational efficiency compared to non-RL alternatives.

Conclusion: The CARLOS algorithm successfully overcomes the time-discretization limitations of classical dynamic programming for optimal stopping problems, enabling accurate pricing at arbitrarily fine time resolution with strong computational performance.

Abstract: Simulation based solvers for optimal stopping problems must discretize the stopping decision. Under classical dynamic programming, a coarse exercise grid with only a few stopping opportunities can materially undervalue the optimal expected reward, whereas on a very fine grid, approximation errors accumulate through the backward recursion. To remove this limitation, we develop a new reinforcement-learning inspired algorithm that enables us to learn the exercise rule at arbitrarily fine time resolution. Our CARLOS (Continuous-time Adaptive Reinforcement Learning for Optimal Stopping) algorithm utilizes an aggregate deep neural network (ADNN) to learn a joint space-time decision boundary. Starting from a coarse time grid, we progressively increase the frequency of stopping opportunities, while in parallel training the ADNN to refine its timing-value estimates. We moreover design an adaptive sampling strategy that gradually concentrates training effort near the stopping boundary. Benchmarked results show that CARLOS delivers higher prices than existing Bermudan solvers, approaching the American upper bound, and achieves high computational efficiency relative to non-RL comparators.

</details>


### [143] [Reversal Q-Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17551)
*Aditya Oberai,Seohong Park,Sergey Levine*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Reversal Q-learning (RQL), an off-policy RL algorithm that trains a flow policy using prior data within an expanded MDP framework, employing virtual on-policy trajectory generation via flow reversal and bias-variance reduction to achieve state-of-the-art offline RL performance on 50 robotic tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing flow-based offline RL methods suffer from limitations such as backpropagation through time, inefficient use of learned value functions, and restricted policy expressiveness. The authors aim to develop a flow-based offline RL algorithm that overcomes these drawbacks while remaining compatible with static, pre-collected datasets.

Method: The method builds on an expanded MDP framework where flow refinement steps are treated as separate actions. Two key techniques enable off-policy learning: (1) reversing flows to generate virtual on-policy trajectories from prior data, making the framework compatible with offline datasets; (2) a bias-and-variance reduction technique to address the horizon curse in off-policy RL. The resulting algorithm, RQL, trains a full expressive flow policy without backpropagation through time and leverages the learned value function effectively.

Result: RQL achieves the best average offline RL performance compared to state-of-the-art flow-based offline RL algorithms across 50 challenging simulated robotic tasks.

Conclusion: RQL demonstrates that iterative generative modeling via flow matching can be effectively adapted for offline RL by addressing the off-policy compatibility and horizon curse problems, yielding superior performance and practical advantages over prior flow-based methods.

Abstract: Iterative generative modeling techniques, such as flow matching, provide powerful tools to model complex behaviors for effective offline reinforcement learning (RL). In this work, we propose a new off-policy RL algorithm that trains a flow policy based on prior data. Our idea starts from the "expanded" Markov decision process (MDP) framework, which treats individual flow refinement steps as separate actions in an MDP. To enable off-policy RL within this framework, we apply two techniques: we generate virtual on-policy trajectories (by "reversing" flows) to make this framework compatible with prior data, and we apply a bias-and-variance reduction technique to mitigate the curse of horizon in off-policy RL. We call the resulting algorithm Reversal Q-learning (RQL). RQL has several advantages over previous flow-based RL methods: it does not suffer from backpropagation through time, makes better use of the learned value function, and directly trains the full, expressive flow policy. Through our experiments on 50 challenging simulated robotic tasks, we show that RQL leads to the best average offline RL performance compared to state-of-the-art flow-based offline RL algorithms.

</details>


### [144] [SpatioTemporal Causal Network Diagnostics for Geographic Tipping Point Early Warning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17553)
*Zhaoyuan Yu,Zhangyong Liang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ST-CND is a novel early warning framework that models geographic fields as time-evolving directed causal networks using transfer entropy, avoiding the spatial dilution, Euclidean assumption, and correlated noise problems of classical indicators like Moran's I. It infers information-flow topology, estimates local recovery rates via dynamic mode decomposition, and identifies vulnerable subnetworks through three signals (internal fluctuation, internal synchronization, low external coupling). Validated on synthetic bifurcations and SST/AMOC benchmarks, it achieves AUROC 0.783 and IoU 0.378 on AMOC, outperforming baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical spatial early warning indicators (e.g., Moran's I) face three critical limitations: (1) spatial dilution — global summaries obscure localized critical transitions; (2) rigid Euclidean neighborhood assumptions that ignore true dynamical dependencies; and (3) susceptibility to false alarms from spatially correlated noise. These issues demand a data-driven, causality-aware method for localized early warning of tipping points in Earth system components like ecosystems, climate subsystems, and ice sheets.

Method: ST-CND proceeds in three stages: (1) Construct a directed causal network by computing transfer entropy between spatial nodes, replacing fixed Euclidean neighborhoods with information-flow topology; (2) Estimate local recovery rates within each candidate subnetwork using dynamic mode decomposition (DMD); (3) Identify the most vulnerable subnetwork by jointly scoring high internal fluctuation, high internal synchronization, and low external coupling — suppressing spatially correlated noise false alarms.

Result: On synthetic bifurcation data, ST-CND provides localized, interpretable early warnings. On Indo-Pacific SST and North Atlantic AMOC observational benchmarks, it outperforms recurrence-network and lambda-AR1 baselines. Specifically on AMOC, it achieves AUROC of 0.783 and a critical-subnetwork IoU of 0.378.

Conclusion: ST-CND provides an interpretable, scalable pipeline for spatial early warning in Earth system science, effectively addressing the three core weaknesses of classical spatial indicators through causal network diagnostics.

Abstract: Geographic tipping points in ecosystems, climate subsystems, or ice sheets pose severe challenges for localized early warning. Classical spatial indicators such as Moran's I summarize global spatial structure, but they struggle with three issues: spatial dilution, Euclidean assumptions, and correlated noise. This paper introduces SpatioTemporal Causal Network Diagnostics (ST-CND), a framework that addresses these three issues by representing the geographic field as a time-evolving directed causal network. The core workflow is as follows: (1) infer which spatial nodes help predict other nodes via transfer entropy, replacing fixed Euclidean neighborhoods with data-driven information-flow topology; (2) estimate local recovery rates within each candidate subnetwork via dynamic mode decomposition; and (3) identify the most vulnerable subnetwork by combining three signals, namely high internal fluctuation, high internal synchronization, and low external coupling, thereby suppressing false alarms from spatially correlated noise. Validated on synthetic bifurcations and two observational sea-surface temperature benchmarks, namely Indo-Pacific SST and North Atlantic AMOC, ST-CND delivers localized and interpretable warnings. On the AMOC task, it achieves an AUROC of 0.783 and a critical-subnetwork IoU of 0.378, outperforming recurrence-network and lambda-AR1 baselines. The framework provides an interpretable and scalable pipeline for spatial early warning in Earth system science.

</details>


### [145] [Reducing Learner Redundancy in Boosting via Residual Orthogonalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17567)
*Ye Su,Jipeng Guo,Yong Liu,Xin Xu,Gangchun Zhang,Jinxin Chen,Di Wu,Longlong Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCBoost replaces traditional boosting's residual fitting with residual orthogonalization via Spectral Residual Projection (SRP) and Covariance-Regularized Weighting (CRW), reducing learner redundancy and improving ensemble efficiency, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance across ten benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard sequential boosting frameworks suffer from learner redundancy because each new learner revisits error components already captured by previous learners. This inefficiency motivates a principled geometric approach to explicitly control redundancy.

Method: SCBoost introduces two complementary mechanisms: (1) Spectral Residual Projection (SRP), which projects residual targets onto the orthogonal complement of the historical prediction subspace during training, forcing successive learners to capture only novel error components; and (2) Covariance-Regularized Weighting (CRW), which optimizes ensemble weights on a validation set with an explicit covariance penalty to mitigate remaining correlations during aggregation.

Result: Theoretically, SRP yields an exact additive residual-energy decomposition (finite-sample geometric characterization), and under isotropic noise, it improves the effective Signal-to-Noise Ratio. Empirically, SCBoost achieves strong out-of-the-box performance across ten benchmark datasets, particularly in accuracy and F1 score.

Conclusion: Boosting can be productively reinterpreted through a geometric lens, and explicit redundancy control via orthogonalization represents a principled and necessary step toward building more efficient ensemble architectures.

Abstract: While sequential residual fitting is the bedrock of standard boosting frameworks, it inherently breeds learner redundancy by repeatedly revisiting correlated error components. To address this bottleneck, we propose a shift from residual fitting to \textit{residual orthogonalization} and introduce SCBoost. Our framework tackles redundancy through two complementary mechanisms: Spectral Residual Projection (SRP) and Covariance-Regularized Weighting (CRW). During training, SRP projects each residual target onto the orthogonal complement of the historical prediction subspace, forcing successive learners to capture only novel empirical innovations. During aggregation, CRW optimizes ensemble weights on a validation set with an explicit covariance penalty to mitigate remaining correlations. Theoretically, we provide a finite-sample geometric characterization proving that SRP yields an exact additive residual-energy decomposition. Furthermore, under an isotropic-noise assumption, we rigorously establish the conditions under which this projection improves the effective Signal-to-Noise Ratio. Extensive experiments across ten benchmark datasets demonstrate that SCBoost delivers strong out-of-the-box performance, particularly in accuracy and F1 score. This work reinterprets boosting through a geometric lens, suggesting that explicit redundancy control is a principled and necessary step toward more efficient ensemble architectures.

</details>


### [146] [When Dynamics Models Read the Wrong Time Steps: Label-Free Event Credit Re-Anchoring for Robust Global Readouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17572)
*Yifan Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies "temporal credit dilution" — a failure mode in learned dynamics models where global readouts rely on smooth, abundant correlates rather than brief physical events. The authors propose CREST, a training-free readout that re-anchors pooled representations around transient event cores, reducing OOD error and restoring event credit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learned dynamics models that answer global physical questions (e.g., fault severity, impact stiffness) typically pool per-step features into a single readout vector with only trajectory-level supervision. This creates a temporal credit assignment problem: models can achieve low training loss by attending to smooth, abundant background signals rather than the brief, physically meaningful events that actually determine the target. Standard physics-informed residuals fail to address this because the error lies in where the global readout assigns functional credit, not in the feature extraction itself.

Method: The authors first formalize the problem, introducing Credit-in-Event — an interface-level probe that measures the fraction of pooled credit landing on event steps. They provide a closed-form proof showing that a pooled linear reader routes credit to a spurious background channel as the event fraction shrinks. They then propose CREST (Credit Re-anchoring via Event-core Selection from Transients), a training-free and label-free readout mechanism. CREST estimates a transient event core from learned features and re-anchors the pooled representation via event-versus-rest contrast, without requiring retraining or additional labels.

Result: CREST was evaluated across simulated gear and impact systems, recurrent and attention encoders, and public bearing vibration data. It consistently reduced out-of-distribution error while restoring event credit. Ablation studies demonstrated that alternatives like stable-step selection and receptive-field shrinking fail, confirming the gain is specifically due to event-core credit re-anchoring rather than generic locality or stability priors.

Conclusion: Temporal credit dilution is a distinct and previously under-studied failure mode in sequence-to-global dynamics models. CREST provides an effective, plug-and-play solution that operates at the readout interface without requiring retraining or labels, and its success stems specifically from re-anchoring credit on transient events rather than from simpler inductive biases.

Abstract: Learned dynamics models often answer global physical questions, such as fault severity or impact stiffness, by pooling a per-step feature sequence into one readout vector. This sequence-to-global interface creates an under-studied temporal credit problem: with only trajectory-level supervision, a model can predict accurately in training conditions while reading from abundant smooth correlates rather than the brief physical events that determine the target. We call this failure temporal credit dilution. It is not exposed by the training loss and is not removed by standard physics-informed residuals, because the error lies in where the global readout assigns functional credit. We introduce Credit-in-Event, an interface-level probe for measuring how much pooled credit lands on event steps, and prove in closed form that a pooled linear reader routes credit to a spurious background channel as the event fraction shrinks. We then propose CREST, a training-free and label-free readout that estimates a transient event core from learned features and re-anchors the pooled representation through event-versus-rest contrast. Across simulated gear and impact systems, recurrent and attention encoders, and public bearing vibration data, CREST reduces out-of-distribution error while restoring event credit. Ablations show that stable-step selection and receptive-field shrinking fail, confirming that the gain comes from event-core credit re-anchoring rather than a generic locality or stability prior.

</details>


### [147] [LLM Features Can Hurt GNNs: Concatenation Interference on Homophilous Graph Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17579)
*Zhongyuan Wang,Pratyusha Vemuri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Concatenating LLM-generated node features to GNNs can systematically degrade accuracy on homophilous benchmarks (up to -17 pp on PubMed), contrary to the common narrative of improvement. The authors introduce a measure called Delta_sig (LLM-alone discriminability) that predicts when concatenation helps vs. hurts, and show the degradation follows a power law in the low-discriminability, small-training-set regime.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The prevailing narrative holds that adding LLM-generated features to GNNs improves accuracy. The authors challenge this by documenting a systematic failure mode: pure input concatenation of LLM features can hurt performance on the very homophilous benchmarks where end-to-end LLM pipelines succeed. They aim to characterize when and why this degradation occurs.

Method: The authors systematically evaluate concatenating SBERT-encoded GPT-4o-mini TAPE features across multiple GNN backbones (MLP, GCN, GCNII, GAT), datasets (Planetoid, WikiCS, ogbn-arxiv), and splits (public vs. random). They introduce Delta_sig — a measure of LLM-alone discriminability — and correlate it with concatenation cost across 9 datasets. They also conduct dimension-controlled ablations (PCA, Gaussian noise) and fit a power law relating concatenation cost to sqrt(d_l/n).

Result: On the Planetoid public split with MLP backbone and bag-of-words features, concatenating TAPE features reduced PubMed accuracy by -17.0±0.3 pp, Cora by -4.3±0.6 pp, and CiteSeer by -0.6±0.8 pp. The drop attenuates with stronger GNN backbones, random splits, and smaller encoders, and reverses on medium-homophily datasets (WikiCS +4.4 pp, ogbn-arxiv +11.7 pp). Delta_sig correlates with concatenation cost at r²=0.38 vs. homophily's r²=0.06. A power law |Δ_concat| ∝ (√(d_l/n))^1.31 fits with r²=0.97; the low-Delta_sig, small-n corner explains the headline PubMed deficit.

Conclusion: LLM feature concatenation is not universally beneficial — it systematically degrades performance under specific conditions (low LLM-alone discriminability, small training sets, weak backbones, homophilous graphs). Delta_sig serves as a useful interpretive lens (classifying 7/9 datasets correctly with τ=13.8 pp) for predicting when concatenation will help vs. hurt, and the degradation follows a predictable power-law scaling.

Abstract: Adding LLM-generated node features to graph neural networks (GNNs) is widely reported to improve accuracy on standard benchmarks. We document a contrasting observation: when LLM features are introduced through pure input concatenation (rather than joint training, distillation, or prompt-conditioning), they can systematically degrade accuracy on the same homophilous benchmarks where end-to-end LLM pipelines succeed. With an MLP backbone on the Planetoid public split and bag-of-words original features, concatenating SBERT-encoded GPT-4o-mini TAPE features reduces PubMed test accuracy by -17.0 +/- 0.3 pp and Cora by -4.3 +/- 0.6 pp (CiteSeer -0.6 +/- 0.8 pp, within seed noise). The drop attenuates as we relax each condition (GCN / GCNII / GAT backbones, random splits, smaller encoders) and reverses on medium-homophily WikiCS (+4.4 pp) and ogbn-arxiv (+11.7 pp). To predict when concatenation helps versus hurts, we report a simple measure of LLM-alone discriminability, Delta_sig. Across 9 datasets Delta_sig correlates with the concatenation cost more strongly than homophily at point estimate (r^2 = 0.38 vs. 0.06; N=9, bootstrap CIs overlap). The bootstrap-best change-point is tau = 13.8 pp, and the rule "Delta_sig <= tau predicts non-positive concat cost" classifies 7/9 datasets correctly; since 60% of bootstrap samples place tau in [5, 30] pp, we treat Delta_sig as an interpretive lens rather than a precision filter. A dimension-controlled ablation on PubMed places the LLM-feature drop between same-source PCA (-2.3 pp) and same-dim Gaussian noise (-37.3 pp), ruling out dimensionality and weight-decay artifacts. Nine PubMed configurations fit a power law |Delta_concat| proportional to (sqrt(d_l/n))^1.31 with r^2 = 0.97; the low-Delta_sig, small-n corner is exactly where the headline -17 pp PubMed deficit appears.

</details>


### [148] [Expanding SPHERE-JEPA: A Family of Statistical Regularizers for the Hypersphere](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17603)
*Léo Nicollier,Enric Meinhardt-Llopis,Max Dunitz,Marc Pic,Pablo Musé,Gabriele Facciolo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper shows that sliced statistical regularizers for uniformity in SSL are Monte Carlo approximations of deterministic Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). By formulating full-dimensional MMD, KSD, and KL divergence objectives with rotationally invariant kernels on the hypersphere, the authors eliminate projection variance, yielding more stable optimization, faster convergence, and consistent gains. The choice of statistical test shapes latent geometry: MMD/KSD favor local clustering; KL divergence promotes fine-grained instance separation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current SSL frameworks (e.g., LeJEPA, SPHERE-JEPA) enforce uniform latent distributions via sliced regularizers (SIGReg, SUSReg) that rely on Monte Carlo sampling along random 1D projections. This stochasticity injects projection variance into training gradients, destabilizing optimization and hindering convergence. The authors aim to eliminate this variance by deriving deterministic, full-dimensional alternatives and to understand how different statistical divergence measures shape latent space geometry.

Method: (1) The authors prove that analytically integrating out random projections in sliced regularizers yields deterministic MMD. (2) They formulate full-dimensional objectives—MMD, Kernel Stein Discrepancy (KSD), and KDE-based KL divergence—directly on the unit hypersphere to enforce uniformity. (3) To avoid spatial bias, they construct rotationally invariant kernels using spectral theory on the sphere, evaluating Heat kernels (smooth exponential decay) and Bandlimited kernels (strict frequency cutoff). (4) Experiments on ImageNet and Galaxy10 compare these deterministic objectives against stochastic sliced baselines.

Result: Removing projection-induced noise leads to more stable optimization, faster convergence, and consistent improvements over SIGReg and SUSReg on ImageNet and Galaxy10. MMD and KSD encourage locally clustered latent organization suited for object-centric domains. The continuous KDE-based KL divergence promotes fine-grained instance separation, achieving the strongest results on unclustered procedural texture retrieval.

Conclusion: Full-dimensional statistical tests with rotationally invariant kernels provide a superior, variance-free alternative to sliced regularizers for enforcing uniformity in SSL. The choice of divergence (MMD, KSD, KL) meaningfully shapes latent geometry, suggesting that practitioners should align the statistical objective with downstream task structure.

Abstract: In Self-Supervised Learning (SSL), preventing representation collapse by explicitly enforcing a uniform distribution on the unit hypersphere has proven to be effective. However, current frameworks typically rely on sliced statistical regularizers such as SIGReg (used in LeJEPA) and SUSReg (used in SPHERE-JEPA), which approximate this continuous objective via Monte Carlo sampling along random 1D directions. This stochasticity injects projection variance into the training gradients, destabilizing optimization, and hindering convergence. In this work, we first show that analytically integrating out these random projections natively yields a deterministic Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), bypassing the variance of sliced methods. Motivated by this equivalence, we formulate full-dimensional objectives for MMD, Kernel Stein Discrepancy (KSD), and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence directly on the sphere to enforce a uniform distribution. To prevent spatial bias, we equip these tests with rotationally invariant kernels constructed via spectral theory, systematically evaluating two canonical families: smooth exponential decay (Heat) and strict frequency cutoff (Bandlimited) filters. Empirically, removing projection-induced noise results in more stable optimization, faster convergence, and consistent improvements over stochastic sliced regularizers on ImageNet and Galaxy10. Furthermore, we reveal that the choice of the statistical test shapes the geometry of the learned latent space: MMD and KSD favor locally clustered organization suitable for object-centric domains, whereas the continuous KDE-based KL divergence promotes fine-grained instance separation, yielding the strongest results on unclustered procedural texture retrieval.

</details>


### [149] [A Risk Decomposition Framework for Pre-Hoc Fine-Tuning Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17649)
*Yuxiang Luo,Chen Wang,Nan Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Pre-hoc LLM performance prediction is formalized as a stochastic estimation problem under information constraints, revealing a fundamental lower bound on how fast optimization variance decays. This yields a budget-optimal probing principle and a predictability phase diagram classifying tasks into three regimes, validated empirically.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The high cost of fine-tuning LLMs creates an economic barrier; pre-hoc performance prediction can mitigate this, but its theoretical limits have not been explored. The authors aim to establish what is fundamentally predictable before training begins.

Method: The problem is cast as stochastic estimation under information constraints. Prediction risk is decomposed into intrinsic (static data-model compatibility) and reducible (optimization variance) components. A lower bound on the decay rate of optimization variance is proven, from which a budget-optimal probing principle and a three-regime predictability phase diagram (Static-Sufficient, Dynamic-Critical, Noise-Dominant) are derived.

Result: Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks validate the existence of the three theoretical regimes and demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed probing strategy for pre-hoc performance prediction.

Conclusion: Pre-hoc performance prediction is fundamentally bounded by both static data-model compatibility and an irreducible optimization variance decay rate. The phase diagram provides a principled framework for understanding when and how probing can be optimally allocated, with practical implications for reducing fine-tuning costs.

Abstract: The high cost of fine-tuning LLMs poses a significant economic barrier; pre-hoc performance prediction offers a critical solution to substantially reduce this expense. However, the theoretical limits of pre-hoc performance prediction remain unexplored. We formulate it as a stochastic estimation problem under information constraints, decomposing prediction risk into two components: an intrinsic limit (static data-model compatibility) and a reducible optimization variance. We prove that optimization variance admits a necessary lower bound on its decay rate, implying fundamental constraints on how quickly uncertainty dissipates, regardless of the predictor used. Based on these dynamics, we derive a budget-optimal probing principle and introduce a predictability phase diagram that organizes tasks into three distinct regimes: Static-Sufficient, Dynamic-Critical, and Noise-Dominant. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks validate these theoretical regimes and demonstrate the efficiency of our probing strategy.

</details>


### [150] [Physics-Constrained Neural Networks for Improved Short-Term Weather Forecasting: A Case Study over the South Pacific](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17659)
*Egor Bugaev,Fedor Buzaev,Dmitry Efremenko,Denis Derkach,Fedor Ratnikov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes three enhancements to physics-constrained neural networks for short-term weather forecasting: a WENO-5-based numerical solver enabling 4× larger time steps with up to 26% lower daily MSE, a unified autoregressive hybrid block to replace 24 specialized modules, and integration with two modern neural backbones (PI-PredFormer, PI-IAM4VP). The hybrids achieve 8–22% RMSE reduction at 1–12h lead times over purely neural counterparts on WeatherBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hybrid physics-neural weather forecasting models suffer from limited numerical integration time steps (restricting efficiency), overfitting to specific lead times due to specialized per-lead-time modules, and suboptimal neural architecture integration. The authors aim to incrementally refine these hybrid components to improve accuracy, stability, and physical consistency.

Method: Three innovations are built upon the WeatherGFT architecture: (1) An upgraded numerical solver employing a fifth-order WENO scheme, beta-plane approximation, and subgrid-scale viscosity, enabling a 1200 s integration time step (4× increase). (2) A unified autoregressive hybrid block that replaces the original chain of 24 specialized modules, training a single module for all lead times. (3) Integration of the physical core with two SOTA neural backbones — PredFormer and IAM4VP — yielding PI-PredFormer and PI-IAM4VP. Evaluation uses the WeatherBench South Pacific subset (2000–2004).

Result: The upgraded solver reduces daily MSE by up to 26% while quadrupling the integration time step. The unified autoregressive block eliminates overfitting to specific lead times. The PI-PredFormer and PI-IAM4VP hybrids reduce RMSE by 8–22% at 1–12 h lead times compared to purely neural counterparts, while better preserving physical consistency.

Conclusion: Incremental refinement of hybrid physics-neural components — solver numerics, autoregressive training strategy, and neural backbone selection — offers a practical and effective route toward more accurate, efficient, and physically consistent short-range weather forecasting.

Abstract: This study introduces enhancements to physics-constrained neural networks (PCNNs) that improve the accuracy and stability of hybrid short-term weather forecasting models. Building on the WeatherGFT architecture, three innovations are proposed. First, an upgraded numerical solver, combining a fifth-order weighted essentially non-oscillatory scheme (WENO-5), a beta-plane approximation, and subgrid-scale viscosity, permits a fourfold increase in the integration time step to 1200 s while reducing the daily mean squared error by up to 26%. Second, a unified autoregressive hybrid block replaces the original chain of 24 specialised modules, eliminating overfitting to specific lead times. Third, the physical core is integrated with two state-of-the-art neural backbones, resulting in PI-PredFormer and PI-IAM4VP. Evaluation on the WeatherBench South Pacific subset from 2000 to 2004 shows that these hybrids reduce root mean squared error at 1-12 h lead times by 8-22% compared to purely neural counterparts, while better preserving physical consistency. These results demonstrate that incremental refinement of hybrid components offers a practical route toward more accurate and efficient short-range weather forecasting.

</details>


### [151] [TuneAhead: Predicting Fine-tuning Performance Before Full Training Begins](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17660)
*Yuxiang Luo,Haonan Long,Chen Wang,Qiqi Duan,Xiaotian Lin,Yanwei Xu,Yuyu Luo,Weikai Yang,Nan Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TUNEAHEAD is a lightweight pre-hoc prediction framework that estimates LLM fine-tuning performance before committing to full training, using meta-features combining dataset descriptors and probe-based features, achieving 1.47 pp RMSE and 95.1% predictions within ±3 pp on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct across 1,300+ runs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuning LLMs is compute-intensive and error-prone, with outcomes highly sensitive to data quality and hyperparameter choices. Naïve runs can even degrade model performance. There is a practical need to predict fine-tuning performance before committing resources to a full training run (pre-hoc prediction), enabling go/no-go screening.

Method: TUNEAHEAD encodes each candidate fine-tuning run as a meta-feature vector combining: (1) static dataset descriptors, and (2) dynamic probe features obtained from a short, standardized probe run. A predictor model maps these features to performance estimates. SHAP-based attributions provide interpretable diagnostics to reveal which features drive each prediction.

Result: Evaluated on 1,300+ fine-tuning runs on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, TUNEAHEAD consistently outperforms baselines (Early-Stop Extrapolation, ProxyLM). On a held-out test set of 370 runs: RMSE of 1.47 percentage points, with 95.1% of predictions falling within ±3 pp of the true score.

Conclusion: Accurate continuous performance predictions from TUNEAHEAD enable practical go/no-go screening policies that can significantly reduce unnecessary full fine-tuning runs while retaining most promising candidates, saving substantial compute resources.

Abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) is compute-intensive and error-prone: model performance depends sensitively on data quality and hyperparameter choices, and naïve runs can even degrade model performance. This raises a practical question:can we predict fine-tuning performance before committing to a full training run? We present TUNEAHEAD, a lightweight framework for pre-hoc prediction of fine-tuning performance. TUNEAHEAD encodes each candidate run as a meta-feature vector that combines static dataset descriptors with dynamic probe features from a short standardized probe. A predictor maps these features to performance estimates, while SHAP-based attributions provide interpretable diagnostics that reveal which specific features drive the prediction. Across 1,300+ fine-tuning runs on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, TUNEAHEAD consistently outperforms strong baselines such as Early-Stop Extrapolation and ProxyLM. On a held-out test set of 370 runs, TUNEAHEAD achieves an RMSE of 1.47 percentage points and places 95.1% of predictions within +3/-3 percentage points of the true score. These accurate continuous predictions support practical go/no-go screening policies that can reduce unnecessary full fine-tuning while retaining most promising runs.

</details>


### [152] [Handling Feature Heterogeneity with Learnable Graph Patches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17667)
*Yifei Sun,Yang Yang,Xiao Feng,Zijun Wang,Haoyang Zhong,Chunping Wang,Lei Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes learnable graph patches as domain-agnostic semantic units to address feature heterogeneity in graph foundation models, enabling cross-domain pre-training and transfer learning without textual information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph foundation models struggle with feature heterogeneity across different graph datasets, particularly when textual information is absent. This limits transferability and prevents effective construction of a universal pre-trained graph model that can generalize across diverse domains.

Method: The authors introduce learnable graph patches — the smallest semantic units of graph data — by decomposing graphs through unfolding node features and constructing corresponding patch structures. A two-component framework is designed: (1) a patch encoder that extracts knowledge from each individual patch unit, and (2) a patch aggregator that learns how these units combine into the whole graph. The approach is domain-agnostic, enabling application to downstream data across diverse domains.

Result: The method enables multi-domain graph pre-training and demonstrates enhanced performance across various downstream datasets and tasks. Notably, consistent improvement in downstream performance is observed as the volume of pre-training data increases, indicating effective utilization of diverse training sources.

Conclusion: Learnable graph patches provide an effective solution to the feature heterogeneity problem in graph foundation models, enabling true cross-domain transferability. The framework's domain-agnostic design and scalability with pre-training data volume position it as a promising direction toward building universal graph foundation models.

Abstract: In recent years, the rapid development of foundation models and graph pre-training technologies has spurred increasing interest in constructing a universal pre-trained graph model or Graph Foundation Model (GFM). However, a significant challenge is that existing models are unable to address feature heterogeneity in graph data without textual information, which hinders the transferability of graph models across different datasets. To bridge this gap, we propose the concept of learnable graph patches, which we regard as the smallest semantic units of any graph data. We decompose the graph into learnable graph patches by unfolding the node features and constructing corresponding patch structures separately. We then design a framework that mines transferable information from graph data across domains. Specifically, after extracting graph patches, we propose a patch encoder to extract knowledge from each unit and a patch aggregator to learn how the units are combined into a whole. Due to its domain-agnostic nature, the model can be applied to downstream data across different domains. Furthermore, we analyze the connection between our method and existing graph models, as well as the transferability of the node embeddings it generates. Empirically, our method not only achieves the capability to use multi-domain graphs for pre-training, but also shows enhanced performance across various downstream datasets and tasks. Moreover, we observe consistent improvement in downstream performance as the volume of pre-training data increases.

</details>


### [153] [ASTEROID: A Spatiotemporal Information Transformer for Forecasting Multi-Step Time Series of Molecular Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17668)
*Kexin Wu,Luonan Chen,Renxiao Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ASTEROID is a Transformer-based framework that predicts multi-step atomic coordinates directly from MD trajectories without iterative integration, using a local-global self-attention mechanism and an encoder-decoder structure to capture multiscale spatiotemporal dependencies, achieving higher accuracy and lower computational cost than existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MD simulations are computationally expensive for large-scale, long-timescale systems. Directly predicting simulation outcomes—rather than performing expensive step-by-step numerical integration—offers substantial scientific and practical value for acceleration.

Method: ASTEROID reformulates MD trajectories as high-dimensional spatiotemporal sequences and incorporates a Spatiotemporal Information (STI) Transformation equation into a Transformer architecture. Spatial dependencies are handled via a local-global self-attention mechanism capturing short- and long-range interactions. Temporal dependencies are modeled with an encoder-decoder structure that combines global context with autoregressive forecasting. The model directly outputs multi-step atomic coordinates.

Result: On quantum-mechanics-derived molecular datasets, ASTEROID outperformed existing methods in multi-step prediction accuracy across benchmarks and significantly reduced computational cost versus conventional MD. It also supports iterative multi-step forecasting over extended timescales.

Conclusion: ASTEROID establishes a robust, generalizable data-driven paradigm for accelerating MD simulations by replacing iterative integration with direct spatiotemporal forecasting of atomic coordinates.

Abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation is computationally demanding, particularly for large-scale systems requiring long-term analysis. Accurate forecast of the outcomes of a MD simulation is not only an attractive scientific challenge but also has substantial practical value. In this work, we developed a data-driven framework, termed ASTEROID (Advanced Spatiotemporal TransformER fOr Inferring Dynamics), that can directly predict multi-step atomic coordinates, avoiding conventional iterative integration. For this purpose, our ASTEROID reformulates MD trajectories as high-dimensional spatiotemporal sequences and integrates the Spatiotemporal Information (STI) Transformation equation into a Transformer architecture. The core innovation of ASTEROID lies in its ability to model multiscale spatiotemporal dependencies. In particular, for spatial dependencies, a local-global self-attention mechanism captures both short- and long-range interactions. For temporal dependencies, an encoder-decoder structure integrates global context with autoregressive forecasting. ASTEROID was evaluated on several quantum-mechanics derived molecular datasets. Our results indicate that ASTEROID achieved not only a higher level of accuracy in multi-step prediction than existing methods on various benchmarks, but also significantly reduced computational cost of conventional MD simulation. Moreover, the model supports iterative multi-step forecasting over an extended time scale. This work establishes a robust and generalizable data-driven paradigm for accelerating MD simulations.

</details>


### [154] [EnvRL: Learn from Environment Dynamics in Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17680)
*Zhitong Wang,Songze Li,Hao Peng,Shuzheng Si,Yi Wang,Maosong Sun,Juanzi Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EnvRL enhances reinforcement learning for LLM agents by adding auxiliary objectives — state prediction and inverse dynamics — that force the agent to learn environment dynamics from its own interaction trajectories, yielding significant success-rate gains on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional RL for long-horizon agentic tasks relies on sparse outcome rewards, ignoring the rich implicit supervision contained in rollout interaction trajectories. These trajectories encode the environment's underlying transition dynamics, which could help the agent build a more accurate internal world model. The authors aim to exploit this overlooked signal to improve policy learning.

Method: EnvRL introduces two auxiliary learning objectives alongside the primary RL objective (e.g., GRPO): (1) **state prediction** — forecasting future states from current state-action pairs, and (2) **inverse dynamics modeling** — inferring the action that produced a given state transition. These objectives are jointly optimized with the RL loss, encouraging the LLM agent to internalize environment dynamics directly from its own rollout experience without requiring a separate world model.

Result: On ALFWorld, EnvRL + GRPO lifts Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct from 72.8% to 77.4% success rate. On WebShop, performance improves from 56.8% to 67.0%. These gains are achieved over RL-only baselines across two distinct long-horizon agentic benchmarks.

Conclusion: Incorporating environment dynamics learning as auxiliary objectives significantly boosts RL-based LLM agent performance. The interaction experience itself provides valuable implicit supervision that helps agents internalize transition mechanisms, leading to more effective policies for long-horizon tasks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for training Large Language Models (LLMs) as agents. However, conventional RL methods for long-horizon agentic tasks often struggle with sparse outcome rewards. Intuitively, this overlooks the rich environment dynamics information contained in rollout interaction trajectories. We argue that the interaction experience inherently serves as an implicit supervision signal, reveals the underlying transition mechanisms of the environment, and enables the agent to construct a more accurate internal model of the environment.. Therefore, in this work, we investigate how to leverage this additional signal to improve policy learning. Specifically, we propose EnvRL, a framework that incorporates environment dynamics learning into agentic RL via two auxiliary objectives: state prediction and inverse dynamics. By jointly optimizing with the primary RL objective, we encourage the agent to internalize environment dynamics from its own interaction experience. Extensive experiments on two long-horizon agentic benchmarks demonstrate that EnvRL achieves significant improvements on success-rates over RL-only baselines, e.g., when trained with GRPO, lifting Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct from 72.8% to 77.4% on ALFWorld, and from 56.8% to 67.0% on WebShop.

</details>


### [155] [Delta-Based Target Reformulation for Short-Term Electricity Load Forecasting Using LSTM and Transformer Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17692)
*Vansh Bansal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes predicting the change (delta) in electricity load between consecutive time steps rather than absolute load values, using deep learning models. Tested on Indian grid data, delta reformulation reduces MAPE by over 50% for hour-ahead forecasts across LSTM, Transformer, and LightGBM; for day-ahead, benefits are specific to deep sequence models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Electricity load data exhibits non-stationarity from weather, calendar effects, and shifting consumption patterns. Existing deep learning studies typically predict absolute load directly without addressing this non-stationarity. The authors are motivated by classical ARIMA differencing and hypothesize that predicting load differences (deltas) stabilizes the target, reducing forecasting difficulty.

Method: The paper introduces a delta-based target reformulation: instead of predicting absolute load values, models are trained to predict the change in load from the previous timestep. Final forecasts are reconstructed by adding the predicted delta to the last observed load. This is evaluated using multi-year hourly electricity load data from India, augmented with NASA POWER meteorological variables and calendar features. Three models — LSTM, Transformer, and LightGBM — are benchmarked under both absolute and delta formulations for hour-ahead and day-ahead horizons, using MAE and MAPE metrics.

Result: Delta reformulation yields MAPE reductions exceeding 50% for hour-ahead forecasts across all models. For day-ahead forecasting, delta targets benefit LSTM and Transformer specifically, while LightGBM remains competitive under the absolute formulation. Efficacy is thus both model-dependent and horizon-dependent.

Conclusion: Delta-based target reformulation serves as a powerful inductive bias for neural network models in short-term load forecasting, but its benefits are not universal — they vary by model architecture and forecast horizon. The approach effectively injects a stationarity-inducing prior that deep sequence models particularly exploit.

Abstract: Accurate short-term electricity load forecasting is critical for the reliable and economic operation of modern power systems, under non-stationarity arising from weather variability, calendar effects, and evolving consumption patterns. While deep learning models such as LSTMs and Transformers show promising performance, most existing studies focus on direct absolute load prediction without explicitly addressing target non-stationarity.
  Motivated by classical time-series differencing techniques in ARIMA models, this paper investigates a delta-based target reformulation for short-term electricity load forecasting using deep learning. Instead of directly predicting absolute load values, the proposed formulation trains models to predict the change in load between consecutive time steps, with final forecasts reconstructed using the last observed load. This aims to stabilize the learning target and reduce forecasting difficulty.
  Using multi-year, hourly real-world electricity load data from India, augmented with meteorological variables from the NASA POWER project and calendar features, this study evaluates LSTM and Transformer models under both formulations, benchmarking them against LightGBM. Experiments are conducted for hour-ahead and day-ahead horizons, assessing performance via Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE).
  Results show that delta-based reformulation consistently improves forecasting accuracy for hour-ahead prediction across all evaluated models, yielding MAPE reductions of over 50% compared to absolute formulations. For day-ahead forecasting, delta targets specifically benefit deep sequence models (LSTM and Transformer), while LightGBM remains competitive under the absolute formulation. These findings indicate that while delta reformulation is a powerful inductive bias for neural networks, its efficacy is model- and horizon-dependent.

</details>


### [156] [Confusion-Aware Transfer Teacher Curriculum Learning Framework: Disentangling Scoring and Pacing Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17706)
*Savini Kommalage,Sanka Mohottala,Asiri Gawesha,Dulara Madhusanka,Menan Velayuthan,Dharshana Kasthurirathna,Mahima Milinda Alwis Weerasinghe,Charith Abhayaratne*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper disentangles curriculum learning's two components—difficulty scoring and pacing—via controlled evaluation protocols, finding that a confusion-aware scoring function yields interpretable difficulty rankings and significant data-efficiency gains (up to 8.7% at 20% data), though it fails to improve full-data accuracy over standard training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Curriculum learning conflates two design choices—how samples are scored by difficulty and how harder samples are paced into training—making it unclear whether observed gains stem from the scoring function or the pacing schedule. The authors aim to disentangle these factors to enable rigorous, independent evaluation of each component.

Method: The authors propose two evaluation protocols within the Transfer Teacher Framework (TTF): (1) stage-wise test subsets that validate scoring functions independently of curriculum training, and (2) a baseline applying the same pacing schedule to randomly ordered data. They introduce a confusion-aware difficulty score based on correct-class confidence and the probability distribution over incorrect classes, and test it on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18 and VGG-16, comparing curriculum, anti-curriculum, and random orderings at various data regimes.

Result: The confusion-aware score produces model-interpretable difficulty rankings aligning with human intuition. At full data, neither curriculum nor anti-curriculum ordering improves accuracy over standard training, indicating scoring improvements alone cannot overcome known TTF failure modes. However, confusion-aware curriculum ordering yields consistent data-efficiency benefits, outperforming random ordering by up to 8.7 percentage points at the 20% data regime.

Conclusion: Improving the difficulty scoring function alone is insufficient to make curriculum learning effective at full data scale in TTF. However, confusion-aware curricula show strong promise as a data-efficient training method, suggesting TTF's practical value lies in low-data regimes rather than in boosting full-dataset performance.

Abstract: Curriculum learning couples two design choices, how samples are scored by difficulty and how harder samples are paced into training, making it difficult to attribute observed gains to either component. We disentangle these factors with two evaluation protocols: stage-wise test subsets that validate scoring functions independently of curriculum training, and a baseline that applies the same pacing schedule to randomly ordered data. Within the Transfer Teacher framework (TTF), we use these protocols to evaluate a confusion-aware difficulty score that considers both correct-class confidence and the probability distribution over incorrect classes. On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18 and VGG-16, the proposed score produces model-interpretable difficulty rankings that align with human intuition. However, at full data, neither curriculum nor anti-curriculum ordering improves accuracy over standard training, indicating that improving the scoring function alone is insufficient to overcome the known failure modes of curriculum learning in TTF. In contrast, We find that confusion-aware curriculum ordering result in consistent data-efficiency benefits, outperforming random ordering by up to 8.7% points at the 20% data regime, suggesting the potential of TTF as a data-efficient training method.

</details>


### [157] [A fairness-aware extension of Stochastic Multicriteria Acceptability Analysis for ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17756)
*Guilherme Dean Pelegrina,Renata Pelissari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SMAA-Fair extends Stochastic Multicriteria Acceptability Analysis to incorporate group fairness by reweighting simulated rankings based on fairness metrics (Statistical Parity, rKL, nDKL), producing fairness-adjusted acceptability indices and central weights. Experiments show improved protected group representation while maintaining robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional SMAA handles uncertainty and incomplete preferences in ranking but ignores fairness concerns, which are critical under Responsible AI. There is a need for a fairness-aware MCDA ranking framework that preserves SMAA's robustness benefits.

Method: SMAA-Fair reweights each simulated ranking by a fairness score derived from group-level metrics (Statistical Parity, rKL, nDKL). These fairness-weighted rankings feed into revised acceptability indices and central weight vectors. Final rankings use expected ranking and maximum acceptability ranking from the fairness-adjusted acceptability matrix. The framework is model-agnostic and metric-flexible.

Result: Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that SMAA-Fair significantly improves the representation of protected groups in top ranking positions compared to standard SMAA, while preserving robustness to preference uncertainty.

Conclusion: SMAA-Fair successfully integrates group fairness into the SMAA framework without sacrificing its core advantages in handling uncertainty, offering a flexible, metric-agnostic solution for fair ranking in MCDA.

Abstract: Fairness has become a central concern in ranking problems involving individuals or social groups, particularly under the Responsible Artificial Intelligence agenda. In Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis, Stochastic Multicriteria Acceptability Analysis (SMAA) provides a robust framework for handling uncertainty and incomplete preference information, but it does not explicitly address fairness in the resulting rankings. This paper proposes SMAA-Fair, a fairness-aware extension of SMAA for ranking problems. The approach reweights the simulated rankings generated by SMAA according to their level of group fairness, so that fairer rankings contribute more strongly to the acceptability indices and central weights vector. The framework is independent of the aggregation model and can incorporate different fairness metrics. In this study, Statistical Parity, normalized discounted Kullback--Leibler divergence (rKL) and normalized discounted cumulative Kullback--Leibler divergence (nDKL) are adopted. Rankings are derived from the fairness-adjusted acceptability matrix using expected ranking and maximum acceptability ranking. We also derive the central weight according to the degree of fairness in the obtained rankings. Numerical experiments with synthetic and real data show that SMAA-Fair improves the representation of protected groups among favourable ranking positions, while preserving robustness to preference uncertainty.

</details>


### [158] [Blind Recovery of Latent Domains via Unsupervised Symmetry Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17782)
*Onur Efe,Arkadas Ozakin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes an unsupervised framework that discovers latent symmetries in data distributions to recover signals and domain structure from unstructured linear measurements, using a shallow group-convolutional network regularized by stationarity and locality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Blind deconvolution fails when corruptions involve general linear transformations that destroy domain structure. Existing blind inverse problem methods cannot handle cases where the obfuscating mechanism is an unknown linear operator that scrambles the underlying domain organization.

Method: Models observations as linear measurements of signals from a latent random field. Optimizes a shallow group-convolutional network with stationarity and locality regularization at the output. The network learns a latent symmetry action (group representation) and an appropriate filter, mapping unstructured observations to a symmetry-based representation.

Result: Demonstrates successful recovery of latent domains and signals across stochastic processes, Ising models, shuffled and bit-scrambled images, and neural recordings.

Conclusion: Symmetry discovery emerges as a viable new direction for unsupervised structure learning and solving blind inverse problems beyond convolutional corruptions.

Abstract: Primary motivation in blind inverse problems is to recover signals of interest from corrupted observations without knowing the obfuscating mechanism. Blind deconvolution is a prominent approach when the corruption is convolutional, but it is not applicable when general linear transformations obfuscate the domain structure. In this work, we propose an unsupervised framework for recovering latent domains and signals by discovering symmetries of the data distribution. Our framework models observations as linear measurements of signals sampled from a latent random field, and optimizes a shallow group-convolutional network by imposing stationarity and locality regularization at the model output. The model learns a latent symmetry action and an appropriate filter, thereby mapping unstructured observations to a symmetry-based representation that reveals latent signals. Experiments on stochastic processes, Ising models, shuffled and bit-scrambled images, and neural recordings show that the method recovers latent domains and signals from unstructured observations, suggesting symmetry discovery as a new direction for unsupervised structure learning and blind inverse problems.

</details>


### [159] [Continual Self-Improvement with Lightweight Experiential Latent Memories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17803)
*Vaggelis Dorovatas,Nancy Kalaj,Rahaf Aljundi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes an online learning method that distills inference-time reasoning traces into lightweight, modular latent memories, enabling LLMs to convert transient computation into persistent reusable knowledge without external supervision, achieving substantial gains on math reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs remain stateless despite generating rich reasoning traces during inference. The authors investigate whether models can learn online from self-produced reasoning experience, converting transient computation into lasting knowledge without external labels or future data access.

Method: Two key findings: (1) ICL over raw reasoning traces fails due to lack of abstraction. (2) Per-instance training with self-generated rewards (majority voting) yields strong gains. The proposed method distills inference-time compute into compact modular latent memories (~0.001% of parameters), stored as soft prompts, trained with few gradient steps, and retrieved for future inputs. Modular design prevents catastrophic forgetting.

Result: The method significantly outperforms zero-shot and raw-data ICL baselines on challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks, often surpassing full-dataset offline training, and transfers effectively across datasets.

Conclusion: Learning compact latent representations from reasoning traces, rather than reusing raw tokens, enables efficient online continual improvement. Lightweight soft prompt memories with modular design provide a practical path toward LLMs that improve from their own inference experience.

Abstract: Large language models achieve strong reasoning performance by scaling inference-time compute, yet remain fundamentally stateless, discarding the rich, self-produced reasoning traces generated during this process. We investigate whether models can instead learn online from this experience, converting transient computation (reasoning traces) into persistent reusable knowledge, and without external supervision or access to future data. We show that In-Context Learning (ICL) over raw reasoning traces fails to generalize, reflecting a fundamental limitation of token-level reuse: individual traces lack the abstraction needed for transfer, even after refinement (e.g. self-reflection). In contrast, drawing inspiration from recent works on unsupervised reinforcement learning, we find that lightweight per-instance training with self-generated test-time signals (majority voting) as rewards yields substantial gains, often surpassing full-dataset offline training, motivating a shift from raw traces to learned latent representations. Building on this insight, we propose an online method that distills inference-time compute spent on encountered problems into compact modular latent memories capturing the underlying reasoning structure. These memories are stored and retrieved for future inputs, enabling continual improvement while avoiding catastrophic forgetting through modular design. Importantly, our method is highly efficient, parametrized as extremely lightweight soft prompt memories (~0.001% of model parameters) and trained with only a few gradient steps, yet achieving performance competitive with full parametric updates and offline training. Across challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks, our approach significantly outperforms zero-shot and raw data ICL baselines, while transferring effectively across datasets.

</details>


### [160] [QueryMarket: Cost-Aware Online Active Learning in Data Markets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17805)
*Xiwen Huang,Pierre Pinson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QueryMarket frames online active learning as a market where labels are purchased based on utility and price. OVBAL, the proposed algorithm, uses D-optimality with exponential forgetting to estimate marginal utility and makes cost-aware queries under a rolling budget, adapting to concept drift and heterogeneous costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data acquisition in real-time streams requires analysts to decide which labels to purchase on the fly under a rolling budget. Existing online active learning methods fail to simultaneously account for pricing, information gain, and rolling budget constraints, especially under concept drift.

Method: The QueryMarket framework treats each incoming data point as a market good. OVBAL estimates each sample's marginal utility using a D-optimality criterion (minimizing posterior parameter covariance) with exponential forgetting to handle nonstationarity. It then executes a cost-aware purchase decision rule that respects a rolling budget constraint, yielding a fully online and adaptive selection policy.

Result: On synthetic data and a real-world solar power forecasting task, OVBAL outperforms baselines under seller-centric pricing and achieves a more favorable long-run error-cost trade-off under both pricing schemes in the real-world task.

Conclusion: OVBAL provides a principled, fully online solution that unifies utility estimation, cost sensitivity, and budget management under concept drift, achieving strong empirical performance where existing methods fall short.

Abstract: Data acquisition is a major bottleneck for learning in real-time streams: analysts must decide on the fly which labels to purchase while respecting a rolling budget. However, existing online active learning rarely unifies pricing, information gain, and rolling budget constraints under concept drift. We introduce QueryMarket, a market-inspired framework that queries each incoming data point based on its estimated utility to the model and its price. Within this framework, we propose OVBAL (online variance-based active learning), which integrates data pricing with information-driven selection by estimating each sample's marginal utility via a D-optimality criterion with exponential forgetting and executing cost-aware purchases under rolling budget constraints. OVBAL yields a simple, fully online decision rule that adapts to nonstationary streams and heterogeneous label costs. Experiments on synthetic data and a real-world solar power generation forecasting task show that OVBAL is particularly effective under seller-centric pricing and yields a more favorable long-run error-cost trade-off in the real-world task under both pricing schemes.

</details>


### [161] [No-Free-Fairness: Fundamental Limits and Trade-offs in Learning Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17810)
*Khoat Than*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper establishes "No-Free-Fairness" theorems identifying three inherent sources of disparity in learning systems: irreducible subgroup cost creating a fairness-cost trade-off frontier; finite-sample learning inducing unavoidable disparity even in ideal settings, with strict fairness requiring exponentially many samples; and model class limitations independently causing disparity when subgroups cannot be accurately represented. Unfairness is shown to stem from intrinsic problem structure, not just biased data or optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To theoretically demonstrate that unfairness in machine learning systems is not merely an artifact of biased data or suboptimal training procedures, but rather arises from fundamental, inescapable structural properties of decision problems, finite-sample constraints, and model expressivity limitations. The authors aim to shift the understanding of fairness from a post-hoc corrective concern to a core design consideration requiring explicit trade-offs.

Method: The authors develop a theoretical framework proving impossibility results across three axes: (1) an information-theoretic analysis showing irreducible subgroup cost forces a Pareto-style fairness--cost frontier; (2) finite-sample learning bounds demonstrating that distribution-free fairness guarantees are impossible and that strict relative fairness creates a statistical bottleneck requiring exponentially many samples; (3) an expressivity analysis showing model class capacity limitations independently preclude fair solutions for certain subgroups.

Result: Three core theorems: (1) Any decision rule under irreducible subgroup cost must trade off overall performance against subgroup disparity. (2) Even with a perfectly fair and accurate solution existing in an ideal setting, finite-sample learning alone induces nontrivial disparity, and strict relative fairness may demand exponentially many samples to achieve low cost. (3) Insufficient model class expressiveness renders fairness unattainable for a subgroup regardless of data quality or training procedure.

Conclusion: Unfairness is not solely caused by biased data or optimization failures but emerges from intrinsic problem structure, finite-data constraints, and model expressivity limits. Fairness must therefore be treated as a core design consideration involving explicit trade-offs rather than an after-the-fact correction. The framework generalizes beyond standard supervised learning.

Abstract: In this paper, we establish a set of theoretical impossibility results, termed the No-Free-Fairness theorems, that identify three fundamental sources of disparity in learning systems. First, we show that when a task exhibits irreducible cost on a subgroup, any decision rule must trade off overall performance with disparity, yielding an inherent fairness--cost frontier. Second, we prove that even in ideal, noise-free settings where a perfectly fair and accurate solution exists, finite-sample learning alone induces nontrivial subgroup disparity, ruling out distribution-free fairness guarantees. More seriously, enforcing strict relative fairness creates a statistical bottleneck: achieving low cost may require exponentially many samples. Third, we show that limitations of the model class can independently induce disparity: if the model cannot represent accurate solutions for a subgroup, fairness remains unattainable regardless of data or training procedure. Overall, these results demonstrate that unfairness is not solely a consequence of biased data or suboptimal optimization, but arises from the intrinsic structure of decision problems, the constraints of finite data, and the expressivity of models. Our framework applies broadly beyond standard supervised learning, and suggests that achieving fairness requires explicit trade-offs and should be treated as a core design consideration.

</details>


### [162] [Conservation Laws for Modern Neural Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17816)
*Viet-Hoang Tran,Vinh Khanh Bui,Tan Lai Ngoc,Nam Nguyen,Tuan Dam,Tan M. Nguyen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A unified framework is developed to characterize conservation laws in gradient flow for modern architectures (GELU, SiLU, SwiGLU, multihead attention with positional encodings, MoE), with experiments validating the predicted invariants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conservation laws in gradient flow are well understood for linear and ReLU networks but remain largely unexplored for modern architectures. Understanding these laws is key to explaining implicit bias in over-parameterized models.

Method: The authors develop a unified theoretical framework that characterizes conservation laws across diverse contemporary architectures, including feedforward networks with GELU/SiLU/SwiGLU activations, multihead attention with sinusoidal and rotary positional encodings, and Mixture-of-Experts with various gating designs.

Result: The framework successfully derives conservation laws (invariants) for all examined architectures. Experiments validate the theoretically predicted invariants.

Conclusion: The unified framework extends the understanding of gradient flow conservation laws to modern architectures, bridging a gap between theory (previously limited to linear/ReLU) and contemporary practice.

Abstract: Understanding gradient descent dynamics is key to explaining the success of over-parameterized models, where implicit bias manifests through conservation laws in gradient flow. While such laws are well understood for linear and ReLU networks, they remain largely unexplored for modern architectures. This work develops a unified framework to characterize conservation laws for contemporary models, including feedforward networks with GELU, SiLU, and SwiGLU activations, multihead attention with sinusoidal and rotary positional encodings, and Mixture-of-Experts architectures under diverse gating designs. Our theoretical findings are supported by experiments that validate the predicted invariants.

</details>


### [163] [Functional Equivalence in Attention: A Comprehensive Study with Applications to Linear Mode Connectivity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17830)
*Viet-Hoang Tran,Vinh Khanh Bui,Van-Hoan Trinh,Tan Lai Ngoc,Tan M. Nguyen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formally analyzes functional equivalence symmetries in Transformer architectures, showing that sinusoidal positional encodings preserve the symmetry group of vanilla attention while rotary positional encodings (RoPE) reduce it, thereby increasing expressivity. This provides a theoretical justification for RoPE's empirical success. The authors also demonstrate that positional encoding choice critically affects linear mode connectivity in Transformer loss landscapes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural network parameter spaces are non-injective due to functional equivalence symmetries. While these symmetries are well-characterized for classical architectures (MLPs, CNNs), they remain poorly understood in modern attention-based models. Crucially, existing analyses of multihead attention symmetries ignore positional encodings, which fundamentally alter the symmetry structure. The paper aims to close this gap, particularly given the practical shift from sinusoidal to rotary positional encodings.

Method: The authors conduct a formal group-theoretic analysis of functional equivalence in Transformers. They characterize the symmetry groups for: (1) vanilla multihead attention (no positional encoding), (2) attention with sinusoidal positional encodings, and (3) attention with rotary positional encodings (RoPE). They compare the invariance structures across these settings. Additionally, they empirically investigate linear mode connectivity under different positional encoding schemes using an alignment algorithm to assess loss landscape geometry.

Result: Sinusoidal positional encodings preserve the full symmetry group of vanilla attention (permutation symmetries within heads and across heads/ layers). In contrast, RoPE breaks a substantial portion of these symmetries, resulting in a strictly smaller equivalence group. This symmetry reduction implies greater expressivity, offering a principled explanation for RoPE's superior empirical performance. Empirically, linear mode connectivity varies significantly with positional encoding type: RoPE-trained models exhibit different connectivity patterns compared to those trained with sinusoidal encodings.

Conclusion: The choice of positional encoding fundamentally shapes the symmetry structure of Transformer parameter spaces. RoPE's symmetry-breaking property enhances representational capacity, explaining its widespread adoption. The findings also reveal that mode connectivity—a property relevant to loss landscape analysis and model merging—is not universal across architectures but depends critically on design choices like positional encodings.

Abstract: Neural network parameter spaces are inherently non-injective, as distinct parameter configurations can realize identical functions through functional equivalence. While this symmetry is well understood in classical fully connected and convolutional models, it becomes substantially more intricate in modern attention-based architectures. Existing analyses of multihead attention have largely focused on the vanilla formulation, overlooking positional encodings that fundamentally reshape architectural symmetries. In this work, we provide a formal study of functional equivalence in Transformers with positional encodings. Focusing on the two most widely used variants--sinusoidal and rotary positional encodings (RoPE)--we show that sinusoidal encodings preserve the equivalence structure of vanilla attention, whereas rotary encodings significantly reduce the symmetry group, thereby enhancing expressivity. This offers a principled explanation for the growing prominence of RoPE in practice. We further examine how positional encodings affect linear mode connectivity, and through an alignment algorithm, empirically demonstrate that the presence and variability of connectivity across Transformer settings crucially depend on the positional encoding.

</details>


### [164] [From Drift to Coherence: Stabilizing Beliefs in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17832)
*SongEun Kim,Seungyoo Lee,Edwin Fong,Hyungi Lee,Juho Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLMs exhibit martingale violations (belief drift) when resampling answers to the same question, but self-stabilize after sufficient steps. Authors propose seed-answer prompting and a self-consistency loss to accelerate stabilization and improve predictive coherence in multiple-choice QA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are hypothesized to perform implicit Bayesian inference, but the martingale property — a key coherence condition for Bayesian beliefs — has been shown to fail in synthetic settings. The authors aim to test whether this holds in realistic multiple-choice QA and to develop methods that restore predictive coherence.

Method: The authors introduce Prompted Predictive Resampling (PPR): an LLM repeatedly answers the same multiple-choice question, and exact predictive distributions are computed over the discrete answer space. They analyze belief dynamics across resampling steps. To mitigate observed early-stage drift, they propose (1) seed-answer prompting, which provides an initial answer to accelerate convergence, and (2) a self-consistency loss for fine-tuning that amortizes early drift directly into model parameters.

Result: PPR reveals early-stage belief drift (martingale violations), but beliefs self-stabilize and converge to a coherent distribution after sufficient resampling. Both seed-answer prompting and self-consistency fine-tuning substantially reduce belief drift and improve predictive coherence on multiple-choice QA benchmarks, all without sacrificing accuracy.

Conclusion: LLMs violate the martingale property in practical QA settings, but their predictive beliefs naturally self-stabilize. The proposed interventions effectively accelerate this stabilization, suggesting practical pathways toward more coherent probabilistic reasoning in deployed LLM systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often hypothesized to perform implicit Bayesian inference, yet a key coherence condition, the martingale property of predictive beliefs, has been shown to fail in controlled synthetic in-context learning settings. We revisit this question in a more typical usage regime: generic multiple-choice question answering. Exploiting the discrete answer space, we compute exact predictive distributions and study belief dynamics induced by autoregressive answer resampling. We introduce prompted predictive resampling (PPR), where an LLM generates a sequence of answers to the same question. Empirically, PPR reveals early-stage belief drift, indicating martingale violations. However, after sufficient resampling steps, the belief process self-stabilizes and converges to a coherent predictive distribution.
