Based on this observation, we further propose (i) a seed-answer prompting strategy to accelerate stabilization, and (ii) a self-consistency loss that amortizes early-stage drift into the model via fine-tuning. Experiments on multiple-choice QA benchmarks show that our methods substantially reduce belief drift and improve predictive coherence without sacrificing accuracy.

</details>


### [165] [Meta-classification of one-class classification models using ranking correlation and nearest neighbor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17858)
*Toshitaka Hayashi,Hamido Fujita,Dalibor Cimr,Richard Cimler,Jitka Kühnová*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper explores the novel direction of applying machine learning to classify ML models themselves, specifically one-class classification (OCC) models. By representing OCC models as normality rankings and using nearest-neighbor and ranking-correlation metrics, the method achieves high accuracy in classifying models by training dataset and can also classify by algorithm when datasets share classes. The approach generalizes to dataset classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Applying ML to ML models (meta-classification) is an underexplored direction. Since all ML models can be approximated as OCC models, the authors propose a unified framework for meta-classification of OCC models, enabling inference about the training dataset, algorithm type, or hyperparameters used to produce a given model.

Method: OCC models are represented as normality rankings over instances. Classification is performed using nearest-neighbor and ranking-correlation metrics to compare these ranking representations. The approach is evaluated on classifying OCC models where class labels correspond to training datasets, algorithms, and hyperparameters. The method is extended to direct dataset classification using sleep-record data.

Result: The proposal achieves high classification accuracy when class labels are datasets. It can also successfully classify algorithms when training datasets share the same class. The discussion shows that classifying OCC models is fundamentally equivalent to classifying datasets (treating multiple samples as a single input).

Conclusion: The proposed method provides a unified solution for classifying OCC models, datasets, and rankings, demonstrating that meta-classification of ML models is feasible and opens a new research direction. Source code is publicly available.

Abstract: Machine Learning (ML) techniques have been applied to various problems. However, applying ML to ML models is an unexplored direction. For this purpose, this paper considers a meta-classification of one-class classification (OCC) models, because all ML models could be approximated as OCC models. The proposal represents OCC models as normality rankings and classifies them using nearest-neighbor and ranking-correlation metrics. The experiment classifies OCC models, where classes correspond to training datasets, algorithms, and hyperparameters. The proposal achieves high accuracy when class labels are datasets. Moreover, it can classify algorithms when the training datasets contain the same class. In addition, the discussion highlights that the classification of OCC models is essentially the classification of datasets that treats multiple samples as a single input. The experiment demonstrates the classification of datasets using sleeping records. The proposed method can provide a unified solution for classifying OCC models, datasets, and rankings. Source code is uploaded to the public repository https://github.com/ToshiHayashi/ClassOCC.

</details>


### [166] [AnchorKV: Safety-Aware KV Cache Compression via Soft Penalty with a Refusal Anchor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17872)
*Ning Ni,Yingjie Lao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AnchorKV is a safety-aware KV cache compression method that biases token retention away from harmful directions in key space, using an offline safety anchor derived from representation engineering. It trades minimal utility for substantially improved safety alignment against jailbreak attacks, and reduces to the original compressor when the safety penalty is zero.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KV cache compression methods (e.g., FastKV, SnapKV, DynamicKV) reduce memory costs but either fail to defend against jailbreak attacks or degrade safety alignment under aggressive token eviction. There is a need for a compression approach that preserves both efficiency and safety.

Method: AnchorKV is a drop-in modification to KV cache compression. It constructs an offline "safety anchor" using a difference-of-means representation engineering approach adapted to the layer-specific key projection space. A soft penalty token selection rule then biases retention scores away from directions associated with harmful prompts, allowing a controlled trade-off between utility and safety alignment.

Result: AnchorKV achieves substantially improved safety alignment compared to baseline KV cache compressors with only a small sacrifice in utility. When the safety penalty is set to zero, the method gracefully reduces to the original compression algorithm.

Conclusion: AnchorKV demonstrates that safety alignment and KV cache compression can be co-optimized, offering a practical, plug-and-play solution for deploying safe and efficient LLMs, particularly in resource-constrained or on-device settings.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) outperform earlier architectures on generative inference and long-context tasks, but their large size introduces significant challenges in memory usage, energy cost, and on-device deployment. Since scaling pre-trained language models improves downstream capability \cite{zhao2023survey}, the key-value (KV) cache becomes a dominant inference bottleneck. Recent KV cache compression methods \cite{jo2025fastkv,li2024snapkv,zhou2024dynamickv} reduce this cost by retaining only a subset of attention-relevant tokens. However, while these approaches preserve accuracy on benign workloads, their compression policies either fail to defend against jailbreak attacks \cite{jiang2024robustkv} or degrade safety alignment under aggressive eviction.
  We propose AnchorKV, a drop-in modification to KV cache compression that biases token retention scores away from directions in key space associated with harmful prompts. AnchorKV constructs an offline safety anchor by adapting a difference-of-means representation engineering approach \cite{arditi2024refusal,zou2023representation} to the layer-specific key projection space used in KV caching. Based on this anchor, a soft penalty token selection rule trades a small amount of utility for substantially improved safety alignment, while reducing to the original compressor when the penalty is zero.

</details>


### [167] [Monotonic Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: A Theoretical and Empirical Study of Monotonicity as an Inductive Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17886)
*Mikhail Krasnov,Carolina Fortuna,Blaž Bertalanič*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MKAN is a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network variant that guarantees hard monotonicity for all parameter values via exponential reparameterization of B-spline coefficients, positive edge weights, and a monotone base activation. The paper provides a representation-cost theorem bounding the size of a monotone realization of any ball-partitioning feature extractor, and shows empirically that MKAN matches SOTA monotone NNs while adding per-edge functional transparency and recovering ground-truth factors with higher Spearman alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing monotonicity-enforcing neural networks (MLP- or flow-based) lack per-edge functional transparency. The only prior KAN variant with monotonicity (MonoKAN) enforces constraints on a restricted parameter subset and requires projection-style training. The authors aim to provide a KAN-based architecture with hard, unconstrained monotonicity guarantees for all parameters while retaining KAN's interpretability.

Method: MKAN enforces hard monotonicity through three mechanisms: (1) exponential reparameterization of B-spline coefficients, (2) strictly positive edge weights (via softplus or similar), and (3) a monotone base activation function. This reduces training to standard unconstrained gradient descent. The theoretical contribution is a representation-cost theorem: any C^K feature extractor inducing a ball-shaped semantic-neighborhood partition admits a monotone realization of equivalent neighborhood structure at size N' = N* + k ≤ 2N*, where k is the number of non-monotone coordinates. An architecture-agnostic sizing rule for monotone encoders follows.

Result: MKAN is competitive with state-of-the-art monotone NNs on the SMM/ICML-2024 benchmark. The 2N* prediction is validated in a self-supervised feature-size sweep across four real datasets. On a controlled monotone-generative dataset, MKAN recovers ground-truth factors with substantially higher Spearman alignment than KAN, MLP, and linear baselines.

Conclusion: MKAN successfully combines hard unconstrained monotonicity with KAN's per-edge functional transparency, closing a gap in the literature. The representation-cost theorem provides a principled sizing rule for monotone encoders, validated empirically. MKAN is the first monotone KAN that requires no constrained/projection training.

Abstract: Monotonicity has been a long-running architectural inductive bias for neural networks, motivated by tabular, scientific, and economic settings where outputs are known to respond monotonically to certain inputs. Existing approaches are MLP- or flow-based and lack per-edge functional transparency; the only Kolmogorov--Arnold Network (KAN) variant with monotonicity, MonoKAN, enforces the constraint only on a restricted parameter subset and requires a projection-style training procedure. We close this gap with \textbf{MKAN}, a KAN with hard monotonicity guaranteed for \emph{all} parameter values via exponential reparameterization of B-spline coefficients, positive edge weights, and a monotone base activation. Training reduces to standard unconstrained gradient descent. Our headline theoretical contribution is a \emph{representation-cost} theorem: any $C^K, K >0$ feature extractor inducing a ball-shaped semantic-neighborhood partition admits a monotone realization of the equivalent neighborhood structure at $N' = N^* + k \le 2N^*$, where $k$ is the number of non-monotone coordinates of the original. The bound is architecture-agnostic and gives a principled sizing rule for monotone encoders. Empirically, MKAN is competitive with state-of-the-art monotone NNs on the SMM/ICML-2024 benchmark while being the only method that combines hard unconstrained monotonicity with KAN's per-edge functional transparency; the $2N^*$ prediction is validated in a self-supervised feature-size sweep on four real datasets, and on a controlled monotone-generative dataset MKAN recovers ground-truth factors with substantially higher Spearman alignment than KAN, MLP, and linear baselines.

</details>


### [168] [Dimensionality Controls When Modularity Helps in Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17889)
*Kathrin Korte,Christian Medeiros Adriano,Joachim Winther Pedersen,Eleni Nisioti,Sebastian Risi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In a sequential A-B-A continual learning paradigm, modular architectures outperform single networks only in a low-dimensional "rich" regime where representations are strongly constrained; in a high-dimensional "lazy" regime, both perform similarly. Modular networks develop graded task-specific subspaces — overlapping for similar tasks, partially aligned for moderately dissimilar ones, and separated for dissimilar ones — suggesting that representational dimensionality, governed by initialization scale, determines when explicit modular structure becomes functionally beneficial.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Compositional learning systems must balance plasticity (acquiring new knowledge) with stability (preserving prior knowledge), particularly when tasks share structure and risk catastrophic interference. It is unclear under what conditions explicit modular architecture actually confers functional benefits over a single network, and how factors like task similarity and representational dimensionality interact to shape this benefit.

Method: The authors compare a task-partitioned modular recurrent network to a single-network baseline in a sequential A-B-A continual learning paradigm. They manipulate representational dimensionality by varying weight initialization scale, inducing either a high-dimensional "lazy" regime or a low-dimensional "rich" regime. They then analyze performance and internal representational geometry across varying degrees of task similarity.

Result: In the high-dimensional lazy regime, both architectures achieve comparable performance and internal geometry. In the low-dimensional rich regime, the modular network significantly outperforms the single network, developing graded task-specific subspaces: overlapping for similar tasks, partially aligned for moderately dissimilar tasks, and separated for dissimilar tasks. This yields a more compositional and interpretable representational organization.

Conclusion: Representational regime — co-varying with initialization scale and dimensionality — is a key factor governing when modular structure is functionally beneficial in continual learning. The findings reframe safety and robustness as problems of adaptive allocation of representational subspaces, rather than a fixed choice between separation and sharing.

Abstract: Compositional learning systems must balance plasticity, the ability to acquire new knowledge, with stability, the preservation of previously learned components, especially when tasks share structure and risk interference. We study how modular architecture, task similarity, and representational dimensionality jointly shape compositional continual learning in a sequential A-B-A paradigm, comparing a task-partitioned recurrent network to a single-network baseline while inducing high- and low-dimensional regimes via weight-scale manipulations. In a high-dimensional "lazy" regime, both architectures achieve similar performance and internal geometry, suggesting that explicit modular structure has little impact when representations are weakly constrained. In a lower-dimensional "rich" regime, modularity becomes decisive: the modular network develops graded task-specific subspaces that overlap for similar tasks, partially align for moderately dissimilar tasks, and separate for dissimilar tasks, yielding a more compositional and interpretable organization than the single network. These findings identify the representational regime induced by initialization scale, which co-varies with representational dimensionality, as a key factor governing when compositional, modular structure is functionally beneficial in continual learning, and support viewing safety and robustness as problems of adaptive allocation of representational subspaces rather than fixed separation versus sharing.

</details>


### [169] [KANLib -- An Modular, Extensible and Fast Kolmogorov-Arnold Network Implementation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17927)
*Julian Hoever,Gregor Schiele*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KANLib is a modular, extensible PyTorch-compatible framework that unifies and optimizes existing KAN implementations, achieving competitive predictive performance and enabling flexible architectural exploration of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Practical research on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) is hindered by high computational costs and inconsistent feature support across existing implementations (PyKAN, EfficientKAN, FastKAN). A unified, efficient, and extensible framework is needed to accelerate KAN research.

Method: KANLib unifies core concepts from existing KAN implementations into a single modular software architecture. It supports two basis function types, adaptive grid rescaling, grid extension, and fine-grained architectural customization while maintaining PyTorch compatibility. Evaluation is performed on the California Housing benchmark, comparing against reference KAN implementations.

Result: KANLib reproduces the predictive behavior of established KAN implementations with competitive computational efficiency. Architectural variations beyond standard KAN formulations can be explored with only minor impacts on predictive performance.

Conclusion: KANLib provides a robust, scalable foundation for future KAN research, lowering the barrier to experimentation while maintaining high performance and broad architectural flexibility.

Abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to traditional multilayer perceptrons by replacing linear weights with learnable univariate functions. Despite their theoretical advantages in interpretability and expressiveness, practical research of KANs remains difficult due to high computational costs and inconsistent feature support across existing frameworks. This paper introduces KANLib, a modular, extensible, and computationally efficient framework for developing and evaluating KAN architectures. KANLib unifies core concepts from existing implementations, including PyKAN, EfficientKAN, and FastKAN, within a consistent software architecture that emphasizes flexibility, feature parity, and high performance. The framework supports two basis function types, adaptive grid rescaling, grid extension, and fine-grained architectural customization while maintaining compatibility with standard PyTorch workflows. Experimental evaluation on the California Housing benchmark demonstrates that KANLib reproduces the predictive behavior of established reference KAN implementations while achieving competitive computational efficiency. Furthermore, the framework enables the exploration of architectural variations beyond standard KAN formulations with only minor impacts on predictive performance. Overall, KANLib provides a robust foundation for future research on scalable and extensible KAN architectures.

</details>


### [170] [Predictive Analytics in E-Commerce for CustomerBehavior Forecasting using hybrid Ret-DNN withXGBoost Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17931)
*Degala Pushpa Sri,Mayank Atreya,Lakshmi. H,Navin Chhibber,Mukesh Soni*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hybrid Ret-DNN + XGBoost model is proposed for customer purchase prediction in e-commerce, achieving an MAE of 0.2193 on a UK retailer dataset of ~500K transactions, outperforming standalone Ret-DNN.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: E-commerce platforms struggle to understand customer behavior and predict future purchases, limiting their ability to optimize retail strategies.

Method: The authors propose a two-stage hybrid model: (1) a Retail Deep Neural Network (Ret-DNN) serves as a feature extractor to capture temporal features and contextual transaction patterns; (2) the extracted features are then fed into an XGBoost classifier for final purchase probability prediction. Data preprocessing includes cleaning, outlier handling, temporal feature extraction, feature encoding, and z-score normalization.

Result: The Ret-DNN + XGBoost hybrid achieved a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.2193, outperforming the baseline Ret-DNN model alone.

Conclusion: Combining deep neural feature extraction with gradient-boosted trees effectively captures both temporal dynamics and tabular patterns in retail transaction data, yielding improved customer purchase forecasting accuracy.

Abstract: In recent years, electronic (E) commerce services have rapidly increased in the daily lives of people, which helpsthem to purchase products online. However, retail platforms have struggled to understand customer behavior and make it difficult to predict their future purchases. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes a hybrid Retail Deep NeuralNetwork (Ret-DNN) with an Extreme Gradient Boosting(XGBoost) model for capturing temporal features and tabular dynamics of retail data. First, data were sourced from a UnitedKingdom (UK)-based online retailer that contains transactions with almost 500,000 records. Then, the collected data were pre-processed using a series of techniques, such as data cleaning, outlier handling, temporal feature extraction, feature encoding, and z-score normalization, to ensure that the data were ready for model training and testing. Subsequently, the preprocessed data were fed into the Ret-DNN model, which acts as a feature extractor to understand the complete context of customer transactions. Further, the extracted data were fed as input into the XGBoost model, which predicted the final output as the purchase probability of customers. Finally, the proposed Ret-DNN XGBoost model achieved better results by attaining aMean Absolute Error (MAE) 0.2193 when compared to the existing Ret-DNN model.
  Keywords: Customer behavior forecasting, extreme gradientboosting, electronic commerce, predictive analytic, retail deepneural networks.

</details>


### [171] [SoftMoE: Soft Differentiable Routing for Mixture-of-Experts in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17952)
*Mikołaj Zasada,Łukasz Struski,Jacek Tabor,Marcin Kurdziel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SoftMoE proposes a differentiable alternative to discrete top-k routing in sparse MoE by using a truncated soft top-k LapSum relaxation with a learnable, globally budget-constrained expert allocation across layers, achieving comparable performance with fewer activated experts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Discrete top-k routing in sparse MoE is non-differentiable and forces a fixed number of active experts per input, leading to computational inefficiency. The authors seek a fully differentiable, gradient-optimizable routing mechanism that can learn how to allocate expert capacity across layers.

Method: SoftMoE replaces discrete top-k routing with a truncated soft top-k LapSum relaxation, making expert routing differentiable. A global budget constraint is imposed, and the mean number of active experts per layer is parameterized, allowing the model to learn non-uniform expert allocation across layers during gradient-based optimization.

Result: SoftMoE achieves performance comparable to or better than standard sparse MoE on language modeling and downstream tasks while activating significantly fewer experts. The learned allocation is highly non-uniform, with later layers activating more experts than earlier layers.

Conclusion: SoftMoE demonstrates that differentiable, budget-constrained expert routing is a viable and efficient alternative to discrete top-k routing, enabling more flexible and computationally efficient use of expert capacity in MoE-based LLMs.

Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable scaling LLM parameters under a fixed inference budget by activating only a small subset of experts via top-$k$ routing. While this preserves causality and suits autoregressive language models, the discrete top-$k$ operator is not differentiable, forcing a fixed number of active experts per input and resulting in inefficient use of computation. We propose SoftMoE, which replaces discrete routing with a truncated soft top-$k$ LapSum relaxation, allowing gradient-based optimization of expert routing. We further parameterize the mean number of active experts per layer and impose a global budget constraint, enabling the model to learn how to allocate expert capacity across layers. SoftMoE remains fully compatible with autoregressive modeling and achieves performance comparable to or better than sparse MoE on language modeling and downstream tasks, while activating significantly fewer experts. Notably, the learned allocation is highly non-uniform, with later layers activating more experts. The source code is publicly available$^\dagger$.

</details>


### [172] [Multiple cyclicity and Wavelet Decomposition with Channel Correlation for Long-term Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17996)
*Bin Wang,Heming Yang,Jinfang Sheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: McWC is a long-term time series forecasting model that separately models cyclicity, trend, and inter-channel correlations using multi-layer cyclicity construction, multi-layer perceptron for channel correlation, and multi-level wavelet decomposition, achieving SOTA performance with high computational efficiency on six real-world datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current long-term time series forecasting methods neglect real-world inter-channel correlations and rely on overly complex designs that capture diverse information at the cost of low computational efficiency, leading to suboptimal predictions.

Method: McWC employs four key components: (1) a multi-layer cyclicity construction module to decouple cyclical information; (2) a multi-layer perceptron to extract inter-channel correlations; (3) a multi-level wavelet decomposition module to model and fuse multi-layer high-frequency and low-frequency information; and (4) aggregation of component results. Additionally, intra-channel autocorrelations are decoupled via a frequency-domain loss function.

Result: Experiments on six real-world datasets show McWC achieves state-of-the-art performance with excellent computational efficiency and strong historical information extraction capabilities.

Conclusion: Separately modeling cyclicity, trend, and inter-channel correlations — rather than using complex monolithic designs — yields both superior forecasting accuracy and computational efficiency in long-term time series forecasting.

Abstract: Cyclicity and trend are important components of time series data and many studies based on cyclicity and trend have achieved good results in long-term time series forecasting. However, we believe that current work neglects the influence of real-world inter-channel correlations in time series data which leads to suboptimal predictions. Furthermore, these models rely on complex designs to capture diverse information so that resulting in low computational efficiency. To address this challenge, we propose McWC, a long-term time series forecasting model that separately models the cyclicity, trend, and inter-channel correlations. Specifically, McWC first decouples cyclical information from data using a multi-layer cyclicity construction module. Then, it extracts inter-channel correlations using multi-layer perceptron. Next, it models and fuses the multi-layer high-frequency and low-frequency information from data using a multi-level wavelet decomposition module. Finally, it aggregates the results of different components to obtain the output. Simultaneously, we decouple intra-channel autocorrelations by calculating a loss function in the frequency domain. Experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that McWC achieves state-of-the-art performance, exhibiting excellent computational efficiency and historical information extraction capabilities.

</details>


### [173] [Half a Link can Be Enough to Predict a Whole Link: Understanding Generalization in Knowledge Graph Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18001)
*Cosimo Gregucci,Obaidah Theeb,Daniel Hernandez,Antonio Vergari,Steffen Staab*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KGFMs generalize well to unseen KGs, but performance varies significantly depending on whether "half-links" (partial triples like (h,r) or (r,t)) have been observed during inference. The paper proposes a taxonomy of four half-link observation scenarios and uses stratified analysis to reveal that SOTA KGFMs exploit seen half-links, while unseen half-links remain challenging — offering a diagnostic framework for evaluating and improving KGFM robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current understanding of when and how KG foundation models robustly generalize across unseen knowledge graphs is limited. The authors aim to dissect the generalization mechanisms of KGFMs, specifically investigating whether observing partial link information (half-links) at inference time explains performance variability.

Method: The authors define "half-links" as partially observed triples — either (h, r) or (r, t). They construct a taxonomy of four scenarios based on whether each half-link of a test triple (h, r, t) is seen or unseen in the inference graph. A rigorous stratified analysis is then conducted over these four scenarios using state-of-the-art KGFMs to quantify how performance varies systematically across the taxonomy.

Result: SOTA KGFMs heavily rely on observed half-links for link prediction; they perform well when half-links are seen but struggle significantly when half-links are unseen. Different half-link combinations pose distinct challenges, revealing non-uniform generalization behavior across the proposed taxonomy.

Conclusion: The proposed half-link taxonomy serves as an effective diagnostic protocol for assessing KGFM generalization robustness. It pinpoints specific weaknesses in current models and provides a roadmap for developing next-generation KGFMs that can better handle unseen half-link scenarios.

Abstract: Knowledge graph (KG) foundation models (KGFMs) are zero-shot generalizers: trained once, they can predict links on unseen graphs without retraining. However, understanding when and how they can robustly generalize across KGs is still an open question. In this paper, we shed some light on their generalization mechanisms highlighting how their performance on unseen KGs is not uniform when it comes to partially seen links, which we call half-links. In fact, we show that to predict a test triple $(h,r,t)$ it might suffice in practice to have observed the half-link $(h,r)$ or $(r,t)$ in the inference graph. This yields a taxonomy of four scenarios when combinations of these half-links are observed or not. In a rigorous stratified analysis over these scenarios, we reveal that SoTA KGFMs use seen half links for predictions, while unseen half-links pose different challenges. As such, our finer-grained taxonomy can be a diagnostic protocol for robust KGFM generalization and highlights where novel KGFMs can improve.

</details>


### [174] [Looped World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18208)
*Hongyuan Adam Lu,Z. L. Victor Wei,Qun Zhang,Jinrui Zeng,Bowen Cao,Lingwei Meng,Mocheng Li,Zezhong Wang,Haonan Yin,Naifu Xue,Minyu Chen,Cenyuan Zhang,Zefan Zhang,Hao Wei,Jiawei Zhou,Haoran Xu,Hao Yang,Ronglai Zuo,Tongda Xu,Yonghao Li,Jian Chen,Hebin Wang,Zeyu Gao,Yang Li,Wei Zhao,Qimin Zhong,Siqi Liu,Yumeng Zhang,Leyan Cui,Zhangyu Wang,Wai Lam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LoopWM introduces iterative, looped transformer architectures for world modeling that achieve up to 100× parameter efficiency by adaptively scaling computation depth per prediction step, establishing iterative latent depth as a new scaling axis orthogonal to model size and data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current world models suffer from a fundamental tension: long-horizon simulation requires deep computation for fidelity, but deeper models are expensive to deploy and susceptible to compounding errors. The authors seek to resolve this trade-off.

Method: LoopWM employs a parameter-shared transformer block that iteratively refines latent environment states. This looped architecture enables adaptive computation, automatically scaling depth to match the complexity of each prediction step rather than using a fixed-depth forward pass.

Result: The approach yields up to 100x parameter efficiency compared to conventional (non-looped) world model architectures, while maintaining or improving simulation fidelity through adaptive depth allocation.

Conclusion: Iterative latent depth represents a novel and promising scaling axis for world simulation, orthogonal to traditional scaling of model size and training data. LoopWM may significantly advance the field by decoupling simulation depth from parameter count.

Abstract: Current world models face a fundamental tension: faithful long-horizon simulation demands deep computation, but deeper models are expensive to deploy and prone to compounding errors. We resolve this by introducing Looped World Models (LoopWM), which are the first looped architectures for world modelling. Our method iteratively refines latent environment states through a parameter-shared transformer block. This yield up to 100x parameter efficiency over conventional approaches with adaptive computation that automatically scales depth to match the complexity of each prediction step. Orthogonal to scaling model size and training data, LoopWM establishes iterative latent depth as a new scaling axis for world simulation, which might significantly push the community forward.

</details>


### [175] [C2FL: Clustered Continual Federated Learning under Spatial and Temporal Drift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18003)
*Davide Domini,Gianluca Aguzzi,Lorenzo Pellegrini,Mirko Viroli,Lukas Esterle*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: C2FL is a fully distributed federated learning approach where nodes self-organize into spatial clusters, using experience replay and dwell-time-aware adaptive averaging to combat temporal drift while preserving privacy, outperforming standard FL under heterogeneous, evolving conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CAS nodes face privacy constraints, spatial heterogeneity (nearby vs. distant observations), and temporal drift from mobility. Standard learning strategies fail under the interplay of these factors across domains like vehicular sensing and crowdsensing.

Method: C2FL enables fully distributed FL with spatial clustering for group self-organization. Each node employs experience replay to retain prior knowledge and a dwell-time-aware adaptive averaging step that progressively incorporates regional consensus based on how long the node stays in an area.

Result: Synthetic experiments systematically reproducing spatial and temporal shifts show that standard federated strategies degrade significantly, while C2FL restores robust collective adaptation under these conditions.

Conclusion: C2FL effectively addresses the combined challenges of privacy, spatial heterogeneity, and temporal drift in CAS, enabling robust decentralized learning through spatial self-organization and temporally adaptive aggregation.

Abstract: Collective Adaptive Systems (CAS) increasingly rely on machine learning to let each node learn from locally sensed data, aligning its behavior with the surrounding environment. Scaling this intelligence, however, raises fundamental challenges: sensed data is often privacy-sensitive, preventing centralized collection; nodes are mobile, traversing regions where nearby nodes perceive similar phenomena while distant ones observe radically different conditions, creating natural spatial clusters; and these distributions evolve over time due to mobility, introducing temporal drift that makes local models progressively stale. These dynamics arise across domains - vehicular sensing, drone-based monitoring, smartphone crowdsensing - yet the interplay of privacy, spatial heterogeneity, and temporal drift severely undermines conventional learning strategies. Therefore, we propose C2FL, a fully distributed Federated Learning (FL) approach where nodes self-organize into learning groups through spatial clustering, reflecting the geographic structure of the environment. To counteract temporal drift, each node combines experience replay with a dwell-time-aware adaptive averaging step, progressively incorporating the regional consensus as it remains longer within the same area, while preserving previously acquired knowledge under evolving distributions. We evaluate our approach on synthetic experiments that systematically reproduce spatial and temporal shifts, showing that standard federated strategies degrade significantly under these conditions and that our method restores robust collective adaptation.

</details>


### [176] [Recursive Scaling in Masked Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18022)
*Alba Carballo-Castro,Julianna Piskorz,Paulius Rauba,Mihaela van der Schaar,Pascal Frossard*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Recursive Masked Diffusion Models (R-MDMs) introduce recursive depth as a third scaling axis for masked diffusion models by repeatedly applying the same denoising transformer within each diffusion step, achieving substantial parameter efficiency gains — an L-iteration recursive model matches non-recursive baselines with roughly L× more parameters — while also enabling partial substitution of denoising steps with recursive refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scaling masked diffusion models has traditionally relied on increasing parameter count or denoising steps. The authors identify an underexplored third axis — recursive depth — that can improve model capacity without inflating parameters, analogous to how recurrence enables deeper computation in RNNs but applied within each diffusion step.

Method: The authors propose Recursive Masked Diffusion Models (R-MDMs), which repeatedly apply the same denoising transformer backbone within each diffusion step. This recursion enables iterative refinement through parameter reuse, increasing effective model depth without increasing the actual parameter count. The method is evaluated on structured generation tasks (Sudoku and Countdown).

Result: An R-MDM with L recursive iterations often matches the performance of non-recursive baselines with roughly L× more parameters, demonstrating substantial parameter efficiency. Additionally, recursive refinement can partially substitute for additional denoising steps, enabling equivalent generation quality with fewer forward passes at inference time.

Conclusion: Recursive depth is a practically useful third scaling axis for masked diffusion models, improving both parameter efficiency and the allocation of test-time compute, and complementing conventional scaling via parameter count and denoising steps.

Abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for sequence generation. Scaling MDMs is conventionally achieved by increasing the parameter count or the number of denoising steps. We introduce Recursive Masked Diffusion Models (R-MDMs), which add recursive depth as a third scaling axis by repeatedly applying the same denoising transformer within each diffusion step. Recursion enables iterative refinement of the output through parameter reuse, increasing effective model depth without increasing parameter count. Across structured generation tasks, including Sudoku and Countdown, we show that R-MDMs achieve substantially improved parameter efficiency: a model with $L$ recursive iterations often matches the performance of non-recursive baselines with roughly $L\times$ more parameters. Moreover, recursive refinement can partially substitute for additional denoising steps, allowing recursive models to reach the same generation quality with fewer forward passes at inference time. These results suggest that recursive depth is a practically useful scaling mechanism for MDMs, improving both parameter efficiency and the allocation of test-time compute.

</details>


### [177] [LoopCoder-v2: Only Loop Once for Efficient Test-Time Computation Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18023)
*Jian Yang,Shawn Guo,Wei Zhang,Tianyu Zheng,Yaxin Du,Haau-Sing Li,Jiajun Wu,Yue Song,Yan Xing,Qingsong Cai,Zelong Huang,Chuan Hao,Ran Tao,Xianglong Liu,Wayne Xin Zhao,Mingjie Tang,Weifeng Lv,Ming Zhou,Bryan Dai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Parallel Loop Transformers enable practical loop-count tuning, but performance is non-monotonic: two loops yield strong gains, while three or more loops regress due to a gain–cost trade-off where fixed positional mismatch costs eventually outweigh diminishing refinement benefits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformers with looped computation scale depth efficiently via weight sharing, but sequential looping introduces latency and memory overhead proportional to loop count. Parallel Loop Transformers (PLT) address this via cross-loop position offsets and shared-KV gated sliding-window attention, making loop count a tunable design parameter. However, the optimal loop count and the trade-offs governing it are not well understood.

Method: The authors frame loop-count selection through a gain–cost lens: additional loops may refine representations (gain) but introduce a positional mismatch at each loop boundary via cross-loop position offsets (cost). They instantiate this by training LoopCoder-v2, a family of 7B PLT-based code generation models with varying loop counts (zero through multiple loops), trained from scratch on 18T tokens with matched instruction tuning. They benchmark across code generation, code reasoning, agentic software engineering, and tool-use tasks, and perform diagnostic analyses on representational diversity, update magnitude, and refinement quality per loop.

Result: The two-loop variant substantially outperforms the non-looped baseline: SWE-bench Verified improves from 43.0 to 64.4, Multi-SWE from 14.0 to 31.0. However, three or more loops cause performance regression, revealing a strongly non-monotonic loop-count effect. Diagnostics show loop 2 provides the primary productive refinement, while later loops produce diminishing, oscillatory updates with reduced representational diversity. The CLP-induced positional mismatch remains roughly constant, so as refinement gains shrink, the offset cost increasingly dominates.

Conclusion: PLT exhibits a saturation point at two loops, explained by a gain–cost trade-off: the cross-loop position offset imposes a fixed mismatch cost at each loop boundary, while refinement gains diminish with additional loops. This framework provides actionable diagnostics and principled guidance for loop-count selection in parallel loop architectures.

Abstract: Looped Transformers scale latent computation by repeatedly applying shared blocks, but sequential looping increases latency and KV-cache memory with the loop count. Parallel loop Transformers (PLT) alleviate this cost through cross-loop position offsets (CLP) and shared-KV gated sliding-window attention, making loop count a practical design choice. We therefore study PLT loop-count selection through a gain--cost view: an extra loop may refine representations, but CLP also introduces a positional mismatch at each loop boundary. We instantiate this study by training LoopCoder-v2, a family of 7B PLT coders with different loop counts, from scratch on 18T tokens, followed by matched instruction tuning and evaluation. Empirically, the two-loop variant delivers broad gains over the non-looped baseline across code generation, code reasoning, agentic software engineering, and tool-use benchmarks, improving SWE-bench Verified from 43.0 to 64.4 points and Multi-SWE from 14.0 to 31.0 points. In contrast, variants with three or more loops regress, revealing a strongly non-monotonic loop-count effect. Our diagnostics show that loop 2 provides the main productive refinement, while later loops yield diminishing, oscillatory updates and reduced representational diversity. Because the CLP-induced mismatch remains roughly fixed as refinement gains shrink, the offset cost increasingly dominates. This gain--cost trade-off explains PLT's saturation at two loops and provides diagnostics for loop-count selection.

</details>


### [178] [Catastrophic Forgetting is Low-Rank: A Function-Space Theory for Continual Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18024)
*Ido Nitzan Hidekel,Dan Raviv*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Forgetting in continual learning is predictable in function space: under the NTK regime, the forgetting vector has a closed-form expression involving the cross-task kernel, concentrates in few NTK eigenmodes, and follows a Kronecker scaling rule for linear-head PEFT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing continual learning analyses focus on parameter drift, replay, or distillation, failing to identify which output-space directions are most vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. The authors aim to provide a function-space understanding of exactly where and why forgetting occurs.

Method: The authors derive a closed-form predictor for the forgetting vector (old-task prediction change) in the NTK regime, using the cross-task kernel between new and old task data. For frozen-backbone linear-head PEFT-CL, the predictor is exact; for nonlinear adapters or full fine-tuning, it is a local NTK approximation. Eigendecomposition of the old-task NTK reveals forgetting concentrates in a few dominant eigenmodes, and a Kronecker scaling rule characterizes the vulnerable rank under frozen linear heads.

Result: The forgetting vector is predictable before any gradient step; forgetting concentrates in a small number of old-task NTK eigenmodes; a Kronecker scaling rule governs the vulnerable rank for linear-head PEFT. The analysis explains why parameter-space regularizers can miss output-space interference and motivates a targeted spectral regularizer.

Conclusion: A function-space NTK-based account of forgetting provides precise, closed-form predictions of which output directions are vulnerable, unifies with prior NTK-overlap theory, exposes limitations of parameter-space regularization, and enables principled spectral regularization for continual learning.

Abstract: Catastrophic forgetting in continual adaptation is usually studied through parameter drift, replay, or distillation, but these views do not identify which output-space directions are vulnerable. We give a function-space account in the NTK regime: new-task training induces old-task prediction drift through the cross-task kernel, yielding a closed-form predictor for the forgetting vector before any new-task gradient step. In frozen-backbone linear-head PEFT-CL, where the model is linear in the trainable parameters, the predictor is exact up to numerical precision; for nonlinear adapters/full fine-tuning, it is a local NTK approximation. The same expression reveals that forgetting concentrates in a small number of old-task NTK eigenmodes and under frozen linear heads gives a Kronecker scaling rule for the vulnerable rank. These results clarify the relation to prior NTK-overlap theory, explain why parameter-space regularizers can miss output-space interference, and motivate a targeted spectral regularizer.

</details>


### [179] [ConTex: Reformulating Counterfactual Generation For Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18049)
*Jan Voets,Hasan Tercan,Tobias Meisen,Sebastian Baum*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ConTex reformulates counterfactual generation for time series forecasting as learning a globally consistent intervention strategy via a decomposed encoder-decoder architecture, achieving state-of-the-art validity, sparsity, and 12-36× speedup over instance-wise methods with ~7ms inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning-based time series forecasting models lack inherent interpretability and actionable guidance—specifically, they cannot indicate how input conditions should be modified to shift predictions toward desired outcomes. Existing counterfactual explanation methods rely on instance-wise optimization, causing inconsistency across instances, high computational cost, and infeasibility for real-time deployment.

Method: ConTex is a model-agnostic, decomposed architecture that learns a single shared function for generating counterfactuals. It consists of a temporal context encoder, a conditional encoder, and two output heads that capture interventions along two axes: temporal relevance (when to intervene) and modification strength (how much to modify). This enables globally consistent counterfactual generation in a single forward pass.

Result: ConTex achieves state-of-the-art validity with sparse counterfactuals (minimizing intervention count), reduces computational cost by at least 12–36× compared to instance-wise generation, and supports real-time inference at approximately 0.007 seconds per sample.

Conclusion: Learning a global intervention function for counterfactual generation in time series forecasting overcomes the instability, inconsistency, and latency of instance-wise optimization, making actionable, interpretable, and real-time explanations feasible across diverse forecasting architectures and datasets.

Abstract: Decision-making with deep learning-based time series forecasting requires not only accurate predictions but also actionable insights. However, current architectures do not inherently provide such information. Specifically, guidance is needed on how current conditions must be modified to shift from a predicted outcome to a desired future scenario. Counterfactual explanations provide a natural framework for this task, as they represent minimal input changes that alter the model's prediction, indicating when and how intervention is required. Existing approaches rely on instance-wise optimization, leading to inconsistency across instances, high computational costs, and limited applicability in real-time settings.
  To address these limitations, we reformulate counterfactual generation for time series forecasting as the problem of learning a globally consistent intervention strategy, allowing counterfactuals to be generated through a single shared function. We propose Counterfactual Time Series Explanations (ConTex), a model-agnostic, decomposed architecture comprising a temporal context encoder and a conditional encoder, followed by two heads that capture interventions in terms of temporal relevance and modification strength. This structure overcomes the instability and inconsistency of instance-based approaches by producing targeted, interpretable interventions across time and feature dimensions in a single forward pass, making it suitable for real-time applications.
  Across multiple forecasting architectures and benchmark datasets, ConTex achieves state-of-the-art validity while generating sparse counterfactuals that minimize the number of necessary interventions. Additionally, our approach reduces computational cost by at least 12-36x compared to instance-wise generation and supports real-time inference at approximately 0.007 seconds.

</details>


### [180] [NoiseTilt: Noise-Tilted Reverse Kernels for Diffusion Reward Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18066)
*Jisung Hwang,Yunhong Min,Jaihoon Kim,I-Chao Shen,Minhyuk Sung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NTRK is a reward-guided diffusion sampler that injects reward gradients through the noise term (not the mean), keeping the reverse kernel unchanged. A whitening operator makes gradient injection safe, achieving state-of-the-art reward alignment without quality loss, using 20× fewer sampling steps than baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reward-guided diffusion sampling methods face a fundamental trade-off: gradient-based guidance (which modifies the reverse mean) achieves high reward but pushes samples off the trained manifold, degrading quality; search-based methods preserve quality but lack gradient signal. No prior method simultaneously achieves both high reward alignment and preserved sample quality.

Method: NTRK keeps the pretrained reverse kernel (mean) unchanged and instead biases the noise term toward high reward by injecting the reward gradient into it. The key innovation is a whitening operator that transforms the reward gradient to be safe for noise injection — removing harmful correlations while preserving the guiding directional signal. This requires only a single sample per step (no search or optimization loops).

Result: Across multiple reward alignment tasks, NTRK outperforms recent state-of-the-art baselines without losing sample quality. On aesthetic generation, NTRK surpasses the best baseline's reward at 500 NFEs using only 25 NFEs — a 20× reduction in compute.

Conclusion: NTRK resolves the quality–reward trade-off in guided diffusion sampling by shifting gradient injection from the mean to the noise term, enabled by the whitening operator. It achieves superior reward alignment with dramatically lower compute, establishing a new state-of-the-art for inference-time reward-guided diffusion.

Abstract: We introduce the Noise-Tilted Reverse Kernel (NTRK), a reward-guided diffusion sampler that injects reward gradients through the noise term, leaving the pretrained reverse kernel unchanged and requiring only a single sample per step. Reward-guided sampling at inference time has greatly expanded the versatility of pretrained diffusion models. Yet existing methods face a trade-off. Gradient-based guidance shifts the reverse mean, steering generation but pushing intermediate states outside the region that the model was trained on and degrading quality. Search-based methods preserve quality but gain no gradient signal. No prior method achieves both. NTRK resolves this by keeping the reverse mean fixed and biasing the noise term toward high reward. We introduce a whitening operator, the central mechanism behind NTRK, that makes the reward gradient safe to inject as noise without losing its guiding signal. Across various reward alignment tasks, NTRK outperforms recent state-of-the-art baselines without losing sample quality. Remarkably, on aesthetic generation, NTRK surpasses the reward of the best baseline at 500 NFEs using only 25 NFEs, a 20$\times$ reduction in compute.

</details>


### [181] [Volterra Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18071)
*Yusen Jia,Bingyan Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Volterra generative models, a score-based diffusion framework replacing memoryless Brownian perturbations with path-dependent fractional noise governed by Volterra kernels. To handle the resulting non-Markovian, non-semimartingale dynamics, the authors construct finite-dimensional Markovian lifts via Gaussian quadrature and hybrid exponential approximations, derive error bounds, and address covariance/reverse-time degeneracies with stabilized conditioning and a Gaussian-bridge reconstruction sampler.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard score-based diffusion models rely on Brownian motion, yielding Markovian forward noising with no memory. Real-world processes often exhibit long-range dependence and path-dependent noise. The authors aim to extend score-based generative modeling to fractional (rough) volatility-type perturbations while maintaining tractable learning and sampling, without blowing up the state dimension.

Method: The forward SDE injects noise through a Volterra (fractional) kernel, producing non-Markovian, non-semimartingale dynamics. Two Markovian lifting strategies are developed: (1) Gaussian quadrature for both rough and smooth kernel regimes, and (2) a hybrid finite-difference exponential approximation in the smooth regime. These lifts yield an augmented linear-Gaussian forward process where learning stays data-dimensional by leveraging residual states and analytic auxiliary Gaussian scores. Covariance degeneracies from shared Brownian factors and signed smooth-regime weights are identified, motivating stabilized conditioning. For stiff larger lifts, a Gaussian-bridge reconstruction sampler is introduced.

Result: Squared error bounds are proved for the approximation schemes. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 demonstrate that persistent fractional perturbations with small Markovian lifts improve score-based generation on MNIST and offer a promising extension to natural images. The bridge sampler provides stability for larger lifts.

Conclusion: Volterra generative models successfully incorporate path-dependent (fractional) noise into score-based generative modeling. Small Markovian lifts suffice for improved generation, and the bridge sampler mitigates instability in larger lifts, opening a new direction for non-Markovian diffusion generative models.

Abstract: Score-based diffusion models typically use Brownian perturbations, which provide tractable reverse-time dynamics but impose memoryless noising. We introduce Volterra generative models, a continuous-time score-based framework whose forward process injects path-dependent noise through fractional kernels. To handle the non-Markovian and non-semimartingale dynamics, we construct finite-dimensional Markovian lifts using Gaussian quadrature in both regimes and a hybrid finite-difference exponential approximation in the smooth regime. We prove squared error bounds, derive an augmented linear-Gaussian forward process, and show that the learning can remain data-dimensional by considering residual states and analytic auxiliary Gaussian scores. We also identify covariance and reverse-time degeneracies caused by shared Brownian factors and signed smooth-regime weights. The degeneracy motivates stabilized conditioning and, for stiff larger lifts, a Gaussian-bridge reconstruction sampler. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 show that persistent fractional perturbations with small Markovian lifts can improve score-based generation on MNIST and provide a promising extension to natural images, while the bridge sampler provides a stability mechanism for larger lifts.

</details>


### [182] [Edge Flow: A Tractable and Predictive Continuous-Time Model for Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18080)
*Pierre Marion*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Edge Flow is a system of three coupled ODEs that models gradient descent at the Edge of Stability, decomposing dynamics into center flow, oscillation direction, and oscillation magnitude, with a self-stabilization feedback loop that resolves sharpness oscillations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical analysis tools (gradient flow, descent lemma) fail when gradient descent operates at the Edge of Stability (EoS), where the largest Hessian eigenvalue hovers near 2/η. Existing continuous-time EoS models cannot resolve the oscillation of sharpness at EoS onset, motivating a more faithful continuous-time model.

Method: The authors propose Edge Flow, a system of three coupled ODEs: (1) a center following modified gradient flow on a symmetrized loss, (2) an oscillation direction tracking a top Hessian eigenvector via Rayleigh quotient dynamics, and (3) an oscillation magnitude that grows/decays exponentially based on whether sharpness exceeds/falls below 2/η. Sharpness stabilization emerges via a self-stabilization feedback loop. Discretization requires only two gradient evaluations and one Hessian-vector product per iteration.

Result: Edge Flow tracks gradient descent dynamics at least as faithfully as prior continuous-time EoS models, while additionally resolving sharpness oscillation at EoS onset. It provides a principled framework for understanding and mitigating instabilities in this regime.

Conclusion: Edge Flow is a tractable, faithful, and predictive continuous-time model for gradient descent at the Edge of Stability, capturing key phenomena (sharpness oscillation, self-stabilization) that prior models miss, with practical discretization for empirical use.

Abstract: Gradient descent in deep learning may operate at the edge of stability (EoS), a regime in which the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian hovers near the stability threshold $2/η$, where $η$ is the learning rate. Classical analysis tools such as gradient flow and the descent lemma do not apply here, motivating the search for a continuous-time model valid at EoS. We propose Edge Flow, a system of three coupled ordinary differential equations that provides a tractable, faithful, and predictive model of gradient descent dynamics at EoS. Edge Flow decomposes the dynamics into a center, an oscillation direction, and an oscillation magnitude. The center follows a modified gradient flow on a symmetrized loss; the direction tracks a top eigenvector of the Hessian via Rayleigh quotient dynamics; and the magnitude grows or decays exponentially depending on whether the sharpness exceeds or falls below the threshold $2/η$. Crucially, sharpness stabilization emerges from the coupled dynamics via a self-stabilization feedback loop. Discretizing Edge Flow only requires two gradient evaluations and one Hessian--vector product at each iteration. We demonstrate empirically that Edge Flow tracks the dynamics of gradient descent at least as faithfully as previously proposed continuous-time EoS models, while in addition resolving the oscillation of the sharpness at the onset of EoS, and that it provides a principled framework for understanding and mitigating instabilities in this regime.

</details>


### [183] [From Reasoning Traces to Reusable Modules: Understanding Compositional Generalization in Language Model Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18089)
*Lingjing Kong,Xin Liu,Guangyi Chen,Martin Q. Ma,Xiangchen Song,Yuekai Sun,Mikhail Yurochkin,Taylor W. Killian,Ruslan Salakhutdinov,Kun Zhang,Eric P. Xing,Zhengzhong Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper argues that the success of SFT+RL pipelines for LLM reasoning stems from compositional generalization. SFT provides compound reasoning traces containing reusable atomic modules (skills and routing mechanisms), while RL decomposes these traces to identify and recombine the latent modules, enabling generalization to novel configurations. Training on compound traces outperforms training on isolated atomic modules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explain why the combination of SFT and RL is so effective for transforming LLMs into strong reasoners, and to formalize the asymmetric, complementary roles these two stages play through the lens of compositional generalization.

Method: The authors propose a hierarchical latent selection model where reasoning traces are generated by cascading discrete latent variables representing atomic modules (skills and routing mechanisms). They theoretically analyze how SFT supplies module materials and RL decomposes traces to identify latent modules. Controlled experiments are designed to validate the theory.

Result: RL successfully extracts atomic modules from SFT-supplied compound traces and recombines them for new configurations. Training on compound traces yields stronger generalization than training on isolated atomic modules. An effective protocol is identified: SFT ensures coverage of all atomic modules via compositional traces, while RL targets novel compositions outside the SFT support.

Conclusion: SFT and RL play asymmetric, complementary roles: SFT supplies raw module materials through compositional traces, and RL decomposes those traces to extract reusable atomic modules, enabling compositional generalization. This framework explains the synergistic success of SFT+RL pipelines for reasoning.

Abstract: Post-training pipelines that combine supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL) have emerged as the key recipe for transforming large language models (LLMs) into robust reasoners. We argue that this combined success is driven by compositional generalization, which we formalize through a hierarchical latent selection model. In this framework, reasoning traces are generated by a cascade of discrete latent selection variables corresponding to reusable atomic modules, including both skills (local operations) and routing mechanisms (how intermediate information is selected, reused, and composed). Within this model, we theoretically show that SFT and RL play asymmetric, complementary roles: SFT supplies the raw module materials in compositional traces, and RL decomposes those traces to identify the latent atomic modules and enable compositional generalization. We design controlled experiments to validate this theory. Our results demonstrate that RL can extract atomic modules from compound traces supplied by SFT and recombine them to solve new configurations. Moreover, we find that training on compound traces yields stronger generalization than training on isolated atomic modules. Finally, we investigate the relationship between SFT and RL data and identify an effective protocol in which SFT ensures coverage of all atomic modules through compositional traces, while RL focuses on novel compositions outside the SFT support to drive exploration.

</details>


### [184] [S4oP: Operator-level Pruning of Structured State Space Models for Resource-Constrained Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18096)
*Marco Deano,Filippo Ziche,Nicola Bombieri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces the first structured operator-level pruning method for S4/S4D state space models, achieving up to 70% operator reduction with preserved performance and substantially lower inference latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: S4 and S4D architectures excel at long-range sequence modeling but suffer from high computational and memory demands, limiting deployment in resource-constrained settings. No prior work has explored structured pruning specifically for SSM operators.

Method: An incremental, operator-level pruning approach that interleaves structured masking with fine-tuning in a unified training/evaluation framework. The method progressively prunes SSM operators while jointly monitoring accuracy and inference latency to systematically explore efficiency-accuracy trade-offs.

Result: Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that pruning up to 70% of model operators preserves original performance in most cases while substantially reducing inference latency.

Conclusion: Structured operator pruning is an effective, previously unexplored strategy for improving SSM efficiency, facilitating deployment in practical resource-constrained scenarios.

Abstract: Structured State Space Models (SSMs), including the S4 and S4D architectures, have recently emerged as powerful alternatives to attention-based models for capturing long-range dependencies in sequential data. Despite their strong empirical performance, deploying these models in time- and resource-constrained settings remains challenging due to their computational and memory demands. In this paper, we propose a novel incremental, operator-level pruning approach for S4- and S4D-based models that significantly reduces inference cost while preserving predictive performance. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to systematically investigate structured operator pruning for SSMs. Our method progressively prunes model operators by interleaving structured masking with fine-tuning, while jointly monitoring accuracy and inference latency. We implement this approach within a unified training and evaluation framework that enables systematic exploration of efficiency-accuracy trade-offs. Experiments across multiple benchmark datasets show that pruning up to 70% of the model operators preserves the performance of the original models in most cases, while substantially reducing inference latency. These results demonstrate that structured operator pruning is an effective and previously unexplored strategy for improving the efficiency of SSMs and facilitate their deployment in practical, resource-constrained scenarios.

</details>


### [185] [Deep Reinforcement Learning for Minimum Zero-Forcing Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18106)
*Steve Halley,Maurício Gruppi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes SD-ZFS, a reinforcement learning framework adapted from S2V-DQN, to solve the NP-hard minimum zero-forcing set problem on undirected graphs, and evaluates its generalization, scalability, and transferability across diverse graph structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The minimum zero-forcing set (ZFS) problem has broad applications in network science, network control, and logic circuit design, but finding the optimal solution is NP-hard. Existing exact methods are computationally intractable for large graphs, motivating the exploration of machine learning approaches that can learn effective heuristics.

Method: The authors propose SD-ZFS, a reinforcement learning framework that adapts the Structure2Vec Deep Q-Network (S2V-DQN) architecture to the ZFS problem. The framework learns to sequentially select nodes for the zero-forcing set. Models are trained and evaluated on graph datasets with varying structural properties to assess generalization, scalability, and transferability.

Result: SD-ZFS demonstrates effectiveness compared to both the optimal solution (on small graphs) and greedy heuristics. The framework shows promising generalization to unseen graph types, scales to larger graphs, and transfers across different network structures.

Conclusion: The adapted S2V-DQN framework provides a viable machine-learning approach to the minimum ZFS problem, offering insights into how network structure influences solution quality and demonstrating that learned policies can outperform greedy baselines while approaching optimality.

Abstract: This paper explores the problem of finding the minimum zero-forcing set on undirected graphs and proposes an adapted machine-learning framework to solve the problem. The minimum zero-forcing set problem is a graph coloring problem where the color of an initial set of nodes propagates throughout a network. The set of nodes is zero-forcing if it forces all uncolored nodes to change color under the constraint of the color-change rule. There are several applications to this problem across different domains such as network science, network control, and designing logical circuits. Finding the minimum zero-forcing set is shown to be NP-hard. We propose a reinforcement learning framework, SD-ZFS, that adapts the S2V-DQN architecture to the ZFS problem. We train several models on this adapted framework and analyze the performance across graph datasets that have varying structures. We evaluate how the models trained on the framework generalize, scale, and transfer to different network types. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework when compared against the optimal solution and greedy heuristic. We provide further insight into how the ZFS problem can be solved through machine-learning and the influence of network structure on the problem.

</details>


### [186] [Learning Fair Pareto-Optimal Policies in Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18111)
*Umer Siddique,Peilang Li,Yongcan Cao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formalizes fair multi-policy MORL, showing that for concave piecewise-linear welfare functions (like GGF), fair policies lie in the convex coverage set. It proposes non-stationary and stochastic policy augmentations with accrued reward histories to dynamically address inequities, and introduces three novel algorithms integrating GGF with multi-policy MOQL, demonstrating empirically that they learn diverse, fair policies across user preferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-policy MORL methods using welfare functions like GGF can learn fair policies for fixed user preferences, but they cannot provide the diverse set of policies needed when user preferences are dynamic or unknown. There is a gap in formalizing and solving the fair optimization problem in the multi-policy MORL setting.

Method: The authors (1) prove that for concave, piecewise-linear welfare functions such as GGF, fair policies reside in the convex coverage set (CCS), an approximated Pareto front from linear scalarization; (2) show that non-stationary policies augmented with accrued reward histories and stochastic policies improve fairness by adapting to historical inequities; (3) propose three novel algorithms: GGF-integrated multi-policy MOQL, state-augmented multi-policy MOQL for non-stationary policies, and a stochastic policy extension.

Result: Empirical evaluations across various domains demonstrate that the proposed methods learn a set of fair policies accommodating different user preferences, outperforming or comparing favorably against state-of-the-art MORL baselines.

Conclusion: The paper successfully bridges fair optimization and multi-policy MORL by establishing theoretical grounding (fair policies in CCS) and providing practical algorithms. Non-stationary and stochastic policies with history augmentation are effective mechanisms for dynamic fairness, enabling a diverse Pareto-optimal policy set for unknown or shifting user preferences.

Abstract: Fairness is an important aspect of decision-making in multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL), where policies must ensure both optimality and equity across multiple, potentially conflicting objectives. While single-policy MORL methods can learn fair policies for fixed user preferences using welfare functions such as the generalized Gini welfare function (GGF), they fail to provide the diverse set of policies necessary for dynamic or unknown user preferences. To address this limitation, we formalize the fair optimization problem in multi-policy MORL, where the goal is to learn a set of Pareto-optimal policies that ensure fairness across all possible user preferences. Our key technical contributions are threefold: (1) We show that for concave, piecewise-linear welfare functions (e.g., GGF), fair policies remain in the convex coverage set (CCS), which is an approximated Pareto front for linear scalarization. (2) We demonstrate that non-stationary policies, augmented with accrued reward histories, and stochastic policies improve fairness by dynamically adapting to historical inequities. (3) We propose three novel algorithms, which include integrating GGF with multi-policy multi-objective Q-Learning (MOQL), state-augmented multi-policy MOQL for learning non-statoinary policies, and its novel extension for learning stochastic policies. We evaluate our algorithms across various domains and compare our methods against the state-of-the-art MORL baselines. The empirical results show that our methods learn a set of fair policies that accommodate different user preferences.

</details>


### [187] [Ternary Mamba: Grouped Quantization-Aware Training of W1.58A16 State Space Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18114)
*Ramprasath Ganesaraja,Sahil Dilip Panse,Swathika N*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Pretrained Mamba-2 can be ternary-quantized via grouped QAT with knowledge distillation in just 102M tokens, achieving competitive accuracy while reducing memory 3.61×, without expensive from-scratch training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SSMs like Mamba-2 offer linear-time inference but are memory-heavy for edge deployment. Previous ternary SSM work required costly from-scratch training on 150B tokens; this paper asks whether a pretrained checkpoint can serve as a sufficient starting point, dramatically reducing the data budget.

Method: Grouped quantization-aware training (QAT) with knowledge distillation from a frozen FP16 teacher is applied to a pretrained Mamba-2 1.3B checkpoint. Only 102M tokens are used for fine-tuning (4 GPU-hours on a single H100), achieving 3.61× compression (2,687 to 744 MB).

Result: The method achieves 48.1% zero-shot accuracy (7-task average), closely matching Bi-Mamba's 48.4% (within ±0.9pp CI). A novel instability termed "zero-ratio collapse" is identified, caused by learnable quantization scales in the QAT-from-pretrained setting. Additionally, Transformer post-hoc correction strategies fail for SSMs due to error accumulation through recurrence.

Conclusion: Ternary SSMs do not require expensive from-scratch training; QAT from pretrained checkpoints with knowledge distillation is a data-efficient alternative, reducing token budget by ~1,000×.

Abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) such as Mamba-2 offer linear-time inference but their memory footprint limits edge deployment. Prior ternary SSM work (Slender-Mamba) trains from scratch on 150B tokens; we show a pretrained checkpoint suffices, reducing the marginal token budget by 1,000x. Using grouped quantization-aware training (QAT) with knowledge distillation from a frozen FP16 teacher, we compress Mamba-2 1.3B to 3.61x (2,687 to 744 MB) and achieve 48.1% zero-shot accuracy (7-task average) in just 102M tokens (4 GPU-hours, single H100) -- approaching Bi-Mamba's 48.4% (within +/-0.9pp CI). This QAT-from-pretrained setting reveals zero-ratio collapse, a novel instability caused by learnable quantization scales that does not arise in from-scratch training. We further show that post-hoc correction strategies effective for Transformers fail for SSMs due to error accumulation through the recurrence. These results demonstrate that ternary SSMs do not require expensive from-scratch training: QAT from pretrained checkpoints with KD is a data-efficient alternative.

</details>


### [188] [Embedded Machine Learning for Microcontroller-Class Edge Devices: Data, Feature, Evaluation, and Deployment Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18122)
*Mostafa Darvishi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A systems-oriented synthesis of embedded machine learning workflows for microcontrollers, covering the full pipeline from data acquisition to streaming deployment, illustrated through inertial motion recognition and keyword spotting case studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embedded ML shifts inference to resource-constrained devices, but existing ML introductions often obscure critical systems-engineering decisions. The paper aims to surface these hidden design choices specific to microcontroller-class platforms.

Method: A workflow synthesis spanning: sampling and buffering strategies, feature extraction as dimensionality reduction (e.g., RMS and spectral features for accelerometer data; MFCCs for audio), validation under class imbalance, model/runtime co-design, and streaming deployment. Two signal families serve as running examples: inertial motion recognition using 2-second 3-axis accelerometer windows, and keyword spotting using 1D convolutional networks on MFCC-processed, anti-aliased audio.

Result: The paper derives practical design rules for robust on-device inference, covering data curation, quantization, thresholding, scheduling, and field monitoring.

Conclusion: Successful embedded ML on microcontrollers demands holistic co-design across the entire workflow—from signal acquisition through deployment—rather than treating the model in isolation.

Abstract: Embedded machine learning moves inference from cloud services to resource-constrained devices that must acquire data, preprocess signals, run a model, and act within tight limits on memory, energy, and latency. This paper presents a systems-oriented synthesis of an embedded machine-learning workflow for microcontroller-class platforms. The emphasis is placed on engineering decisions that are often hidden in generic machine-learning introductions: sampling and buffering, feature extraction as dimensionality reduction, validation under class imbalance, model/runtime co-design, and streaming deployment. Two representative signal families are used throughout the paper. The first is inertial motion recognition, where a two-second, three-axis accelerometer window is transformed from raw samples into root-mean-square and spectral features before classification. The second is keyword spotting, where audio is sampled, anti-aliased, transformed into mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, and processed by a compact one-dimensional convolutional network.
