The paper concludes with practical design rules for robust on-device inference, including data curation, quantization, thresholding, scheduling, and field monitoring.

</details>


### [189] [Kolmogorov Regression for Robust Diffusion Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18186)
*Lekan Molu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper replaces stochastic score matching in diffusion policies with a deterministic boundary-value PDE based on the backward Kolmogorov equation in Cameron-Martin space, yielding convergence guarantees, improved trajectory regularity, and a reward-free failure detector. Validated on robotic manipulation (PushT) and manufacturing line control (CONWIP), it achieves significant gains in reward, drift reduction, RMSE, and deadlock prevention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Finite-dimensional diffusion policies suffer from temporal drift due to discretization artifacts, which degrades long-horizon deployment performance on physical systems. The authors aim to resolve this by reformulating diffusion policy training as a deterministic PDE problem with theoretical regularity and convergence guarantees.

Method: The method lifts diffusion policies into a Cameron-Martin space (a subset of Hilbert space) using the backward Kolmogorov equation, converting stochastic score matching into a deterministic boundary-value PDE. A Gaussian measure framework is employed where the diffusion noise covariance is derived from a colored noise distribution, imposing regularity on samples. Training uses a precision-weighted Cameron-Martin loss, and a Kolmogorov residual serves as a PDE diagnostic (failure detector) at inference. Convergence bounds depend on the effective kernel rank rather than action dimension. Policies are certified via Hamilton-Jacobi reachability theory.

Result: On PushT manipulation: 17% improvement in max episode reward (0.95 vs 0.78 MSE baseline), 67.6% reduction in inter-step drift via residual magnitude. On CONWIP manufacturing: 28.4% lower RMSE vs LSTM baselines, starvation recall of 1.0, Precision@1 of 1.0 for bottleneck identification, 13× signal-to-noise ratio. Hamilton-Jacobi reachability certification reduced deadlock events by 96% (351 events prevented over 100 simulated runs).

Conclusion: The proposed Cameron-Martin reformulation of diffusion policies effectively eliminates discretization-induced drift, provides formal convergence guarantees, enables deterministic failure detection without reward signals, and generalizes across both robotic manipulation and industrial manufacturing control domains with substantial practical improvements.

Abstract: Finite-dimensional (FD) diffusion policies exhibit temporal drift owing to discretization artifacts that degrade long-horizon performance (when deployed on physical systems). We introduce a backward Kolmogorov equation that lifts diffusion policies to a Cameron-Martin space -- a subset of the Hilbert space. Essentially, replacing stochastic score matching with a deterministic boundary-value PDE problem. Our core innovation thrives on Gaussian measure theory whereupon the diffusion noise covariance operator is realized from a colored noise distribution which prescribes a notion of regularity on samples from the model at inference time. We train the diffusion model with a derived precision-weighted Cameron- Martin loss and a Kolmogorov residual is introduced as a PDE diagnostic during inference. These substitutions yield (i) convergence guarantees where the bound's constants depend on the effective rank of the kernel rather than action dimension, (ii) improved trajectory regularity via spectral weighting, and (iii) a deterministic failure detector without reward signals. Validation across two application domains demonstrates substantial improvements: on the PushT manipulation benchmark, the Cameron-Martin loss achieves a 17% improvement in maximum episode reward (0.95 vs. 0.78 for MSE) and 67.6% reduction in inter-step drifts during inference via the introduced residual magnitude. Similarly, on a 6-station manufacturing line with constant work-in-process (CONWIP) flow control, we achieve 28.4% lower RMSE than classical LSTM baselines; a high starvation-event recall (1.0 in test cycles), and effective bottleneck identification (Precision@1 = 1.0 in test set, 13x signal-to-noise ratio). We then certify the dispatch policies with Hamilton-Jacobi reachability theory which reduces deadlock events by 96% compared to uncontrolled dispatch over 100 simulated runs (351 events prevented).

</details>


### [190] [Rethinking Dataset Distillation for Classification: Do Distilled Sets Outperform Coresets?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18209)
*Trisha Mittal,Akshay Mehra,Joshua Kimball*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A large-scale empirical study revealing that state-of-the-art dataset distillation methods offer limited practical advantages over simpler coreset selection baselines on ImageNet-scale datasets, often performing comparably or worse while incurring substantially higher construction costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dataset distillation research suffers from inconsistent evaluation protocols that conflate distillation quality with training recipe choices. Furthermore, claims that DD outperforms coreset selection rest on untested assumptions about the expressiveness limits of real-sample subsets. The authors seek to isolate the intrinsic effectiveness of distilled data through standardized, large-scale benchmarking.

Method: The authors benchmark seven SOTA DD methods (including MTT, DM, IDM, SRe2L, etc.) on ImageNet-1K, ImageNet-100, and ImageNette under three standardized training protocols (standard ERM, single-teacher, multi-teacher). They compare against three coreset selection strategies (random, herding, k-center) using uniform evaluation settings. Beyond accuracy, they assess representativeness, diversity, and distributional coverage of the condensed sets.

Result: Several DD methods fail to beat random subset baselines. The best DD approaches are at best comparable to or worse than coresets on large-scale datasets, with dramatically higher construction cost (orders of magnitude). Coresets consistently achieve better coverage of the original data distribution in terms of representativeness and diversity metrics.

Conclusion: Current DD methods offer limited practical advantages over coreset selection for data-centric learning, especially at scale. Coresets remain a competitive, computationally efficient alternative. The field needs standardized evaluation protocols and greater scrutiny of cost-effectiveness.

Abstract: Dataset distillation (DD) has emerged as a prominent approach in data centric machine learning, aiming to synthesize compact training sets for efficient training by compressing the information in large datasets into a small number of synthetic samples. However, DD methods are often evaluated under inconsistent evaluation protocols, ranging from standard ERM to single/multi-teacher supervision, making it difficult to isolate the effectiveness of distilled data from evaluation. Moreover, many prior methods claim that DD outperforms data pruning approaches such as coreset selection (CS), based on the assumption that restricting condensed datasets to subsets of real samples fundamentally limits their expressiveness. In this work, we critically evaluate DD methods through large-scale experiments using standardized datasets and evaluation protocols to assess their intrinsic effectiveness. We benchmark seven state-of-the-art (SOTA) DD methods on ImageNet-1K, ImageNet100, and ImageNette, using three widely adopted training protocols against three CS strategies. Our results show that while some DD methods fail to outperform even simple random subsets, the SOTA DD approaches are comparable to or worse than coresets on large-scale datasets and incur a substantially higher cost for construction. Beyond accuracy, we also evaluate the representativeness, diversity, and quality of condensed sets, and find that coresets consistently achieve better coverage of the original data distribution. These findings highlight the limited practical advantages of current DD methods and show that coresets remain competitive and are often a more computationally efficient alternative for data-centric learning.

</details>


### [191] [Sign-Rank, Index, and List Replicability: Connections and Separations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18236)
*Ari Blondal,Hamed Hatami,Pooya Hatami,Chavdar Lalov,Sivan Tretiak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper establishes a hierarchy among lower-bound measures for sign rank: the Z₂-index is linearly bounded by the list replicability number, yielding a strong separation between sign rank and Z₂-index. It then studies list replicability thoroughly, providing upper bounds via height and minimum star number, and proving a composition theorem for products of concept classes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lower bounds on sign rank are notoriously difficult to obtain. Recent work introduced two more tractable surrogate measures—the Z₂-index and the list replicability number—but their relationship and relative strength were poorly understood. Resolving a question by Frick, Hosseini, and Vasileuski about whether these measures are equivalent or separable drives the investigation.

Method: The authors order the two surrogate measures by proving that the Z₂-index is upper-bounded by a linear function of the list replicability number. This yields a strong separation between sign rank and Z₂-index. They then conduct a combinatorial study of list replicability, establishing upper bounds via height and minimum star number, and proving a composition result: the list replicability number of a product class is at most the sum of those of the factors.

Result: Key results: (1) Z₂-index ≤ O(list replicability number), implying a strong separation between sign rank and Z₂-index. (2) Upper bounds on list replicability via height and minimum star number. (3) A composition theorem: for concept classes C₁, C₂, the list replicability number of C₁ × C₂ is bounded by the sum of their individual list replicability numbers.

Conclusion: List replicability is the stronger lower-bounding measure for sign rank among the two surrogates. The separation result resolves an open question and motivates deeper study of list replicability as a combinatorial parameter in its own right, with height, star number, and product behavior providing structural insight.

Abstract: In learning theory, the sign rank of a binary concept class captures the smallest dimension in which it can be represented by points and halfspaces. Despite tremendous interest, lower bounds on sign rank are notoriously difficult to come by. Two recent approaches to the problem establish lower bounds on sign rank by measures that are easier to analyze: the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-index and the list replicability number.
  We order these measures, showing that the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-index is upper-bounded by a linear function of the list replicability number. As a main consequence, we obtain a strong separation between sign rank and $\mathbb{Z}_2$-index, thereby resolving a question of Frick, Hosseini, and Vasileuski.
  This motivates a thorough study of list replicability, the stronger of the two lower-bounding measures. We establish upper bounds on the list replicability number by two combinatorial measures: height and minimum star number. We also prove a fundamental composition result, showing that the product of two concept classes has list replicability number bounded by the sum of the list replicability numbers of the two classes.

</details>

### [192] [Security and Human-Centered Assessment of BACnet-Controlled DALI Infrastructure in an Educational Building Automation Testbed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17089)
*Ariton Verush*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A case study documenting BACnet/IP and DALI building automation exploration during a 2026 cybersecurity hackathon, emphasizing that effective BACS security assessment requires not only protocol analysis but also usable tools, physical observability, interpretable naming, and safe mental models for command priorities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building automation and control systems (BACS) create complex cyber-physical environments that are difficult to inspect, secure, and explain to new analysts. The work is motivated by the gap between protocol-level security analysis and the human-centered, educational, and physical-world dimensions of understanding these systems.

Method: The study employs four complementary approaches: (1) network-oriented enumeration of BACnet services, (2) object-level inspection to reconstruct structured object hierarchies, (3) physical rack analysis to map BACnet objects to DALI group-level lighting infrastructure, and (4) reflective HCI analysis of tool-supported learning using Yabe and BACteria, conducted within a domotics-oriented hackathon setting.

Result: The work documents observable BACnet services, reconstructs structured object hierarchies, identifies room-level lighting-control paths, and successfully maps BACnet objects to DALI group-level infrastructure. The reflective analysis reveals that usable tool interfaces, physical observability, interpretable naming conventions, and safe mental models for command priorities are critical for effective BACS assessment.

Conclusion: BACS security assessment is not merely a technical protocol task; it requires human-centered tooling and educational approaches. The paper contributes implications for cybersecurity education, human-centered security tool design, and responsible experimentation practices in cyber-physical building environments.

Abstract: Building automation and control systems integrate heating, ventilation, air conditioning, lighting, sensing, and management functions through specialized communication protocols. While this integration enables flexible building operation, it also creates complex cyber-physical environments that are difficult to inspect, secure, and explain to new analysts. This paper presents a practical security and human-centered case study of a BACnet/IP building automation testbed with DALI lighting infrastructure, investigated during a domotics-oriented cybersecurity hackathon in Thun, Switzerland in April 2026. The study combines network-oriented enumeration, object-level inspection, physical rack analysis, and reflective HCI analysis of tool-supported learning. Using Yabe and BACteria, the work documents observable BACnet services, reconstructs structured object hierarchies, identifies room-level lighting-control paths, and maps BACnet objects to DALI group-level infrastructure. The analysis emphasizes that BACS assessment is not only a technical protocol task: it also requires usable tool interfaces, physical observability, interpretable naming conventions, and safe mental models for command priorities. The paper contributes a compact case study of BACnet/DALI exploration in an educational testbed and discusses implications for cybersecurity education, human-centered security tooling, and responsible experimentation in cyber-physical building environments.

</details>


### [193] [Securing Multi-Agent GIS Systems: Risk Evaluation and Prompt Hardening Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17092)
*Kyle Gao,Pranavi Kotta,Linlin Xu,Jonathan Li,David A. Clausi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A security framework for multi-agent GIS systems is proposed, featuring modular orchestration, red-teaming with an adaptive attacker LLM, and prompt optimization via structured signatures with adversarial demonstrations to enhance resilience without compromising task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As agentic systems integrate with GIS for conversational and spatial analysis, multi-agent coordination introduces security vulnerabilities. Existing approaches lack systematic methods for risk identification, evaluation, and mitigation tailored to multi-agent geospatial contexts while preserving generalizability to broader agentic architectures.

Method: The authors develop a modular state-machine-based orchestration framework that abstracts agent behavior into reusable components. Security evaluation employs a red-teaming framework featuring an adaptive attacker LLM and a deterministic judge LLM that generates binary outcomes with rationales across multi-turn attack scenarios. For mitigation, a prompt optimization framework treats prompts as structured signatures and injects adversarial demonstrations to systematically harden the system.

Result: The framework is tested on a commercial geospatial partner's agentic system. The red-teaming approach effectively identifies vulnerabilities through multi-turn attacks with deterministic, rationale-supported judgments. The prompt optimization framework improves security resilience without degrading task performance.

Conclusion: Modular orchestration combined with adaptive red-teaming and signature-based prompt optimization provides an effective, generalizable security framework for multi-agent GIS systems, balancing robustness with functional performance.

Abstract: Agentic systems are increasingly integrated with geographic information systems (GIS), where multi-agent coordination enables complex conversational and spatial analysis but introduces security risks. This work presents a security-oriented framework for risk identification, evaluation, and mitigation in a multi-agent GIS system while maintaining adaptability to broader agentic architectures. We test the agentic system of a commercial geospatial partner while developing a modular state-machine-based orchestration framework that abstracts agent behavior into reusable components. We evaluate robustness using a red-teaming framework with an adaptive attacker LLM and a deterministic judge that produces binary outcomes with supporting rationales across multi-turn attacks. We further improve resilience with a prompt optimization framework that treats prompts as structured signatures and injects adversarial demonstrations, enabling systematic security improvements without degrading task performance.

</details>


### [194] [Timestamp-Aware Spatio-Temporal Graph Contrastive Learning for Network Intrusion Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17109)
*Jianli Dai,Guangwei Wu,Jiacheng Li,Weiping Wang,An He,Xinjun Xiao*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A self-supervised GNN framework for network intrusion detection that leverages real timestamps via temporal graphs, E-GraphSAGE + LSTM encoding, and multi-view graph contrastive learning (temporal, spatial, feature contrasts) with adaptive loss weighting, achieving state-of-the-art performance comparable to supervised methods while remaining computationally efficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GNN-based NIDS methods treat traffic flows as temporally independent and rely on supervised/semi-supervised learning, limiting their ability to handle evolving attacks and generalize to unseen threats. Real temporal dependencies remain underexploited in self-supervised GNN-NIDS.

Method: (1) Temporal graph construction from flows using real timestamps; (2) E-GraphSAGE + LSTM encoder for joint spatial-temporal feature extraction without expensive attention; (3) Multi-view GCL with three contrast types: temporal contrast (captures temporal continuity), spatial contrast (preserves structural consistency), and feature contrast (improves generalization/robustness); (4) Gradient-norm-based adaptive weighting to balance contrastive loss components.

Result: The method significantly outperforms existing self-supervised approaches and achieves performance comparable to the supervised state-of-the-art GNN method on four representative NIDS datasets with real timestamps, while maintaining high computational efficiency.

Conclusion: Self-supervised GNN-based NIDS with explicit temporal modeling and multi-view GCL can match supervised SOTA performance without requiring labeled attack data, offering a practical and efficient solution for detecting both known and unseen network attacks.

Abstract: Given their effectiveness in modeling the relational structure among network traffic flows, graph neural networks (GNNs) have been widely adopted in network intrusion detection systems (NIDSs). However, most existing GNN-based NIDS approaches focus on the relational structure of traffic flows, and treat them as temporally independent, which limits their ability to cope with evolving attack behaviors. Moreover, their reliance on supervised or semi-supervised learning often restricts generalization to unseen attacks. To address these limitations, we propose a novel self-supervised GNN-based framework. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed model is among the first self-supervised GNN-based NIDS models to explicitly leverage real timestamps, which provides faithful temporal dependencies for representation learning. We first construct a series of temporal graphs from network traffic flows according to their timestamps, and then employ an E-GraphSAGE and LSTM based encoder to fully extract temporal information and spatial dependencies of network traffic, without introducing time-costly attention mechanisms. A multi-view graph contrastive learning (GCL) scheme is introduced, where temporal, spatial, and feature contrasts are jointly performed to capture temporal continuity, preserve structural consistency, and improve the generalization and robustness of the learned representations, respectively. In addition, a gradient-norm-based adaptive weighting strategy is designed to optimize the contrastive loss weights. Experimental results on four representative NIDS datasets with real timestamps demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing self-supervised approaches and achieves performance comparable to the supervised state-of-the-art GNN method, while maintaining high computational efficiency.

</details>


### [195] [Loss Landscape Poisoning: Targeted Extraction of Unseen Training Data from LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17110)
*Md Abdullah Al Mamun,Ngoc Phu Doan,Pedram Zaree,Ihsen Alouani,Nael Abu-Ghazaleh*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that an attacker who can poison training data can induce leakage of a separate target record they cannot access. The attack works by reshaping the loss landscape to create a sharp local minimum at the target, forcing memorization. It succeeds across language (up to 100%) and vision-language models (up to 90%), and a new variant bypasses even differential privacy defenses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs trained on private/sensitive data face extraction attack risks. Prior work focused on direct access or inference attacks; the authors ask a novel question: can poisoning a portion of training data facilitate leakage of a separate, inaccessible target record? This represents an underexplored indirect attack vector where the attacker lacks direct access to the target but can influence training.

Method: The core mechanism is loss-landscape poisoning: the attacker crafts poisoned training samples that create a sharp local minimum at the target completion while elevating loss on nearby alternatives. This forces the model to memorize the target as the unique low-loss solution in its neighborhood. The attack requires no architectural modifications and generalizes across centralized and federated learning. A secondary contribution is a probing attack that directly interrogates the loss landscape to infer target information, bypassing DP defenses.

Result: The attack achieves up to 100% successful extraction on language models and up to 90% on vision-language models. Differential privacy training thwarts the primary poisoning attack, but the authors introduce a new loss-landscape probing attack that circumvents DP protections.

Conclusion: Training-data poisoning can be weaponized to leak specific target records without direct access, exposing a serious privacy vulnerability in ML training pipelines. Even differential privacy—considered a gold standard—can be partially bypassed via loss-landscape probing, suggesting the need for stronger or complementary defenses.

Abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly trained on proprietary or sensitive data, from private healthcare and financial records to user conversations containing secrets. Ensuring the privacy of such data against extraction attacks has become a central concern. In this paper, we ask whether an attacker who can poison a portion of the training data can facilitate the leakage of a separate target record they have no access to. We answer in the affirmative and show that such leakage can be induced by a poisoning mechanism that reshapes the model's local loss landscape around the target completion. Our key insight is that poisoning to create a sharp loss minimum at the target, surrounded by elevated loss on nearby alternatives, forces the model to memorize the target as the unique low-loss solution in its neighborhood. The attack requires no architectural changes, and generalizes across centralized and federated learning settings. We demonstrate that the attack amplifies privacy leakage across language (up to 100% successful extraction), and vision-language models (up 90% successful extraction). We show that the attack is thwarted when the model is trained to be differentially private. However, we introduce a new attack that directly probes the loss landscape bypassing even differential privacy defenses.

</details>


### [196] [Fractional Verkle Trees: A Hypertree Decomposition and Verified Proof Serialization Architecture for High-Performance Blockchain State Accumulators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17111)
*Ekleen Kaur,Everton Fraga*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Fractional Verkle Trees (FVT) decompose global state into N independent sub-accumulators coordinated by a Merkle tree, achieving 5000x faster root recomputation (91 μs vs ~500 ms), 57% heap allocation reduction, and elimination of 4.85 PB/year network-wide bandwidth. Four critical inefficiencies in go-verkle are patched: phantom nodes, bloated LSM keys, redundant copies, and non-deterministic serialization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ethereum's transition to Verkle Trees for stateless operation faces critical implementation bottlenecks in the go-verkle reference that burden home validators. Verkle Trees reduce proof sizes from O(width * depth) to O(depth), but the current implementation introduces pathological behaviors including excessive memory allocation, I/O amplification from LSM-tree compaction, and non-deterministic wire formats. These inefficiencies undermine the scalability goals of Ethereum's stateless roadmap.

Method: The authors propose Fractional Verkle Trees (FVT), which partition global state into N independent sub-accumulators under a Merkle commitment tree. This hypertree decomposition yields: (1) improved cache locality; (2) zero-lock-contention goroutine-parallel commitment computation; (3) fast root recomputation at 91 μs. Four concrete patches address go-verkle inefficiencies: existence checks eliminate phantom nodes on non-existent account deletion; 32-byte SHA256 node references replace 64-byte keys to reduce LSM compaction; zero-copy reference-counted buffers eliminate redundant deserialization copying; and HashMap-based lexicographic deduplication fixes Proof of Absence wire format non-determinism.

Result: Benchmarks on Apple M1 Pro demonstrate: 57% heap allocation reduction (566,760 → 242,004 bytes per 10K proofs); parallel insertion at 2,433 ns/op; network-wide elimination of 4.85 PB/year bandwidth across 6,000 full nodes. Root recomputation is ~5000x faster (91 μs vs ~500 ms).

Conclusion: FVT and its accompanying patches directly advance the Ethereum stateless roadmap by making Verkle Tree commitment computation practical for home validators, eliminating memory bloat, I/O amplification, and serialization non-determinism. The decomposition approach provides a scalable path toward production-grade stateless Ethereum clients.

Abstract: Modern blockchain state management faces a critical scalability bottleneck: maintaining cryptographic commitments over hundreds of millions of entries becomes computationally prohibitive. Ethereum's transition to Verkle Trees: polynomial commitment accumulators reducing proof sizes from O(width * depth) to O(depth) via constant-size IPA vector commitments, is a critical step toward stateless operation. Yet, current implementations exhibit pathological characteristics that burden home validators.
  We identify four inefficiencies in the reference go-verkle implementation \cite{kaur2025goverkle, kaur2025goethereum}: (1) phantom node creation during non-existent account deletion; (2) 64-byte database keys triggering excessive LSM-tree compaction; (3) redundant memory copying in proof deserialization; (4) a Proof of Absence wire format incompatibility causing non-deterministic serialization.
  We present Fractional Verkle Trees (FVT), a hypertree decomposition partitioning global state into N independent sub-accumulators coordinated by a Merkle commitment tree, achieving improved cache locality, zero-lock-contention goroutine-parallel commitment computation, and faster root recomputation (91 $μ$s vs $\sim$500 ms). We address each inefficiency via existence checks, 32-byte SHA256 node references, zero-copy reference-counted buffers, and HashMap-based lexicographic deduplication.
  Benchmarks on Apple M1 Pro show 57\% heap allocation reduction (566,760 to 242,004 bytes per 10K proofs), parallel insertion at 2,433 ns/op, and network-wide elimination of 4.85 PB/year across 6,000 full nodes, advancing the Ethereum stateless roadmap.

</details>


### [197] [An Evaluation of Data Leakage Risks in Tool-Using LLM Agents in Realistic Scenarios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17114)
*Hankyul Baek,Jaewon Noh,Sang Seo,Yongsu Kim,Gabriel Waikin Loh Matienzo,Young Il Kim,Ee Wei Seah,Akriti Vij*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A joint evaluation by Singapore and Korea AI Safety Institutes tested three AI agents across 12 non-adversarial real-world tasks, finding that none achieved both fully correct and fully safe execution. Successful task completion frequently coincided with data-handling failures, revealing that operational data leakage is a first-order safety concern distinct from adversarial exfiltration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior research on agent data leakage has focused on adversarial threats (prompt injections, jailbreaks), but sensitive information can also be exposed during benign, non-adversarial use. The authors aim to systematically evaluate this underexplored category of operational data leakage.

Method: Two independent AI safety institutes jointly evaluated three AI agents across 12 realistic, non-adversarial scenarios spanning customer support, DevOps, web automation, and enterprise/personal productivity. Five risk types were assessed: lack of data awareness, audience awareness, policy compliance, data minimization, and access-boundary awareness. Task-specific LLM-judge rubrics were used in independent testing environments.

Result: No agent achieved fully correct and fully safe execution across all scenarios. Successful task completion frequently co-occurred with data-handling failures (e.g., accessing unnecessary data, disclosing to wrong recipients), suggesting capability and data-handling safety are orthogonal dimensions. Qualitative review uncovered claim-action mismatches, simulation-aware behavior, user-simulator role reversal, and interpretation gaps in automated judging.

Conclusion: Operational data leakage constitutes a first-order agent-safety concern distinct from adversarial exfiltration. The study provides a replicable methodology for evaluating agent data-handling safety and demonstrates that capability and safety must be assessed independently.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly being adopted in enterprise and personal settings with access to emails, databases, documents, and other tools where they can read, update, and disseminate sensitive information. Much of prior research on data leakage risks in agents has focused on adversarial data exfiltration through prompt injections and jailbreaks. However, sensitive information may also be exposed during non-adversarial use, creating leakage risks even when users issue benign requests.
  We report a joint evaluation by the Singapore AI Safety Institute and the Korea AI Safety Institute examining agent data leakage in 12 realistic, non-adversarial tasks spanning customer support, DevOps, web automation, and enterprise and personal productivity. The evaluation covers five risk types: lack of data awareness, audience awareness, policy compliance, data minimization, and access-boundary awareness. Both institutes tested a common set of scenarios mirroring real-world deployments using independent testing environments and task-specific LLM-judge rubrics.
  Across the three tested agents, none achieved fully correct and fully safe execution across all scenarios. Successful task completion often coincided with data-handling failures such as accessing unnecessary information or disclosing information to inappropriate recipients, indicating that capability and data-handling safety should be evaluated separately. Qualitative review also revealed claim-action mismatches, simulation-aware behavior, user-simulator role reversal, and interpretation gaps in automated judging. Overall, the results indicate that operational data leakage is a first-order agent-safety concern distinct from adversarial exfiltration and provide a methodology for future evaluations of agent data-handling safety.

</details>


### [198] [Quantifying quantum risk: a measure of crypto agility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17116)
*Coryan Wilson-Shah*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces "rotation time" as a metric for crypto agility and derives a formula linking rotation time tolerance to security risk tolerance. Using historical CVE data, it estimates rotation time tolerances on the order of hours to days, showing that crypto agility combined with hybrid encryption is effective for quantum-resilient systems but demands stringent operational tolerances.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantum computers threaten current cryptographic algorithms, and "harvest now, decrypt later" attacks necessitate mitigations today. While advances in cryptography and security architecture support quantum-resilient system design, a key gap exists in the literature: no method for deriving tolerances (e.g., how quickly cryptographic components must be rotated) for such systems.

Method: The authors introduce "rotation time" as a measure of crypto agility. They derive an analytical approximation that mathematically links rotation time tolerance to an organization's security risk tolerance. Historical CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) data is then used to compute illustrative numerical values for rotation time tolerance.

Result: The derived rotation time tolerance is on the order of hours to days. This demonstrates that crypto agility combined with hybrid encryption is an effective design approach for quantum-resilient systems, but meeting organizational risk tolerances may require challenging technical and operational tolerances.

Conclusion: Crypto agility paired with hybrid encryption is a viable strategy for building quantum-resilient systems. However, the short rotation time tolerances (hours to days) impose demanding operational requirements that organizations must address to align with their risk appetite.

Abstract: Because of their ability to enable new forms of cryptanalysis, quantum computers pose a threat to the cryptographic algorithms that are widely used to secure contemporary computer systems. A practical quantum computer may emerge within the next ten years or so, but due to theorised "harvest now, decrypt later" style attacker behaviour, mitigations are necessary today. Recent advances in cryptography and security architecture show promise in supporting the design of systems that exhibit resilience against quantum-enabled cryptanalysis, however there is a key gap in the literature around the subject of deriving tolerances for such systems. In this paper, we introduce the concept of rotation time as a measure of crypto agility, and derive an approximation that links rotation time tolerance to security risk tolerance. Historical CVE data is used to calculate illustrative values for rotation time tolerance, which is found to be of the order of hours to days. This demonstrates that using crypto agility in conjunction with hybrid encryption is an effective approach for designing quantum-resilient systems, but may necessitate challenging technical and operational tolerances in order to meet organisational risk tolerances.

</details>


### [199] [Graph neural networks at war: integrating cybersecurity and drone intelligence in the Israeli-Iranian conflict](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17119)
*Sozan Sulaiman Maghdid,Tarik Ahmed Rashid,Shavan Askar*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Graph Neural Network (specifically GraphSAGE) based framework for integrated cyber intrusion detection and UAV response coordination in cyber-physical systems, achieving 94.2% detection rate, 0.955 AUC-ROC, and 1.4s average response time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cyber-physical systems introduce novel threats requiring both rapid intrusion detection and coordinated physical response. Existing approaches lack integration between structural network understanding and drone-based countermeasures, motivating a unified graph learning framework.

Method: The authors develop a GraphSAGE-based intrusion detection system that learns underlying network topologies to identify malicious activity, coupled with drone response coordination. Effectiveness is evaluated through an emulation-based case study with modeled cyberattacks, comparing GraphSAGE against GCN and GAT baselines.

Result: The proposed GraphSAGE model achieved a 94.2% detection rate, an average AUC-ROC of 0.955, and an average response time of 1.4 seconds. GraphSAGE outperformed both GCN and GAT in identical experimental conditions.

Conclusion: Graph neural networks, particularly GraphSAGE, are effective for integrated intrusion detection and adaptive UAV response in dynamic cyber-physical systems, enhancing situational awareness and swarm coordination.

Abstract: Physical cyber systems have brought about new threats and challenges in detection and immediate response. This study examines how Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can be used to aid cybersecurity and drone management in a physical cyber system comprising of cyber intrusions and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). By providing a bridge between structural understanding of graphical neural networks, this work has provided an integrated procedure that allows intrusion detection systems to educate on underlying network structures, identify malicious activity, and facilitates drone response measures. Based on an emulation-based case study, cyberattacks models were created to provoke the responses of the drones, which proved that graph-based learning can assist with the situational awareness, swarm coordination, and adaptive maneuver. According to the performance valuation, this method has a detection rate of 94.2, average area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) of 0.955 and an average response time of 1.4 seconds. Comparative experiments reveal that proposed GraphSAGE network is more effective than the Graphical Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and Graphical Attention Networks (GATs) in the identical situation. Such findings prove that graphical neural networks can be used to avert intrusion and response of dynamic cyber-physical systems.

</details>


### [200] [TrustErase: Auditable Instant Machine Unlearning with Passport-Embedded Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17122)
*Rutger Hendrix,Leonardo G. Russo,Concetto Spampinato,Matteo Pennisi,Giovanni Bellitto*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: TrustErase proposes a verifiable, data-free machine unlearning framework that uses passport-embedded representations in parameter-efficient adaptation layers, enabling instant forgetting of specific classes/datasets by deactivating cryptographic keys without retraining or data access.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing machine unlearning methods (retraining or distillation-based) are computationally expensive and lack verifiability. There is a critical need for privacy-compliant AI systems that can provably and efficiently forget designated data without requiring access to original training data.

Method: TrustErase embeds passports (treated as cryptographic keys) into parameter-efficient adaptation layers. A singular value decomposition conceals these passports within model weights. Specific classes or datasets are forgotten by simply deactivating the corresponding passport, requiring no retraining, fine-tuning, or original data access. The approach is modular and leaves a transparent audit trail for compliance verification.

Result: Evaluations on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 demonstrate that TrustErase matches or exceeds state-of-the-art methods (DELETE, L2UL, Boundary Shrink) while operating in a strictly data-free regime.

Conclusion: TrustErase establishes a new paradigm for trustworthy, accountable, and instantly forgettable AI systems, combining verifiability with computational efficiency in a data-free unlearning framework.

Abstract: The demand for privacy-compliant AI has amplified the need for machine unlearning; yet, existing retraining or distillation-based methods remain unverifiable and computationally costly. We introduce TrustErase, a verifiable, data-free unlearning framework leveraging passport-embedded representations for instant, modular, and auditable forgetting. By treating passports as cryptographic keys within parameter-efficient adaptation layers, TrustErase enables the removal of specific classes or datasets through simple deactivation, without retraining, fine-tuning, or access to the original data. A singular value based decomposition conceals passports within model weights, ensuring that unlearning actions remain transparent and provably compliant. Evaluations on MNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 show that TrustErase matches or exceeds state-of-the-art benchmarks such as DELETE, L2UL, and Boundary Shrink, while operating in a strictly data-free regime. Ultimately, TrustErase establishes a new paradigm for trustworthy, accountable, and instantly forgettable AI systems.

</details>


### [201] [LineageMark: Multi-user White-box Watermarking for Contribution Tracing in Model Derivation Chains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17123)
*Bingxue Zhang,Xiaofeng Xu,Feida Zhu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: LineageMark is a multi-user white-box watermarking framework that uses projection-based encoding on stable parameter carriers to preserve contributor watermarks across multi-stage model derivation chains, with robustness against re-watermarking, fine-tuning, quantization, and pruning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In open LLM ecosystems, models undergo frequent adaptation across multiple domains, creating multi-stage derivation chains. Existing watermarking methods are designed for single-user, one-time embeddings and fail under repeated derivation and incremental updates. There is a need for provenance tracking and IP protection that survives multi-stage model evolution.

Method: LineageMark encodes watermarks directly into model parameters using a projection-based white-box approach. It first selects stable carriers (parameters less sensitive to model changes), then represents each watermark bit as a projection statistic over these carriers. New watermark insertions are constrained to introduce only bounded perturbations in the projection space, with margin constraints preserving signal integrity across successive insertions.

Result: Experimental results demonstrate that LineageMark successfully preserves contributor watermarks across multi-stage derivation chains, supports incremental multi-user watermark insertion, and exhibits robustness against perturbations including re-watermarking, fine-tuning, quantization, and pruning.

Conclusion: LineageMark provides an effective solution for tracking model provenance and protecting intellectual property in open LLM ecosystems with multi-stage derivation chains, overcoming the limitations of single-user watermarking schemes.

Abstract: In open large language model (LLM) ecosystems, models are frequently adapted across multiple domains and applications, forming multi-stage derivation chains. Consequently, tracking and verifying historical contributions is essential for model provenance and intellectual property protection. However, existing watermarking methods are mainly designed for single-user, one-time embeddings, often fail under repeated model derivation and incremental updates. To address this problem, we propose LineageMark, a multi-user white-box watermarking framework for model derivation chains. The framework encodes watermarks in model parameters using a projection-based approach. Stable carriers are first selected to reduce sensitivity to model changes, each watermark bit is then represented as a projection statistic over these carriers. Additional watermark insertions introduce only bounded perturbations in the projection space, and margin constraints are used to maintain signal integrity. We evaluate the effectiveness of LineageMark in multi-stage model derivation chains. Experimental results show that LineageMark preserves contributor watermarks across multi-stage derivation and supports incremental multi-user watermark insertion. Furthermore, it exhibits robustness against perturbations such as re-watermarking, fine-tuning, quantization, and pruning.

</details>


### [202] [Safety, Security, and Cognitive Risks in Neuro-Symbolic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17223)
*Manoj Parmar*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper systematically analyzes the enlarged attack surface of Neuro-Symbolic AI (NeSy), formalizes key concepts like Symbolic Integrity Violation (SIV) and Cross-Layer Amplification Ratio, extends MITRE ATLAS with NeSy-specific threats, catalogs symbolic-layer attacks (KG poisoning, ontology subversion), identifies cognitive risks amplified by explicit logical explanations, proposes mitigations aligned to NIST/EU standards, and provides three empirical benchmarks demonstrating vulnerabilities in medical KG, DistilBERT+ProbLog, and OWL ontology pipelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neuro-symbolic AI is increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains requiring both perception and structured reasoning, yet its hybrid neural-symbolic architecture introduces a uniquely expanded attack surface spanning five layers — neural perception, symbolic knowledge bases, reasoning engines, agentic orchestration, and data stores — with exploit pathways absent from purely neural systems. No prior work has systematically formalized, taxonomized, and empirically demonstrated these cross-layer vulnerabilities.

Method: (1) Formal definitions of NeSy Attack Surface, SIV, and Cross-Layer Amplification Ratio (decomposed into neural-caused and autonomous symbolic sensitivity); (2) a unified threat model extending MITRE ATLAS with 11 NeSy-specific tactics and a five-profile attacker taxonomy; (3) a symbolic-layer threat catalogue; (4) cognitive bias analysis; (5) interdisciplinary mitigations with NIST AI 600-1 / EU AI Act acceptance criteria; (6) three empirical benchmarks: targeted KG poisoning on a 205-entity medical KG, PGD-10 adversarial attack on DistilBERT+ProbLog pipeline, and single-axiom OWL edits with Pellet consistency stealth and STIX detection evaluation.

Result: (E1) Targeted KG poisoning achieves break-even SIV at injection budget B=5, with a stealth/SIV trade-off; (E2) PGD-10 at ε=0.01 yields a Cross-Layer Amplification Ratio of 5.884 (95% CI [4.64, 8.00], p<0.0001), with a matched-random baseline confirming adversarial specificity; (E3) single-axiom OWL edits achieve 93.3% SIV success with 100% Pellet-consistency stealth, yet STIX-based detection fails at 50% (random-guessing level), constituting an open problem.

Conclusion: NeSy systems exhibit severe, empirically validated cross-layer vulnerabilities where small neural perturbations or minimal symbolic injections can be structurally amplified through the reasoning chain. Current detection mechanisms (e.g., STIX for ontologies) are inadequate. The paper calls for integrated mitigations spanning all five layers, measurable against NIST and EU regulatory frameworks, and identifies ontology-level attack detection as a critical open problem.

Abstract: Neuro-symbolic AI (NeSy) pairs neural perception with symbolic reasoning, making it attractive for high-stakes domains where explainability and structured inference are required. However, this hybrid architecture introduces an enlarged attack surface spanning five layers: neural perception, symbolic knowledge bases, reasoning engines, agentic orchestration, and data stores -- each exploitable in ways absent from purely neural systems.
  This paper makes six contributions: (1) formal definitions of NeSy Attack Surface, Symbolic Integrity Violation (SIV), and Cross-Layer Amplification Ratio $\mathcal{X}$, decomposed into neural-caused and autonomous symbolic sensitivity components; (2) a unified threat model extending MITRE ATLAS with 11 NeSy-specific tactic extensions and a five-profile attacker taxonomy; (3) a symbolic-layer threat catalogue covering knowledge graph (KG) poisoning, ontology-merging, and inference-engine subversion; (4) analysis of cognitive risks -- automation bias, authority bias, and sycophantic reinforcement -- structurally amplified by NeSy's explicit logical explanations relative to black-box neural outputs; (5) interdisciplinary mitigations with measurable acceptance criteria aligned to NIST AI 600-1 and the EU AI Act; (6) three empirical benchmarks: (E1) targeted KG poisoning achieves break-even SIV at injection budget $B=5$ on a 205-entity medical KG, with a KG-specific stealth/SIV trade-off; (E2) PGD-10 at $\varepsilon=0.01$ yields $\mathcal{X}=5.884$ (95% CI $[4.64,\, 8.00]$, $p<0.0001$), confirmed adversarially specific by a matched-random baseline ($E^{R}_{\mathrm{rand}}=0$), on a DistilBERT+ProbLog pipeline; (E3) single-axiom OWL edits achieve 93.3% SIV success with 100% Pellet-consistency stealth, but held-out STIX detection fails at 50% (random-guessing level), an open problem.

</details>


### [203] [Cache to the Future: A Distributed Webpage Archive for Internet Blackouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17245)
*Ross Evans,Diogo Barradas*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Cache to the Future (CttF) is a system that caches and delivers static web content during internet blackouts using distributed community ratings, crowdsourced caching, and cryptographic safeguards (digital signatures, proof-of-work) to resist adversarial interference, demonstrated effective at city-scale via realistic simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Internet blackouts — whether accidental or government-imposed — deny citizens web access. While blackout-resistant technologies using mobile mesh networks exist for basic messaging, no solution provides continued access to knowledge sources on the web during a blackout. This gap motivates CttF.

Method: CttF employs a distributed community rating system for crowdsourcing cached content at scale, combined with cryptographic constructs including digital signatures (for authenticity) and proof-of-work (to thwart adversarial manipulation). The system is evaluated through realistic city-scale simulations under both benign and adversarial conditions.

Result: Realistic simulations show that CttF successfully delivers static web content at city scale across a wide range of scenarios, including those with adversarial interference.

Conclusion: CttF fills a critical gap in blackout-resistant communication by enabling continued access to web knowledge sources, complementing existing mesh-based messaging solutions with a robust, crowdsourced, cryptographically secured caching architecture.

Abstract: Internet blackouts, occurring due to technological mishaps or intentional governmental action, prevent citizens from accessing the internet. Citizens in regions where internet blackouts are common have utilized blackout-resistant technologies to maintain communication. Such technologies often rely on mobile mesh networks to provide limited messaging services. However, no technology currently exists which can provide continued access to knowledge sources on the web during a blackout.
  We present Cache to the Future (CttF): a system to cache and deliver static content hosted on the web during a blackout. CttF's distributed community ratings crowdsources caching at scale while cryptographic constructs (digital signatures, proofs-of-work) mitigate adversarial interference. Our realistic simulations demonstrate CttF delivering content at city-scale across a wide range of benign and adversarial scenarios.

</details>


### [204] [ARVO: Atlas of Reproducible Vulnerabilities for Open-Source Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17283)
*Xiang Mei,Jordi Del Castillo,Pulkit Singh Singaria,Haoran Xi,Abdelouahab Benchikh,Tiffany Bao,Ruoyu Wang,Yan Shoshitaishvili,Adam Doupé,Hammond Pearce,Brendan Dolan-Gavitt*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: ARVO introduces a method to create a large-scale, reproducible vulnerability dataset from OSS-Fuzz, containing over 6,100 vulnerabilities across 311 projects. It achieves 81% reproduction rate and 89.4% patch identification accuracy, breaking the traditional trade-off between reproducibility, quantity, and diversity in security datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vulnerability datasets have historically faced a three-way trade-off among reproducibility, quantity, and diversity, with reproducibility being the most neglected. This lack of reproducibility limits automated analysis of historical bug data and reduces utility for downstream security research. The authors aim to break this trade-off by enabling full reproducibility at scale.

Method: The authors identify key obstacles to large-scale bug reproduction and address them with general solutions. Their method is applied to the OSS-Fuzz dataset (the largest open-source software vulnerability dataset), transforming it into the ARVO dataset. Each vulnerability is packaged in a form that can be consistently rebuilt, triggered, and analyzed across versions. Reproducibility further enables automatic identification of corresponding patches and supports direct interaction with vulnerabilities after code changes.

Result: ARVO comprises over 6,100 real-world vulnerabilities across 311 projects. It achieves an 81% vulnerability reproduction success rate and 89.4% accuracy in locating corresponding patches. These capabilities—consistent rebuilding, triggering, cross-version analysis, and automatic patch identification—are not provided by existing large-scale datasets.

Conclusion: The ARVO dataset demonstrates that reproducibility can be achieved alongside quantity and diversity in vulnerability datasets, overcoming the longstanding three-way trade-off. The work also discusses ARVO's influence on both upstream development practices and downstream security research, suggesting broad impact across the software security ecosystem.

Abstract: Achieving reproducibility, quantity, and diversity in vulnerability datasets has long been viewed as an inherent three-way trade-off, where improving one dimension often comes at the cost of the others. In practice, reproducibility has been the dimension most often neglected. This has limited what can be automatically extracted from historical bug datasets, and has reduced their utility for downstream security research.
  In this work, we propose a method to produce a new security dataset which ensures reproducibility for diverse vulnerabilities at scale by identifying the key obstacles to large-scale bug reproduction and addressing them with general solutions. Using this method, we introduce full reproducibility to the largest open source software vulnerability dataset (OSS-Fuzz) and construct the ARVO dataset (an Atlas of Reproducible Vulnerabilities in Open-source software). ARVO is a large-scale dataset consisting of over 6,100 real-world vulnerabilities across 311 projects. Focusing on reproducibility, ARVO differs from existing datasets by providing each vulnerability in a form that can be consistently rebuilt, triggered, and analyzed across versions. Reproducibility also enables automatic identification of the corresponding patch for each vulnerability and supports direct interaction with vulnerabilities after code changes, capabilities that existing large-scale datasets do not provide. In our evaluation, ARVO successfully reproduces 81% of vulnerabilities and achieves 89.4% accuracy on the located patches. We also discuss ARVO's influence on both upstream practices and downstream security research.

</details>


### [205] [OTRO: Oblivious Tokenization Path with Square-Root ORAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17358)
*Jonghyun Lee,Yongqin Wang,Rachit Rajat,Daniel Wong,Mengyuan Li,Murali Annavaram*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: OTRO is an oblivious tokenization system for LLM serving in confidential computing that uses replicated square-root ORAM with epoch-based rotation and KV-cache-aware rebuild overlapping to prevent side-channel leakage from tokenizer memory access patterns while keeping time-to-first-token (TTFT) overhead under 4.5%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CPU-side LLM tokenizers in TEE-based confidential computing stacks leak user prompts through table-driven memory access patterns. Existing defenses using tree-based ORAM (e.g., PathORAM) impose ~13× tokenizer slowdown and 10-58% higher TTFT, which is unacceptable for latency-critical LLM serving.

Method: OTRO employs three innovations: (1) a pool of replicated square-root ORAM instances exploiting the read-only nature of the tokenizer table to avoid rebuild costs; (2) an epoch-based rotation policy that decouples accesses from rebuilds, padding epochs with dummy accesses to bound leakage; and (3) chunked KV-cache-aware tokenization that overlaps rebuilds with GPU prefill, minimizing instance count. Implemented in HuggingFace Tokenizers and nano-vLLM on Intel TDX with NVIDIA H100 GPU.

Result: OTRO limits TTFT overhead to at most 4.5%, keeps tokenizer-induced latency under 10% of total TTFT, adds less than 0.5 GB memory overhead, and significantly reduces observable tokenizer leakage across diverse model families and sizes.

Conclusion: OTRO demonstrates that efficient, practical oblivious tokenization is feasible for production LLM serving in confidential computing environments, effectively closing a critical side-channel gap without prohibitive performance penalties.

Abstract: The CPU-side large language model (LLM) tokenizer is a critical security gap in LLM serving through a confidential computing stack with CPU and GPU trusted execution environments (TEEs). Tokenizers converts the prompts through table-driven lookups, and the resulting memory access patterns are a powerful source of side-channel leakage. Recent work demonstrates end-to-end recovery of user prompts from tokenizer access pattern on production Intel TDX. However, a drop-in use of the popular tree-based Oblivious RAMs (e.g., PathORAM) to prevent access-pattern leakage introduces $\sim$13$\times$ tokenizer slowdown, resulting in 10-58% higher time-to-first-token (TTFT).
  In this paper, we present OTRO, an efficient, oblivious tokenization path tailored to latency-critical LLM serving. OTRO relies on square-root ORAM for fast single-access lookups, but avoids its prohibitive $O(N\log^2N$) rebuild cost every $\sqrt{N}$ accesses through three key innovations. First, OTRO provides a pool of replicated square-root ORAM instances that utilize the read-only nature of tokenizer table. Second, an epoch-based rotation policy decouples accesses from rebuilds and pads each epoch with dummy accesses to its boundaries, minimizing observable information. Lastly, chunked KV-cache-aware tokenization further overlaps rebuilds with GPU prefill and minimizes the instance count. Implemented as modules in HuggingFace Tokenizers and nano-vLLM, running within a TDX-enabled CVM with an NVIDIA H100 GPU, OTRO limits TTFT overhead to at most 4.5%, keeps tokenizer-induced latency under 10\% of total TTFT, and adds less than 0.5 GB of memory overhead while reducing the tokenizer's observable leakage across various model families and sizes.

</details>


### [206] [SoK: AI-Augmented Binary Reversing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17398)
*Yujeong Kwon,Yiyue Zhang,Shakhzod Yuldoshkhujaev,Kexin Pei,Dokyung Song,Hyungjoon Koo*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A systematic literature review of 144 papers (2015–present) on AI-augmented binary reversing, organizing the field into 22 inference task domains and proposing a unified taxonomy that connects traditional analysis, artifact representations, learning paradigms, and emerging LLM/agentic AI roles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Binary reversing is critical for security applications but fundamentally difficult due to compile-time semantic loss. AI-augmented approaches have proliferated rapidly, yet the research landscape is fragmented across domains, representations, learning methods, and evaluation standards, lacking a cohesive structure or common vocabulary.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic literature review of 144 papers from 2015 onward. They classify these into 22 binary reversing domains by inference task and introduce a unified taxonomy integrating: (1) conventional and AI-augmented reversing pipelines, (2) binary-derived artifacts, (3) representation strategies, (4) learning paradigms, and (5) downstream inference tasks, with explicit treatment of LLM and agentic AI system roles.

Result: The taxonomy reveals common structural patterns across seemingly disparate approaches. The analysis identifies persistent technical challenges (e.g., semantic gap, scalability), gaps in evaluation practices, and promising future directions, providing a holistic decade-scale view of the field's evolution.

Conclusion: The SoK establishes foundational clarity for AI-augmented binary reversing, offering a structured framework and shared vocabulary to guide future research toward more reliable, scalable, and systematically evaluable systems.

Abstract: Binary reversing is fundamental to software understanding, vulnerability discovery, malware investigation, and firmware auditing. However, it remains inherently challenging due to the irreversible loss of semantic information during compilation. Recent advances in machine learning, large language models (LLMs), and agentic AI systems have accelerated the adoption of AI-augmented binary reversing. Yet, the resulting body of work has become increasingly fragmented across reversing domains, artifact representations, learning approaches, and evaluation practices. This paper presents the first comprehensive systematization of knowledge on AI-augmented binary reversing. We analyze 144 research papers published since 2015, and organize them into 22 binary reversing domains according to the inference tasks. We further introduce a unified taxonomy spanning conventional and AI-augmented reversing pipelines. Our taxonomy connects traditional analysis techniques, binary-derived artifacts, representation strategies, learning paradigms, and downstream inference tasks, while clarifying the emerging roles of LLMs and agentic AI systems. By establishing a common vocabulary and structured framework, we provide a holistic view of the field's evolution over the past decade. Our study reveals common structures underlying seemingly disparate approaches, highlights persistent technical challenges and evaluation gaps, and identifies promising opportunities for future research. Collectively, these insights clarify the current state of the field and provide a foundation for the next generation of reliable and scalable AI-augmented binary reversing systems.

</details>


### [207] [Bifrost: Hybrid TEE-FHE Inference for Privacy-Preserving Transformer and LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17421)
*Chenghao Chen,Kailun Qin,Xiaolin Zhang,Chi Zhang,Dawu Gu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Bifrost presents a hybrid TEE-FHE architecture for confidential LLM serving, where a CPU TEE handles non-linear operations and state management while FHE (CKKS) delegates linear projection layers to an untrusted accelerator. Bifrost+ adds a prefill/decode split to keep prompt-side KV state in the TEE, achieving 9–10× latency reduction on larger models and 14–53× TTFT improvements on smaller models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cloud LLM inference exposes sensitive user prompts to untrusted software stacks and accelerators. Pure FHE is too expensive for end-to-end inference due to interleaved non-linear operators, while CPU TEEs alone lack a secure mechanism for accelerator participation. A hybrid approach is needed to balance confidentiality with performance.

Method: Bifrost provisions secrets exclusively to an attested CPU TEE and uses FHE (CKKS) as a delegation mechanism for linear projection/feed-forward layers on an untrusted accelerator. Non-linear operators (attention softmax, GELU, etc.), KV-cache state transitions, and decrypt-then-encrypt refresh execute inside the TEE. Bifrost+ further splits prefill (prompt KV built in TEE) from decode (hybrid ciphertext path).

Result: Using Euston's methodology for estimator comparison: Bifrost reduces projected latency by 9.25× on GPT-2 (1.5B) and 9.91× on LLaMA 3 (8B). For direct CKKS/FHE deployments: Bifrost+ reduces TTFT by 14.6–45.8× on GPT-2 (124M) and 15.3–53.4× on Qwen3 (0.6B).

Conclusion: Selective encrypted execution is the key principle: use FHE only where ciphertext-only accelerator delegation is needed (linear layers), and keep non-linear, refresh, and prompt-side computation inside the CPU TEE. This hybrid partitioning achieves substantial latency improvements over pure-FHE approaches.

Abstract: Cloud-hosted transformer and large language model (LLM) inference creates a direct confidentiality problem: user prompts may contain sensitive code, business data, personal information, or regulated documents, yet remote serving exposes intermediate state to the cloud software stack and accelerator runtime. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) keeps accelerator-side execution ciphertext-only, but end-to-end LLM inference remains expensive because linear layers are interleaved with non-linear, cache-state, and refresh-sensitive operators. CPU trusted execution environments (TEEs) can execute those operators natively, but a CPU TEE alone does not define how an untrusted accelerator should participate.
  We present Bifrost, a hybrid TEE-FHE serving architecture in which secrets are provisioned only to an attested CPU TEE, while the accelerator, device memory, driver/runtime stack, and host software remain outside the trusted computing base. Bifrost uses FHE as a secure delegation mechanism for projection and feed-forward linear layers on accelerator-backed CKKS, while non-linear operators, attention-side control logic, KV-state transitions, and decrypt-then-encrypt refresh execute inside the CPU TEE.
  Bifrost+ further applies a prefill/decode split: prompt-side KV state is built inside the CPU TEE, and only decode-side state enters the hybrid ciphertext path. In an estimator-style comparison matching Euston's methodology, Bifrost reduces projected latency by 9.25x on GPT-2 (1.5B) and 9.91x on LLaMA 3 (8B). In direct CKKS/FHE deployments, Bifrost+ reduces TTFT by 14.6-45.8x on GPT-2 (124M) and 15.3-53.4x on Qwen3 (0.6B). The systems lesson is selective encrypted execution: use FHE only where ciphertext-only accelerator delegation is required, and keep non-linear, refresh, and prompt-side work inside the CPU TEE.

</details>


### [208] [PARSE: Provenance-Aware Retrieval Sanitization for Professional Domain LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17467)
*Aaditya Pai*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Synthetic benchmarks for prompt injection defenses fail to generalize to real enterprise documents. The authors introduce a real-document benchmark across five professional domains and propose PARSE, a provenance-aware sanitization pipeline that significantly reduces attack success while preserving utility, unlike prior defenses like paraphrasing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing prompt injection defenses are evaluated on synthetic benchmarks that do not reflect the characteristics of real enterprise documents — which are longer, denser, and interleave authoritative language with factual content. This creates a dangerous evaluation gap where defenses that appear effective in synthetic settings may fail in production.

Method: The authors construct a real-document benchmark of 122 tasks spanning financial (SEC filings), legal (Federal Register), medical (PubMed), scientific (arXiv), and DevOps (GitHub postmortems) domains. They then introduce PARSE (Provenance-Aware Retrieval Sanitization), a pipeline that: (1) classifies each sentence by injection likelihood, (2) extracts structured facts before rewriting, (3) verifies fact preservation through a consistency-checking loop, and (4) employs a directiveness gate that routes 59% of documents to a lightweight path, concentrating computation on high-risk documents.

Result: Paraphrasing — the strongest defense on synthetic benchmarks — shows no statistically significant attack success rate reduction on real documents (p=0.500) while degrading utility from 91.8% to 82.8%. PARSE achieves a 15.6% attack success rate (a 38% reduction from the 25.4% baseline) at 86.9% utility. This is the only condition that is both statistically significant (p=0.014, adequately powered) and maintains near-baseline utility.

Conclusion: Practitioners should evaluate prompt injection defenses on domain-matched real documents rather than synthetic proxies. PARSE demonstrates that domain-aware, fact-preserving sanitization with adaptive computational routing can meaningfully reduce injection risk without sacrificing utility in real enterprise settings.

Abstract: Prompt injection defenses evaluated on synthetic benchmarks do not generalize to real enterprise documents, which are longer, denser, and interleave legitimate authority language with factual content. We demonstrate this gap with a real-document benchmark of 122 tasks across five professional domains (financial, legal, medical, scientific, DevOps) using actual SEC filings, Federal Register rules, PubMed abstracts, arXiv papers, and GitHub postmortems. Paraphrasing, the strongest defense on synthetic benchmarks, shows no statistically significant attack success rate reduction on real documents (p=0.500) while degrading utility from 91.8% to 82.8%. We introduce PARSE (Provenance-Aware Retrieval Sanitization), a domain-aware, fact-preserving sanitization pipeline that classifies each sentence by injection likelihood, extracts structured facts before rewriting, and verifies fact preservation via a consistency-checking loop. A directiveness gate routes 59% of real enterprise documents to a lightweight path, concentrating computational cost on high-risk documents. PARSE achieves 15.6% attack success rate -- a 38% reduction versus the 25.4% baseline -- at 86.9% utility, the only condition that is both statistically significant (p=0.014, adequately powered) and maintains near-baseline utility. Practitioners should evaluate defenses on domain-matched real documents, not synthetic proxies.

</details>


### [209] [SNAS: A Multi-Layer Defense-in-Depth Architecture for Secure Egress in Sandboxed Workloads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17533)
*Niranjan Kumar Sharma,S Muralidhar,Samy Boshra-Riad,Mike Halcrow,Yuxiong He,Nitya Kumar Sharma,Shawn Xia,Haowei Yu,Elliott Brossard,Derek Denny-Brown,Choden Konigsmark,Bhanu Prakash,Brandon Baker,Andong Zhan*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Snowflake's SNAS architecture uses eBPF filtering, GENEVE overlay networks, and distributed egress proxies to enable secure, policy-driven external network access from sandboxed Snowpark workloads while preserving multi-tenant isolation and resource fairness at production scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Snowpark workloads running in secure sandboxes require external connectivity to cloud APIs, databases, and feature stores. The core challenge is providing transparent network access while simultaneously maintaining strict multi-tenant isolation and resource fairness — a dependability problem that existing sandboxing approaches do not adequately solve.

Method: SNAS employs a three-layer architecture: (1) eBPF-based packet filtering for fine-grained network control within sandboxes, (2) GENEVE overlay networks for tenant traffic isolation, and (3) distributed egress proxies for policy-driven egress control. Key components include an Earliest Departure Time (EDT) algorithm-based bandwidth limiter, dual-tier policy enforcement, and safeguards against connection limiting and port exhaustion.

Result: SNAS is deployed across all Snowflake regions and supports large-scale production workloads, including petabyte-scale data transfer and latency-sensitive external integrations, with low overhead.

Conclusion: SNAS demonstrates that combining eBPF, GENEVE, and distributed proxies yields a viable production architecture for secure multi-tenant external network access in sandboxed execution environments, successfully balancing the tension between connectivity and isolation.

Abstract: Snowpark enables data engineering and AI/ML workloads in Snowflake by executing user-defined functions in secure sandboxes. Many of these workloads require external connectivity to access cloud APIs, external databases, or feature stores, creating a dependability challenge: how to provide transparent network access while preserving strict multi-tenant isolation and resource fairness. This paper presents Secure Network Access in Snowpark (SNAS), a production architecture for secure external communication from sandboxed workloads. SNAS combines Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) packet filtering, Generic Network Virtualization Encapsulation (GENEVE) overlay networks, and distributed egress proxies for policy-driven egress control with low overhead. We describe the design, deployment, and measured production behavior of SNAS, including an eBPF-based bandwidth limiter using the Earliest Departure Time (EDT) algorithm, dual-tier policy enforcement, and safeguards for connection limiting and port exhaustion. SNAS is deployed across all Snowflake regions and supports large-scale production workloads including petabyte-scale data transfer and latency-sensitive external integrations.

</details>


### [210] [An AI Security Agent for Banking: Multi-Vector Fraud and AML Detection Across Retail and Corporate Accounts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17555)
*Joseph Walusimbi,Joshua Benjamin Ssentongo*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A three-component AI security agent fusing LSTM behavioral models, statistical velocity monitors, and graph-based network analysis across dual transaction/session streams achieves F1 scores of 0.787/0.867, substantially outperforming rule-based (0.562/0.733) and LSTM-only (0.655/0.713) baselines on synthetic banking data, with sub-millisecond critical-tier response latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional static rule engines in banking effectively detect high-velocity, brute-force fraud but are structurally incapable of identifying sophisticated threats like business email compromise, session hijacking, and money-laundering layering — attacks engineered to mimic legitimate activity at the individual transaction or session level. This duality demands a detection architecture bridging both signature-based fraud and behavioral financial crime.

Method: A fusion architecture with three components operating on two parallel event streams: (1) a transaction stream covering card fraud, ACH/wire fraud, and AML categories; (2) a session stream covering account takeover, session hijacking, SIM-swap, and insider abuse. Each stream integrates an LSTM sequence model for per-account behavioral history, a statistical velocity/threshold monitor, and a graph/network module capturing account-counterparty relationship patterns (fan-in, fan-out, pass-through ratio). The system also includes a customer-facing transaction-verification chatbot and an analyst case-summary assistant.

Result: Evaluated on a synthetic dataset of 237,669 transactions and 113,508 sessions across 13 threat categories and 3,470 simulated accounts. The proposed fusion model achieved F1 of 0.787 (transaction stream) and 0.867 (session stream), compared to 0.562/0.733 for rule-based baselines and 0.655/0.713 for LSTM-only baselines. The verification chatbot reached 96.6% identity verification accuracy and 86.8% mass-reset attack detection; the analyst assistant achieved 99.3% action-recommendation F1. Critical-tier automated response latency was under 0.43 ms at the 95th percentile.

Conclusion: The three-component fusion architecture — combining sequential behavioral modeling, statistical velocity checks, and graph-based relationship analysis across dual event streams — effectively bridges the detection gap between signature-based fraud and behavioral financial crime, delivering strong performance improvements over both purely rule-based and purely LSTM-based approaches while maintaining operational viability through sub-millisecond critical response latency and deployable customer/analyst-facing auxiliary tools.

Abstract: Banks simultaneously face signature-based fraud (card-not-present attacks, account takeover, ATM cloning) and behavioural financial crime (structuring, layering, mule networks, business email compromise) -- two threat families with fundamentally different detection requirements. Static rule engines that reliably catch brute-force and high-velocity events are structurally blind to business-email-compromise (BEC) payment redirection, session hijacking, and money-laundering layering, which are engineered to appear indistinguishable from legitimate activity at the individual transaction or session level. This paper presents an AI security agent for retail and corporate banking that addresses this gap through a three-component fusion architecture operating on two parallel event streams: a transaction stream (card fraud, ACH/wire fraud, AML categories) and a session stream (account takeover, session hijacking, SIM-swap, insider abuse). Each stream combines an LSTM sequence model capturing per-account behavioural history, a statistical velocity/threshold monitor, and a graph/network module capturing account-counterparty relationship patterns (fan-in, fan-out, pass-through ratio) for money-laundering detection.
