Experiments on a synthetic event log of 237,669 transactions and 113,508 sessions across 13 threat categories and 3,470 simulated accounts demonstrate overall F1 of 0.787 (transaction stream) and 0.867 (session stream) for the proposed model, versus 0.562/0.733 for a rule-based baseline and 0.655/0.713 for an LSTM-only baseline. The agent includes a customer-facing transaction-verification chatbot (96.6% identity verification accuracy, 86.8% mass-reset attack detection) and an analyst case-summary assistant (99.3% action-recommendation F1), with Critical-tier automated response latency under 0.43 ms at the 95th percentile.

</details>


### [211] [Anywhere, Any-Stymie: Remote Activation of Trojan Malware on LiDAR with Modulated Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17562)
*R. Spencer Hallyburton,Miroslav Pajic*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper reveals a novel attack vector where dormant malware embedded in LiDAR firmware can be remotely triggered via an optical signal to manipulate point cloud data in real time, enabling false object injection and real object suppression that compromise autonomous system safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LiDAR sensors are critical for 3D perception in autonomous systems, yet existing security analyses focus on network-based or physical spoofing attacks. The authors identify a gap: no prior work has explored malware embedded at the firmware level that lies dormant during normal operation and can be externally activated post-deployment without network or hardware access.

Method: The authors design dormant malware that manipulates low-level point cloud data and embed it into LiDAR firmware. They implement an optical trigger mechanism using a modulated optical signal delivered into the sensing environment to remotely activate the malware. Once triggered, the malware performs real-time point cloud manipulation. Evaluation includes static tests at 300 ft, drive-by activation at up to 35 mph, semantic detectability analysis using a state-of-the-art 3D object detector, and demonstration of safety-critical impacts on a deployed tactical autonomous vehicle.

Result: The attack is feasible: optical triggering works at 300 ft static range and during drive-by scenarios at 35 mph. Injected person-like artifacts remain semantically detectable by a modern 3D object detector. Multiple modes of safety-critical impact are demonstrated on an operational tactical autonomous vehicle.

Conclusion: The LiDAR sensing pipeline lacks sufficient integrity guarantees. The demonstrated attack — dormant firmware-level malware with optical remote activation — exposes a critical, previously unexplored threat surface that demands stronger security measures throughout the sensor development and deployment lifecycle.

Abstract: LiDAR sensors are widely deployed in autonomous systems for 3D perception and safety-critical decision-making. We identify a previously unexplored attack surface in which dormant malware embedded in the LiDAR sensing pipeline remains inactive during normal operation and can be externally triggered after deployment, without requiring access to sensor hardware or networking at attack time. To operationalize this threat, we design malware capable of low-level point-cloud manipulation and embed it into LiDAR firmware. This malware was developed in a closed research test environment with vendor technical support, rather than by exploiting an inherent production supply-chain vulnerability. To selectively trigger attack activation, we design and implement an optical trigger that remotely activates the malware by delivering a modulated signal into the sensing environment. Once triggered, the malware performs real-time point cloud manipulation, and we demonstrate false object injection and real object suppression on static and mobile victim platforms. Our evaluation first establishes attack feasibility, including static operation at 300~ft and recorded drive-by runs reaching 35~mph. We then illustrate quantitatively that injected person-like artifacts can remain semantically detectable by a state-of-the-art 3D object detector. Finally, we demonstrate multiple modes of safety-critical impact on a deployed tactical autonomous vehicle. Together, these results highlight the need for stronger integrity guarantees throughout the LiDAR sensor development and deployment pipeline.

</details>


### [212] [Children Are Not the Enemy: Child-Fit Security as an Alternative to Bans and Surveillance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17957)
*Kopo M. Ramokapane,Rui Huan,Zaina Dkaidek,Awais Rashid*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper critiques containment-based approaches to children's online safety (bans, age gates, parental controls) and proposes "Child-fit security," a paradigm where children are treated as legitimate users whose wellbeing, development, privacy, safety, agency, and rights constitute core security requirements — shifting protection from restricting access to fostering healthy child-system relationships.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current dominant approaches to children's online safety frame child protection as a problem of restricting access to adult-designed systems, treating children as attackers, vulnerabilities, or risks to be managed. This framing is inadequate for the reality that digital technologies are central to children's learning, play, communication, identity formation, and social participation. A new security paradigm is needed.

Method: The authors engage in conceptual analysis and paradigm design: they characterize and critique containment-oriented approaches, then construct an alternative framework — Child-fit security — by defining its core principles, contrasting it with existing paradigms, and mapping its implications for security design. They conclude with a research agenda for operationalization.

Result: The paper delivers a conceptual framework for Child-fit security organized around core principles: treating children as legitimate users, making children's wellbeing and developmental needs into security requirements, and focusing protection on the child-system relationship rather than on apps, accounts, or data in isolation.

Conclusion: Child-fit security represents a necessary paradigm shift from containment to relationship-centered protection. The paper outlines a research agenda for making this paradigm operational, inviting the security community to redesign systems with children's rights, agency, and participation as foundational security requirements.

Abstract: Digital technologies are now central to children's learning, play, communication, identity formation, and social participation. Yet dominant approaches to children's online safety often rely on containment mechanisms, including bans, age gates, parental controls, monitoring, and screen-time restrictions. These approaches can be useful in specific contexts, but they often frame child protection primarily as a problem of restricting access to systems designed for adults. In this paper, we argue that this framing is inadequate for children's digital lives and insufficient as a security paradigm. We propose Child-fit security, a design paradigm in which technologies likely to be used by children treat a child as legitimate users, not attackers to be excluded, vulnerabilities to be patched, or risks to be managed. In this paradigm, children's wellbeing, development, privacy, safety, agency, and rights become core security requirements. This shifts the focus of protection from apps, accounts, and data to the child-system relationship, which means protecting both the child and their participation. We conceptualise child-fit security, contrast it with containment-oriented approaches, define its core principles, and discuss its implications for security design. We conclude by presenting a research agenda for making child-fit security operational.

</details>


### [213] [Beyond Native Success: Auditing Deployment-Interface Exposure of CLIP Backdoors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17815)
*Kunlan Xiang,Haomiao Yang,Wenbo Jiang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: DIFE is a framework for auditing backdoored CLIP models across diverse deployment interfaces, revealing that attack success is interface-specific rather than checkpoint-level. The authors identify a gap — no existing attack compromises the textual encoder as a reusable carrier — and fill it with BadTextTower, which produces strong text-conditioned exposure while keeping visual-only reuse clean.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CLIP backdoor attacks are validated only on narrow, attack-native tasks, leaving uncertainty about whether and how poisoned checkpoints remain dangerous when reused through different downstream interfaces (retrieval, reranking, feature extraction, selection). There is a need for systematic cross-interface auditing.

Method: The authors propose DIFE, a Deployment-Interface Footprint Evaluation framework that standardizes auditing by specifying five dimensions per interface: component readout, trigger channel, target event, reference condition, and metric. DIFE also includes effective-footprint diagnosis to identify which CLIP components carry adversarial exposure. They then introduce BadTextTower, a novel backdoor attack designed to poison the textual encoder into a reusable carrier of adversarial behavior.

Result: Auditing reproduced CLIP backdoors with DIFE reveals: (1) native attack success does not certify checkpoint-level risk; (2) exposure follows component footprints; (3) text-side poisoning fails to control the textual encoder; (4) some coupled attacks remain mechanism-bound. BadTextTower achieves strong text-conditioned exposure in retrieval, reranking, and selection while leaving visual-only reuse nearly clean.

Conclusion: CLIP backdoor risk is interface-dependent, not monolithic. DIFE enables structured, comparable cross-interface auditing. BadTextTower fills the critical gap of a text-encoder-carried backdoor, demonstrating that targeted component-level poisoning is both feasible and dangerous across deployment scenarios.

Abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training models are widely reused across downstream interfaces, including feature extraction, retrieval, reranking, and selection. Existing CLIP backdoor, however, usually validate attacks on a small attack-native task, leaving unclear whether the same poisoned checkpoint remains exposed, weakens, or becomes not applicable when reused through other interfaces. We introduce DIFE, a Deployment-Interface Footprint Evaluation framework that audits backdoored CLIP checkpoints across deployment interfaces. DIFE makes various evaluations comparable by specifying each interface's component readout, trigger channel, target event, reference condition, and metric. DIFE also introduces effective-footprint diagnosis to identify the reusable CLIP component or component combination that carries exposure and explains where risk transfers. Auditing reproduced CLIP backdoors with DIFE reveals a structured landscape: native success is not a checkpoint-level risk certificate, exposure follows component footprints, text-side poisoning does not yield textual-encoder control, and some coupled attacks remain mechanism-bound. This audit reveals a import gapin existing CLIP backdoors: a textual encoder that itself becomes a reusable carrier of adversarial behavior. We therefore introduce BadTextTower to fill this gap. BadTextTower produces strong text-conditioned retrieval, reranking, and selection exposure while leaving visual-only reuse nearly clean.

</details>


### [214] [ShellGames: Speculative LLM-Driven SSH Deception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17986)
*Umberto Salviati,Fabio De Gaspari,Mauro Conti,Luigi Vincenzo Mancini*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: ShellGames is an LLM-based SSH shell simulator for cyber deception that addresses key LLM limitations (state persistence, consistency, hallucinations, latency, subversion) through five complementary techniques. It achieves significant accuracy gains across correctness, consistency, state tracking, and robustness benchmarks, with user studies confirming realism comparable to real shells.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cyber deception and Moving Target Defense aim to disrupt adversaries via uncertainty, but maintaining long-lived, credible interactive sessions is difficult. While LLMs offer potential for dynamic deception, they suffer from critical limitations: lack of persistent state, output inconsistencies, hallucinations, high latency, and susceptibility to behavioral subversion that could expose the deception.

Method: ShellGames integrates five complementary techniques: (i) Automatic Chain-of-Thought with few-shot learning to improve command correctness; (ii) memory management for persistent system state coherency; (iii) speculative command execution to reduce response latency; (iv) smart routing of complex interactive commands to a sandboxed environment; and (v) subversion detection leveraging the constrained input-output domain of shell environments. Evaluation uses a standardized benchmarking protocol and dataset covering correctness, consistency, state tracking, and robustness tasks, plus a user study (n=20).

Result: ShellGames achieves 0.898 command accuracy on correctness (+5.3pp over baselines), 0.918 sequence-level accuracy on consistency (+36pp), 0.98 state tracking accuracy (+18.3pp), and 0.95 robustness accuracy (+37pp). The user study (n=20) confirms realism comparable to a real shell under free exploration and outperforms traditional honeypots on perceived command coverage.

Conclusion: ShellGames demonstrates that LLM-based deception systems can achieve high-fidelity, stateful, and robust interactive deception when augmented with memory management, speculative execution, sandboxed routing, and subversion detection. It sets a new standard for realistic, long-lived cyber deception environments suitable for engaging and studying adversaries.

Abstract: Cyber deception and Moving Target Defense are promising strategies that aim to disrupt adversaries by increasing uncertainty. However, sustaining long-lived, credible interactive sessions with adversaries remains an open challenge. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising path toward more dynamic deception systems, but suffer from key limitations that fundamentally limit their applicability, including: lack of persistent state, output inconsistencies, hallucinations, latency, and susceptibility to behavioral subversion that may reveal the deception.
  We propose ShellGames, an SSH shell simulator based on LLM designed to address these limitations. ShellGames combines five complementary techniques: (i) Automatic Chain-of-Thought and few-shot learning to improve correctness; (ii) memory management to maintain system state coherency; (iii) speculative command execution to reduce response latency; (iv) smart routing of complex interactive commands to a sandboxed environment; and (v) subversion detection leveraging the constrained input-output domain of shell environments. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce a standardized benchmarking protocol and dataset spanning correctness, consistency, state tracking, and robustness tasks. ShellGames achieves $0.898$ command accuracy on correctness ($+5.3pp$ over baselines), $0.918$ sequence-level accuracy on consistency ($+36pp$), $0.98$ state tracking accuracy ($+18.3pp$), and $0.95$ accuracy on robustness ($+37pp$). A user study with $n=20$ participants confirms that ShellGames achieves realism comparable to a real shell under free exploration and outperforms traditional honeypots on perceived command coverage.

</details>


### [215] [An Empirical Analysis of AI Slop in Music Streaming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18052)
*Stanley Wu,Josephine Passananti,Viresh Mittal,Wenxin Ding,Haitao Zheng,Ben Y. Zhao*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper investigates the emerging "AI slop" phenomenon in the music industry — mass-produced, low-quality AI-generated music distributed via streaming platforms for profit. Through analysis of Spotify data, the authors find that 93% of AI music receives negligible listener engagement. They demonstrate the ease of publishing AI-generated tracks through 11 distributors with inconsistent policies, and show that current detection methods are unreliable. The paper concludes that without intervention, AI music slop could become a self-sustaining shadow industry as generation costs decline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI has dramatically lowered barriers to content creation, enabling a cottage industry of "AI slop" — mediocre AI-generated content produced for revenue through misrepresentation or scams. While parallels exist with email spam, it remains unclear whether AI slop in music can evolve into a self-sustaining shadow industry. The authors aim to characterize this emerging threat and determine whether it can be prevented from taking root in the music streaming ecosystem.

Method: The study employs a multi-pronged approach: (1) Characterization of the current AI music slop landscape by analyzing growth and engagement metrics on Spotify; (2) Empirical testing of the AI slop pipeline by generating and publishing their own AI tracks through 11 independent music distributors to evaluate policy enforcement; (3) Assessment of existing AI music detection methods for accuracy and robustness.

Result: Key findings include: (a) 93% of AI-generated music on Spotify receives minimal to no listener plays and is rarely recommended by the platform's algorithms; (b) AI musicians adopt a "spray and pray" strategy, releasing large volumes across multiple genres seeking occasional hits; (c) Indie music distributors have inconsistent and largely unenforced policies on AI music, making mass publication trivially easy; (d) Current AI music detection methods lack sufficient accuracy or robustness for reliable enforcement.

Conclusion: As generation costs continue to decrease, AI slop in music is likely to become a self-sustaining shadow industry unless concrete countermeasures are adopted. The authors discuss potential mitigation strategies based on their empirical findings, emphasizing that proactive steps by the music industry — including stronger distributor policies and improved detection techniques — are necessary to prevent this outcome.

Abstract: Generative AI models lower the bar for content creation, making it easy for any user to create professional-looking images, text and music with minimal effort. This has enabled a new cottage industry around creation of "AI slop" mass quantities of mediocre content produced to generate revenue, often through misrepresentation as human-authored content, or scams involving automated scripts and fake consumption.
  While there are obvious parallels between the AI-slop industry and "traditional" email spam networks, it might be too early to determine if AI slop generation can grow into a similar self-sustaining industry. In this paper, we look specifically at the music industry, and explore the question: Can we prevent AI music slop from growing into a self-sustaining shadow industry?
  To answer this question, we characterize the current state of AI slop in music, and its pipeline from generation, distribution, and consumption by users on streaming platforms. By examining growth and engagement on Spotify, we confirm that AI music exhibits AI slop characteristics: the overwhelming majority (93%) of AI music receive few, if any listener plays, and are rarely recommended. AI musicians "spray and pray," releasing large volumes of music across multiple genres in hopes of generating a hit. We also explore the AI slop pipeline by generating and publishing our own AI tracks onto streaming through 11 indie music distributors. We find distributors have inconsistent and largely unenforced policies on AI music, making it surprisingly easy to publish mass produced AI songs. Finally, we consider AI music detection, and find that current methods lack accuracy or robustness. As generation costs decrease, we believe slop generation in music will become self-sustainable, unless concrete steps are taken by the music industry. We consider and discuss potential mitigation methods based on our findings.

</details>


### [216] [Structural Role Injection in Handlebars-Templated LLM Prompts: Triple-Brace Interpolation, Delimiter Family, and the Limits of HTML Auto-Escaping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18120)
*Mohammadreza Rashidi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Handlebars' double-brace HTML escaping as a prompt-template default provides inconsistent protection against structural role injection attacks — it neutralizes angle-bracket-based delimiters (ChatML, Llama-3, XML) but leaves colon-, square-bracket-, and Markdown-based delimiters (Llama-2, legacy Human:/Assistant:, Markdown ###) fully intact, a finding confirmed through model-free analysis and 5,760 empirical trials across four models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prompt templates using Handlebars (the default in Microsoft Semantic Kernel) rely on HTML escaping as a security mechanism, but the adequacy of this escaping against structural role injection — where attacker-controlled data injects forged chat role delimiters to hijack conversations — had not been systematically evaluated across diverse delimiter schemes and models.

Method: A two-phase approach: (1) model-free analysis establishing which delimiter characters survive Handlebars escaping across seven families (ChatML, Llama-3, XML, Llama-2 [INST], legacy Human:/Assistant:, Markdown ###); (2) 5760 empirical trials across four models (GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4.1 mini, Claude Haiku 4.5), two attack objectives (task-hijack and secret-exfiltration), comparing raw vs. escaped templates at a total API cost of $1.63 USD.

Result: GPT-3.5 Turbo followed task-hijack instructions in 97% (raw) and 91% (escaped) of trials. Protection from escaping was concentrated in angle-bracket families (0.00 survival rate) and absent for colon- and Markdown-based families (1.00 survival rate). The secret-exfiltration objective revealed the same family interaction pattern more cleanly. Claude Haiku 4.5 resisted both objectives almost entirely regardless of escaping.

Conclusion: HTML escaping as a prompt-injection defense is fundamentally limited: it protects only delimiter schemes whose characters happen to be covered by HTML escaping, and cannot substitute for proper structural separation of instruction and data. The escaped default creates a false sense of security for colon- and Markdown-based delimiter families.

Abstract: Large language model applications build prompts from templates, and Handlebars is a widely used templating engine and the default prompt-template format in Microsoft Semantic Kernel. Its double-brace {x} expression HTML-escapes the interpolated value and is documented as the safe default; its triple-brace {x} expression inserts the value raw. We show that this choice silently governs an application's exposure to structural role injection, where attacker-controlled data carries chat role delimiters that forge a higher-privilege turn. A model-free analysis establishes the mechanism: Handlebars escaping rewrites angle brackets but not square brackets, colons, or Markdown hashes, so it neutralises ChatML, Llama-3, and XML role delimiters (survival rate 0.00) while leaving Llama-2 [INST], legacy Human:/Assistant:, and Markdown ### delimiters intact (survival rate 1.00 for the last two). We then run 5760 trials across seven delimiter families, two attack objectives, and four models (GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4.1 mini, Claude Haiku 4.5) at a combined API cost of 1.63 USD. GPT-3.5 Turbo follows the task-hijack instruction in 97% of raw and 91% of escaped trials, with the escaping protection concentrated in the angle-bracket families and absent for the colon- and Markdown-based families; the harder secret-exfiltration objective, which does not saturate, exposes the same family interaction more cleanly. Claude Haiku 4.5 resists both objectives almost entirely. The escaped default protects only the delimiter schemes whose characters HTML escaping happens to cover, gives no protection for the rest, and cannot substitute for a structural separation of instruction and data.

</details>


### [217] [Evaluating Open-Source LLMs for Multi-Label ATT&CK Technique Classification on CTI Reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18166)
*Ahmed Ryan,Saad Sakib Noor,Md Erfan,Shaswata Mitra,Sudip Mittal,Md Rayhanur Rahman*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper constructs a realistic, human-annotated dataset from complex unstructured CTI reports and benchmarks seven open-source LLMs (8B–236B parameters) for multi-label ATT&CK technique classification. The best model achieved only a 0.22 micro-averaged F1 score, demonstrating that current open-source LLMs are inadequate for production-grade CTI classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM evaluations for ATT&CK classification use simplified, single-technique sentences that inflate performance and fail to reflect the multi-label, multi-step complexity of real-world unstructured CTI reports. The baseline performance of open-source LLMs on genuinely complex CTI data had not been established.

Method: The authors constructed a ground-truth dataset of 2,076 human-annotated sentences (1,281 positive, 795 negative) from 83 complex unstructured CTI reports, mapping to 114 unique ATT&CK techniques via a six-phase annotation process (κ=0.68). They evaluated seven open-source LLMs (8B to 236B parameters) under varied prompt strategies and temperature settings, measuring micro-averaged F1 for multi-label classification.

Result: The best-performing LLM achieved only a 0.22 micro-averaged F1 score. Model parameter size showed a statistically significant positive correlation with F1 score, while prompt strategy and temperature yielded no statistically significant gains. All models fell far short of production-grade requirements.

Conclusion: Current open-source LLMs are insufficient for production-grade ATT&CK classification on complex unstructured CTI reports. The dataset, benchmark, and findings provide a reproducible foundation for future research. Significant improvements in model capability or methodology are needed before these systems can be deployed operationally.

Abstract: Classifying Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) using MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK) is essential for proactive defense, but historically required extensive human effort. Pre-Large Language Model (LLM) automation sped up this process, but could not resolve the complex language and multi-step attack patterns found in unstructured CTI reports. LLMs addressed previous limitations by using contextual reasoning to understand unstructured text. However, current evaluations rely on simplified, single-technique sentences that ignore the complexity of real-world CTI reports, which often leads to inflated performance results. Consequently, the baseline performance of open-source LLMs on complex unstructured CTI reports remains unevaluated. To address this gap, we constructed a ground-truth dataset of 2,076 human-annotated sentences (1,281 technique-positive, 795 negative) from 83 complex unstructured CTI reports. These sentences were mapped to 114 unique ATT&CK techniques using a six-phase annotation process, achieving \k{appa} = 0.68 inter-annotator agreement. Using this dataset, we evaluated seven open-source LLMs ranging from 8B to 236B parameters across prompt strategy and temperature configurations. The highest-performing LLM achieved a micro-averaged F1 score of 0.22, establishing the empirical baseline for multi-label ATT&CK classification on complex unstructured CTI. Parameter size showed a statistically significant positive correlation with F1 score. Prompt strategy and temperature produced no statistically significant gains across model configurations. These results indicate that current open-source LLMs are insufficient for production-grade ATT&CK classification. The dataset, benchmark, and findings provide a reproducible foundation for future CTI research.

</details>


### [218] [Multi-Source Cybersecurity Logs: An ATT&CK-Labeled Dataset and SLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18190)
*Abir Ashab Niloy,Ahmed Ryan,Imamul Hossain Rafi,Md Erfan,Md Rayhanur Rahman*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces the first public multi-source log dataset combining system, network, and browser events with per-entry MITRE ATT&CK technique labels. It contains 870 sessions (~2.3M events) across 53 techniques and 12 tactics, generated using real attack tools. Fine-tuning SLMs with LoRA on this dataset raised chunk classification accuracy from ~8% to 90–97%, while ATT&CK technique identification reached 42% exact match, with strong partial-match performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: No existing public dataset simultaneously provides system, network, and browser logs with fine-grained, per-entry MITRE ATT&CK technique labels. This gap prevents training ML models to detect multi-stage cyberattacks that span all three telemetry sources. The authors aim to close this gap to enable and benchmark cross-source attack detection research.

Method: The authors constructed a multi-source dataset by capturing system, network, and browser events from Windows endpoints during 870 sessions (70 attack, 800 benign), yielding ~2.3 million labeled events. Attacks were executed with real tools (RATs, C2 tunnels, cloud exfiltration) and manually labeled with ATT&CK technique IDs across 12 tactics and 53 techniques. To validate learnability, they fine-tuned three SLMs (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-3B, Phi-4-Mini) using LoRA and evaluated them against base variants on chunk classification and ATT&CK technique identification across ten metrics.

Result: Fine-tuning improved every model on every metric. Chunk classification accuracy rose from ~8% (base models) to 90–97% after fine-tuning. ATT&CK technique identification proved harder, with the best exact-match accuracy reaching only 42%, though high partial-match scores indicated the models captured most of the underlying reasoning.

Conclusion: The dataset successfully fills a critical gap in multi-source, ATT&CK-labeled cyberattack data. It enables effective training for coarse-grained attack detection and shows promise for fine-grained technique identification, though the latter remains a challenging open problem.

Abstract: Multi-stage cyberattacks span system, network, and browser logs. Detecting them requires correlating events across all three sources. Machine learning methods can learn these cross-source patterns, but they need labeled multi-source data. Existing public datasets fall short. Network-only datasets such as CICIDS and UNSW-NB15 miss host and browser activity. Host-focused datasets such as LMDG and CICAPT-IIoT lack browser telemetry. ATLAS includes all three sources but labels events only as malicious or benign, without MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK) technique granularity. No public dataset combines all three sources with per-entry ATT&CK technique labels. We close the gap by building a multi-source log dataset of 870 sessions (70 attack, 800 benign) and approximately 2.3 million events. We captured system, network, and browser activity simultaneously on Windows endpoints. We labeled malicious events with ATT&CK technique IDs, covering 12 tactics and 53 techniques. We generated all attack data using real tools, including Remote Access Trojan (RAT), Command and Control (C2) tunnels, and cloud exfiltration. To demonstrate learnability, we fine-tuned three Small Language Models (SLMs) (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-3B, Phi-4-Mini) using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). We compared each against its base variant across ten metrics on two tasks: chunk classification and ATT&CK technique identification. Fine-tuning improved every model on every metric. Chunk classification accuracy rose from approximately 8% in the base variants to between 90% and 97% after fine-tuning. Technique identification remained challenging, with the best exact-match accuracy at 42%, although high partial-match scores show the models captured most of the underlying reasoning.

</details>


### [219] [A Red-Team Study of Anthropic Fable 5 & Opus 4.8 Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18193)
*Nicola Franco*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A red-teaming evaluation of two frontier LLMs (Anthropic's Fable 5 and Opus 4.8) across 7,826 harmful intents reveals that while both resist most attacks, adaptive iterative attacks—particularly tree-of-attacks—consistently break them, producing hundreds to thousands of panel-confirmed harmful completions across all harm categories with minimal refinement steps and no human intervention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aggregate jailbreak success rates can misleadingly suggest frontier LLMs are robust. The authors aim to reveal the residual attack surface that persists even in hardened models, demonstrating that low aggregate rates still translate to a practically significant volume of harmful outputs, and that adaptive iterative attacks remain a credible threat requiring sustained attention.

Method: The HackAgent red-teaming framework was used to generate hundreds of thousands of adversarial attempts against two Anthropic frontier models (Fable 5 and Opus 4.8) across 7,826 harmful intents in a ten-category harm taxonomy. Four families of automated jailbreak attacks were evaluated, including static obfuscation and adaptive iterative methods (notably tree-of-attacks). Every apparent success was re-adjudicated by a panel of three independent judge models using majority voting.

Result: Both models resisted the majority of attacks. Static obfuscation was nearly fully neutralized. However, adaptive iterative attacks dominated the residual surface: tree-of-attacks broke Opus 4.8 on 11.5% of intents and Fable 5 on 6.1%. This yielded 1,620 (Opus 4.8) and 702 (Fable 5) panel-confirmed harmful completions spanning all ten harm categories, achieved automatically, cheaply, and within one or two refinement steps by an attacker model without any human expert in the loop.

Conclusion: Even the best and most extensively tested frontier LLMs remain reliably breakable under sustained automated adversarial pressure. Aggregate robustness metrics obscure a practically dangerous residual attack surface, and adaptive iterative attacks represent a persistent, low-cost, and scalable threat that current safety measures do not fully mitigate.

Abstract: We evaluate the adversarial robustness of two frontier large language models (LLMs) developed by Anthropic, Fable 5 and Opus 4.8, against four families of automated jailbreak attack across 7 826 harmful intents spanning a ten-category harm taxonomy. Using the HackAgent red-teaming framework, hundreds of thousands of adversarial attempts were generated and every apparent success was independently re-adjudicated by a panel of three judge models (majority vote). Both models resist the majority of attacks, but the residual surface is larger than aggregate framing suggests: it is dominated by adaptive iterative attacks, while static obfuscation is near-fully neutralised. The strongest adaptive search (tree-of-attacks) breaks Opus 4.8 on 11.5% of intents overall, whereas Fable 5 stays in the single digits (6.1% worst-case). Aggregate rates therefore should not be read as reassurance. Even in these hardened configurations, the two models produced 1 620 (Opus 4.8) and 702 (Fable 5) panel-confirmed harmful completions spanning every harm category, located automatically, cheaply, and within the first one or two refinement steps by an attacker model with no human expert in the loop. The reasonable conclusion is that even the best, most-tested frontier models remain reliably breakable under sustained automated pressure.

</details>


### [220] [Seeing Is Not Screening: Multimodal Hidden Instruction Attacks on Agent Skill Scanners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18198)
*Xiaojun Jia,Jie Liao,Simeng Qin,Ke Ma,Wenbo Guo,Yebo Feng,Aishan Liu,Yang Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper identifies a blind spot in LLM skill security: malicious instructions hidden in images can bypass text-based scanners yet be executed by multimodal agents. The authors propose SkillCamo, an attack embedding harmful instructions in images with benign textual framing, and ExecScan, a multimodal defense using execution-grounded simulation to detect such threats.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM skill scanners rely on textual descriptions, manifests, and source code, creating a gap where visually conveyed malicious intent goes unexamined. As multimodal agents become capable of interpreting images during deployment, hidden instructions in bundled images pose a practical threat that existing defenses miss.

Method: The attack side, SkillCamo, conceals malicious instructions within images bundled with a skill, rewriting surrounding documentation so images appear as part of normal workflow—relying on joint text-image interpretation at execution. The defense side, ExecScan, is an execution-grounded multimodal scanner performing: (1) intent extraction, (2) behavior reconstruction, (3) abuse assessment, and (4) deliberative execution simulation over all skill artifacts (docs, code, resources, visuals) to recover hidden instructions and identify risks like exfiltration, destruction, persistence, deception, and privilege escalation.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that image-hidden malicious instructions successfully evade existing skill scanners, while ExecScan significantly improves detection performance against such multimodal threats.

Conclusion: Image-mediated malicious instructions represent a critical, underexamined attack surface in LLM agent ecosystems. Execution-grounded multimodal scanning, as implemented in ExecScan, provides an effective defense by jointly reasoning over textual and visual artifacts to uncover hidden malicious behaviors.

Abstract: Agent skills are emerging as an important attack surface in LLM-based systems. Through an empirical study of existing skill scanners, we find that current defenses primarily rely on textual descriptions, manifests, and source code as the main signals for security analysis, which can leave visually conveyed malicious intent insufficiently examined. This creates a practical blind spot: harmful operational instructions hidden in images may bypass scanning while still being recoverable by multimodal agents during deployment. To systematically investigate this threat, we propose SkillCamo, a document-mediated multimodal instruction attack that conceals malicious instructions within images bundled with a skill while rewriting the surrounding documentation to naturally reference those images as part of the normal workflow. Thus, the attack does not rely on the image alone, but on the joint interpretation of textual guidance and visual payload at execution time. To defend against such attacks, we further propose ExecScan, an execution-grounded multimodal scanning module that performs intent extraction, behavior reconstruction, abuse assessment, and deliberative execution simulation over skill artifacts. ExecScan jointly analyzes documentation, code, referenced resources, and visual content to recover hidden instructions, reconstruct executable behavior chains, and identify downstream risks such as exfiltration, destruction, persistence, deception, and privilege escalation. Extensive experiments show that image-hidden malicious instructions challenge existing skill scanners, while ExecScan can improve the skill scanning performance.

</details>


### [221] [Gatling: Rapid-Fire Consensus from Parallel Composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18220)
*Giulia Scaffino,Max Resnick,Joachim Neu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Gatling is an atomic broadcast protocol that achieves arbitrarily small inter-proposal times (below one network delay) by running multiple parallel instances of a black-box consensus protocol with staggered proposal schedules and merging their outputs via a deterministic interleaving rule.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior work has established tight lower bounds on confirmation latency that modern consensus protocols already achieve, it remains an open problem whether inter-proposal time can be reduced below the state-of-the-art of one network delay. Reducing inter-proposal time directly improves good-case transaction latency in fault-free executions.

Method: Gatling runs multiple parallel instances of any black-box atomic broadcast protocol with staggered proposal schedules under a rotating leader schedule. A deterministic interleaving rule merges instance outputs into a single global log. The paper analyzes head-of-line blocking from crashed leaders, derives the optimal number of parallel instances, and presents two variants preserving predictable validity.

Result: Gatling achieves arbitrarily small inter-proposal times (smaller than one network delay). The paper analytically derives the optimal number of parallel instances considering crash-induced head-of-line blocking. Experiments confirm Gatling works with off-the-shelf component protocols to achieve low latency without per-protocol tuning.

Conclusion: Gatling demonstrates that inter-proposal time can be reduced below one network delay, closing a previously open problem. This enables lower good-case transaction latency in consensus protocols without modifying or fine-tuning the underlying component protocol.

Abstract: Consensus protocols form the core of blockchains and other replicated state machines, ensuring that all correct nodes process the same totally ordered log of input transactions. In fault-free executions, performance is driven by the good-case transaction latency -- the time between a transaction becoming known to all nodes and its confirmation by the consensus protocol -- which depends on both how frequently proposals are made and, once made, how quickly they are confirmed. While prior work has established tight lower bounds on confirmation latency that modern protocols already achieve, it remains open whether the inter-proposal time can be further reduced below the state-of-the-art of one network delay.
  We introduce Gatling, an atomic broadcast protocol that achieves arbitrarily small inter-proposal times under rotating leader schedules; in particular, smaller than the network delay. Gatling runs multiple parallel instances of a black-box atomic broadcast protocol and staggers their proposal schedules to generate proposals in faster succession than state-of-the-art protocols. A deterministic interleaving rule merges the outputs of these instances into a single global log. We analyze the effects of head-of-line blocking caused by crashed leaders, and derive Gatling's optimal number of parallel instances. We further study the impact of Gatling on predictable validity and present two variants that retain this property. Finally, our experiments confirm that Gatling can be used with off-the-shelf component protocols to achieve low latency without fine-tuning the component protocol for minimum latency.

</details>


### [222] [Learning Red Agent Policy from Observations for Neurosymbolic Autonomous Cyber Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18223)
*Ankita Samaddar,Sandeep Neema,Daniel Balasubramanian,Xenofon Koutsoukos*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Proposes an imitation learning-based policy learning technique for partially observable RL environments with discrete state-action spaces, applied to cyber-defense to predict attacker actions from network observations and defender actions, achieving high accuracy when integrated with neurosymbolic agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern autonomous cyber-defense agents using RL suffer from partial observability — the attacker's (red agent's) actions are hidden, making it difficult for the defender to predict red actions, learn red policies, or assess intrusion levels. Existing neurosymbolic approaches (behavior trees with LECs) lack robust solutions for this problem.

Method: A Policy Learning Technique based on imitation learning designed for partially observable RL agents with discrete state and action spaces. The method learns to predict the red agent's actions using only network observations and known defender actions, and is integrated into a neurosymbolic cyber-defense agent architecture.

Result: The proposed method effectively handles diverse red (attacker) policies and achieves high prediction accuracy across multiple simulated autonomous cyber-environment scenarios.

Conclusion: Imitation learning can successfully address the partial observability challenge in autonomous cyber-defense by enabling defenders to infer attacker policies from limited observations, enhancing the effectiveness of neurosymbolic RL-based defense agents.

Abstract: With sophisticated cyber-attacks becoming increasingly prevalent, modern networks require intelligent autonomous cyber-defense agents trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL). These agents employ neurosymbolic approaches such as behavior trees with learning-enabled components (LECs) to learn, reason, adapt, and implement security rules while maintaining critical operations. However, these autonomous networks are partially observable systems, i.e., the cyber-attacker's (red agent's) actions are not observable, making it difficult for the defender to predict red actions, learn red policies, or assess the attacker's intrusion levels. To address this, we propose a Policy Learning Technique using imitation learning to learn policies for partially observable RL agents with discrete states and discrete actions. We apply this technique in an autonomous cyber environment to predict red agent's actions from network observations and defender actions. Integrated with a neurosymbolic cyber-defense agent, our method effectively handles different red policies and achieves high prediction accuracy across diverse simulated scenarios.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [223] [Beyond Parallel Sampling: Diverse Query Initialization for Agentic Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17209)
*Sidhaarth Murali,João Coelho,Jingjie Ning,João Magalhães,Bruno Martins,Chenyan Xiong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DivInit improves agentic search by diversifying first-turn queries: instead of sampling k independent queries (which often overlap), it generates n candidates and selects k diverse seeds, yielding 5–7 point gains on multi-hop QA across five models and eight benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard parallel sampling (breadth scaling) for agentic search suffers from diminishing returns because models tend to issue similar first-turn queries across rollouts, leading to redundant retrieval and shared conditioning in subsequent turns.

Method: DivInit is a training-free intervention: at the first turn, instead of sampling k independent queries, it draws n > k candidates from a single model call, then selects k diverse seeds (e.g., via diversity-based filtering) to launch parallel trajectories.

Result: Across five open-weight models and eight benchmarks, DivInit consistently outperforms standard parallel sampling, achieving average improvements of 5–7 points on multi-hop QA tasks at matched compute budgets.

Conclusion: Diversifying initial queries is a simple, effective, training-free method to mitigate redundancy in parallel agentic search trajectories, substantially improving multi-hop reasoning performance without additional compute cost.

Abstract: Test-time scaling for agentic search typically increases depth (i.e., more turns and tokens per trajectory) or breadth (i.e., more parallel rollouts). Here we focus on breadth scaling, showing that standard parallel sampling yields diminishing returns, tracing this to query redundancy at the first turn. When models issue similar first queries across rollouts, the threads retrieve overlapping evidence, and subsequent turns are conditioned on this shared retrieval. We address this limitation with DivInit, a training-free intervention at the first turn. Rather than sampling k independent first queries, DivInit draws n candidates from a single call, picks k < n diverse seeds, and runs them as parallel trajectories. Across five open-weight models and eight benchmarks, DivInit consistently improves over standard parallel sampling, with average gains of five to seven points on multi-hop QA at matched compute. Code available at https://github.com/cxcscmu/diverse-query-initialization

</details>


### [224] [When Rules Learn: A Self-Evolving Agent for Legal Case Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17220)
*Mingxu Tao,Jiawei Hu,Xian Zhou,Wenpeng Hu,Jiajun Cheng,Yunbo Cao,Zhunchen Luo,Guotong Geng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a self-evolving, rule-driven query rewriting framework that enhances BM25 for legal case retrieval without parameter training. An LLM agent iteratively generates rewriting rules, validates them, and prunes ineffective ones using automatic evaluation feedback, outperforming static baselines on LeCaRD-v2.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite advances in dense retrieval, BM25 remains a strong baseline in legal case retrieval due to the domain's need for precise lexical matching. Existing query rewriting methods rely on human expertise or one-shot LLM generation and lack iterative refinement, motivating an automated, self-improving rule discovery process.

Method: A self-evolving framework where an LLM-based agent operates within an automatic evaluation loop. The agent iteratively: (1) creates candidate rewriting rules, (2) plans combinatorial validation experiments over rule sets, and (3) eliminates underperforming rules based on historical feedback. This rule-driven rewriting augments BM25 queries without any parameter fine-tuning.

Result: On the LeCaRD-v2 Chinese legal case retrieval benchmark, the self-evolving framework outperforms non-evolutionary baselines (human-designed rules, greedy rule selection), especially with high-capacity LLMs. Ablation analyses show that the LLM's ability to leverage past experimental results and its intrinsic knowledge for rule elimination are critical to the self-evolution mechanism.

Conclusion: Self-evolving rule discovery via LLM agents is a viable, training-free approach to enhance sparse retrieval in specialized domains like law. Success hinges on the core LLM's capacity for experimental reasoning and knowledge-driven rule pruning.

Abstract: Legal case retrieval remains challenging due to the complexity of legal language and the need for precise lexical alignment between queries and relevant cases. Although dense retrieval models have achieved notable progress, empirical studies show that BM25 continues to serve as a strong baseline in this domain. It motivates us to propose a self-evolving framework for rule-driven query rewriting that enhances BM25 without any parameter training. The framework equips an LLM-based agent with an automatic evaluation environment, enabling it to iteratively create rewriting rules, plan validation experiments over rule combinations, and eliminate ineffective rules based on historical feedbacks. We evaluate our method on the Chinese legal case retrieval benchmark LeCaRD-v2. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms non-evolutionary baselines, including human-designed rules and greedy rule selection, particularly when powered by a highcapacity core LLM. We also conduct detailed analyses to investigate the mechanisms underlying self-evolution. Our findings reveal that LLM's capabilities to leverage previous experimental results and its intrinsic knowledge of rule elimination play critical roles in refining the rule set via self-evolution.

</details>


### [225] [SkillChain-Gym: A Benchmark for Reskilling-Aware Production-Inventory Control under Disruptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17266)
*Carlos Eduardo Sanoja*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillChain-Gym is a new open-source benchmark for studying production-inventory control under workforce skill dynamics, including certification lapses, forgetting, and training-time trade-offs. Across multiple policies and disruption scenarios, no single policy class dominates; the optimal choice depends on forecast visibility, capacity slack, and forgetting rates, motivating hybrid controllers that balance skill insurance with reactive training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production planning increasingly requires treating workforce capability as a decision variable due to skill decay, new product demands, and competition between production and training hours. Existing benchmarks treat labor as exogenous, and workforce-planning models with skill dynamics are rarely released as reusable testbeds, creating a gap in reproducible research infrastructure.

Method: The authors introduce SkillChain-Gym, a benchmark specification featuring a single-site environment with stylized worker skill-state dynamics, hard-threshold certification, forgetting mechanisms, and capacity-consuming training actions constrained by per-worker time budgets. The benchmark includes seed-controlled disruption scenarios, three feasibility modes with projection diagnostics, deterministic replay, and comprehensive metrics (operations, resilience, capability growth, training-access distribution). They evaluate four policy families — production-only, reactive adaptive, water-filling adaptive, and static-insurance — with budget variants over 60-shift horizons using paired statistical tests.

Result: Results are regime-dependent: training-capable policies consistently outperform the production-only baseline, and maintenance training is necessary under forgetting even without disruptions. Adaptive training excels when bottlenecks are visible in forecasts, while lean static cross-training provides strong insurance under surprise shocks and absenteeism. Capacity slack and forgetting rates govern the boundary between these regimes. No single policy class dominates across all conditions.

Conclusion: The lack of a universally dominant policy motivates the development of forecast-driven controllers that can dynamically decide when to invest in skill insurance versus when to react to observed bottlenecks, adapting to the governing regime.

Abstract: Production planning increasingly has to treat workforce capability as a decision variable: certifications lapse when skills are not maintained, new products require skills the current workforce does not hold, and reskilling competes for the same worker hours needed for production. Existing operations benchmarks usually treat labor as exogenous, while workforce-planning models with skills and learning are rarely released as reusable testbeds. We introduce SkillChain-Gym, a benchmark specification for reskilling-aware production-inventory control: a single-site environment with stylized worker skill-state dynamics, hard threshold certification, forgetting, and capacity-consuming training actions constrained by the same per-worker time budget as production. The benchmark includes seed-controlled disruption scenarios, three feasibility modes with projection diagnostics, deterministic replay, and metrics covering operations, resilience, capability growth, and training-access distribution. We evaluate production-only, reactive adaptive, water-filling adaptive, and static-insurance policies with budget variants over 60-shift horizons with paired statistical tests. The results are regime-dependent rather than a ranking. Training-capable policies dominate the production-only baseline, and maintenance training is necessary under forgetting even without disruptions. Among training-capable classes, adaptive training helps when bottlenecks are visible in the forecast, while a lean static cross-training plan, a deliberately favorable comparator whose structure encodes relevant skill contingencies, acts as strong insurance under surprise shocks and absenteeism. Capacity slack and the forgetting rate govern the boundary between these regimes. No policy class dominates across regimes, motivating forecast-driven controllers that decide when to buy skill insurance and when to react.

</details>


### [226] [Skill-Constrained Model Predictive Control for Resilient Manufacturing Supply Chains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17269)
*Carlos Eduardo Sanoja*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper examines a model predictive control (MPC) approach for production-inventory systems where worker certifications decay over time, requiring ongoing training decisions that compete directly with production for scarce labor hours. Evaluated on synthetic SkillChain-Gym scenarios, the MPC controller shows regime-dependent performance: it excels when skill or labor bottlenecks are forecastable early, but lean static cross-training insurance remains competitive under surprise shocks and near demand-capacity boundaries. The key finding is that forecastability, not adaptivity per se, determines when predictive control pays off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In production systems requiring certified workers, firms face a fundamental tension: production consumes worker hours today, but training consumes those same hours to build certified capacity for tomorrow. Certifications decay unless maintained. The authors aim to understand when a closed-loop, optimization-based controller that jointly plans production and training outperforms simpler static or reactive policies, and to isolate the mechanisms (maintenance, re-acquisition, or greenfield training) driving any gains.

Method: The authors formulate a closed-loop model predictive controller (MPC) that solves a finite-horizon mixed-integer program at each shift, jointly optimizing production, inventory, backlog, and training decisions. The formulation includes binary predicted certification variables, hard production eligibility constraints, and an interpretable terminal value function that penalizes certified-capacity gaps at the planning horizon. Only the first-period action is implemented before replanning. The controller is benchmarked on synthetic, seed-controlled SkillChain-Gym environments against: (1) production-only and maintenance-only ablations, (2) static cross-training insurance plans, and (3) a strong reactive heuristic. Scenarios include announced and surprise skill shocks, demand shocks, absenteeism, forecast-quality variations, and systematic sweeps of capacity boundaries and training rates. Attribution ablations separate the effects of certification maintenance, re-acquisition of lapsed certifications, and greenfield skill acquisition.

Result: No single policy class dominates. Predictive control is beneficial when skill or labor bottlenecks can be forecasted sufficiently early to complete training before the bottleneck materializes. Lean static cross-training insurance remains hard to beat under surprise shocks, near the demand-capacity boundary, and in regimes where pre-shock slack makes insurance cheap. The attribution analysis shows that the relative contribution of maintenance, re-acquisition, and greenfield training varies across scenarios. The decisive factor is forecastability, not the controller's adaptivity.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that regime dependence, not universal superiority, characterizes the value of predictive control in skill-constrained production-inventory systems. Practitioners should assess the forecast horizon relative to training lead times: when bottlenecks can be anticipated early, MPC adds value; when shocks are unforecastable, cheap static insurance may suffice. The work provides a structured evaluation framework (SkillChain-Gym) and attribution methodology for making this assessment.

Abstract: In skill-constrained production-inventory systems, the qualified human capacity available tomorrow depends on training decisions made today: production requires certified workers, certifications decay unless maintained, and training consumes the same scarce worker hours that production needs now. We study a closed-loop skill-constrained model predictive controller that, at every shift, solves a finite-horizon mixed-integer program over production, inventory, backlog, and training, with binary predicted certification, hard production eligibility, and an interpretable terminal value that prices certified-capacity gaps at the horizon boundary; only the first-period action is applied before replanning. On synthetic, seed-controlled SkillChain-Gym scenarios - announced and surprise new-skill shocks, demand shocks, absenteeism, forecast- and availability-quality modes, capacity-boundary and training-rate sweeps, and negative controls - we evaluate the controller against production-only and maintenance-only ablations, static cross-training insurance plans, and a strong reactive heuristic, under an ex-ante locked configuration and paired statistics. The result is regime dependence, not superiority: no policy class dominates. Predictive control helps when skill or labor bottlenecks are forecastable early enough for training to complete; lean static insurance remains hard to beat under surprise shocks, near the demand-capacity boundary, and wherever pre-shock slack makes insurance cheap. Attribution ablations separate certification maintenance, re-acquisition of lapsed certifications, and greenfield skill acquisition. Forecastability, not adaptivity per se, decides when predictive control pays.

</details>


### [227] [Nothing from Something: Can a Language Model Discover 0?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17289)
*Phoebe Zeng,Thomas L. Griffiths,Brenden M. Lake*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether neural network models can discover the concept of "zero" — a case study in out-of-distribution generalization for mathematical reasoning. The authors find that GPT-2-sized language models fail to generalize to zero at test time without explicit training, but can learn it with tens to hundreds of examples. Language pretraining reduces the required examples by approximately 50%, suggesting language abilities scaffold mathematical discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mathematical discovery demands a strong form of out-of-distribution generalization — the capacity to hypothesize genuinely novel mathematical structures that may be logically more powerful than those seen during training. The paper examines whether modern AI models possess this capacity, using the discovery of "zero" in arithmetic as a tractable case study. It also tests the hypothesis that language abilities support such generalizations, mirroring claims about human cognition.

Method: The authors use simple arithmetic tasks as a controlled testbed. They evaluate GPT-2-sized language models on their ability to generalize to the concept of zero at test time. Two conditions are compared: (1) models tested without any exposure to zero during training, and (2) models fine-tuned on varying numbers of zero examples (tens to hundreds). The effect of language pretraining is isolated by comparing pretrained versus non-pretrained models.

Result: Key findings: (1) GPT-2-sized language models fail to generalize to zero at test time without explicit training, regardless of whether they received language pretraining. (2) Models improve substantially after training on tens or hundreds of zero examples. (3) Language pretraining reduces the number of required training examples by approximately 50%, providing evidence that linguistic knowledge scaffolds mathematical concept acquisition.

Conclusion: While current neural models cannot spontaneously discover zero through pure out-of-distribution generalization, they can acquire the concept efficiently with limited examples. Language pretraining serves as a meaningful scaffold, substantially accelerating this learning process. This suggests that combining linguistic knowledge with targeted mathematical training may be a productive path toward AI systems capable of genuine mathematical discovery.

Abstract: AI systems based on artificial neural networks are being developed with aspirations of pushing the boundary of human mathematical knowledge. A key question for these systems is how much they can reach beyond their training data. Mathematical discovery requires a strong form of out of distribution generalization; the ability to hypothesize genuinely new - and potentially logically more powerful - mathematical structures. It has been hypothesized that language abilities support such generalizations in human cognition. In this work, we use simple arithmetic as a case study for examining how modern AI models could expand their mathematical horizons, evaluating whether these models can independently discover the concept of "zero". We show that We show that (1) language models of a GPT-2 size are unable to perform this generalization at test time regardless of language pretraining, but (2) models can improve substantially after training on tens or hundreds of examples of zero. Additionally, we find that language pretraining reduces the number of required examples by approximately $50\%$, showing that language abilities can scaffold mathematical discovery in neural models.

</details>


### [228] [LegalHalluLens: Typed Hallucination Auditing and Calibrated Multi-Agent Debate for Trustworthy Legal AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18021)
*Lalit Yadav,Akshaj Gurugubelli*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Legal AI systems hallucinate at ~52% on aggregate, but this masks where and how errors occur. LegalHalluLens introduces typed hallucination profiles across four claim categories, a Risk Direction Index (RDI) to quantify omission-vs-invention bias, and a typed debate pipeline that reduces fabricated detections by 45% using a small 4B-parameter model, matching commercial APIs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aggregate hallucination metrics (~52%) in legal AI systems conceal critical failure patterns: which claim types (numeric, temporal, obligation/entitlement, factual) concentrate errors, and whether errors skew toward omission or invention. This opacity prevents compliance officers from making informed deployment decisions. The paper aims to surface these hidden failure modes to enable direction-aware procurement, accountability, and safer agent design.

Method: LegalHalluLens comprises three components: (1) Typed hallucination profiling across four legally-motivated claim categories (numeric, temporal, obligation/entitlement, factual) using the CUAD benchmark; (2) A Risk Direction Index (RDI) that collapses omission-vs-invention bias into a single deployment-comparable scalar; (3) A typed debate pipeline with Skeptic challenges and asymmetric gates calibrated to measured failure modes. Evaluation covers 510 contracts and 249,252 clause-level instances, using a 4B-parameter backbone.

Result: A within-model gap of approximately 38-40 percentage points exists between obligation/numeric and temporal claims that aggregate reporting hides. Two systems with matched 52% hallucination rates can carry opposite RDIs (opposite omission/invention biases). The typed debate pipeline reduces fabricated detections by 45%, with per-category gains tracking the diagnosis, matching commercial API performance despite the small model size.

Conclusion: Typed hallucination profiles and RDI surface failure modes that aggregate metrics conceal and serve as effective calibration inputs for multi-agent debate pipelines. Targeted, diagnosis-driven debate (with asymmetric gates keyed to measured failure modes) outperforms generic debate tuning. The framework supports direction-aware deployment decisions, accountability mechanisms, and agent design for legal AI in production settings.

Abstract: AI systems deployed in legal workflows hallucinate at rates that aggregate metrics report at ~52%, but this average conceals where errors concentrate and in which direction they run, leaving compliance officers without an actionable signal for trustworthy deployment. We present LegalHalluLens, an auditing framework with three components: typed hallucination profiles across four legally-motivated claim categories (numeric, temporal, obligation/entitlement, factual) over CUAD (Hendrycks et al., 2021); a Risk Direction Index (RDI) that reduces omission-versus-invention bias to a single deployment-comparable scalar; and a typed debate pipeline calibrated to both magnitudes and directions. Across 510 contracts and 249,252 clause-level instances we measure a within-model gap of approximately 38-40 pp between obligation/numeric and temporal claims that aggregate reporting hides, and show that two systems with matched 52% rates can carry opposite RDIs. The debate pipeline reduces fabricated detections by 45% with per-category gains tracking the diagnosis, matching commercial APIs with a substantially smaller backbone (4B active parameters). Typed profiles and RDI surface failure modes that aggregate metrics hide; we further show these diagnostics serve as calibration inputs for multi-agent debate pipelines, where Skeptic challenges and asymmetric gates targeted at measured failure modes outperform generically-tuned debate. The framework supports direction-aware procurement, accountability, and agent design for legal AI deployed in the wild.

</details>


### [229] [Quantifying Consistency in LLM Logical Reasoning via Structural Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17312)
*Baishali Chaudhury,Mengdie Flora Wang,Hyunji Hayley Park,Rahul Ghosh,Sungmin Hong,Jae Oh Woo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes "structural uncertainty," a framework that evaluates LLM reliability by measuring the stability of self-preference rankings across multiple sampled reasoning paths, rather than relying solely on answer dispersion. It decomposes uncertainty into across-trial ranking instability and within-trial candidate ambiguity, showing these signals complement answer dispersion and are particularly informative for logical/mathematical reasoning but collapse for factual retrieval tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reliability assessment methods for LLMs focus on output dispersion (how much sampled answers differ), ignoring whether models can consistently rank competing reasoning candidates. This is especially problematic for multi-step deductive reasoning, where models may reach the same answer via unstable or contradictory paths.

Method: For a given query, multiple candidate reasoning solutions are generated. The LLM judges pairwise preferences among its own outputs. Self-preferences are aggregated into ranking distributions via Bradley-Terry modeling with PageRank. The signal is decomposed into two entropy-based components: (1) across-trial ranking instability — how much rankings vary across repeated sampling trials, and (2) within-trial candidate ambiguity — how evenly distributed preferences are within a single trial.

Result: Tested across five LLMs and eight benchmarks: (1) Structural signals complement answer dispersion, improving identification of unreliable instances on logical/mathematical reasoning tasks. (2) On factual retrieval, structural signals collapse toward uniformity, marking a regime boundary where reasoning-level consistency is uninformative. (3) Within-trial ambiguity correlates positively with correctness (multiple plausible paths remain competitive), while across-trial instability correlates negatively (signaling unreliable reasoning).

Conclusion: Structural uncertainty is not a universal confidence estimator but a regime-sensitive evaluator of logical reasoning consistency. It is most valuable for multi-step deductive reasoning and becomes uninformative in factual retrieval settings, providing a diagnostic for when reasoning-level consistency evaluation is appropriate.

Abstract: Large language models can arrive at the same answer through reasoning paths that are unstable, contradictory, or difficult to rank consistently -- a failure mode especially prevalent in multi-step deductive reasoning. Existing methods assess reliability primarily through output dispersion -- measuring how much sampled answers differ -- but this discards a complementary signal: whether the model can consistently rank competing reasoning candidates. We propose structural uncertainty, a consistency-aware framework derived from the stability of self-preference-induced rankings over sampled reasoning solutions. Given a query, we generate multiple candidate solutions and ask the model to judge pairwise preferences among its own outputs. We aggregate self-preferences into ranking distributions via Bradley-Terry modeling with PageRank, and decompose the signal into two entropy-based components: across-trial ranking instability and within-trial candidate ambiguity. Across five LLMs and eight benchmarks, structural signals provide information complementary to answer dispersion: on logical and mathematical reasoning tasks, the combination improves identification of unreliable instances, while on factual retrieval the structural signal collapses toward uniformity, diagnosing a regime boundary where reasoning-level consistency evaluation is uninformative. The two components relate differently to accuracy: within-trial ambiguity correlates positively with correctness -- consistent with settings where multiple plausible solution paths remain competitive -- while across-trial instability correlates negatively, signaling unreliable reasoning. Structural uncertainty is best understood not as a universal confidence estimator, but as a regime-sensitive evaluator of logical reasoning consistency.

</details>


### [230] [ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18037)
*Ander Alvarez,Santhiya Rajan,Samuel Mugel,Román Orús*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ProvenanceGuard is a source-aware verifier for MCP-grounded LLM answers that detects cross-source conflation—where claims are factually supported but attributed to the wrong source. It decomposes answers into atomic claims, routes them to source-specific evidence, checks support via NLI and token alignment, and compares stated vs. actual source attribution. Evaluated on 281 medical MCP-agent traces, it achieves block F1 of 0.802 and source accuracy of 0.858, outperforming source-blind baselines, and detects all injected attribution swaps in clinical conflation probes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard factuality metrics test whether an answer is supported by pooled evidence but miss a critical failure mode: cross-source conflation, where a claim is factually supported somewhere but attributed to the wrong evidence source. This provenance-sensitive error is particularly dangerous in MCP-based agents that draw from heterogeneous sources (search, APIs, databases, clinical records), as incorrect attribution can lead to misplaced trust and clinical/operational harm.

Method: ProvenanceGuard operates by: (1) capturing MCP traces with stable tool IDs, source IDs, and raw outputs; (2) decomposing LLM answers into atomic claims; (3) routing each claim to source-specific evidence; (4) verifying support using NLI and a token-alignment proxy; (5) comparing the agent's stated attribution against the routed source; and (6) returning per-claim verdicts plus an answer-level allow/block decision. Blocked answers can be repaired via retrieval-augmented revision and re-verified.

Result: On a 266-trace adjudicated subset yielding 2,325 LLM-assisted claim labels (361 human-verified), ProvenanceGuard achieved block F1 of 0.802 and source accuracy of 0.858 on the 40-trace held-out split over 260 source-eligible claims, outperforming source-blind baselines. On a harder multi-source benchmark, block F1 was 0.846 but source-plus-relation accuracy dropped to 0.229, revealing difficulty with semantically close sources. Repair-and-reverify resolved all blocked answers. In 50 controlled clinical conflation probes, all injected attribution swaps were detected with zero retained wrong attributions.

Conclusion: Source attribution constitutes an independent axis for factuality verification in MCP-based agents, orthogonal to traditional evidence-support checks. ProvenanceGuard demonstrates that explicit source tracking and claim-to-source routing can effectively detect cross-source conflation, though precision degrades when sources are semantically proximate. The repair-and-reverify loop offers a practical mitigation path for blocked answers.

Abstract: Tool-using LLM agents increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to answer from heterogeneous evidence sources, including search, APIs, databases, clinical records, and formulary tools. Standard factuality metrics usually test whether an answer is supported by pooled evidence, missing a provenance-sensitive failure mode: a claim may be supported somewhere while being attributed to the wrong source. We call this cross-source conflation.
  We introduce ProvenanceGuard, a source-aware verifier for MCP-grounded answers. It consumes captured MCP traces with stable tool IDs, source IDs, and raw outputs; decomposes answers into atomic claims; routes claims to source-specific evidence; checks support with NLI and a token-alignment proxy; compares stated attribution with the routed source; and returns per-claim verdicts plus an answer-level allow/block decision. Blocked answers can be repaired with retrieval-augmented answer revision and re-verified.
  We evaluate on 281 medical-domain MCP-agent traces. A 266-trace adjudicated subset yields 2,325 LLM-assisted claim labels split by trace; 361 held-out labels are human-verified. On the 40-trace held-out split, ProvenanceGuard achieves block F1 0.802 and source accuracy 0.858 over 260 source-eligible claims, outperforming source-blind baselines that do not emit claim-to-source IDs. On a harder multi-source benchmark it reaches block F1 0.846, while source-plus-relation accuracy drops to 0.229, showing that exact source ownership remains difficult with semantically close sources. Repair-and-reverify resolves all blocked answers in the full trace set, often via conservative fallback. In 50 controlled clinical conflation probes, ProvenanceGuard detects all injected attribution swaps with no retained wrong attribution. These results show that source attribution is an independent axis for factuality verification in MCP-based agents.

</details>


### [231] [MemTrace: Probing What Final Accuracy Misses in Long-Term Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17328)
*Xianxuan Long,Zhikai Chen,Shenglai Zeng,Shouren Wang,Kai Guo,Jiliang Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemTrace introduces a benchmark that evaluates LLM long-term memory at the granularity of individual "knowledge points" (typed user facts) across three dimensions—memory age, question type, and evidence condition—revealing that pooled accuracy masks distinct failure modes and that the primary bottleneck is evidence utilization rather than retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
