TL;DR: EComAgentBench is a benchmark of 662 shopping tasks where agents must uncover requirements scattered across queries, profiles, and clarifications, then commit to a single product within 100 tool calls. Even the best model achieves only 57.1% accuracy, with typed rubrics attributing failures to specific requirement sources.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM shopping agent benchmarks are inadequate because they expose full user intent upfront and only grade the final product choice. This fails to capture how real shopper requirements emerge: implicitly in queries, stored in profiles, or surfaced through clarification dialogues. These benchmarks cannot pose long-horizon challenges or explain which specific requirement caused an agent's failure.

Method: The authors construct EComAgentBench with 662 tasks grounded in real Amazon products and reviews. Each task distributes requirements across three sources: a visible query, a tool-gated profile, and scripted clarification interactions. Agents must discover hidden intent, verify candidates against attributes and review evidence, and select a single product within a 100-tool-call budget. Every task is graded using typed, source-tagged rubrics that attribute failures to specific requirements and their sources. Construction is automated but code-verified before text generation, with every sample validated for reliability.

Result: Evaluation across seven models shows the strongest model reaches only 57.1% overall accuracy. Rubric satisfaction degrades systematically from visible requirement sources to hidden ones (profile and clarification), demonstrating the benchmark's capacity to diagnose where agents fail to elicit or utilize requirements.

Conclusion: EComAgentBench provides a reproducible foundation for advancing shopping agents beyond single-query search toward dependable, long-horizon assistance, with fine-grained failure attribution enabling targeted improvement.

Abstract: As LLM-based shopping agents enter production, existing benchmarks fail to capture how a shopper's requirements arrive: stated implicitly in the query, recorded in a profile, or revealed only when the right question is asked. Benchmarks that expose full intent upfront and grade only the final choice can neither pose this long-horizon challenge nor explain which requirement an agent missed. To address this gap, we introduce EComAgentBench, a benchmark of 662 tasks grounded in real Amazon products and reviews. Each task scatters these requirements across a visible query, a tool-gated profile, and scripted clarification; an agent must uncover hidden intent, verify candidates against attributes and review evidence, and commit to a single product within 100 tool calls. Moreover, typed, source-tagged rubrics grade every task, attributing each failure to a requirement and its source. Construction is automated yet reliable, with every answer fixed in code before any text is generated and every sample validated. Our evaluation of seven models reveals that even the strongest attains only 57.1% overall accuracy, and rubric satisfaction degrades from visible to hidden sources. Overall, we believe EComAgentBench will serve as a reproducible foundation for moving shopping agents from single-query search toward dependable assistance over long horizons.

</details>


### [253] [LongWebBench: Evaluating Structural and Functional Webpage Generation in Long-Horizon Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17727)
*Yi Zhao,Zhen Yang,Mengpan Chen,Mingde Xu,Shanghui Gong,Xijun Liu,Jibing Gong,Jie Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LongWebBench introduces a benchmark with 490 real-world long webpages for structural fidelity evaluation and 507 interaction tasks over 129 pages for functional evaluation. It reveals that VLM-generated long webpages degrade in structure with length and fail at executable multi-step interactions, advocating for interaction-based evaluation beyond visual similarity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations for VLM-based webpage generation focus on short, single-screen, static pages, ignoring the challenges of long-horizon, multi-screen webpages that require both structural coherence and functional interactivity.

Method: LongWebBench employs two complementary protocols: (1) a multi-dimensional VLM-based metric for assessing long-range structural coherence, and (2) a DOM-augmented agent-based pipeline for end-to-end functional verification of goal-oriented interaction tasks. Human agreement analysis validates the automatic evaluation protocols.

Result: Experiments with state-of-the-art open-source and proprietary VLMs show that structural fidelity degrades with increasing webpage length, and visually plausible generations frequently fail to support executable multi-step interactions, exposing a critical gap in current VLM capabilities.

Conclusion: Long-horizon webpage generation must be evaluated beyond surface-level visual similarity; executable, multi-step interaction should serve as a core evaluation criterion. LongWebBench provides the infrastructure to drive this shift.

Abstract: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) have shown promising progress in generating webpages from visual inputs, yet existing evaluations mainly focus on short, single-screen, and largely static webpages. We introduce LongWebBench, a benchmark for evaluating long-horizon webpage generation from both structural and functional perspectives. LongWebBench contains 490 real-world long webpages for structural fidelity evaluation and 507 goal-oriented interaction tasks over 129 webpages for functional evaluation. It employs two complementary protocols: a multi-dimensional VLM-based metric for assessing long-range structural coherence, and a DOM-augmented agent-based pipeline for end-to-end functional verification. We further examine the automatic evaluation protocols through human agreement analysis. Experiments with state-of-the-art open-source and proprietary VLMs under single-image and multi-image settings reveal that structural fidelity degrades as webpage length increases, while visually plausible generations often fail to support executable multi-step interactions. These results highlight the need to evaluate long webpage generation beyond visual similarity, with executable interaction as a core criterion. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/zheny2751-dotcom/LongWebBench.

</details>


### [254] [Shattering the Autoregressive Curse: Dynamic Epistemic Entropy Orchestrated Erasable Reinforcement Learning for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17735)
*Ziliang Wang,Kang An,Faqiang Qian,Jialu Cai,Cijun Ouyang,Yuhang Wang,Qibing Ren,Yichao Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: E³RL addresses the "autoregressive curse" in long-horizon RL for LLMs — where early errors cascade irreversibly — by using intrinsic cross-entropy as an epistemic uncertainty signal, segment-level dynamic thresholds, and KV-cache reuse to enable self-healing reasoning. It achieves SOTA gains of 5.35% (4B) and 6.51% (8B) on AIME.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning for LLMs suffers from the autoregressive curse in long-horizon logical reasoning: small early perturbations propagate irreversibly along the Markov decision process, causing cascading failures that collapse the entire reasoning trajectory. Existing methods rely on external signals and cannot self-correct localized errors without discarding prior computation.

Method: E³RL uses the model's endogenous local autoregressive cross-entropy as an intrinsic epistemic uncertainty coordinate, eliminating reliance on external feedback. It introduces segment-level adaptive dynamic thresholds and advantage allocation to identify and excise localized logical defects. Crucially, it reuses historical KV-cache streams from unafflicted segments, enabling self-healing without full regeneration. Training is conducted on the DeepMath-103k dataset, maintaining linear memory overhead.

Result: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks (AIME), E³RL achieves substantial gains: 4B models surpass prior SOTA by 5.349%, 8B models by 6.514%. It also improves long-sequence reasoning exploration efficiency and sample efficiency while maintaining linear memory overhead.

Conclusion: E³RL effectively shatters the autoregressive curse in long-sequence reasoning, providing both a theoretical and systems-level foundation for self-healing capabilities in next-generation AGI.

Abstract: Although reinforcement learning (RL) has expanded the cognitive boundaries of large language models (LLMs), it often remains vulnerable to the autoregressive curse in long-horizon logical reasoning: small epistemic perturbations introduced early in generation can propagate irreversibly along the Markov decision process flow, triggering cascading failures that drive the reasoning trajectory toward collapse. To overcome this autoregressive cascade, in which a single early mistake can compromise all subsequent reasoning steps, we propose dynamic epistemic entropy orchestrated erasable reinforcement learning ($\text{E}^3\text{RL}$). $\text{E}^3\text{RL}$ eliminates reliance on external signals by grounding the model's endogenous local autoregressive cross-entropy as an intrinsic coordinate of epistemic uncertainty. By introducing segment-level adaptive dynamic thresholds and advantage allocation, $\text{E}^3\text{RL}$ enables the model to precisely excise localized logical defects while reusing historical key-value (KV) cache streams, thereby endowing the reasoning process with a self-healing capability. We train $\text{E}^3\text{RL}$ on the DeepMath-103k dataset. Experimental results show that $\text{E}^3\text{RL}$ reshapes the exploration efficiency of long-sequence reasoning and improves sample efficiency while maintaining linear memory overhead. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks such as AIME, $\text{E}^3\text{RL}$ achieves substantial performance gains, with the 4B and 8B parameter models surpassing previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) results by 5.349\% and 6.514\%, respectively. These findings suggest that $\text{E}^3\text{RL}$ shatters the autoregressive curse in long-sequence reasoning and establishes a theoretical and systems-level foundation for the next generation of self-healing artificial general intelligence (AGI).

</details>


### [255] [DecoSearch: Complexity-Aware Routing and Plan-Level Repair for Text-to-SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17821)
*Esteban Schafir,Xu Zheng,Hojat Allah Salehi,Zhuomin Chen,Mo Sha,Wei Cheng,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DecoSearch is a training-free, model-agnostic framework that routes NL-to-SQL queries by complexity: simple queries are handled directly, while complex ones are decomposed into a DAG of atomic sub-questions. It achieves state-of-the-art execution accuracy among training-free methods on BIRD (70.53%) and Spider (88.31%) with significantly lower token consumption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based NL-to-SQL methods struggle with complex queries requiring multi-step, data-aware reasoning. The authors aim to bridge this gap without training, by adaptively allocating reasoning effort based on query complexity and intelligently handling decomposition failures.

Method: DecoSearch uses four core components: (1) a lightweight Schema Selector that prunes irrelevant tables/columns; (2) an LLM Judger that routes simple queries to direct generation and complex ones to decomposition; (3) a DAG-based decomposer that breaks complex queries into atomic sub-questions solved by targeted SQL generation, grounded by a RAG component with semantically similar examples; and (4) a Topology Refiner that restructures the reasoning plan when execution failures indicate flawed decomposition rather than correctable SQL errors.

Result: With a DeepSeek backbone, DecoSearch achieves 70.53% execution accuracy on BIRD and 88.31% on Spider, outperforming all training-free baselines while using an order of magnitude fewer tokens than competing methods. It also consistently improves fine-tuned SQL generation backbones when used as a model-agnostic wrapper.

Conclusion: Adaptive routing of queries by complexity, combined with DAG-based decomposition and failure-aware topology refinement, yields substantial gains in NL-to-SQL accuracy and efficiency. DecoSearch's training-free, model-agnostic design makes it broadly applicable as a plug-and-play enhancement for existing SQL generation pipelines.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in translating natural language to SQL, yet existing methods still falter on complex queries requiring multi-step, data-aware reasoning. We introduce DecoSearch, a training-free framework that addresses this by routing each query to the appropriate level of reasoning effort. A lightweight Schema Selector first prunes the full database schema to the relevant tables and columns. An LLM Judger then decides whether the question requires decomposition: straightforward questions follow a direct generation path and complex ones are escalated to a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of atomic sub-questions, each solved by a targeted SQL generation step. A RAG component grounds the decomposer with semantically similar training examples, and a Topology Refiner restructures the reasoning plan when execution failures signal a flawed decomposition rather than a fixable SQL error. DecoSearch achieves 70.53% execution accuracy on BIRD and 88.31% on Spider with a DeepSeek backbone, surpassing all training-free baselines while consuming an order of magnitude fewer tokens than competing methods. It also functions as a model-agnostic wrapper, consistently improving fine-tuned SQL generation backbones without any modification to the pipeline.

</details>


### [256] [WallZero: Mastering the Game of WallGo with Strategic Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17847)
*Hsing-Yu Chen,Jérôme Arjonilla,I-Chen Wu,Ti-Rong Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WallZero is an AlphaZero-based agent for the board game WallGo, featuring tailored action and feature designs that outperform professional Go players. The agent is also used to analyze game fairness and identify optimal strategies, revealing that the Netflix series' opening leads to a more balanced game.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: WallGo is a newly popularized strategic board game with high game-tree complexity but remains largely underexplored in AI research. There is a need for a strong AI agent to play the game competitively and to analyze its strategic properties.

Method: The authors develop WallZero, an agent based on the AlphaZero architecture, incorporating game-specific action representations and feature engineering tailored to WallGo's dual mechanics of stone movement and wall placement on a 7×7 board.

Result: WallZero defeats two professional Go players, capturing on average 1.98x more territory per game. Analysis using WallZero further reveals that the opening sequence featured in the Netflix series The Devil's Plan produces a more balanced game state.

Conclusion: WallZero demonstrates that AlphaZero-style reinforcement learning, combined with domain-specific modifications, can achieve superhuman performance in WallGo. The agent also serves as a valuable analytical tool for evaluating game balance and strategic principles.

Abstract: WallGo is a recently introduced strategic board game popularized by the 2025 Netflix series The Devil's Plan. Although played on a small 7 x 7 board, its combination of stone movement and wall placement yields high game-tree complexity and intricate strategic interactions. Despite its growing popularity, WallGo remains underexplored. This paper presents WallZero, an AlphaZero-based agent for the two-player WallGo setting. We introduce tailored action and feature designs to improve playing performance significantly. In the evaluation, WallZero defeats two professional Go players who participated in this study, securing on average 1.98x more territory per game. Beyond its strength, we use WallZero to assess game fairness and identify key strategies for mastering WallGo. Interestingly, our results show that the opening used in the Netflix series yields a more balanced game. Our code is available at https://rlg.iis.sinica.edu.tw/papers/wallzero.

</details>


### [257] [A homotopy-type-theoretic generalization of neurosymbolic inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17851)
*Fernando Zhapa-Camacho,Robert Hoehndorf*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper reformulates neurosymbolic (NeSy) computation by replacing set-theoretic foundations with homotopy type theory (HoTT), preserving symmetry and proof-relevance information that sets discard. The resulting belief-weighted homotopy cardinality naturally handles reasoning shortcuts, yielding a closed-form symmetry-invariant concept posterior that matches or exceeds ensemble methods on MNIST benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard neurosymbolic systems compute a belief-weighted sum over a set of σ-structures, but sets deliberately forget two critical pieces of information: (1) when structures are identical up to symmetries of the theory, and (2) how many distinct proofs witness a query. This information loss causes NeSy systems to mishandle reasoning shortcuts — spurious correlations that models exploit instead of learning intended concepts. The authors aim to restore this lost structure using type theory.

Method: The authors develop a HoTT-based framework from scratch for NeSy systems, replacing sets with types (specifically groupoids/1-types). The key technical move is replacing the classical belief-weighted sum with a belief-weighted homotopy cardinality, which counts each object inversely proportional to its automorphism group size. They prove a conservativity theorem showing recovery of the classical functional when symmetries are trivial, and demonstrate that the symmetry exposed by their framework exactly captures reasoning-shortcut structure. This yields a closed-form, symmetry-invariant concept posterior obtained by averaging a single model over the symmetry group.

Result: On MNIST reasoning-shortcut benchmarks (e.g., colored MNIST variants where color spuriously correlates with digit labels), the proposed single-model wrapper achieves better calibration than diversity-trained ensembles while preserving label accuracy and identifiable concepts. The symmetry-invariant posterior is computable in closed form without expensive ensembling or expressive density estimation.

Conclusion: Reframing NeSy computation in homotopy type theory provides a principled account of reasoning shortcuts through symmetry. The framework yields practical benefits: a simple, theoretically-grounded single-model method that outperforms ensemble baselines on shortcut benchmarks, with freely available code.

Abstract: A wide range of neurosymbolic (NeSy) systems compute one functional: a belief-weighted sum of a logical quantity over a space of $σ$-structures, of which weighted model counting, fuzzy logic, and probabilistic logic are special cases. This account is built on sets, and a set deliberately forgets two things that are important for NeSy: when two $σ$-structures are the same up to a symmetry of the theory, and how many distinct proofs witness a query. Replacing the underlying sets by types, in the sense of homotopy type theory, preserves this information, and turns this functional into a belief-weighted homotopy cardinality, a notion of size that counts each object in inverse proportion to its symmetries. We develop the framework from scratch for NeSy systems, prove a conservativity theorem that recovers the classical functional when symmetries are trivial, and show that the symmetry our framework exposes is exactly the one behind reasoning shortcuts. The payoff is concrete: the shortcut-aware concept posterior that recent methods reach by ensembling or expressive density estimation is the only symmetry-invariant point of the confusion-set simplex, computable in closed form by averaging a single model over the symmetry group. On MNIST reasoning-shortcut benchmarks this single-model wrapper is better calibrated than a diversity-trained ensemble, while leaving label accuracy and identifiable concepts untouched. Code is freely available at https://github.com/bio-ontology-research-group/hott-nesy.

</details>


### [258] [FlowRAG: Synergizing Explicit Reasoning via Frequency-Aware Multi-Granularity Graph Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17856)
*Bihao Zhan,Zongsheng Cao,Jie Zhou,Bo Zhang,Liang He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FlowRAG introduces a semantic-aware retrieval framework that uses a quad-level heterogeneous graph (passages, summaries, sentences, entities) with dual-granularity activation and frequency-weighted flow routing to improve multi-hop reasoning in GraphRAG, achieving SOTA on complex reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GraphRAG methods primarily rely on entity-based graphs with implicit semantic relevance propagation, leading to two key failures: (1) under-retrieval when user queries are abstract and semantically sparse at the entity level, and (2) brittle multi-hop reasoning where noisy activations derail entity-to-entity transitions, corrupting the inferred relation chain and producing unreliable conclusions.

Method: FlowRAG constructs a quad-level heterogeneous graph over passages, summaries, sentences, and entities, where summary nodes act as coarse semantic hubs. At retrieval time, a dual-granularity activation module combines summary-query alignment with sentence-level matching to robustly activate relevant entities under paraphrase and abstraction. A frequency-aware weighted flow module then routes relevance through entity-passage links weighted by within-passage term frequency, pruning noisy connections and extracting high-confidence reasoning paths as an explicit logic skeleton for generation.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlowRAG achieves state-of-the-art performance on complex reasoning benchmarks.

Conclusion: FlowRAG effectively addresses the under-retrieval and brittle multi-hop reasoning limitations of prior GraphRAG methods by combining semantic-aware dual-granularity retrieval with frequency-weighted flow routing, yielding robust and reliable reasoning for knowledge-intensive tasks.

Abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) is effective for knowledge-intensive and multi-hop query tasks; however, many existing methods primarily seed entity-based graphs and rely on implicit semantic relevance propagation. This often (i) under-retrieves when user queries are abstract and semantically sparse at the entity level, and (ii) suffers from brittle multi-hop reasoning, where noisy activations can derail entity-to-entity transitions and corrupt the inferred relation chain, yielding unreliable conclusions. To this end, we propose \texttt{FlowRAG}, a semantic-aware retrieval framework that improves both semantic recall and explicit reasoning. Specifically, \texttt{FlowRAG} constructs a quad-level heterogeneous graph over passages, summaries, sentences, and entities, where summary nodes serve as a coarse semantic hub. At retrieval time, a dual-granularity activation module combines summary--query alignment with sentence-level matching to activate relevant entities under paraphrase and abstraction robustly. We then introduce a frequency-aware weighted flow module that routes relevance through entity--passage links weighted by within-passage term frequency, pruning noisy connections and extracting high-confidence reasoning paths as an explicit logic skeleton for generation. Extensive experiments show that \texttt{FlowRAG} obtains state-of-the-art performance on complex reasoning benchmarks.

</details>


### [259] [StepGuard: Guarding Web Navigation via Single-Step Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17871)
*Zhihao Cui,Yuchen Zhang,Xiyang Sun,Yaxiong Wang,Li Zhu,Jinpeng Hu,Liu Liu,Mengjia Li,Yujiao Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: StepGuard is a web navigation framework that combines Dynamic Dual-Policy Optimization (DDPO) to resolve reward conflicts between navigation and answering, and Confidence-Guided Adaptive Navigation Reflection (CANR) to calibrate per-step errors via confidence estimation and contrastive self-correction. It achieves state-of-the-art on standard benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing web navigation agents suffer from two key problems: (1) reward entanglement/conflict between navigation exploration and question-answering objectives, and (2) single-step fragility caused by error propagation and reward misalignment. These issues degrade both navigation and answer accuracy.

Method: StepGuard consists of two main components: (1) DDPO — dynamically switches between a navigation-first policy (exploration) and an answer-first policy (QA), mitigating reward conflict; (2) CANR — estimates per-step confidence scores, triggers reflection only when confidence is low, and employs contrastive rewards to drive self-correction of single-step inaccuracies.

Result: StepGuard achieves significant improvements in both navigation accuracy and answer accuracy, establishing new state-of-the-art results on standard web navigation benchmarks.

Conclusion: By addressing reward entanglement and single-step error propagation through DDPO and CANR, StepGuard provides a robust framework for web navigation agents, advancing the state of the art.

Abstract: Web navigation requires agents to follow natural language goals, interact with web pages, and produce accurate answers. While recent advances leverage vision-language models and reinforcement learning, existing methods still suffer from single-step fragility due to reward misalignment and error propagation. To tackle the reward entanglement, we design Dynamic Dual-Policy Optimization (DDPO), which dynamically switches between a navigation-first mode for exploration and an answer-first mode for question-answering to mitigate reward conflict. To calibrate the single-step error, we propose Confidence-Guided Adaptive Navigation Reflection (CANR), a mechanism that estimates per-step confidence, triggers reflection only when necessary, and uses contrastive rewards to encourage self-correction to calibrate the single-step inaccuracy. With the above as the main components, we finally develop our StepGuard, a new framework of Guarding Web Navigation via Single-Step Calibration. Experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves navigation and answer accuracy, setting new state-of-the-art performance on standard web navigation benchmarks.

</details>


### [260] [Structural Preservation and the Logical Expressiveness of Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17882)
*Przemysław Andrzej Wałęga,Bernardo Cuenca Grau*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper characterizes the logical expressiveness of classes of GNN classifiers based on structural preservation properties (embeddings, injective homomorphisms, homomorphisms), establishing correspondences with fragments of graded modal logic. The approach introduces a novel well-quasi-order result for bounded-height trees to obtain finite representations of unravelling-invariant classes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work established GNN-logic correspondences by fixing specific architectural choices (aggregation, combination, activation functions), yielding tight but narrow results tied to particular GNN architectures. The authors aim to provide a semantic, architecture-independent characterization of GNN expressiveness, capturing broad classes of GNNs through structural preservation properties rather than syntactic architectural constraints.

Method: The authors adopt a semantic approach: they classify GNNs by the structural properties under which their classifications are preserved—namely embeddings (extensions), injective homomorphisms, and homomorphisms. For each preservation property, they identify the corresponding fragment of graded modal logic: existential graded modal logic, its existential-positive fragment, and existential-positive modal logic. Technically, they prove a new well-quasi-order result for trees of bounded height, enabling finite representations of classes invariant under unravelling. This yields characterizations of logical expressiveness that hold independently of architectural choices, while also demonstrating that each class admits a concrete GNN architecture matching that expressiveness.

Result: The paper proves that: (1) GNN classifiers preserved under embeddings correspond exactly to existential graded modal logic; (2) those preserved under injective homomorphisms correspond to the existential-positive fragment of graded modal logic; (3) those preserved under homomorphisms correspond to existential-positive modal logic. Each class admits a GNN architecture achieving the same expressiveness, bridging the architecture-independent semantic characterization with constructive realizability.

Conclusion: The semantic perspective on GNN expressiveness, grounded in structural preservation properties and modal logic fragments, provides a robust, architecture-independent framework for understanding what broad classes of GNNs can express. The well-quasi-order result for bounded-height trees is a key technical contribution with potential applications beyond this work.

Abstract: Bridges between graph neural networks (GNNs) and logical formalisms have been established by fixing architectural choices, such as the types of aggregation, combination, and activation functions. These choices define restricted classes of GNNs for which tight correspondences with logical formalisms can be obtained, by showing that logical formulae can be translated into equivalent GNNs and, conversely, that GNNs can be translated into equivalent formulae.
  In this paper we take a semantic perspective by establishing the logical expressiveness of classes of GNN classifiers that are preserved under structural properties: embeddings (extensions), injective homomorphisms, and homomorphisms. We show that, for each such property, there exists a fragment of graded modal logic characterising the class of GNNs. In particular, preservation under embeddings, injective homomorphisms, and homomorphisms corresponds to existential graded modal logic, its existential-positive fragment, and existential-positive modal logic, respectively. These results characterise the expressiveness of broad classes of GNNs independently of specific architectural choices, but we also show that each of these classes admits a GNN architecture of the same expressiveness.
  Technically, our approach uses a new well-quasi-order result for trees of bounded height, yielding finite representations of unravelling-invariant classes.

</details>


### [261] [MathVis-Fine: Aligning Visual Supervision with Necessity via Progressive Dependency-Guided Training for Multimodal Mathematical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17888)
*Wanshi Xu,Haokun Zhao,Haidong Yuan,Songjun Cao,Long Ma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a framework for fine-grained visual dependency modeling in multimodal mathematical reasoning, introducing the MathVis-Fine dataset with visual dependency ratings and a two-stage progressive training paradigm that balances answer correctness and visual grounding rewards based on sample-specific visual dependency levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal CoT methods treat visual inputs homogeneously, ignoring sample-specific text-image dependencies. This leads to coarse-grained, non-adaptive visual supervision and inaccurate training feedback due to uniformly applied visual rewards without accounting for complementary relationships among inputs.

Method: (1) Construction of MathVis-Fine dataset with fine-grained visual annotations and visual dependency ratings. (2) A two-stage progressive visual enhancement training paradigm that dynamically balances answer correctness rewards and visual grounding rewards according to each sample's intrinsic visual dependency level, mitigating reward bias.

Result: Extensive experiments show that MathVis-Fine effectively enhances visual perception progressively based on visual dependency, yielding improved multimodal mathematical reasoning performance.

Conclusion: The proposed framework offers a more precise training approach for multimodal mathematical reasoning by modeling fine-grained visual dependencies, addressing key limitations of homogeneous visual treatment in prior CoT methods.

Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has extended from purely linguistic domains to multimodal scenarios; however, existing approaches often treat visual inputs as homogeneous or auxiliary signals, failing to capture the intricate and sample-specific dependencies between text and images in mathematical problem-solving. This gives rise to two core issues: first, the supervisory signals for visual content are generalized and coarse-grained, lacking adaptation to the actual necessity of visual information in each sample; second, training feedback becomes inaccurate when visual rewards are uniformly applied without distinguishing the complementary relationships among inputs. These limitations hinder models from achieving precise multimodal reasoning. In this work, we propose a framework for modeling fine-grained visual dependencies in mathematical reasoning. We first construct the MathVis-Fine dataset, augmenting fine-grained visual annotations with visual dependency ratings. Building upon this dataset, we introduce a two-stage progressive visual enhancement training paradigm that balances answer correctness rewards and visual grounding rewards according to the intrinsic visual dependency level of each sample, thereby mitigating reward bias and improving supervision accuracy. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the MathVis-Fine framework effectively enhances visual perception progressively based on visual dependency, offering a more precise training framework for multimodal mathematical reasoning. We will release the dataset upon acceptance.

</details>


### [262] [Learn to Quantify Social Interaction with Constraints for Pedestrian Walking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17897)
*Xiaodan Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes "Learn to Cluster," a probabilistic latent variable generative method that discovers, quantifies, and categorizes social interaction patterns among pedestrians directly from trajectory data. These learned interaction clusters serve as interpretable labels and are integrated into trajectory prediction models, improving long-term human path forecasting in crowds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing pedestrian trajectory prediction methods consider social interactions but fail to explicitly identify what kinds of interactions occur and how they influence pedestrian decision-making. Social interactions are massive, hard to label, and difficult to quantify manually, limiting both interpretability and robustness.

Method: A probabilistic latent variable generative approach that clusters social interactions directly from sequential trajectory observations without requiring manual labels. The method learns interaction patterns in an unsupervised manner and is designed to scale to an arbitrary number of pedestrians. The learned latent variables serve as categorical labels for social interactions and are naturally integrated into the training process of a trajectory prediction model.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple trajectory prediction benchmarks show the method successfully learns meaningful social interaction patterns and effectively integrates them into pedestrian trajectory prediction.

Conclusion: Learning to cluster social interactions in a label-free, generative manner yields interpretable interaction categories that enhance pedestrian trajectory forecasting performance.

Abstract: Long-term human path forecasting in crowds is critical for autonomous moving platforms (like autonomous driving cars and social robots) to avoid collision and make high-quality planning. Although the current research take into account social interactions for prediction, they don't reveal the exact kinds of social interactions happened among people and how the social interactions affect the decision-making process of pedestrians, which further limits its robustness. Social interactions in pedestrian walking are intuitively massive and hard to label and quantify. In this paper, we explore creatively to quantify and interpret how pedestrians interact with others by proposing Learn to Cluster. Our clustering social interactions is probabilistic latent variable generative, learning directly from sequential trajectory observations, scalable to arbitrary number of pedestrians. Learn to cluster is label-free and can be naturally integrated into the training process of the prediction model. The latent variables will then serve as 'labels' to categorize social interactions. Extensive experiments over several trajectory prediction benchmarks demonstrate that our method is able to learn the patterns of social interactions and effectively integrate the patterns to pedestrian trajectory prediction.

</details>


### [263] [DiagFlowBench: Evaluating How Language Models Handle Off-Procedure Inputs in Grounded Diagnostic Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17904)
*Guillermo Gil de Avalle,Laura Maruster,Shaina Raza,Christos Emmanouilidis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DiagFlowBench introduces a benchmark of 1,676 multi-turn diagnostic conversations from 50 industrial flowcharts, testing how language models handle out-of-scope queries in maintenance settings. Evaluation of ten models reveals that grounding reduces hallucination but introduces a new failure mode: confidently selecting real but contextually inappropriate steps, exposing a critical vulnerability in advisory systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models deployed as maintenance advisors typically use procedural documentation to ground responses and prevent hallucination. However, real operators frequently ask out-of-scope questions mid-conversation, and existing benchmarks fail to evaluate how models recognize and abstain from such queries. The paper addresses this gap by systematically studying model behavior when faced with plausible but unsupported requests.

Method: The authors construct DiagFlowBench by converting 50 authentic industrial diagnostic flowcharts from a consumer manufacturer into 1,676 multi-turn conversations. Each conversation deliberately contrasts compliant, in-scope utterances with out-of-scope ones, requiring models to detect when a query cannot be answered from the provided documentation. Ten commercial and open-weight models are then evaluated on their abstention behavior and failure modes.

Result: Models exhibit high variability in abstention rates. Rather than generating fabrications (hallucinations), models predominantly fail by selecting a real, grounded step that is contextually inadequate — a "mapped but wrong" response. This advice carries the authority of approved documentation yet is incorrect for the situation, making it a particularly deceptive and dangerous failure mode for grounding systems.

Conclusion: Grounding models in procedural documentation successfully curtails hallucination but introduces a subtler vulnerability: plausible yet contextually misaligned recommendations drawn from real steps. DiagFlowBench reveals that current models struggle with out-of-scope recognition in multi-turn diagnostic dialogue, highlighting an urgent need for robust abstention mechanisms and better benchmark coverage of this realistic operational dynamic.

Abstract: Language models increasingly serve as advisory systems in maintenance operations. To prevent hallucination, recent systems ground these models in procedural documentation to constrain them to approved steps. In practice, however, operator queries frequently stray from this path, requiring models to recognise out-of-scope inputs mid-conversation, a dynamic that current benchmarks rarely prioritise. We introduce DiagFlowBench, a dataset of 50 industrial diagnostic flowcharts from a consumer manufacturer converted into 1,676 multi-turn conversations that contrast compliant with out-of-scope utterances. Evaluating a panel of ten commercial and open-weight models reveals high variability in abstention rates, with models commonly selecting a real but contextually inadequate step rather than fabricating facts. The inherent plausibility and authority of this mapped but wrong advice exposes a challenging vulnerability for grounding systems.

</details>


### [264] [PreAct: Computer-Using Agents that Get Faster on Repeated Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17929)
*Bojie Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PreAct compiles successful agent task executions into small state-machine programs that can be replayed 8.5–13× faster without per-step LM calls, using screen-state verification at each step and an independent evaluator to gate program admission to the store.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Computer-using agents solve every task from scratch — re-reading the screen, re-reasoning each action, and incurring full LLM inference costs on every run — even for repetitive tasks. This is inefficient in both time and compute.

Method: PreAct compiles a successful agent trajectory into a state-machine program (states = screen checks, transitions = actions). On reuse, it replays the program directly with per-step screen-state verification; if the screen diverges from expectations, control reverts to the agent. A compiled program is admitted to the store only if an independent evaluator confirms (from a clean-slate re-run) that the program actually solved the task. A fallback exploration strategy is used when no stored program fits.

Result: Replay is 8.5–13× faster than the original agent with no per-step LM calls. The store-time evaluator check improves robustness, yielding gains of 1.75–2.6 tasks across mobile, desktop, and web benchmarks. PreAct matches a strong record-and-replay baseline when using afresh exploration fallback. Prompt wording, runtime guardrails, and the choice of LM vs. embedding-based retrieval had negligible impact.

Conclusion: Safe, verified replay of compiled agent programs dramatically reduces inference cost and latency for repeated tasks, and the independent evaluator gate is critical for preventing faulty program accumulation in the store.

Abstract: Computer-using agents drive real software through the screen -- clicking and typing -- but they solve every task from scratch: asked to repeat a task, an agent re-reads the screen, re-reasons every tap, and pays the full cost again. We present PreAct, which lets such an agent get faster on tasks it has done before. The first time it succeeds, PreAct compiles the run into a small state-machine program-states that check the screen, transitions that act-and on later runs replays it directly instead of invoking the agent 8.5-13x faster, with no per-step language-model calls. Replay is not blind: at each step PreAct checks that the screen matches what the program expects before acting, and hands control back to the agent the moment something is off.
  PreAct applies the same discipline when deciding what to keep: a freshly compiled program enters the store only if, re-run from a clean state, an independent evaluator confirms it solved the task-catching programs that replay to their last step yet leave the task undone. Across a mobile, a desktop, and a web benchmark, this store-time check separates repeated runs that improve from ones that degrade as faulty programs accumulate, worth 1.75-2.6 tasks per benchmark, the same direction on all three; a fallback that explores afresh when no program fits brings PreAct level with a strong record-and-replay baseline. We also report what did not matter: prompt wording, runtime guardrails, and whether a language model or a plain embedding retriever selects which program to reuse.

</details>


### [265] [How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17930)
*Jessica McFadyen,Ole Jorgensen,Harry Coppock,Kevin Wei,Cozmin Ududec*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Frontier LLMs evaluated on 7 challenging benchmarks show performance is highly sensitive to inference-time compute allocation. Larger token budgets, context compaction, and repeated submissions substantially improve scores. Fixed-budget evaluations increasingly understate true capability, especially for newer models. The authors argue evaluations should report performance as a function of inference compute rather than at a single restrictive budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI evaluations are shifting toward harder, tool-use-intensive tasks, making performance increasingly sensitive to inference compute. Yet many benchmarks report scores at a single restrictive budget, potentially conflating evaluation design limitations with model capability. The authors aim to demonstrate that fixed-budget evaluations can systematically understate frontier model performance, with implications for safety and policy assessments.

Method: Twelve frontier language models were evaluated across seven challenging benchmarks (software engineering, mathematics, medicine, cybersecurity). A controlled setup applied three inference-scaling interventions: (1) larger token budgets, (2) context compaction, and (3) repeated submission attempts with either self-guidance or minimal correctness feedback. Performance was measured across varying compute budgets to assess sensitivity.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Larger token budgets substantially improved performance on cybersecurity, FrontierMath, Humanity's Last Exam, and TerminalBench. (2) Fixed-budget evaluations increasingly understate frontier capability as models advance; newer models unlock harder tasks at larger budgets. (3) Benchmarks differ in which inference-scaling methods help most — repeated submission broadly improves performance, while the value of larger budgets, external feedback, and parallel attempts varies by benchmark.

Conclusion: Benchmark scores are protocol-dependent. Evaluations should report capability as a function of inference-time compute, explicitly specify protocol choices, and compare models over a shared compute range at matched budgets — especially in safety- and policy-relevant settings.

Abstract: AI evaluations are shifting toward harder tasks that benefit from longer trajectories involving tool use and iterative problem solving. As a result, performance is increasingly sensitive to the amount and allocation of compute available at test time ("inference compute"). Yet many evaluations still report performance at a single restrictive budget, meaning that low scores may reflect the evaluation setup rather than the model's underlying capability. To test this, we evaluate up to 12 frontier language models on seven challenging benchmarks spanning software engineering, mathematics, medicine, and cybersecurity. We use a controlled setup combining three simple inference-scaling interventions: larger token budgets, context compaction, and repeated submission attempts, guided either by the model itself or by minimal correctness feedback. We find three main results. First, larger token budgets substantially improve performance on benchmarks across multiple domains, including cybersecurity, FrontierMath, Humanity's Last Exam, and TerminalBench. Second, fixed-budget evaluations can increasingly understate frontier capability as models advance. Newer models reach higher performance at large budgets, where they unlock harder tasks and solve them more reliably. Third, benchmarks differ in which inference-scaling methods help most: repeated submission broadly improves performance, but the value of larger token budgets, external feedback, and parallel attempts varies by benchmark. Overall, our results show that benchmark scores are protocol-dependent. We therefore argue that evaluations should report capability as a function of inference-time compute, specify protocol choices explicitly, and compare model generations over a large shared compute range at matched budgets, especially in safety- or policy-relevant settings.

</details>


### [266] [Small Initialization Matters for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17945)
*Liangkai Hang,Junjie Yao,Zhiyu Li,Feiyu Xiong,Hongkang Yang,Zhi-Qin John Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Smaller parameter initialization scales act as a gene-like determinant that consistently improves LLM pretraining, especially on reasoning tasks. The authors identify a critical initialization point balancing reasoning and training, reveal that small initialization drives a "compression-first, expansion-later" developmental trajectory, and propose a simple γ-initialization rule as a cost-free intervention for better model capacity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to understand how intelligence emerges in LLMs by treating them as tractable scientific objects, rather than merely engineering artifacts. They challenge the dominant narrative that scale, data, and architecture are the primary drivers of progress, proposing instead that parameter initialization plays a fundamental, gene-like role in determining model capacity and training outcomes.

Method: The paper systematically varies parameter initialization scale across different model sizes and tasks. It identifies two widely used empirical settings that mask the benefits of small initialization, relaxes them to restore favorable scaling, and uncovers a critical initialization threshold. Mechanistic analysis includes tracking the developmental trajectory of parameter structures (condensation-to-expansion), and token-level analysis comparing performance on trivial vs. context-constrained predictions.

Result: Reducing initialization scale consistently improves pretraining, with largest gains on reasoning-demanding tasks. Small initialization produces a distinct trajectory where parameters first form low-complexity structures, then expand into richer representations — giving concrete form to "compression is intelligence." Gains concentrate on non-trivial, context-constrained token predictions. The proposed γ-initialization rule (defaulting to small initialization) is a near-zero-cost intervention effective across model scales.

Conclusion: Parameter initialization is an underappreciated, gene-like determinant of emergent intelligence in LLMs. Small initialization is a simple, cost-free intervention that reliably improves pretraining and reasoning. The "compression first, expansion later" developmental trajectory provides a mechanistic lens for understanding how intelligence emerges, and the γ-initialization rule offers practical guidance for training stronger models.

Abstract: Large language models provide a tractable system for asking how intelligence itself emerges, rather than only how LLMs can be engineered. Although progress is usually attributed to scale, data and architecture, we show that parameter initialization is a gene-like determinant of training and, in particular, of model capacity. Reducing the initialization scale consistently improves pretraining, with the largest gains on reasoning-demanding tasks. We identify two widely used empirical settings that restrain the advantage of small initialization, and show how relaxing them restores favorable scaling. We further uncover a critical initialization that balances the reasoning and training. Mechanistically, small initialization drives a distinct developmental trajectory: parameters first condense into low-complexity structures and later expand into richer representations, giving concrete form to the idea that compression is intelligence. Token-level analyses show that the gains concentrate on non-trivial, context-constrained predictions rather than all tokens uniformly. These results motivate a simple $γ$-initialization rule: expose initialization rage as an explicit knob and use small initialization by default, an almost cost-free intervention that improves pretraining and strengthens reasoning across model scales.

</details>


### [267] [MoCo-AIS: A Contrastive Learning Framework for Similarity Computation of Vessel Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17978)
*Ruixin Song,Md Mahbub Alam,Zahra Sadeghi,Amilcar Soares,José F. Rodrigues-Jr,Gabriel Spadon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MoCo-AIS proposes a unified self-supervised framework based on Momentum Contrast (MoCo) for learning vessel trajectory embeddings, enabling consistent benchmarking of DL models for trajectory similarity without requiring extensive labeled data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional distance-based trajectory similarity measures are computationally expensive. Supervised learning-based approaches rely on labels derived from these same measures and tend to reproduce them, limiting generalization. Self-supervised contrastive learning offers a solution but currently lacks a unified framework, making it difficult to fairly compare different deep learning models for consistent trajectory representation.

Method: The authors propose MoCo-AIS, a unified framework built on the Momentum Contrast (MoCo) paradigm. It formulates trajectory similarity learning using positive and negative trajectory pairs. The framework is evaluated by integrating a diverse set of leading deep learning models and testing them on large-scale, real-world AIS vessel-tracking datasets that span varied navigation behaviors and operating conditions.

Result: The MoCo-AIS framework significantly improves similarity learning performance over existing baselines and serves as an effective benchmarking platform for evaluating trajectory representation models.

Conclusion: MoCo-AIS provides a standardized self-supervised learning framework for vessel trajectory similarity, demonstrating that the MoCo paradigm effectively unifies trajectory embedding learning while enabling consistent comparison across diverse DL architectures.

Abstract: Trajectory similarity is a fundamental task in analyzing mobility patterns, essential for applications such as route pattern extraction, mobility prediction, and anomaly detection. Traditional distance-based measures for computing similarity incur high computational cost, driving the adoption of lightweight learning-based approaches. Supervised methods rely on extensive labels derived from traditional distance measures and often reproduce these metrics, which limits generalization. While self-supervised learning addresses this issue through contrastive learning, it lacks a unified framework, making it difficult to compare deep learning (DL) models for consistent trajectory representation. Accordingly, this paper presents MoCo-AIS, a unified framework for learning vessel trajectory embeddings based on the Momentum Contrast (MoCo) paradigm, which formulates similarity learning through positive and negative trajectory pairs. Within this framework, we evaluate a diverse set of leading DL models on large-scale, real-world vessel-tracking AIS datasets that capture diverse navigation behaviors and operating conditions. Results demonstrate that our framework significantly improves similarity learning over existing baselines, while providing a benchmarking platform for evaluating trajectory representation models.

</details>


### [268] [STAR: SpatioTemporal Adaptive Reward Allocation for Text-to-Image RL Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17979)
*Jinjie Shen,Wei Deng,Xian Hu,Daiguo Zhou,Jian Luan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: STAR proposes a spatiotemporally adaptive reward allocation method for RL post-training of text-to-image models, directing stronger policy updates to the latent regions and denoising steps that most affect text alignment, achieving state-of-the-art results on GenEval, OCR, and PickScore.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL post-training methods apply a single scalar reward uniformly across the entire denoising trajectory, ignoring the temporal and spatial structure inherent in text-to-image generation. Different denoising steps serve distinct generation stages, and text-alignment-critical content often occupies only a localized portion of the image. This granularity mismatch prevents policy updates from focusing on the components that truly influence the reward.

Method: STAR leverages text-image cross-attention maps within the generative model to identify core content regions relevant to user-specified prompt elements. It constructs dynamic spatial allocation maps that vary across both denoising timesteps and rollouts, then allocates group-relative advantages preferentially to more relevant latent regions. A spatially resolved policy objective applies stronger updates to these high-importance regions, all with negligible computational overhead.

Result: Using Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium as the base model, STAR achieves 0.9759 on GenEval, 0.9757 on OCR text rendering, and 23.60 on PickScore, improving compositional semantic alignment, text rendering, and human preference optimization without modifying the external reward source.

Conclusion: Spatiotemporally adaptive reward allocation effectively addresses the granularity mismatch in RL post-training for text-to-image models. By focusing policy updates on the most reward-relevant regions and timesteps, STAR yields consistent improvements across multiple evaluation dimensions while introducing minimal computational cost.

Abstract: Existing RL post-training methods for text-to-image generation usually convert the final-image reward into a single scalar advantage and apply it with the same strength to the entire generative trajectory. However, text-to-image generation naturally has temporal and spatial structure: different denoising steps are responsible for different generation stages, and the content that truly determines text alignment often appears only in part of the image. This granularity mismatch makes it difficult for policy updates to focus on the generative components that actually affect the reward. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{SpatioTemporal Adaptive Reward (STAR) Allocation} for RL post-training of text-to-image diffusion and flow models. STAR uses text-image attention inside the generative model and starts from the core content that the user truly cares about in the prompt. It constructs spatial allocation maps that dynamically vary across denoising steps and rollouts, and allocates the same group-relative advantage to more relevant latent regions with almost no additional computational overhead. STAR then applies stronger policy updates to these regions through a spatially resolved policy objective. We use Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium as the base model and evaluate on three tasks: GenEval, OCR text rendering, and PickScore. Experimental results show that STAR improves compositional semantic alignment, text rendering, and preference optimization without changing the external reward source, achieving $\mathbf{0.9759}$, $\mathbf{0.9757}$, and $\mathbf{23.60}$ on GenEval, OCR, and PickScore, respectively.

</details>


### [269] [LLM Consumer Behavior Theory: Foundations of a Novel Research Field](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18005)
*Manon Reusens,Sofie Goethals,David Martens*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces LLM Consumer Behavior Theory, a new field that formalizes how LLM-based agents make consumption decisions, how human preferences are reflected in agent actions, and how these decisions aggregate into market demand, while identifying open research questions on alignment, preference representation, and market dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents making consumption decisions for users, traditional consumer theory—which models humans as primary decision-makers—faces fundamental challenges. There is a need to formalize how agentic markets operate and unify fragmented research on LLM decision-making, human behavior simulation, and preference elicitation under an economic framework.

Method: The authors draw on classical and behavioral economics alongside advances in Natural Language Processing to conceptually formalize: (1) how human preferences are reflected and acted upon by LLM-based agents, and (2) how agent-level decisions aggregate into market demand. They unify previously fragmented literature under a common economic lens and highlight where traditional assumptions (rationality, heterogeneity) may break down in agentic markets. This is a theoretical/scoping paper without empirical validation.

Result: The paper does not provide empirical results. Instead, it delineates the scope of LLM consumer behavior as a new field of study and identifies key open research questions concerning alignment, preference representation, and market dynamics in agentic markets.

Conclusion: LLM Consumer Behavior Theory is proposed as a necessary new subfield at the intersection of economics and NLP. The paper calls for further research into how traditional economic assumptions hold in agentic markets and highlights unresolved issues in alignment and preference aggregation that warrant empirical investigation.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that make consumption decisions on behalf of users. This shift raises fundamental questions for consumer theory, which has traditionally modeled humans as the primary decision-makers. In this paper, we introduce LLM Consumer Behavior Theory, a new field of study concerned with analyzing consumer behavior in agentic markets. Drawing on classical and behavioral economics alongside recent advances in Natural Language Processing, we formalize how human preferences are reflected and acted upon by LLM-based agents, and how agent-level decisions aggregate into market demand. We unify previously fragmented literature on LLM decision-making, human behavior simulation, and preference elicitation under a common economic lens, highlighting where assumptions, such as rationality and heterogeneity, may fail in agentic markets. Rather than providing empirical validation, this paper outlines the scope of LLM consumer behavior and identifies open research questions related to alignment, preference representation, and market dynamics.

</details>


### [270] [PseudoBench: Measuring How Agentic Auto-Research Fuels Pseudoscience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18060)
*Xinyang Liao,Lingyu Li,Huacan Liu,Tianle Gu,Yang Yao,Tong Zhu,Yan Teng,Yingchun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PseudoBench evaluates whether LLM-based research agents can resist pseudoscience. Testing seven SOTA agents across 200 claim-evidence pairs in five domains, the study finds near-zero refusal rates and a maximum resistance of only 27.4%, with stronger agents packaging pseudoscience in more sophisticated language, raising concerns about scientific alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM-based agents increasingly participate in autonomous scientific research, there is a critical risk that these systems will generate plausible-sounding but pseudoscientific studies that contaminate academic literature and undermine trust in science. The authors aim to systematically assess whether current agentic systems possess any inherent safeguards against pseudoscience.

Method: The authors introduce PseudoBench, an adversarial benchmark comprising 200 curated pseudoscientific claim-evidence pairs spanning five domains. Agents are evaluated through an end-to-end research pipeline covering experimental design, execution, and manuscript writing. Seven state-of-the-art agents are tested on their ability to identify and resist pseudoscientific narratives, with resistance measured via refusal rates and other behavioral indicators.

Result: All seven tested agents show near-zero refusal rates when confronted with pseudoscientific premises. The highest observed resistance rate is only 27.4%. More capable agents tend to produce more persuasive and scientifically sophisticated reports that reinforce pseudoscientific claims, paradoxically increasing their apparent credibility rather than challenging them.

Conclusion: Current LLM-based research agents exhibit an alarming capacity to amplify pseudoscience by generating convincingly formatted but misleading scientific outputs. This highlights an urgent need for "scientific alignment" — training and safeguards that enable agents to recognize and resist pseudoscience — before these systems are widely deployed in autonomous research roles.

Abstract: As Large Language Model based agents enter autonomous scientific research, their ability to resist pseudoscience becomes increasingly important. Otherwise, such systems may rapidly generate plausible yet misleading studies that contaminate academic literature and erode trust in science. We present PseudoBench, an adversarial benchmark for evaluating whether agentic auto-research systems can identify and resist pseudoscientific narratives. PseudoBench contains 200 curated pseudoscientific claim-evidence pairs across five domains and evaluates agents through an end-to-end research pipeline from experiments to writing. Testing seven state-of-the-art agents, we find that current systems readily produce persuasive reports that align with pseudoscientific premises with near-zero refusal rates and the highest resistance of only 27.4%. Stronger agents risk packaging pseudoscience in more sophisticated scientific language, increasing its apparent credibility. These findings reveal an alarming capacity to fuel pseudoscience, calling for scientific alignment before widespread deployment.

</details>


### [271] [Agentic AI-based Framework for Mitigating Premature Diagnostic Handoff and Silent Hallucination in Healthcare Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18068)
*Divyansh Srivastava,Shreya Ghosh,Anshul Verma,Rajkumar Buyya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multi-agent medical reasoning framework replaces LLM-as-a-judge routing with deterministic orchestration constraints, using a neuro-symbolic gate to enforce OLDCARTS protocol completeness and an epistemic uncertainty quantification gate to intercept divergent diagnoses, achieving 49.3% precision (an 11.3 pp gain) and showing a negative correlation between protocol completeness and semantic entropy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical conversational agents suffer from two critical failure modes: premature diagnostic handoff (rushing to a diagnosis before gathering sufficient clinical information) and silent clinical hallucinations (confidently delivering incorrect diagnoses that go undetected). Existing LLM-as-a-judge routing approaches fail to reliably prevent these errors, motivating the need for more constrained, safety-oriented orchestration mechanisms.

Method: The authors propose a multi-agent framework with two deterministic safety gates: (1) a neuro-symbolic state-tracking gate that enforces completeness of the OLDCARTS clinical protocol (Onset, Location, Duration, Character, Aggravating/Alleviating factors, Radiation, Timing, Severity), blocking diagnostic transitions until all eight dimensions are collected; (2) an epistemic uncertainty quantification gate that computes semantic entropy (H) across K=5 independent diagnostic samples to identify and intercept divergent outputs. The system is evaluated using simulated patient agents powered by llama-3.1-70b-instruct on 150 test cases.

Result: The full architecture achieves 49.3% diagnostic precision, an absolute improvement of 11.3 percentage points over the unconstrained baseline. A statistically significant negative correlation (r = -0.181, p < 0.05) was observed between OLDCARTS completeness (σ) and semantic entropy (H), indicating that more complete structured information gathering is associated with reduced diagnostic uncertainty.

Conclusion: Replacing LLM-as-a-judge routing with deterministic neuro-symbolic orchestration constraints and epistemic UQ can meaningfully improve diagnostic precision and safety in medical conversational agents. Structured clinical protocol adherence (OLDCARTS) may serve as a practical mechanism for reducing diagnostic uncertainty.

Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and multi-agent systems have driven the rise of Agentic AI, showing promise for medical reasoning. However, open-ended conversational agents remain prone to two critical failure modes: premature diagnostic handoff and silent clinical hallucinations that may go undetected before reaching the patient. In this work, we propose a multi-agent framework that addresses both issues by replacing ``LLM-as-a-judge'' routing with deterministic orchestration constraints. The framework incorporates two safety mechanisms. First, a neuro-symbolic state-tracking gate enforces completeness of the OLDCARTS clinical protocol (Onset, Location, Duration, Character, Aggravating/Alleviating factors, Radiation, Timing, and Severity) by blocking diagnostic transitions until all required dimensions are collected. Second, an epistemic uncertainty quantification (UQ) gate computes semantic entropy (H) across K=5 independent diagnostic samples to identify and intercept divergent outputs before delivery.
  We evaluate the system using simulated patient agents powered by the llama-3.1-70b-instruct model on 150 test cases. The full architecture achieves 49.3% diagnostic precision, representing an absolute improvement of 11.3 percentage points over an unconstrained baseline. Additionally, we observe a statistically significant negative correlation (r = -0.181, p < 0.05) between OLDCARTS completeness (σ) and semantic entropy (H), suggesting that structured information gathering is associated with reduced diagnostic uncertainty.

</details>


### [272] [A Unified Framework for Context-Aware and Relation-Aware Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18075)
*Haoyang Zhong,Yifei Sun,Antong Zhang,Chunping Wang,Lei Chen,Yang Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyGRAG introduces a hierarchical graph RAG framework that synthesizes chunk and entity representations through iterative clustering and LLM-based summarization, enabling emergent knowledge retrieval across abstraction levels with dynamic update capabilities, achieving 9.7% accuracy gains on multi-hop reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-based RAG methods (entity-centric and chunk-centric) operate on representations anchored to original text without true knowledge fusion. They retrieve information separately through similarity search, missing emergent understanding that arises from synthesizing contextual and relational information across different granularities.

Method: HyGRAG proposes: (1) hierarchical index structures over hybrid graphs containing both chunk and entity nodes, iteratively clustered with LLM-generated summaries; (2) context- and relation-aware retrieval that searches across all abstraction levels and expands through community membership; (3) dynamic knowledge update via attachment-based algorithms requiring only local re-summarization.

Result: HyGRAG improves average accuracy on multi-hop reasoning tasks by 9.7% compared to baselines, while maintaining reasonable computational efficiency.

Conclusion: The hierarchical hybrid graph approach effectively synthesizes contextual and relational knowledge, overcoming the limitations of single-perspective retrieval in existing graph RAG systems. The framework demonstrates that fusing entity and chunk representations across abstraction levels yields emergent understanding beneficial for complex reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a paradigm for enhancing large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge, yet existing graph-based methods face a fundamental limitation: entity-centric and chunk-centric approaches operate on representations anchored to original text without true knowledge fusion. While entity-centric methods connect logically related content and chunk-centric methods preserve context, both retrieve information separately through similarity search, missing emergent understanding from their synthesis. In this paper, we propose HyGRAG, a hierarchical graph RAG framework that transcends source documents by addressing three core challenges: constructing summaries that genuinely integrate contextual and relational information, leveraging these synthesized representations to access emergent knowledge during retrieval, and efficiently updating hierarchical structures for dynamic corpora. Specifically, we design hierarchical index structures over hybrid graphs with both chunk and entity nodes, then iteratively cluster them and generate LLM-based summaries. Then, we design context and relation-aware retrieval that searches across all abstraction levels while expanding through community membership. Moreover, we enable dynamic knowledge update through attachment-based algorithms with only local re-summarization. Experimental results show that HyGRAG improves the average accuracy of multi-hop reasoning tasks by 9.7%, while maintaining reasonable efficiency.

</details>


### [273] [IsabeLLM: Automated Theorem Proving Applied to Formally Verifying Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18098)
*Elliot Jones,William Knottenbelt*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper enhances IsabeLLM, an automated theorem proving tool for Isabelle, by adding Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), error tracing, and counterexample generation. The authors benchmark the improved version against the original on verifying Bitcoin's Proof of Work consensus protocol.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Formal verification is critical for blockchain systems — particularly consensus protocols like Bitcoin's Proof of Work — which are frequent targets of attacks causing significant financial losses. However, formal verification demands high expertise and effort. AI-assisted theorem proving can democratize and automate this process, making verification more accessible and scalable.

Method: The authors extend IsabeLLM (an LLM-based automated theorem prover for the Isabelle proof assistant) with three key improvements: (1) a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework to supply richer context, (2) error tracing mechanisms, and (3) counterexample generation to guide the LLM toward correct proofs. Compatibility with the latest Isabelle and Sledgehammer versions is also updated for efficiency gains.

Result: The paper presents a comparative performance evaluation between the original IsabeLLM and the enhanced version, specifically measured on their ability to complete verification of Bitcoin's Proof of Work consensus protocol.

Conclusion: While the abstract does not explicitly state the final conclusion, the work implies that augmenting LLM-based theorem provers with RAG, error feedback, and counterexamples improves their capability to formally verify complex, real-world protocols such as blockchain consensus mechanisms.

Abstract: Advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have led AI for Theorem Proving to become a promising means of formally verifying computer systems. Whilst formal verification is traditionally reserved for safety-critical systems due to the required amount of expertise and effort, AI can help to automate a large amount of this workload and make it far more accessible. Blockchain-based systems are becoming increasingly popular and are frequently targeted by malicious actors, often resulting in huge financial losses, highlighting the need to better verify these systems and mitigate vulnerabilities. Arguably the most important component of these systems is the consensus protocol, which allows nodes to agree on decisions in a potentially adversarial environment. In this paper, we improve upon IsabeLLM, the automated theorem proving tool in Isabelle. Namely, we implement a Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, Error tracing and counterexample generation for improved context supplied to the Large Language Model. Compatibility with the latest version of Isabelle and Sledgehammer is also implemented for improved efficiency. We compare the performance of the two versions of IsabeLLM in their ability to complete the verification of Bitcoin's Proof of Work consensus.

</details>


### [274] [Trust the Right Teacher: Quality-Aware Self-Distillation for GUI Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18101)
*Jingyuan Huang,Zuming Huang,Yucheng Shi,Tianze Yang,Xiaoming Zhai,Wei Chu,Ninghao Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Quality-Aware Self-Distillation (QASD) improves VLM-based GUI grounding by combining soft correctness-aware gating and teacher-probability scaling to filter unreliable coordinate-token supervision. Neither component works alone, but together they consistently boost performance across six benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers dense token-level supervision useful for GUI grounding, but suffers from degraded teacher signal quality when the student-generated prefix deviates from the target coordinate. This makes naive OPSD unreliable for coordinate-sensitive tasks.

Method: The proposed Quality-Aware Self-Distillation (QASD) introduces two complementary mechanisms: (1) Soft correctness-aware gating — checks if the teacher's current coordinate-token prediction under the student prefix can still reach the ground-truth box; if not, the signal is down-weighted. (2) Teacher-probability scaling — uses teacher confidence as a lightweight factor to further calibrate the gated supervision strength.

Result: A key finding is that neither component improves performance individually, but their combination yields consistent gains. QASD outperforms strong baselines and consistently improves the base model across six GUI grounding benchmarks.

Conclusion: Correctness-aware gating and teacher-probability scaling are complementary: the former suppresses unreliable coordinate-token supervision, while the latter calibrates remaining signal strength. Together they enable effective self-distillation for coordinate-sensitive GUI grounding.

Abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) grounding requires vision-language models (VLMs) to identify small target elements in high-resolution screenshots and predict precise screen coordinates. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a promising post-training approach for this coordinate-sensitive task, since it provides dense token-level teacher signals beyond hard coordinate labels. However, naive OPSD is not well suited to GUI grounding: OPSD evaluates the teacher on student-generated prefixes, the quality of coordinate-token teacher signals can degrade when the prefix has already deviated from the target coordinate, leading to unreliable teacher signal. To mitigate this, We propose quality-aware self-distillation for VLM-based GUI grounding, which improves coordinate-token teacher-signal quality through soft correctness-aware gating and teacher-probability scaling.
