The soft correctness-aware gate checks whether the teacher's current coordinate-token prediction can still be completed into the ground-truth box under the student-generated prefix. If not, the corresponding teacher signal is down-weighted. Teacher-probability scaling then uses the teacher's confidence as a lightweight factor to further calibrate the strength of the gated supervision. A key empirical finding is that neither component alone improves overall performance, whereas combining them consistently improves performance. This suggests that the two mechanisms play complementary roles: correctness-aware gating suppresses unreliable coordinate-token supervision, while teacher-probability scaling calibrates the strength of the remaining signals. Experiments across six GUI grounding benchmarks show that our method consistently improves the base model and outperforms strong baselines.

</details>


### [275] [First Proof Second Batch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18119)
*Mohammed Abouzaid,Nikhil Srivastava,Rachel Ward,Lauren Williams*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study evaluates the ability of current AI systems to solve research-level mathematics problems by testing them on ten problems spanning diverse mathematical fields, contributed by active researchers from their own work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To rigorously assess whether contemporary AI systems can correctly solve authentic, research-level mathematics problems that arise naturally in mathematicians' work, rather than curated benchmarks or competition problems.

Method: A set of ten unsolved or recently solved research problems across a broad range of mathematical fields were contributed by practicing mathematicians. Multiple AI systems were tested on these problems. The study documents the problems, methodology, AI-generated solutions, human solutions, and referee evaluations.

Result: The paper presents the outcomes of AI testing on these ten problems, with supplementary materials including AI-generated solutions, human benchmark solutions, and referee reports evaluating the AI outputs.

Conclusion: The abstract does not state explicit conclusions, but the study implies a structured, expert-validated framework for benchmarking AI mathematical reasoning at the research level, with full transparency via linked supplementary materials.

Abstract: To assess the ability of current AI systems to correctly solve research-level mathematics problems, we tested several AI systems on a set of ten problems in a broad range of mathematical fields; these problems arose naturally in the research process of the contributors. This document includes the problems, our methodology, and the results of our testing. We provide links to supplementary documents including the human solutions, the AI-generated solutions, and the referee reports and logs for the AI-generated solutions.
  The ten problems were contributed by the following mathematicians: (1) Dariusz Kalociński and Theodore A. Slaman, (2) Richard Schwartz, (3) Aleksa Milojevic and Benny Sudakov, (4) Larry Guth, (5) Oleg Butkovsky, Jonathan Mattingly, and Lorenzo Zambotti, (6) Joshua Evan Greene and Duncan McCoy, (7) Sucharit Sarkar, (8) Sam Payne and Jidong (Jayden) Wang, (9) Sylvie Corteel and John Lentfer, (10) Srivatsav Kunnawalkam Elayavalli.

</details>


### [276] [Knowledge Reutilization in Meta-Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18132)
*Yuan Meng,Bo Wang,Juan de los Rios Ruiz,Xiangtong Yao,Zhenshan Bing,Fuchun Sun,Alois Knoll*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A meta-knowledge reutilization framework decouples task inference from embodiment-specific control by learning task-level knowledge on a simplified agent and transferring it to heterogeneous agents via a semantic-magnitude interface and temporal adaptor, achieving dramatic reductions in tracking error (94.75%–99.79%) with only ~23.8% of the interaction data required by state-of-the-art baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing end-to-end meta-reinforcement learning methods tightly couple task inference with embodiment-specific control, which obscures non-parametric task semantics, reduces sample efficiency, and impedes cross-agent knowledge reuse. The authors aim to disentangle task-level knowledge from embodiment-specific execution to enable efficient transfer across heterogeneous agents.

Method: The proposed framework consists of: (1) a dynamics-simplified agent where task-level knowledge is learned; (2) a Bayesian non-parametric prior to organize latent task modes; (3) a high-level policy generating task-level magnitude guidance; (4) a semantic-magnitude interface that converts frozen meta-knowledge into temporally aligned subgoals; and (5) a lightweight temporal adaptor that bridges reusable task knowledge to embodiment-specific low-level controllers on heterogeneous agents.

Result: On multiple locomotion agents, the framework reduces final-step tracking error by 94.75% to 99.79% compared to recent state-of-the-art baselines. It also achieves comparable deployment performance while requiring only approximately 23.8% of the interaction data used by those baselines.

Conclusion: Decoupling task inference from embodiment-specific control via a meta-knowledge reutilization framework enables highly sample-efficient transfer across heterogeneous agents, dramatically improving tracking accuracy while drastically reducing the data requirements for deployment.

Abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning enables fast adaptation by extracting shared structure from related tasks, but existing end-to-end methods often couple task inference with embodiment-specific control. This coupling can obscure non-parametric task semantics, reduce sample efficiency, and limit cross-agent reuse. We propose a meta-knowledge reutilization framework that learns task-level knowledge on a dynamics-simplified agent and transfers it to heterogeneous agents. The framework uses a Bayesian non-parametric prior to organize latent task modes and a high-level policy to generate task-level magnitude guidance. To bridge reusable task knowledge with different embodiments, we introduce a semantic-magnitude interface and a lightweight temporal adaptor, which convert frozen meta-knowledge into temporally aligned subgoals for embodiment-specific low-level controllers. Experiments on multiple locomotion agents show that our framework reduces final-step tracking error by 94.75% -- 99.79% compared with recent state-of-the-art baselines and achieves comparable deployment performance with about 23.8% of their interaction data.

</details>


### [277] [Your AI Travel Agent Would Book You a Bullfight: An Agentic Benchmark for Implicit Animal Welfare in Frontier AI Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18142)
*Jasmine Brazilek,Oliver Tulio,Joel Christoph,Miles Tidmarsh,Carol Kline,Arturs Kanepajs*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TAC (Travel Agent Compassion) is the first agentic benchmark testing whether AI agents avoid animal-exploitative options when booking travel. Across 48 scenarios, all seven frontier models score below chance (64%), with the best at 53%. Adding a welfare-aware sentence to system prompts dramatically improves performance in most models, but base-condition transcripts show no signs of evaluation awareness, suggesting genuine welfare-reasoning failures rather than gaming.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents transition from passive advisors to autonomous actors executing real-world tasks, existing welfare benchmarks only evaluate text responses to Q&A prompts. It is unknown whether welfare reasoning expressed in text transfers to agentic deployment where models take tool-based actions. The authors aim to close this gap by measuring whether frontier models actually avoid animal exploitation when making consequential choices on behalf of users.

Method: The authors construct TAC, a benchmark comprising 12 hand-authored travel booking scenarios spanning six categories of animal exploitation (e.g., trophy hunting, captive cetacean shows, elephant rides), augmented to 48 samples controlling for price, rating, and position confounds. Seven frontier models from four labs are evaluated in an agentic setting where models use tools to book travel. Two conditions are tested: a base condition and a condition with a single welfare-aware sentence added to the system prompt. An auxiliary "Inspect Scout" audit uses Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite to judge 288 base-condition transcripts for evaluation awareness.

Result: All seven models score below the 64% chance level in the base condition; the best performer, Claude Opus 4.7, achieves only 53%. Adding one welfare-aware system-prompt sentence yields gains of 47–63 percentage points in Claude and GPT-5.5, 26 points in GPT-5.2, and under 12 points in DeepSeek and Gemini. The Inspect Scout audit flags zero of 288 transcripts for evaluation awareness, indicating below-chance rates are not due to models detecting the test.

Conclusion: Frontier AI agents systematically fail to avoid animal-exploitative options when acting autonomously, despite being capable of welfare reasoning when prompted. This demonstrates a significant transfer gap from text-based welfare benchmarks to agentic deployment. The authors highlight implications for category-level cultural variation, the insufficiency of text-response benchmarks for agentic safety, and relevance to the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice systemic risk framework.

Abstract: AI agents are moving from advisors to actors, booking travel, planning menus, and running procurement on behalf of users. Existing benchmarks for AI and animal welfare evaluate model text responses to question-answer prompts, leaving open whether the welfare reasoning surfaced in those responses transfers to agentic deployment where the model must take actions with tools. We introduce TAC (Travel Agent Compassion), the first agentic benchmark measuring whether AI agents avoid options involving animal exploitation when acting on behalf of users. TAC presents an AI agent with twelve hand-authored travel booking scenarios across six categories of animal exploitation, augmented to forty-eight samples to control for price, rating, and position confounds. We evaluate seven frontier models from four labs. Every model scores below the chance level of sixty-four percent, with the best performer (Claude Opus 4.7) at fifty-three percent. A single welfare-aware sentence in the system prompt yields gains of forty-seven to sixty-three percentage points in Claude and GPT-5.5, twenty-six points in GPT-5.2, and under twelve points in DeepSeek and Gemini. An auxiliary Inspect Scout audit of 288 base-condition transcripts from the top two performers, using Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite as judge, flags zero transcripts for evaluation awareness, suggesting the below-chance rates do not stem from the models recognising the evaluation. We discuss implications for category-level variation across cultural domains, the limits of text-response welfare benchmarks, and the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice systemic risk framework.

</details>


### [278] [Memory as a Wasting Asset: Pricing Flash Endurance for Embodied Agents, and the Limits of Doing So](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18144)
*Josef Liyanjun Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Embodied robot memory is modeled as depreciating capital with a finite program/erase endurance budget. A single shadow price $η$ yields a cost-optimal placement threshold across RAM/NVM/cloud, which becomes non-monotone when value and write frequency correlate positively ($χ > 0$). Empirical measurement on real robot logs shows $χ$ is positive for recurrent long-horizon manipulation, null for short-horizon tasks, and negative for non-recurrent teleoperation. Wear-aware routing matches price-based routing on task value because realized value is tier-invariant, but whether it improves task value remains an open question.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: No deployed robot memory system currently prices which memories are worth consuming a scarce program/erase cycle, despite NVM flash endurance being a finite, non-renewable resource (thousands of P/E cycles). This leads to suboptimal allocation of writes across the RAM/on-board NVM/cloud hierarchy.

Method: The authors model embodied memory as depreciating capital and introduce a single endurance shadow price $η$. This yields a wear-augmented per-byte index for cost-minimizing placement across the memory hierarchy. The placement policy reduces to a threshold that can become non-monotone when the value-write association $χ > 0$. The sign of $χ$ is measured empirically on real robot logs across three deployment regimes: recurrent long-horizon manipulation, shorter-horizon suites, and non-recurrent teleoperation. A learned wear-aware controller is compared against price-based routing.

Result: $χ$ is positive ($\hatχ ≈ +1.0 × 10^{-3}$, replicated at full power) for recurrent long-horizon manipulation, null on shorter-horizon suites, and negative on non-recurrent teleoperation. The endurance budget is irrelevant on premium 3,000-P/E TLC at datasheet prices but binding on commodity QLC/eMMC (~1,000 P/E) typical of cheaper edge robots. Where the budget binds, wear-aware routing matches price-based routing on task value because realized value is tier-invariant across RAM, NVM, and cloud. The non-monotone optimum, though proven theoretically, is not yet observed in data.

Conclusion: The sign of $χ$ is a property of the deployment regime, determining whether flash endurance pricing is necessary. On cheap edge robots with commodity flash, endurance-aware placement governs device lifetime and cost rather than task performance. Whether wear-aware placement improves task value remains open — the non-monotone optimum is proven but not empirically observed, and $χ$ is measured against a value proxy.

Abstract: A robot's flash endurance is a non-renewable stock: every persisted write spends one of a few thousand program/erase cycles and never refills, yet no fielded robot memory system prices which memories are worth an erase cycle. We treat embodied memory as depreciating capital and price that stock with a single endurance shadow price $η$, which makes cost-minimizing placement across a RAM / on-board NVM / cloud hierarchy a threshold in a wear-augmented per-byte index. The index is cost-optimal whatever the sign of the value-write association $χ$; only when $χ> 0$ does the optimum turn non-monotone, sending a robot's most valuable memories off its flash.
  The pivot is thus empirical, and we measure $χ$ on real robot logs at a pre-specified gate: its sign is a property of the deployment regime -- positive on recurrent long-horizon manipulation ($\hatχ \approx +1.0 \times 10^{-3}$, replicated at full power), null on a shorter-horizon suite, and negative on non-recurrent teleoperation. Two boundaries scope the result. The endurance budget is dormant on premium 3,000-P/E TLC at datasheet prices and binding on the commodity QLC/eMMC ($\sim$1,000 P/E) that cheaper edge robots run. And where it binds, a learned wear-aware controller only ties price-based routing on task value, because realized value is tier-invariant across RAM, NVM, and cloud: the rent governs device lifetime and cost, not task performance. Whether wear-aware placement improves task value remains open -- $χ$ is measured against a value proxy, and the non-monotone optimum, while proven, is not yet observed in data.

</details>


### [279] [WEQA: Wearable hEalth Question Answering with Query-Adaptive Agentic Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18147)
*Yuwei Zhang,Tong Xia,Bianca Emmerich,Yu Yvonne Wu,Dimitris Spathis,Xin Liu,Daniel McDuff,Cecilia Mascolo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WEQA is a query-adaptive agent framework that routes wearable health data questions to specialized analytical tools and pretrained models via an LLM controller, achieving 24% higher accuracy than baselines and superior clinical soundness in expert evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Answering questions about wearable health data is challenging because such data are continuous, high-dimensional, longitudinal, and misaligned with text-centric LLM pretraining. Additionally, the diversity of sensor modalities and user intents cannot be handled by fixed reasoning workflows or a single foundation model.

Method: WEQA uses an LLM controller that synthesizes execution plans and dynamically routes each query to appropriate combinations of sensor analysis tools and pretrained models. It also performs grounded response auditing against external knowledge. Evaluation uses a curated benchmark across four open wearable datasets covering analytic and predictive tasks in three health domains, plus a blinded study with 12 medical experts and 8 users.

Result: WEQA achieves 24% higher accuracy than LLM and agentic baselines. A blinded study with 12 medical experts and 8 users demonstrates substantial gains in both usefulness and clinical soundness.

Conclusion: A query-adaptive agent architecture that dynamically orchestrates specialized tools outperforms monolithic LLM approaches for wearable health data QA, suggesting a promising direction for deploying LLMs in ubiquitous health monitoring contexts.

Abstract: Language models are remarkably capable at medical question answering, in some cases surpassing the accuracy of general physicians. However, answering questions about wearable health data remains challenging and understudied, as these ubiquitous sensors produce continuous, high-dimensional, and longitudinal data, which is non-trivial to align with text-centric distributions in LLM pretraining. The diversity of sensor modalities and user intents cannot be effectively handled by a fixed reasoning workflow or a single pretrained foundation model. To address these challenges, we propose WEQA, a query-adaptive agent framework that unifies LLM reasoning with specialized wearable analytical and modeling tools. An LLM controller is employed to synthesize execution plans and dynamically route each query to the appropriate combination of sensor analysis and pretrained models, and perform grounded response auditing with external knowledge. We also curate a benchmark spanning four open wearable datasets comprising analytic and predictive tasks in three different health domains. Experiments show that our framework is 24% more accurate than LLM and agentic baselines, and a blinded study with 12 medical experts and 8 users shows substantial gains in usefulness and clinical soundness.

</details>


### [280] [Learning Cardiac Electrophysiology Digital Twins Through Agentic Discovery of Hybrid Structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18154)
*Ziqi Zhou,Yubo Ye,Sumeet Atul Vadhavka,Linwei Wang,Zhiqiang Tao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LEADS frames cardiac EP domain knowledge as a structured action space, enabling an LLM agent to iteratively discover physically grounded, numerically stable hybrid models through a reasoning-and-action loop, with gradient descent handling parameter fitting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building personalized cardiac digital twins requires identifying the correct model structure per patient, not just parameter fitting. Existing approaches either demand expert manual design (non-transferable) or use LLMs that lack the structural priors needed for stable cardiac simulations.

Method: LEADS formalizes cardiac EP domain knowledge as a structured action space. An LLM agent operates in an iterative reasoning-and-action loop to select, combine, and refine hybrid physics-neural model architectures. Candidate models are constrained to be physically grounded, interpretable, and numerically stable. Parameter fitting is delegated to gradient descent.

Result: LEADS outperforms both human-designed hybrid models and existing LLM-based hybrid modeling approaches on synthetic data (three ground-truth reaction models) and on real cardiac EP data.

Conclusion: LEADS demonstrates that constraining LLM-based architectural search with domain-specific structural priors yields superior hybrid models for cardiac EP digital twins, enabling open-ended discovery while maintaining physical validity and numerical stability.

Abstract: Building personalized cardiac electrophysiology (EP) digital twins requires identifying the appropriate model structure for each patient, not merely fitting parameters. Traditional methods rely on experts to manually prescribe hybrid physics-neural architectures, which requires deep domain expertise and does not transfer across patients. Recent works have applied large language models (LLMs) to generate or act as hybrid models. However, despite their promising generalization capacity, these LLM-based methods lack the structural priors needed for stable cardiac simulations. Hence, we propose LEADS, a framework that formulates cardiac EP domain knowledge as a structured action space and utilizes an LLM agent to discover hybrid models. The agent follows an iterative reasoning-and-action loop to select, combine, and refine hybrid models, whilst gradient descent handles parameter fitting. The proposed LEADS designs every candidate model towards physically grounded, interpretable, and numerically stable, while allowing open-ended architectural discovery. We validate LEADS on synthetic data with three ground-truth reaction models and on real cardiac EP data, demonstrating that it outperforms both human-designed hybrid models and other LLM-based hybrid modeling.

</details>


### [281] [The Stanford EDGAR Filings Dataset: Reconstructing U.S. Corporate and Financial Disclosures into Layout-Faithful and Token-Efficient Pretraining Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18192)
*Nick Bettencourt,Xiaowei Ding,Kay Giesecke*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Stanford EDGAR Filings Dataset (SEFD) is an open-source, 152B-token reconstruction of SEC filings into layout-faithful MultiMarkdown, providing clean long-context training data for financial LLMs with minimal overlap with existing web corpora. It also introduces two benchmarks: EDGAR-Forecast for numerical forecasting and EDGAR-OCR for table transcription.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-quality public web corpora are becoming exhausted, and clean long-context documents for LLM training are scarce, expensive, proprietary, synthetic, or narrowly domain-specific. SEC filings represent a rich, audited, multi-domain source of long-context documents that remains underutilized in open pretraining data.

Method: SEFD reconstructs SEC filings from the EDGAR system into layout-faithful MultiMarkdown format, preserving document structure, tables, and formatting. The corpus is filtered for token efficiency and model readiness, with explicit verification of less than 0.1% overlap with Common Crawl-derived corpora. Two benchmarks are derived: EDGAR-Forecast tests numerical forecasting grounded in filings after knowledge cutoffs, and EDGAR-OCR evaluates transcription accuracy on complex financial tables.

Result: SEFD-v1 provides a 152B-token public snapshot, with the full archive spanning 18.5 million filings estimated at 550B tokens. The corpus achieves less than 0.1% overlap with Common Crawl data, ensuring training novelty.

Conclusion: SEFD offers a high-quality, open, domain-rich long-context corpus for financial language modeling, addressing the scarcity of clean long-document pretraining data. The accompanying benchmarks enable rigorous evaluation of financial reasoning, forecasting, compliance, and document understanding capabilities in LLMs.

Abstract: As high-quality public web corpora become increasingly exhausted, clean long-context documents have become a scarce and expensive source of training data for large language models (LLMs). Existing long-context corpora are often proprietary and costly to acquire, synthetically generated, or concentrated in narrow domains such as programming. We introduce the Stanford EDGAR Filings Dataset (SEFD), an open reconstruction of SEC filings into layout-faithful MultiMarkdown for financial language modeling and evaluation. SEFD makes audited financial statements, risk disclosures, ownership reports, accounting notes, and market-moving event filings usable as long-context pretraining data and as a basis for financial reasoning, forecasting, compliance, and document understanding. The resulting corpus is token-efficient, model-ready, and has less than 0.1% overlap with Common Crawl-derived corpora. We release SEFD-v1, a 152B-token initial public snapshot, and provide corpus-level analyses of a larger 18.5M-filing archive estimated at 550B tokens. We further introduce two SEFD-derived benchmarks: EDGAR-Forecast, which evaluates filing-grounded numerical forecasting after model knowledge cutoffs, and EDGAR-OCR, which evaluates transcription of complex financial tables.

</details>


### [282] [Fixed-Point Reasoners: Stable and Adaptive Deep Looped Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18206)
*Sajad Movahedi,Vera Milovanović,Shlomo Libo Feigin,Alexander Theus,Thomas Hofmann,Valentina Boeva,T. Konstantin Rusch,Antonio Orvieto*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes FPRM, a Transformer-based Fixed-Point Reasoning Model that addresses signal propagation issues in looped architectures using pre-norm layers and residual scaling. It employs fixed-point convergence as an end-to-end halting mechanism, enabling adaptive computation based on task difficulty, and demonstrates effectiveness on Sudoku, Maze, state-tracking, and ARC-AGI benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Looped architectures, while beneficial for learning compositional step-by-step procedures, suffer from signal propagation problems as depth increases when halting is postponed. Existing solutions to this depth-induced degradation are insufficient, motivating the need for architectural modifications that stabilize signal propagation while preserving the benefits of iterative computation.

Method: The authors introduce FPRM, a Transformer-based looped architecture with two key modifications: (1) pre-norm layers (applying normalization before sublayer transformations) and residual scaling to mitigate signal propagation issues. (2) Fixed-point convergence as an end-to-end halting mechanism, where computation terminates when internal representations reach a stable fixed point, allowing the model to dynamically allocate compute proportional to task difficulty.

Result: FPRM achieves strong performance on reasoning benchmarks including Sudoku, Maze, state-tracking, and ARC-AGI. The fixed-point halting mechanism successfully adapts computational depth to the difficulty of each task instance, demonstrating that the model can scale its reasoning steps without explicit depth specification.

Conclusion: Fixed-point convergence provides an effective, adaptive halting mechanism for looped Transformer architectures. Combining this with pre-norm and residual scaling resolves signal propagation issues, yielding a model that autonomously determines how many iterations to spend on a given reasoning problem, with promising results across diverse compositional reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Looped architectures provide an inductive bias toward learning step-by-step procedures for tasks that require compositional reasoning. The number of effective layers reached by looping determines the quality of the solution these models find. Like deep architectures, looped architectures are prone to a signal propagation problem induced by depth as the halting decision is postponed. In this paper, we address this signal propagation issue using pre-norm layers and residual scaling. Building on these architectural modifications, we propose FPRM, a Transformer-based Fixed-Point Reasoning Model that uses fixed-point convergence as an end-to-end halting mechanism in a looped architecture. We show that fixed-point halting allows FPRM to adapt its compute to task difficulty. FPRM is effective on common reasoning benchmarks, namely Sudoku, Maze, state-tracking, and ARC-AGI.

</details>


### [283] [EvolveNav: Proactive Preflection and Self-Evolving Memory for Zero-Shot Object Goal Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18235)
*Qi Chai,Wenhao Shen,Nanjie Yao,Yue Xia,Kaiyong Zhao,Jie Ma,Guosheng Lin,Hao Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A self-evolving framework for zero-shot object-goal navigation that extracts actionable rules from past trajectories, retrieves them via upper confidence bound, and uses memory-guided preflection to forecast outcomes, achieving 10.1% improvement in success rate with fewer wasted steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ZS-OGN methods rely on foundation models with static priors and lack test-time adaptation, leading to repeated errors and inefficient trial-and-error exploration.

Method: The authors propose: (1) an agentic rule memory that extracts actionable knowledge from past trajectories; (2) a retrieval strategy based on upper confidence bound (UCB) that balances semantic relevance and historical success when selecting rules; (3) a memory-guided preflection module that predicts potential outcomes before executing actions to reduce inefficient exploration.

Result: The method outperforms existing zero-shot baselines, achieving a 10.1% improvement in success rate while requiring fewer unnecessary steps.

Conclusion: Self-evolving memory mechanisms and outcome preflection enable continuous test-time improvement for zero-shot object-goal navigation, significantly boosting success rates and exploration efficiency.

Abstract: Zero-Shot Object-Goal Navigation (ZS-OGN) requires embodied agents to explore and locate target objects without any prior training. To this end, recent methods leverage foundation models. But they typically rely on static priors and lack adaptation, which leads to repeated errors and costly trial and error. In this paper, we propose a self-evolving ZS-OGN framework that enables continuous test-time improvement. Specifically, we build an agentic rule memory by extracting actionable knowledge from past trajectories. Then, we propose a retrieval strategy based on upper confidence bound, selecting effective rules by balancing semantic relevance and historical success. In addition, we introduce a memory-guided preflection module that forecasts potential outcomes before action, reducing inefficient exploration. Extensive experiments show that our method outperforms existing zero-shot baselines, achieving a 10.1\% improvement in success rate with fewer unnecessary steps.

</details>
